docs.text: Table 7.2. Comparison of attitude sensor specifications for space applications. Sensor Accuracy Update Rate Mass (kg) Typical Use Star Tracker 1–10 arcsec 1–10 Hz 0.3–2.0 Precision 3-axis Fine Sun Sensor 0.01–0.1 10–100 Hz 0.05–0.3 Sun vector, array pointing Coarse Sun Sensor 1–5 \(>\)100 Hz 0.01–0.05 Acquisition, safe mode Earth Horizon Sensor 0.05–0.1 1–10 Hz 0.3–1.5 Nadir vector, backup Magnetometer (FOG) \(\pm 1\)–100 nT 1–100 Hz 0.05–0.5 Rate sensing, LEO MEMS Gyroscope 0.1–1/\(\sqrt{\mathrm{h}}\) ARW 100–1000 Hz 0.01–0.2 Rate sensing, CubeSats HRG 0.0001/\(\sqrt{\mathrm{h}}\) ARW 200–400 Hz 0.5–2.0 Precision, long-life GPS (single) 3–10 m position 1–10 Hz 0.1–0.5 Orbit determination GPS (multi-antenna) 0.1–1 attitude 1–10 Hz 0.5–2.0 Attitude, baselines

docs.title: 7.12 Micro-Vibration and Jitter Analysis
docs.text:
For optical imaging satellites with resolution requirements of sub-meter at altitude, micro-vibration from rotating machinery (reaction wheels, cryocoolers, compressors) can be the dominant error source limiting image quality. The metric is the line-of-sight (LOS) jitter expressed as an angle (arcseconds RMS) in the focal plane.

Reaction wheel imbalance produces disturbances at the wheel spin frequency \(f_w\) and harmonics \(n f_w\). The structural response of the spacecraft amplifies disturbances near modal frequencies. The LOS jitter is computed through a transfer function from wheel force/torque to LOS angle, integrated over all wheel speeds and frequencies.

Passive isolation mounts (such as the Moog CSA hexapod isolator) provide 6-DOF isolation, attenuating disturbances above the corner frequency (typically 10–40 Hz) by 20–40 dB/decade. Active isolation using accelerometer-based control further extends the isolation bandwidth.

docs.title: 7.13 Summary
docs.text: The ADCS constitutes one of the most mathematically rich subsystems of the spacecraft. From the reference frames that define the context for attitude measurement, through the singularity-free quaternion representation of attitude and its kinematic equations, to the Euler rigid-body equations of motion coupling attitude dynamics to external torques—the theoretical foundation provides the tools for analysis. Environmental disturbances (SRP, gravity gradient, aerodynamic, magnetic) drive the actuator sizing. Sensor technologies spanning coarse photodiodes to precision star trackers and HRG gyroscopes provide the measurements for the EKF attitude estimator. Reaction wheels provide precision torque; magnetorquers enable efficient momentum management in LEO; CMGs provide high agility. The PD and LQR control laws, with their known stability properties, complete the closed-loop system. Chapter 8 addresses the propulsion system, which interfaces closely with the ADCS through orbit maintenance manoeuvres and angular momentum desaturation.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Satellite Propulsion Systems
docs.text:
Key Concepts: Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, specific impulse, chemical propulsion (monopropellant, bipropellant, cold gas), electric propulsion (gridded ion, Hall effect, electrospray, PPT), propellant budgeting, all-electric GEO satellites, advanced and nuclear propulsion.

Propulsion is a critical enabling technology for satellite missions. Whether correcting orbital injection errors, executing station-keeping maneuvers over a 15-year operational lifetime, or raising a spacecraft from low Earth orbit to geostationary orbit, the propulsion system determines mission feasibility, lifetime, and mass budget. This chapter provides a comprehensive treatment of the physical principles, hardware implementations, performance trade-offs, and mission applications of satellite propulsion systems, from classical chemical thrusters to modern electric propulsion that is transforming commercial satellite operations.

docs.title: 8.1.1 The Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation
docs.text:
The foundational relationship governing all rocket propulsion is the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, derived in 1903. It relates the velocity change achievable by a spacecraft to the mass of propellant consumed:

\[\Delta v = v_e \ln\!\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right) = I_{sp}\, g_0 \ln\!\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)\tag{8.1}\]

where \(\Delta v\) is the total velocity change (m/s), \(v_e\) is the effective exhaust velocity (m/s), \(m_0\) is the initial (wet) mass, \(m_f\) is the final (dry) mass, \(I_{sp}\) is the specific impulse (s), and \(g_0 = 9.80665\) m/s\(^2\) is standard gravitational acceleration. The ratio \(m_0/m_f\) is the mass ratio, and the propellant mass fraction is \(\zeta = (m_0 - m_f)/m_0\).

For a spacecraft requiring multiple \(\Delta v\) maneuvers, the total propellant mass required for each maneuver \(i\) is:

\[m_{p,i} = m_{i-1}\left(1 - e^{-\Delta v_i / (I_{sp} g_0)}\right)\tag{8.2}\]

This exponential dependence on \(\Delta v / (I_{sp} g_0)\) is crucial: doubling \(I_{sp}\) for the same \(\Delta v\) reduces propellant fraction dramatically, which is why electric propulsion with \(I_{sp} > 1500\) s is so attractive for large \(\Delta v\) missions.

docs.title: 8.1.2 Thrust and Specific Impulse
docs.text:
The thrust force produced by a rocket engine is:

\[F = \dot{m}\, v_e + (P_e - P_a) A_e\tag{8.3}\]

where \(\dot{m}\) is the propellant mass flow rate (kg/s), \(v_e\) is the exhaust velocity at the nozzle exit (m/s), \(P_e\) is the nozzle exit pressure (Pa), \(P_a\) is the ambient pressure (Pa, effectively zero in space), and \(A_e\) is the nozzle exit area (m\(^2\)). The first term is the momentum thrust; the second is the pressure thrust. In the vacuum of space, \(P_a = 0\), and for a well-designed nozzle with exit pressure matched to near-vacuum conditions, the two terms combine into an effective exhaust velocity:

\[c = \frac{F}{\dot{m}} = v_e + \frac{(P_e - P_a) A_e}{\dot{m}}\tag{8.4}\]

Specific impulse is defined as thrust per unit weight flow of propellant:

\[I_{sp} = \frac{F}{\dot{m}\, g_0} = \frac{c}{g_0}\tag{8.5}\]

\(I_{sp}\) has units of seconds and is the primary figure of merit for propellant efficiency: higher \(I_{sp}\) means less propellant is consumed for the same impulse delivered. The total impulse delivered by a thruster is \(J = F \cdot t_{burn} = \dot{m} \cdot I_{sp} \cdot g_0 \cdot t_{burn}\).

docs.title: 8.1.3 Nozzle Theory and the Ideal Rocket
docs.text:
For an ideal rocket with isentropic flow through a converging-diverging (de Laval) nozzle, the theoretical exhaust velocity is:

\[v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1} \frac{R_u T_c}{M_w}\left[1 - \left(\frac{P_e}{P_c}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\right]}\tag{8.6}\]

where \(\gamma\) is the ratio of specific heats, \(R_u = 8.314\) J/(mol\(\cdot\)K) is the universal gas constant, \(T_c\) is the combustion chamber temperature (K), \(M_w\) is the molecular weight of the exhaust products (kg/mol), and \(P_c\), \(P_e\) are chamber and exit pressures. This equation reveals the key drivers of high \(I_{sp}\): high combustion temperature \(T_c\) and low exhaust molecular weight \(M_w\). This is why hydrogen (\(M_w = 2\)) is such a valuable rocket propellant (Sutton and Biblarz 2017).

docs.title: 8.2 Chemical Propulsion Systems
docs.text: Chemical propulsion exploits exothermic chemical reactions to heat propellant and expel it through a nozzle. It offers high thrust and heritage reliability at the cost of modest \(I_{sp}\) compared to electric alternatives (Wertz et al. 2011).

docs.title: 8.2.1 Cold Gas Propulsion
docs.text:
Cold gas thrusters are the simplest propulsion devices: a pressurized inert gas (typically nitrogen N\(_2\), or occasionally helium or R-134a refrigerant) is stored in a tank and expelled through a small nozzle. No combustion or heating occurs.

Performance is limited by the speed of sound in the stored gas. For nitrogen at 20\(^\circ\)C, the theoretical maximum \(I_{sp}\) is approximately 80 s, with practical values of 50–75 s. Thrust levels are typically 0.05–10 N, and system simplicity (no pyrotechnic valves, no propellant compatibility issues, no ignition system) makes cold gas ideal for:

  • CubeSat attitude control where volume and cost constraints dominate.

  • Proximity operations and formation flying where contamination of sensitive surfaces by chemical exhaust products must be avoided.

  • First-generation micro-satellite propulsion serving as a technology baseline.

The PRISMA mission (2010) used a cold gas system for close-proximity demonstration experiments. Many 6U CubeSats now fly MEMS-fabricated cold gas micro-thrusters with nozzle throats of 100–500 \(\mu\)m diameter, produced by companies such as Vacco Industries and Bradford ECAPS. The key limitations are low \(I_{sp}\) (limiting \(\Delta v\) budget severely) and the large propellant tank volume required to store gas at useful pressures (typically 100–300 bar).

docs.title: 8.2.2 Monopropellant Hydrazine Systems
docs.text:
Hydrazine (N\(_2\)H\(_4\)) monopropellant thrusters have been the workhorse of satellite propulsion since the 1960s. The propellant decomposes exothermically when passed over a catalytic bed:

\[3\,\mathrm{N_2H_4} \rightarrow 4\,\mathrm{NH_3} + \mathrm{N_2} \quad \Delta H = -157\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}\tag{8.7}\]

followed at high temperatures by:

\[4\,\mathrm{NH_3} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{N_2} + 6\,\mathrm{H_2} \quad \Delta H = +184\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}\tag{8.8}\]

The net reaction produces a gas mixture (N\(_2\), H\(_2\), NH\(_3\)) at temperatures of 600–900\(^\circ\)C, yielding an \(I_{sp}\) of 220–235 s in vacuum (Pisacane 2005). The Shell 405 catalyst (granular iridium on alumina support) is the industry standard, developed at Shell Development Company and qualified for space use in the 1960s. More recent catalysts include the S-405 successor and Aerojet’s MR-509 for improved ignition reliability at low temperatures (\(-10^\circ\)C to \(+60^\circ\)C operational range).

Hydrazine thrusters range from 0.5 N (attitude control, \(< 1\) g/s flow rate) to 22 N (orbit adjust, \(\sim 10\) g/s). The system architecture uses one of two pressurization schemes:

  • Regulated: A pressurant gas (N\(_2\) or He) maintains constant feed pressure through a pressure regulator, providing constant thrust and \(I_{sp}\) throughout the mission but requiring a separate pressurant tank.

  • Blowdown: The pressurant and hydrazine share the same tank; as propellant is consumed, pressure drops (typically by a factor of 4:1 from 28 to 7 bar), reducing thrust and \(I_{sp}\) by 10–15% over the mission. Simpler and lighter, this is the preferred choice for small satellites.

Hydrazine is classified as a toxic, carcinogenic substance (REACH SVHC list in Europe), requiring full SCAPE (Self-Contained Atmospheric Protective Ensemble) suit handling and specialized ground facilities. This has driven significant investment in green propellant development.

docs.title: 8.2.3 Green Monopropellants
docs.text:
Two ionic liquid-based green propellants have reached flight maturity as hydrazine replacements:

AF-M315E (ASCENT – Advanced Spacecraft Energetic Non-Toxic): Developed by AFRL (Air Force Research Laboratory) and commercialized by Aerojet Rocketdyne, AF-M315E is a hydroxyl ammonium nitrate (HAN)-based ionic liquid blend. Key properties:

  • \(I_{sp} \approx 257\) s (approximately 12% improvement over hydrazine at same chamber conditions).

  • Specific gravity \(\approx 1.47\) (50% denser than hydrazine at 1.004, reducing tank volume for the same propellant mass).

  • Non-toxic handling eliminates SCAPE suit requirements; classified as a Class 1.3C explosive only.

  • Flash point \(>\)107\(^\circ\)C (much safer than hydrazine flash point of \(\sim\)52\(^\circ\)C).

  • Higher catalyst preheat required: 800–900\(^\circ\)C versus 80–100\(^\circ\)C for hydrazine, adding preheat time and power draw.

AF-M315E was first demonstrated in orbit on the GPIM (Green Propellant Infusion Mission, 2019) aboard a Ball Aerospace BCP-100 spacecraft, completing 1317 s of thruster operation and validating the ASCENT-MONARC-1 thruster.

LMP-103S (HPGP – High Performance Green Propellant): Developed by ECAPS (a Bradford ECAPS / Bradford Space company) as an ammonium dinitramide (ADN) and water/fuel blend. Demonstrated on the PRISMA spacecraft (2010) at 1 N and 22 N thrust levels, it achieves \(I_{sp} \approx 252\) s and has been baselined for ESA missions including the MATS satellite (2022) and studied for SMILE.

docs.title: 8.2.4 Bipropellant Systems
docs.text:
Bipropellant engines use separate fuel and oxidizer streams that combust upon mixing. This enables higher combustion temperatures and thus higher \(I_{sp}\) than monopropellants, at the cost of two independent propellant feed systems (valves, lines, tanks, and mixture ratio control).

The most common satellite bipropellant is MMH/MON-3 (monomethylhydrazine fuel / mixed oxides of nitrogen with 3% NO oxidizer), which is hypergolic – spontaneously ignites on contact – eliminating the need for an ignition system:

\[\mathrm{CH_3NHNH_2} + \frac{5}{4}\,\mathrm{N_2O_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{CO_2} + 3\,\mathrm{H_2O} + \frac{1}{4}\,\mathrm{N_2} + \text{(minor products)}\tag{8.9}\]

MMH/MON-3 achieves \(I_{sp} \approx 315\) s at a mixture ratio (O/F by mass) of approximately 1.65:1. The Marquardt R-4D thruster (490 N, \(I_{sp} = 311\) s) and its variants are used on hundreds of GEO spacecraft for liquid apogee engine (LAE) burns and attitude control. For apogee burns with thrust of 400–1000 N, bipropellant engines deliver GTO-to-GEO transfer in 1–3 firing sequences spanning 24–72 hours, compared to 6–12 months for all-electric orbit raising.

The N\(_2\)O\(_4\)/UDMH (unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine) combination has been widely used by European Ariane upper stages and Russian/Chinese spacecraft, with \(I_{sp}\) of 310–316 s. The Russian S5.92 engine (4 kN, \(I_{sp} = 326\) s, used on Fregat upper stage) exemplifies mature UDMH engine technology.

For future missions requiring higher performance without the toxicity of storable propellants, LOX/LCH\(_4\) (liquid oxygen/liquid methane) offers \(I_{sp} \approx 363\) s in vacuum. SpaceX Raptor achieves \(I_{sp} = 380\) s (vacuum) and is non-toxic, with potential for in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) at Mars where CH\(_4\) can be synthesized from atmospheric CO\(_2\) via the Sabatier reaction.

docs.title: 8.3 Electric Propulsion
docs.text:
Electric propulsion (EP) uses electrical power from solar arrays or a radioisotope/fission source to accelerate propellant to exhaust velocities far exceeding those achievable by chemical combustion. The \(I_{sp}\) is not thermodynamically limited by combustion temperature but by the available electrical energy per unit propellant mass. The key trade is power: EP thrusters require substantial electrical power (100 W to 100 kW) but consume far less propellant for the same \(\Delta v\) (Wertz et al. 2011).

The jet power efficiency of an EP thruster is:

\[\eta_{thrust} = \frac{F^2}{2 \dot{m} P_{in}} = \frac{F \cdot v_e / 2}{P_{in}}\tag{8.10}\]

Typical EP thruster efficiencies are 40–70%, depending on technology. For a given power \(P_{in}\) and efficiency \(\eta\), there is a fundamental trade between thrust and \(I_{sp}\): for fixed power, increasing \(I_{sp}\) (exhaust velocity) reduces propellant flow rate and thus thrust.

docs.title: 8.3.1 Gridded Ion Thrusters
docs.text:
Gridded ion thrusters (GITs), also known as electrostatic ion thrusters, use a plasma discharge to ionize propellant (typically xenon Xe, occasionally krypton Kr or iodine I\(_2\)) and then electrostatically accelerate ions through precision-drilled metal grids.

The Kaufman-type thruster (named for Harold Kaufman, NASA Lewis Research Center, 1960s) operates in three stages:

  1. Ionization: Xenon gas is fed into a cylindrical discharge chamber where electron bombardment from a hollow cathode creates a dense plasma (\(> 90\)% ionization efficiency). The discharge chamber operates at 25–35 V.

  2. Extraction: A multi-aperture screen grid (at plasma potential, \(+\)1000 to \(+\)5000 V) and accel grid (at negative high voltage, typically \(-200\) V, to prevent back-streaming electrons) extract and collimate positive Xe\(^+\) ions from the plasma boundary.

  3. Acceleration: The net beam voltage \(V_b\) (sum of screen and accel potentials, 1000–5000 V) accelerates ions to exit velocity:

\[v_{exit} = \sqrt{\frac{2 q V_b}{m_i}}\tag{8.11}\]

where \(q = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\) C is the elementary charge and \(m_i\) is the ion mass. For Xe\(^+\): \(m_i = 2.18 \times 10^{-25}\) kg (atomic mass 131.3 amu). For \(V_b = 1800\) V (NSTAR full throttle operating point), \(v_{exit} \approx 31\) km/s, corresponding to:

\[I_{sp} = \frac{v_{exit}}{g_0} = \frac{31{,}000}{9.806} \approx 3160\,\mathrm{s}\tag{8.12}\]

The general relationship between \(I_{sp}\) and beam voltage for a gridded ion thruster is:

\[I_{sp} = \frac{\eta_b}{g_0}\sqrt{\frac{2 q V_b}{m_i}}\tag{8.13}\]

where \(\eta_b \approx 0.95\)–0.98 accounts for the fraction of accelerated ions that exit as beam (versus charge-exchange losses). Total thruster efficiency (beam power / input DC power) ranges from 60% to 80%.

Key flight examples of gridded ion thrusters:

  • NSTAR (NASA Solar Electric Propulsion Technology Application Readiness): 30 cm diameter thruster, 2.3 kW input power, \(I_{sp} = 3100\) s at full throttle, 93 mN thrust, throttle range 0.5–2.3 kW (\(I_{sp} = 1979\)–3100 s). Flew on Deep Space 1 (1998-2001, first deep-space EP primary propulsion) and Dawn (2007–2018, Vesta and Ceres orbit insertion).

  • T6 (QinetiQ, now the Moog T6 for ESA): 22 cm thruster, 4.26 kW input, 145 mN thrust, \(I_{sp} = 4120\) s at design point. Four T6 thrusters power the BepiColombo Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) for the ESA/JAXA Mercury mission (launched 2018, Mercury orbit insertion 2025), providing \(> 5\) km/s of \(\Delta v\) for solar system braking.

  • NEXT-C (NASA Evolutionary Xenon Thruster - Commercial): 7.7 kW input, 236 mN, \(I_{sp} = 4190\) s. Single unit flew on the Psyche Discovery mission (2023 launch). Long-duration qualification life test exceeded 50,000 hours.

  • RIT-22 (Airbus Defence and Space): Radio-frequency ion thruster using RF inductive discharge (eliminating hollow cathode life limits), 22 cm beam, \(I_{sp} = 4600\) s at 5 kW, used on Eutelsat Quantum (2021) as primary electric propulsion for all-electric orbit raising and station keeping.

A critical component is the neutralizer cathode, which emits electrons into the ion beam downstream to prevent spacecraft charging to multi-kV potentials that would attract the beam back, and to prevent repulsion of subsequent ion beam pulses.

Grid erosion via charge-exchange (CEX) ion sputtering limits thruster life. NSTAR completed a 30,472-hour extended life test (ELT) with acceptable grid erosion, demonstrating the feasibility of multi-year deep space missions.

docs.title: 8.3.2 Hall Effect Thrusters
docs.text:
Hall Effect Thrusters (HETs), also called Hall thrusters, Closed Drift Thrusters (CDTs), or Stationary Plasma Thrusters (SPT, the Soviet/Russian designation), are the dominant electric propulsion technology for commercial GEO satellite station keeping. They have accumulated hundreds of thousands of hours of flight operation since the Soviet SPT-50 flew in 1971 on Meteor weather satellites.

The operating principle exploits the \(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\) drift of electrons in crossed electric and magnetic fields:

  1. A radial magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) (100–300 G) is applied across the annular discharge channel by electromagnets or permanent magnets.

  2. An axial electric field \(\mathbf{E}\) is applied between the anode (upstream, at \(+V_d\)) and the external hollow cathode (at ground or negative potential).

  3. Electrons emitted by the hollow cathode drift into the channel but are trapped by the crossed fields in an azimuthal Hall current (the \(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\) drift), forming a rotating electron cloud that acts as a virtual cathode for ionizing neutral xenon.

  4. Positive Xe\(^+\) ions, being far too massive to be significantly magnetized (ion Larmor radius \(\gg\) channel length), experience the full axial electric field and are accelerated out of the thruster.

The discharge voltage \(V_d\) (200–800 V for typical operation) determines exhaust velocity and \(I_{sp}\):

\[I_{sp} \approx \frac{1}{g_0}\sqrt{\frac{2 q \alpha V_d}{m_i}}\tag{8.14}\]

where \(\alpha \approx 0.85\)–0.95 accounts for the effective voltage fraction used for ion acceleration (the remainder drives ionization and electron heating). At \(V_d = 300\) V with xenon, \(I_{sp} \approx 1600\) s; at \(V_d = 1000\) V, \(I_{sp} \approx 2800\) s.

HETs have significantly lower \(I_{sp}\) than gridded ion thrusters but substantially higher thrust density (thrust per unit channel area) and simpler construction with no fragile high-voltage grids subject to ion sputtering. Practical discharge voltages for commercial GEO station keeping are 300–500 V, giving 1500–2000 s \(I_{sp}\).

Key flight Hall thruster examples:

  • SPT-100 (Fakel Enterprise, Russia / licensed by Safran, France): 100 mm mean channel diameter, 1.35 kW, 83 mN, \(I_{sp} = 1600\) s, 9 kg dry mass. Over 200 spacecraft have flown SPT-100 or direct derivatives since 1994; it is the single most flown Hall thruster in history.

  • PPS-1350 (Safran Snecma, France): 1.5 kW, 90 mN, \(I_{sp} = 1650\) s. Used on ESA SMART-1 lunar mission (2003–2006, demonstrated feasibility of EP for lunar orbit insertion), Alphabus GEO platform, Galileo NSSK backup.

  • BHT-200 (Busek, USA): 200 W small HET, 12.8 mN, \(I_{sp} = 1390\) s. Flew on AFRL TacSat-2 (2006), multiple DoD small satellites, and commercial small GEO. The most flown US commercial HET.

  • PPS-5000 (Safran, France): 5 kW, 330 mN, \(I_{sp} = 1800\) s. Primary propulsion for all-electric Eutelsat-115 West B (first operational all-electric commercial GEO satellite on Boeing 702SP, 2015).

  • X3 (University of Michigan / NASA Glenn): Multi-channel (nested) HET, demonstrated 100 kW operation (5.4 N thrust, \(I_{sp} = 1800\) s at 100 kW). Intended for future crewed Mars missions requiring megawatt-class SEP.

  • H9 (Aerojet Rocketdyne): 6 kW, 600 mN, \(I_{sp} = 2000\) s. Baseline for POWER and Gateway logistics development.

Krypton propellant for LEO constellations: SpaceX adopted krypton (Kr, atomic mass 83.8 amu, versus Xe at 131.3 amu) for Starlink Gen1 satellite HETs (approximately 250 W per thruster, four thrusters per satellite). At the same discharge voltage, krypton produces higher exhaust velocity (lower mass) for \(I_{sp} \approx 1800\)–2000 s, but with lower mass efficiency than xenon because krypton ionizes less efficiently. The dominant motivation is economics: krypton costs approximately $2–5/kg compared to xenon at $500–1200/kg. With over 5000 Starlink Gen1 and Gen2 satellites requiring propellant, this cost differential is decisive. The Starlink constellation represents the largest fleet of HET-propelled spacecraft in history.

docs.title: 8.3.3 Electrospray Thrusters
docs.text:
Electrospray thrusters (also known as field-emission electric propulsion, FEEP, when using liquid metals, or colloid thrusters when using ionic liquids) extract and accelerate charged species from a liquid surface at a sharp emitter tip subject to a strong electric field.

When the applied voltage exceeds a threshold, the balance between electrostatic pressure and surface tension forms a Taylor cone at the tip apex, from which a fine jet of ions or charged droplets is emitted. For ionic liquid propellants (e.g., 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate, [EMIm][BF\(_4\)]), both positive and negative ions are emitted alternately (or from dual emitter arrays), avoiding spacecraft charging issues.

Key performance characteristics:

  • Thrust range: 1–1000 \(\mu\)N (micro-Newton class), making them uniquely suited to precision drag-free and attitude control applications.

  • \(I_{sp}\): 500–5000 s depending on whether droplet mode (lower, 500–1000 s) or ion evaporation mode (higher, 3000–5000 s) dominates.

  • Power: 1–50 W per thruster head; very power-efficient at micro-Newton thrust.

  • No moving parts; fast electrical response (millisecond time constant, limited by propellant wetting dynamics).

  • Propellant stored as liquid at room temperature in simple reservoirs; no pressurization required.

The LISA Pathfinder mission (ESA/NASA, launched December 2015) demonstrated drag-free control at the \(10^{-15}\) m/\(\sqrt{\text{Hz}}\) displacement noise level using electrospray thrusters as the primary actuation mechanism. The NASA Disturbance Reduction System (DRS) used Busek ST7-DRS thrusters (six \(\times\) micro-Newton class); the ESA GAIA-heritage system used MOOG Coloid Micro-Newton Thrusters (CMNTs). The force noise requirement below \(0.1\) \(\mu\)N/\(\sqrt{\text{Hz}}\) over 1–30 mHz was achieved, validating the propulsion technology for the full LISA gravitational wave observatory (planned launch 2034).

Commercial electrospray systems include Accion Systems TILE (Tiled Ionic Liquid Electrospray) modules, which integrate arrays of hundreds of silicon micro-fabricated emitter tips for 0.3–3 mN total thrust at 1 W/mN. Designed for 6U CubeSats, TILE has flown on multiple commercial small satellite missions since 2018.

docs.title: 8.3.4 Pulsed Plasma Thrusters
docs.text:
Pulsed Plasma Thrusters (PPTs) ablate a solid Teflon (PTFE, polytetrafluoroethylene) propellant bar using a pulsed capacitor discharge, producing a plasma that is electromagnetically accelerated by Lorentz forces. Each pulse operates as follows:

  1. A high-voltage capacitor (charged to 1–2 kV, energy \(E_{cap} = \frac{1}{2}CV^2\), typically 2–20 J) discharges across a spark-plug triggered electrode gap adjacent to the Teflon face.

  2. The spark ionizes a thin surface layer of Teflon, forming a transient plasma. The plasma current (\(10^4\)–\(10^5\) A flowing for \(\sim\)5 \(\mu\)s) interacts with the self-generated magnetic field.

  3. Lorentz force \(\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}\) accelerates the plasma axially, while the ablated neutral gas is also entrained and heated, contributing to thrust.

  4. The Teflon bar is spring-fed (or gravity-fed in testing) to advance fresh surface into the discharge gap.

Each pulse delivers an impulse bit (\(I_{bit}\)) of typically 100–500 \(\mu\)N\(\cdot\)s, with \(I_{sp}\) of 500–1500 s and pulse repetition rates of 1–100 Hz. Total thruster efficiency (jet power / input power) is low (5–20%) due to late-time ablation of neutral gas that does not participate in electromagnetic acceleration.

PPT advantages: solid propellant eliminates all feed system components (valves, lines, tanks, regulators); extremely simple and low-cost; propellant is non-toxic; capable of very small impulse bits useful for attitude control. EO-1 (NASA, 2000) was the first satellite to use a PPT for primary attitude control. The Mars Cube One (MarCO) CubeSats used PPT attitude control alongside cold gas for trajectory correction. The Zacube-2 (South Africa, 2018) and various university CubeSats have used commercial PPT units from Clyde Space and CU Aerospace.

docs.title: 8.4 All-Electric GEO Satellites
docs.text:
Traditional GEO satellites use a chemical bipropellant liquid apogee engine (LAE, \(\Delta v \approx 1800\) m/s, firing duration 1–3 hours) to transfer from geostationary transfer orbit (GTO, \(e \approx 0.73\), \(a \approx 24{,}500\) km) to GEO, then chemical or electric thrusters for station keeping. All-electric satellites eliminate the LAE entirely, using electric thrusters for the complete GTO-to-GEO transfer and all subsequent station-keeping (Wertz et al. 2011).

The Boeing 702SP (small platform) was the first operational all-electric GEO satellite platform. ABS-3A and Eutelsat-115 West B were launched simultaneously in March 2015 aboard a Falcon 9. The 702SP architecture uses four SPT-140D Hall thrusters (25 cm diameter, 4.5 kW each from Fakel/SPT, two operating simultaneously). The orbit raising from GTO to GEO requires 6–12 months of continuous thrusting (vs. days for chemical).

The mass advantage of all-electric propulsion is derived from the Tsiolkovsky equation. For NSSK over 15 years with total \(\Delta v \approx 800\) m/s:

\[\begin{align*} m_{prop,chem} &= m_{dry}\left(e^{800/(235 \times 9.806)} - 1\right) \approx 0.42\, m_{dry} \notag \\ m_{prop,EP} &= m_{dry}\left(e^{800/(1800 \times 9.806)} - 1\right) \approx 0.047\, m_{dry} \end{align*}\]

For a 2000 kg dry satellite, this represents 840 kg (chemical) versus 94 kg (EP) for station-keeping propellant – a saving of 746 kg that can be applied to payload capacity or reduced launch cost. Adding the elimination of the LAE propellant (\(\sim\)1050 kg for a 3000 kg wet satellite) yields total propellant savings of \(>\)1500 kg, allowing an all-electric satellite to launch at half the GTO mass of its chemical equivalent.

The all-electric orbit-raising trajectory is a low-thrust spiral from GTO to GEO. The spacecraft fires thrusters near apogee (to raise perigee) and near perigee (to raise apogee and reduce inclination). The spiral passes through the Van Allen radiation belts for 6–12 months, requiring:

  • Radiation-hardened electronics (total ionizing dose of 30–100 krad, versus \(<\)5 krad for chemical orbit raising).

  • Radiation-resistant solar cells (triple-junction GaAs with increased cover glass thickness, 500 \(\mu\)m vs. 150 \(\mu\)m for chemical).

  • Careful thermal management during long-duration thrusting.

Subsequent all-electric GEO platforms include Airbus Eurostar 3000 Neo (Eutelsat-36C, 2016; Al Yah 3, 2018 with six PPS-5000 thrusters), Boeing 702X (four 25-cm XIPS gridded ion thrusters, Intelsat IS-29e, 2016), and Thales Spacebus Neo (4 PPS-5000, operational from 2019).

docs.title: 8.5 Propellant Budget Analysis
docs.text:
A systematic propellant budget quantifies all \(\Delta v\) demands across the mission lifetime and derives total propellant mass. The sequence accounts for each maneuver separately (Eq. (8.2)) since spacecraft mass decreases with each consumption event (Wertz et al. 2011).

For a GEO communications satellite with 15-year design life, the major \(\Delta v\) requirements are:

Table 8.2. GEO Satellite 15-Year Propellant Budget (3000 kg dry mass, chemical station keeping) Maneuver \(\Delta v\) (m/s) Prop. Mass (kg) \(I_{sp}\) (s) System GTO apogee kick (LAE) 1,820 1,050 315 Bipropellant Inclination trim at GEO 50 22 315 Bipropellant Injection error correction 30 13 315 Bipropellant N–S station keeping (15 yr) \(15 \times 50 = 750\) 310 235 Hydrazine E–W station keeping (15 yr) \(15 \times 2 = 30\) 12 235 Hydrazine Attitude control (momentum dump) 20 8 230 Hydrazine Repositioning maneuvers 20 8 235 Hydrazine End-of-life disposal to graveyard 11 5 230 Hydrazine Uncertainties and residuals (5%) — 71 — — Total wet mass \(\sim\)2731 \(\sim\)1499

The north–south station-keeping (NSSK) \(\Delta v\) of \(\sim\)50 m/s/year is driven by solar and lunar gravitational perturbations that cause orbital inclination to increase at approximately 0.75/year without correction. Maintaining the inclination within \(\pm\)0.05 of the equatorial plane requires biannual NSSK maneuvers. East–west station keeping (EWSK) corrects longitudinal drift caused by Earth’s equatorial ellipticity (triaxiality), requiring only \(\sim\)2 m/s/year.

End-of-life disposal to a graveyard orbit at least 300 km above GEO requires \(\Delta v = 11\) m/s, mandated by ITU-R S.1003 and FCC regulations. The graveyard orbit lies at \(\sim\)36,086 km altitude where the satellite will remain for hundreds of years (there is no atmospheric drag at GEO altitudes).

docs.title: 8.6.1 Nuclear Thermal Propulsion
docs.text:
Nuclear Thermal Propulsion (NTP) heats hydrogen propellant using a fission reactor, achieving exhaust temperatures of 2500–3000 K – far exceeding the 3500 K adiabatic flame temperature limit of chemical combustion (limited by dissociation). The theoretical \(I_{sp}\) for hydrogen heated to 3000 K:

\[I_{sp,NTP} = \frac{1}{g_0}\sqrt{\frac{2 \gamma R_u T_c}{(\gamma-1) M_w}} \approx \frac{1}{9.806}\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.4 \times 8314 \times 2700}{0.4 \times 2}} \approx 900\,\mathrm{s}\tag{8.16}\]

where \(M_w = 2\) kg/kmol for molecular hydrogen and \(T_c = 2700\) K is a representative reactor exit temperature. The NERVA (Nuclear Engine for Rocket Vehicle Application) program (1955–1972) demonstrated ground test engines (Phoebus-2A, XE-Prime) achieving \(I_{sp} = 825\)–850 s at 4.4 GN thrust, validating NTP for crewed Mars missions before cancellation.

NASA’s current DRACO (Demonstration Rocket for Agile Cislunar Operations) program, contracted to BWX Technologies for reactor and General Atomics for propulsion system integration (Phase 1 awarded 2021, launch target late 2020s), aims to demonstrate NTP in Earth orbit. NTP’s principal appeal is cutting the crewed Mars transit time from \(\sim\)9 months (chemical \(\Delta v \approx 3.6\) km/s) to \(\sim\)4 months (\(\Delta v\) achieved more efficiently), dramatically reducing crew radiation exposure from galactic cosmic rays.

docs.title: 8.6.2 Solar Electric Propulsion at Scale
docs.text:
SEP performance scales directly with available solar power. The BepiColombo mission (ESA/JAXA, launched 2018, Mercury arrival 2025) operates four T6 ion thrusters at 22 kW total at 1 AU (degrading to 6 kW at Mercury’s 0.31 AU), executing a complex planetary gravity-assist trajectory requiring \(> 5\) km/s of deep-space \(\Delta v\).

NASA’s Dawn mission (2007–2018) accumulated 51,445 hours of ion thruster operation on NSTAR thrusters powered by 10.3 kW solar arrays (at 1 AU), consuming 425 kg of xenon over the 11-year mission. Dawn remains the only spacecraft to orbit two extraterrestrial bodies (Vesta and Ceres).

For future high-power applications, the 100 kW Hall thruster X3 has been demonstrated at NASA Glenn Research Center, while the Advanced Electric Propulsion System (AEPS) – a 13 kW HET for Gateway’s Power and Propulsion Element (PPE) – has been developed by Aerojet Rocketdyne. Megawatt-class nuclear electric propulsion (NEP), combining fission reactors with ion thruster clusters, has been studied for crewed Mars missions (Isp \(>\) 5000 s, continuous thrust for months) and rapid cargo delivery to the outer solar system.

Table 8.3. Comprehensive Propulsion System Comparison System \(I_{sp}\) (s) Thrust Power TRL Best Application Cold gas (N\(_2\)) 50–75 0.05–10 N None 9 CubeSat ACS Hydrazine monoprop 220–235 0.5–22 N Heater only 9 Small sat \(\Delta v\), ACS Green prop. docs.title: 8.7 Thruster Selection and System Design
docs.text:
Selecting a propulsion system for a given mission requires balancing multiple constraints simultaneously. The primary decision variables are:

\(\Delta v\) requirement and time budget: High \(\Delta v\) (\(>\)1 km/s) strongly favors EP if sufficient power is available and if schedule permits slow orbit raising. For rapid maneuvering (\(<\)days), chemical high-thrust systems are necessary. Mixed architectures (chemical for apogee and emergency, EP for station keeping) are common in traditional large GEO satellites.

Power availability: EP requires electrical power proportional to thrust level. At 60% total efficiency, generating 200 mN at 1800 s \(I_{sp}\) requires \(\sim\)3 kW. Large GEO satellite solar arrays provide 10–25 kW, easily supporting one to four HETs in parallel. CubeSats generating 5–30 W can only support micro-thrusters (electrospray, cold gas, micro-PPT).

Contamination: Ion thruster charge-exchange (CEX) products deposit on solar cell cover glass (sputtered molybdenum, tungsten), reducing transmission. Hall thruster backflux contains sputtered boron nitride channel material. Electrospray ionic liquid droplets can deposit on optical surfaces. Thruster placement geometry and solar array orientation during thrusting are designed to minimize plume impingement.

End-of-life compliance: ITU, FCC, and ESA guidelines require LEO satellites to deorbit within 5 years and GEO satellites to achieve graveyard orbit. Propulsion systems must retain sufficient propellant for deorbit (LEO) or raise to graveyard (GEO). Passivation (venting remaining propellant) is required to prevent on-orbit breakup from residual energy sources.

docs.title: 8.8 Summary
docs.text:
This chapter has surveyed the full breadth of satellite propulsion technologies from first principles. The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation (Eq. (8.1)) remains the central governing relationship: the exponential dependence of propellant mass on \(\Delta v / (I_{sp} g_0)\) drives the quest for higher specific impulse and makes electric propulsion with \(I_{sp} > 1500\) s enormously attractive for high-\(\Delta v\) missions.

Chemical propulsion (hydrazine monopropellant, MMH/MON-3 bipropellant) dominates where high thrust, rapid maneuvering, or power-limited environments prevail. Green propellants (AF-M315E, LMP-103S) are progressively replacing toxic hydrazine as regulatory pressure increases. Electric propulsion, particularly Hall effect thrusters, has transformed commercial GEO satellite architecture: the all-electric 702SP and Eurostar 3000 Neo platforms eliminate the heavy liquid apogee engine, saving 400–600 kg of launch mass. The Starlink constellation’s krypton HET fleet represents the largest deployment of electric propulsion in history.

Looking forward, nuclear thermal propulsion (NASA DRACO program) offers a path to crewed Mars missions with substantially reduced transit times, while high-power SEP (BepiColombo T6, NEXT-C, X3) is enabling increasingly ambitious robotic science missions to the inner and outer solar system (Sutton and Biblarz 2017; Wertz et al. 2011; Pisacane 2005).

Chapter Summary – Key Equations:

  • Tsiolkovsky: \(\Delta v = I_{sp} g_0 \ln(m_0/m_f)\)

  • Thrust equation: \(F = \dot{m} v_e + (P_e - P_a)A_e\)

  • Ion exit velocity: \(v_{exit} = \sqrt{2qV_b/m_i}\)

  • GEO NSSK budget: \(\approx 50\) m/s/year; EWSK: \(\approx 2\) m/s/year

  • GEO disposal: minimum \(\Delta v = 11\) m/s to graveyard (\(+\)300 km above GEO)

docs.title: Chapter 9: Thermal Control Systems
docs.text:
Key Concepts in This Chapter

  • Heat transfer mechanisms in the space environment: conduction, radiation, and the absence of convection

  • Orbital thermal environment characterisation including solar, planetary infrared, and albedo heat loads

  • Passive thermal control: multilayer insulation, optical coatings, and heat pipes

  • Active thermal control: heaters, louvers, mechanically pumped fluid loops, and cryocoolers

  • Thermal mathematical modelling methodology and verification by test

  • Special thermal design challenges: cryogenic instruments and battery thermal management

docs.title: 9.1 Introduction and Design Philosophy
docs.text:
The thermal control system (TCS) of a spacecraft is responsible for maintaining all components within their allowable temperature ranges throughout every phase of the mission, from integration and test on the ground to end-of-life on-orbit operations. Unlike terrestrial engineering where convection dominates heat transfer, spacecraft thermal engineers must work exclusively with conduction and radiation, two fundamentally different mechanisms that demand careful systems-level reasoning.

The consequence of thermal failure can be severe. Battery cells that freeze below \(-20\,^{\circ}\)C lose capacity irreversibly; reaction wheels overheat and seize if their lubricant degrades above \(+60\,^{\circ}\)C; optical detector arrays must often be maintained within \(\pm 0.1\,^{\circ}\)C to preserve calibration stability; and electronic components exposed to thermal cycling beyond their qualified range rapidly develop solder joint fatigue. The thermal design engineer must simultaneously satisfy conflicting requirements: electronics generate heat that must be rejected to space, yet sensitive detectors must be shielded from solar and planetary heating, and batteries must be kept warm during eclipse.

This chapter presents the fundamental physics governing spacecraft thermal behaviour, surveys the suite of passive and active thermal control hardware available to the designer, introduces the computational methods used to model and predict temperatures, and describes the test methodologies used to validate thermal models prior to launch (Gilmore 2002).

docs.title: 9.2 Heat Transfer Fundamentals in the Space Environment
9.2.1 Conduction
docs.text:
Heat conduction within solid bodies obeys Fourier’s Law. For steady-state one-dimensional conduction through a slab of cross-sectional area \(A\), thermal conductivity \(k\), and temperature gradient \(dT/dx\):

\[Q_{\mathrm{cond}} = -k \, A \, \frac{dT}{dx}\tag{9.1}\]

For a composite multi-layer structure (e.g., a panel sandwich of aluminium face-sheets and honeycomb core), thermal resistances are combined in series or parallel analogously to electrical resistors. The thermal resistance of a layer of thickness \(\delta\) is:

\[R_{\mathrm{cond}} = \frac{\delta}{k \, A}\tag{9.2}\]

Aluminium alloy Al-6061 has \(k \approx 167\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}\), making it the dominant structural material for heat spreading. Titanium (\(k \approx 7\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}\)) is used as a thermal isolator, while carbon-fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) panels used for dimensional stability have \(k\) ranging from \(5\) to \(700\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}\) depending on fibre orientation. Thermal interface resistance between mechanical surfaces can dominate the conductive path; this is discussed in Section 9.6.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Thermal Radiation
docs.text:
All surfaces emit thermal radiation according to the Stefan-Boltzmann law. For a surface of emittance \(\varepsilon\), temperature \(T\), and area \(A\):

\[Q_{\mathrm{rad}} = \varepsilon \, \sigma \, T^4 \, A\tag{9.3}\]

where \(\sigma = 5.6704 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}\) is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. The net radiation exchange between two large parallel plates of emittances \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) at temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) is:

\[Q_{\mathrm{net}} = \frac{\sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)}{\frac{1}{\varepsilon_1} + \frac{1}{\varepsilon_2} - 1}\tag{9.4}\]

For arbitrarily oriented surfaces, the geometric view factor \(F_{ij}\) represents the fraction of diffuse radiation leaving surface \(i\) that is intercepted by surface \(j\). The view factor integral is:

\[F_{ij} = \frac{1}{\pi A_i} \int\!\!\int_{A_i} \int\!\!\int_{A_j} \frac{\cos\theta_i \, \cos\theta_j}{\pi r^2} \, dA_i \, dA_j\tag{9.5}\]

where \(\theta_i\) and \(\theta_j\) are the angles between the surface normals and the line joining the area elements, and \(r\) is the distance between them. View factors obey the reciprocity relation \(A_i F_{ij} = A_j F_{j i}\) and the enclosure summation rule \(\sum_j F_{ij} = 1\).

docs.title: 9.2.3 Absence of Convection
docs.text: In the space vacuum (\(p < 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Pa}\)), there are essentially no gas molecules available to carry heat convectively. This has profound implications: heat generated inside a spacecraft can only leave by radiation from an external surface, with conduction providing the internal transport path. The thermal engineer must therefore create a low-resistance conductive path from every heat-generating component to a radiating surface, while simultaneously insulating the spacecraft from external heat fluxes. In pressurised volumes (crew modules, battery enclosures) convective effects are present and must be accounted for.

docs.title: 9.3.1 Solar Irradiance
docs.text:
The solar irradiance (solar constant) at 1 AU from the Sun is:

\[S_0 = 1361 \pm 0.5 \,\mathrm{W/m^2}\tag{9.6}\]

This value varies seasonally by \(\pm 3.5\%\) due to Earth’s orbital eccentricity, reaching a maximum of approximately \(1414\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\) at perihelion (January) and a minimum of \(1322\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\) at aphelion (July). For missions at other distances from the Sun, the irradiance scales as the inverse square:

\[S(r) = S_0 \left(\frac{1\,\mathrm{AU}}{r}\right)^2\tag{9.7}\]

yielding \(S = 9126\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\) at Mercury (0.387 AU) and \(S = 50\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\) at Jupiter (5.2 AU).

docs.title: 9.3.2 Earth Infrared Emission and Albedo
docs.text:
The Earth emits thermal infrared radiation at a disk-averaged flux of approximately:

\[Q_{\mathrm{IR}} = 250 \pm 20 \,\mathrm{W/m^2}\tag{9.8}\]

This flux varies with latitude, season, and cloud cover. For thermal design, worst-case hot and cold values must be separately analysed. The Earth also reflects solar radiation with an average albedo factor of:

\[a = 0.30 \pm 0.05\tag{9.9}\]

The albedo heat flux absorbed by a spacecraft surface facing the Earth is:

\[Q_{\mathrm{alb}} = a \cdot S \cdot \alpha_s \cdot A_{\mathrm{proj}} \cdot F_{\mathrm{Earth}}\tag{9.10}\]

where \(\alpha_s\) is the solar absorptance of the surface, \(A_{\mathrm{proj}}\) is the projected area toward the Earth, and \(F_{\mathrm{Earth}}\) is the view factor from the surface to the Earth disk.

docs.title: 9.3.3 Spacecraft Energy Balance
docs.text:
The transient energy balance for a spacecraft thermal node of mass \(M\) and specific heat \(C_p\) is:

\[M \, C_p \, \frac{dT}{dt} = Q_{\mathrm{solar}} \cdot \alpha_s \cdot A_{\mathrm{proj}} + Q_{\mathrm{IR}} \cdot \varepsilon \cdot A_{\mathrm{Earth-facing}} + Q_{\mathrm{alb}} \cdot \alpha_s \cdot A_{\mathrm{proj}} + Q_{\mathrm{int}} - \varepsilon \, \sigma \, T^4 \, A_{\mathrm{rad}}\tag{9.11}\]

In steady-state (\(dT/dt = 0\)), the equilibrium temperature of a simple isothermal spacecraft body is:

\[T_{\mathrm{eq}} = \left[ \frac{\alpha_s \, A_{\mathrm{sun}} \, S + \varepsilon \, Q_{\mathrm{IR}} \, A_{\mathrm{earth}} + Q_{\mathrm{int}}} {\varepsilon \, \sigma \, A_{\mathrm{rad}}} \right]^{1/4}\tag{9.12}\]

The ratio \(\alpha_s/\varepsilon\) is arguably the most important single parameter in spacecraft thermal design. A high ratio causes the spacecraft to run hot; a low ratio causes it to run cold. Passive thermal control is largely the art of selecting surface finishes with appropriate \(\alpha_s/\varepsilon\) ratios.

Table 9.1. Thermo-optical properties of common spacecraft surface finishes (BOL = Beginning of Life). Note that \(\alpha_s\) degrades with radiation dose (UV darkening). docs.title: 9.4 Passive Thermal Control
docs.text: Passive thermal control encompasses all techniques that operate without power consumption: surface coatings, multilayer insulation blankets, heat pipes (which require no electrical power), and structural design for thermal paths.

docs.title: 9.4.1 Multilayer Insulation
docs.text:
Multilayer insulation (MLI) blankets are the workhorse of spacecraft thermal control. A typical blanket consists of 10 to 30 layers of \(6\)–\(25\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) Mylar or Kapton film with a thin vacuum-deposited aluminium coating, separated by Dacron mesh spacers to prevent direct contact between layers. The Dacron spacers have very low area contact fraction (typically \(\sim 2\%\)), minimising conductive bridging.

The effective emittance \(\varepsilon^*\) of an \(N\)-layer MLI blanket, accounting for both radiation and residual conduction through spacers, can be estimated. For a perfect MLI with \(N\) shields of individual emittance \(\varepsilon_s\) (both sides), the radiation component gives:

\[\frac{1}{\varepsilon^*_{\mathrm{rad}}} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon_1} + \frac{N}{\varepsilon_s / 2} + \frac{1}{\varepsilon_2} - (N+1) \approx \frac{N+2}{\varepsilon_s}\tag{9.13}\]

For adjacent layer pairs with emittances \(\varepsilon_a\) and \(\varepsilon_b\), the effective emittance of that pair is:

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pair}} = \frac{\varepsilon_a \, \varepsilon_b}{\varepsilon_a + \varepsilon_b - \varepsilon_a \, \varepsilon_b}\tag{9.14}\]

The total heat flux through an \(N\)-shield MLI in the radiation limit is:

\[Q_{\mathrm{MLI}} = \frac{\sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)}{N+2} \cdot A \cdot \varepsilon^*\tag{9.15}\]

In practice, effective emittances \(\varepsilon^* \approx 0.010\)–\(0.025\) are achievable for well-fabricated 20-layer blankets. The actual performance is degraded by edges, seams, penetrations (for cables, tubes, and bolts), and handling damage. A conservative design value of \(\varepsilon^* = 0.03\)–\(0.05\) is often used for budgeting.

Table 9.2. MLI blanket performance data for typical configurations used in spacecraft thermal control. Configuration Layers \(\varepsilon^*\) Heat Flux (W/m\(^2\)) Application (typical) (at 300–77 K) Double Aluminised Mylar (DAM) + Dacron 10 0.030 3.5 Instrument covers DAM + Dacron 20 0.015 1.8 Spacecraft body Aluminised Kapton + Dacron 20 0.025 2.9 External (UV stable) Single-sided aluminised Mylar 30 0.008 1.0 Cryogenic dewar NRC-2 foil 10 0.050 5.8 High-temperature

docs.title: 9.4.2 Optical Solar Reflectors
docs.text:
Optical solar reflectors (OSRs) consist of thin (\(0.1\)–\(0.5\,\mathrm{mm}\)) fused silica or ceria-stabilised glass tiles with a silver or aluminium metallic backing. The glass transmits solar radiation (\(\lambda < 5\,\mu\mathrm{m}\)) and reflects it from the backing, giving a very low solar absorptance. The glass itself is opaque to thermal infrared (\(\lambda > 5\,\mu\mathrm{m}\)) and radiates with high emittance. The resulting thermo-optical properties are excellent:

  • Solar absorptance: \(\alpha_s = 0.06\)–\(0.08\)

  • Infrared emittance: \(\varepsilon = 0.78\)–\(0.82\)

  • Ratio: \(\alpha_s / \varepsilon \approx 0.08\)–\(0.10\)

  • End-of-life (post-radiation): \(\alpha_s \approx 0.10\)–\(0.13\) (slight UV darkening of glass)

OSRs are radiation-stable compared to paints (which suffer UV darkening and particle radiation damage). They are commonly used on GEO satellite radiator panels where the 15+ year mission duration demands BOL-to-EOL stability. Typical radiator specific rejection capacity with OSR cover is \(250\)–\(300\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\).

docs.title: 9.4.3 Heat Pipes
docs.text:
Heat pipes are passive two-phase heat transport devices exploiting the latent heat of vaporisation of a working fluid. The principle of operation involves:

  1. Evaporator: heat input vaporises the working fluid, raising local vapour pressure.

  2. Vapour transport: pressure difference drives vapour flow through the central vapour core from evaporator to condenser.

  3. Condenser: vapour condenses, releasing latent heat to the heat sink, and the liquid is returned to the evaporator.

  4. Wick: a porous capillary structure (screen mesh, sintered powder, grooves) pumps liquid by capillary action back to the evaporator, requiring no mechanical pump.

The maximum heat transport capability (limited by capillary pumping) is:

\[Q_{\max} = \frac{r_e A_v \rho_v h_{fg}}{\mu_v L_{\mathrm{eff}}} \left[ \frac{2\sigma_l}{r_c} - \rho_l g L \sin\phi \right]\tag{9.16}\]

where \(r_e\) is the effective pore radius, \(A_v\) is the vapour space cross-sectional area, \(\rho_v\) is the vapour density, \(h_{fg}\) is the latent heat of vaporisation, \(\mu_v\) is the vapour dynamic viscosity, \(L_{\mathrm{eff}}\) is the effective length, \(\sigma_l\) is the liquid surface tension, \(r_c\) is the capillary pore radius, and \(\phi\) is the tilt angle relative to horizontal.

The most common spacecraft heat pipe working fluid is ammonia (NH\(_3\)), which has an excellent figure of merit \(N_l = \sigma_l \rho_l h_{fg} / \mu_l\) in the temperature range \(-60\) to \(+60\,^{\circ}\)C covering the typical spacecraft operating range. Propylene (\(-50\) to \(+45\,^{\circ}\)C) and ethane (\(-120\) to \(-10\,^{\circ}\)C) serve lower temperature applications.

A variable conductance heat pipe (VCHP) contains a reservoir of non-condensable gas (NCG, typically nitrogen or helium) connected to the condenser end. As the heat source temperature rises, the working fluid vapour pressure increases and compresses the NCG, exposing more condenser area and increasing the effective thermal conductance. This provides passive temperature control without any power input. The conductance varies as:

\[G_{\mathrm{eff}} = G_{\max} \cdot F_{\mathrm{condenser}}(T_{\mathrm{source}})\tag{9.17}\]

Loop heat pipes (LHPs) use the same two-phase cycle but with a mechanically separate evaporator/compensation chamber and remote condenser connected by flexible transport lines, enabling heat transport over distances of \(10\)–\(30\,\mathrm{m}\). LHPs are used on the GOES-R weather satellite series and ESA’s MetOp spacecraft.

docs.title: 9.5.1 Electrical Heaters
docs.text:
Electrical heaters are used to maintain components above their minimum allowable temperature (MAT). Two distinct classes are employed:

Survival heaters are powered from the battery during eclipse or emergency power mode. They maintain non-operating components (e.g., propulsion lines, battery cells during launch, pyrotechnic initiators) above their survival lower limit (SLL). Typical temperature set-point: \(-20\,^{\circ}\)C.

Operational heaters are thermostatically controlled (via bimetal thermostats or software-commanded solid-state relays) during normal operations. They compensate for variations in internal dissipation and orbital environment. Heater sizing requires:

\[P_{\mathrm{heater}} = Q_{\mathrm{loss}} - Q_{\mathrm{int,\min}} = (\varepsilon \sigma T^4 A + G \Delta T) - Q_{\mathrm{int,\min}}\tag{9.18}\]

Resistive foil heaters (Kapton-encapsulated etched-foil elements) are applied directly to component surfaces or structural panels. Typical power densities are \(0.5\)–\(3\,\mathrm{W/cm^2}\).

docs.title: 9.5.2 Louvers
docs.text:
Louver assemblies (also called jalousie shutters) provide variable effective emittance by opening and closing bi-metallic actuated blades over a radiator surface. As temperature rises, the blades open, exposing the high-emittance radiator coating; as temperature falls, blades close and the low-emittance blade back-surface reduces radiative loss.

  • Fully open effective emittance: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{open}} \approx 0.60\)–\(0.70\)

  • Fully closed effective emittance: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{closed}} \approx 0.05\)–\(0.10\)

  • Temperature control range: \(\pm 5\)–\(10\,^{\circ}\)C

  • Control range (open to closed): \(15\)–\(30\,^{\circ}\)C

Louvers require no power and represent a well-proven heritage technology (used since early US and Soviet satellites). Their disadvantages are mass, complexity, potential for jamming, and susceptibility to contamination of sliding surfaces.

docs.title: 9.5.3 Mechanically Pumped Fluid Loops
docs.text:
For high-power spacecraft (\(>5\,\mathrm{kW}\) total dissipation), mechanically pumped single-phase fluid loops offer efficient heat collection from distributed sources and rejection at centralised radiators. The heat transport capacity is:

\[Q = \dot{m} \, C_p \, \Delta T = \rho \, \dot{V} \, C_p \, (T_{\mathrm{out}} - T_{\mathrm{in}})\tag{9.19}\]

The International Space Station (ISS) uses two independent mechanically pumped single-phase ammonia loops in the External Active Thermal Control System (EATCS), each capable of rejecting up to \(70\,\mathrm{kW}\) through large (\(700\,\mathrm{m^2}\)) deployable radiator panels. Commercial GEO satellites such as Boeing 702 and Airbus Eurostar E3000 use MPFL with Novec 7100 (methoxy-nonafluorobutane, \(\rho = 1528\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(C_p = 1183\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}\)) as the working fluid, which is non-toxic, non-flammable, and compatible with all spacecraft materials.

docs.title: 9.5.4 Cryocoolers
docs.text:
Cryocoolers are mechanical refrigerators that maintain sensors and detectors at temperatures from \(4\,\mathrm{K}\) to \(150\,\mathrm{K}\) by actively pumping heat from the cold stage to a warm rejection point. The thermodynamic efficiency is characterised by the coefficient of performance (COP):

\[\mathrm{COP} = \frac{Q_{\mathrm{cold}}}{W_{\mathrm{input}}} = \frac{Q_{\mathrm{cold}}}{Q_{\mathrm{hot}} - Q_{\mathrm{cold}}}\tag{9.20}\]

The Carnot COP provides the theoretical maximum:

\[\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{Carnot}} = \frac{T_{\mathrm{cold}}}{T_{\mathrm{hot}} - T_{\mathrm{cold}}}\tag{9.21}\]

Practical cryocoolers achieve \(10\)–\(30\%\) of Carnot COP. Major types used in space:

  • Stirling cryocoolers: linear piston compressor + displacer piston, \(20\)–\(100\,\mathrm{K}\) cooling, heritage on IRAS, Landsat, and numerous military IR satellites. Lockheed Martin ACTDP Stirling cooler provides \(600\,\mathrm{mW}\) at \(55\,\mathrm{K}\) consuming \(46\,\mathrm{W}\).

  • Pulse tube cryocoolers: no moving displacer (replaced by inertance tube and reservoir), lower vibration than Stirling, \(30\)–\(100\,\mathrm{K}\), used on ASTER/Terra, GOES-R ABI.

  • Joule-Thomson (JT) cryocoolers: expansion of pre-cooled gas through throttling valve, \(<20\,\mathrm{K}\) achievable, used as a final stage, no moving parts in cold head.

  • Adiabatic demagnetisation refrigerators (ADR): paramagnetic salt demagnetised to reach \(<1\,\mathrm{K}\), used on XMM-Newton RGS and Astro-H SXS to achieve \(50\,\mathrm{mK}\).

  • Dilution refrigerators: \(^3\)He/\(^4\)He dilution, sub-millikelvin temperatures, planned for future quantum sensor missions.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) operates at \(6.7\,\mathrm{K}\), achieved by a dedicated Joule-Thomson cryocooler (the MIRI cooler system, \(5.6\,\mathrm{W}\) input for \(160\,\mathrm{mW}\) at \(6.2\,\mathrm{K}\)) combined with the telescope’s passive cooling to \(40\,\mathrm{K}\) provided by its L2 orbit and multi-layer sunshield.

docs.title: 9.5.5 Thermoelectric Coolers (Peltier Devices)
docs.text:
Thermoelectric coolers (TECs) use the Peltier effect: when current flows through a junction of two dissimilar semiconductor materials (bismuth telluride Bi\(_2\)Te\(_3\) alloys), heat is pumped from the cold face to the hot face. The heat pumped and electrical power consumed are:

\[Q_{\mathrm{cold}} = \alpha_P \, I \, T_{\mathrm{cold}} - \frac{1}{2} I^2 R - K (T_{\mathrm{hot}} - T_{\mathrm{cold}})\tag{9.22}\]

where \(\alpha_P\) is the Seebeck coefficient of the thermocouple pair, \(I\) is the current, \(R\) is the electrical resistance, and \(K\) is the thermal conductance of the module. TECs are used for small precise temperature control applications: focal plane array (FPA) temperature stabilisation (\(\pm 0.01\,^{\circ}\)C), laser diode temperature control, and electronics boxes where \(\Delta T < 40\,^{\circ}\)C is needed.

docs.title: 9.6 Thermal Interface Materials
docs.text:
Even highly polished metal surfaces in intimate contact leave microscopic air gaps that dominate thermal resistance at the interface. Thermal interface materials (TIMs) fill these gaps and dramatically reduce contact resistance. The interface thermal resistance is:

\[R_{\mathrm{int}} = \frac{1}{h_c \, A_{\mathrm{contact}}}\tag{9.23}\]

where \(h_c\) is the contact conductance (\(\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}\)). Table 9.3 summarises common TIM options.

Table 9.3. Thermal interface material (TIM) properties and typical applications in spacecraft. TIM Type Conductivity Contact Conductance Notes \(k\) (W m\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\)) \(h_c\) (W m\(^{-2}\) K\(^{-1}\)) Indium foil (0.1 mm) 81 \(5000\)–\(15000\) Reusable, soft metal Thermal grease (Apiezon N) 0.2 \(3000\)–\(8000\) Low temp, pumpout risk Thermal grease (Dowsil TC-5026) 4.0 \(8000\)–\(20000\) High conductivity Graphite pad (Grafoil) 5 (in-plane), 3 (thru) \(4000\)–\(12000\) Compressible, EMC too Phase change material (PCM) 0.7 \(5000\)–\(18000\) Reflows at 52C Bare Al-Al joint (bolted) — \(500\)–\(3000\) Highly bolt-torque dependent

The contact conductance between two bolted aluminium surfaces increases approximately as:

\[h_c \approx h_{c,0} \left( \frac{P}{P_0} \right)^{0.7}\tag{9.24}\]

where \(P\) is the contact pressure (MPa) and \(P_0\) is a reference pressure. The strong dependence on bolt torque means that the TCS thermal model must track the bolt torque specification and any relaxation due to vibration or thermal cycling.

docs.title: 9.7.1 Geometric Math Model and View Factor Calculation
docs.text:
The thermal mathematical model (TMM) consists of a network of thermal nodes connected by conductors, implemented in commercial software such as ESATAN-TMS (European Standard Analysis Tool for Thermal Networks), Thermal Desktop/SINDA (Cullimore & Ring), or MSC Nastran thermal. The modelling process begins with a Geometric Math Model (GMM) that captures the spacecraft geometry for view factor and absorbed flux computation.

View factor calculation for complex geometries uses the Monte Carlo ray-tracing method: \(N_{\mathrm{rays}}\) rays are launched from surface \(i\) in random directions weighted by the cosine law; the fraction intercepting surface \(j\) gives \(F_{ij}\). The statistical uncertainty is:

\[\sigma_{F_{ij}} = \sqrt{\frac{F_{ij}(1-F_{ij})}{N_{\mathrm{rays}}}}\tag{9.25}\]

Typically \(N_{\mathrm{rays}} = 10^6\) to \(10^8\) are used to achieve \(\sigma < 0.001\).

docs.title: 9.7.2 Node Network and Conductors
docs.text:
The TMM discretises the spacecraft into a set of thermal nodes. For a network of \(n\) nodes, the thermal state is described by the vector \(\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^n\). The governing equations are:

\[C_i \frac{dT_i}{dt} = Q_{\mathrm{ext},i} + Q_{\mathrm{int},i} + \sum_{j \neq i} G_{ij}^{\mathrm{cond}} (T_j - T_i) + \sum_{j \neq i} G_{ij}^{\mathrm{rad}} (T_j^4 - T_i^4)\tag{9.26}\]

where \(C_i = M_i C_{p,i}\) is the thermal capacitance of node \(i\), \(G_{ij}^{\mathrm{cond}}\) is the linear conductive conductor, \(G_{ij}^{\mathrm{rad}} = \varepsilon^* \sigma A_i F_{ij}\) is the radiative conductor (radiation exchange factor, REF), and \(Q_{\mathrm{ext},i}\) includes solar, IR, and albedo inputs computed by the GMM for each orbital position.

The system of equations can be written in matrix form:

\[\mathbf{C} \dot{\mathbf{T}} = \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{ext}} + \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{int}} + \mathbf{G}^{\mathrm{cond}} (\mathbf{T}_j - \mathbf{T}_i) + \mathbf{G}^{\mathrm{rad}} (\mathbf{T}_j^4 - \mathbf{T}_i^4)\tag{9.27}\]

docs.title: 9.7.3 Thermal Analysis Cases
docs.text:
Four primary analysis cases bound the temperature range:

  1. Hot case: maximum solar (perihelion), maximum internal dissipation (payload fully on), orbit with maximum sunlit time, BOL surface properties (clean surfaces, low \(\alpha_s\)).

  2. Cold case: minimum solar (aphelion), minimum internal dissipation (safe mode, minimum equipment on), maximum eclipse fraction, EOL degraded surface properties (UV-darkened, high \(\alpha_s\)).

  3. Eclipse start/end transient: rapid temperature change as spacecraft enters/exits Earth’s shadow, driving thermal cycling fatigue analysis.

  4. Transfer orbit: applicable to GEO satellites during the apogee engine firing phase when attitude is constrained by the engine pointing requirement.

docs.title: 9.8.1 Thermal Balance Test
docs.text:
The thermal balance test (TBT) is conducted in a large thermal vacuum (TV) chamber at pressures below \(10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Pa}\). The spacecraft is placed on a support structure surrounded by a cold shroud (liquid nitrogen cooled, \(T_{\mathrm{shroud}} \approx 100\,\mathrm{K}\)) to simulate the cold space sink. Solar simulation is provided by infrared heater arrays or, for higher fidelity, quartz lamp arrays. The test sequence includes:

  1. Pump down to vacuum (\(< 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Pa}\))

  2. Cold soak stabilisation (typically 12–24 h)

  3. Hot case stabilisation at maximum internal dissipation

  4. Eclipse simulation (heater arrays off)

  5. Additional cases per test plan

Correlation between test-measured temperatures and TMM-predicted temperatures is performed. Acceptance criteria typically require:

\[|T_{\mathrm{predicted}} - T_{\mathrm{measured}}| < 3\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} \quad \text{for critical nodes}\tag{9.28}\]

Parameters adjusted during correlation include conductances, heater powers, and surface properties, following a systematic sensitivity analysis.

docs.title: 9.8.2 Thermal Cycling
docs.text: Thermal cycling tests subject the spacecraft or unit to repeated temperature excursions between \(T_{\min} = -40\,^{\circ}\)C and \(T_{\max} = +70\,^{\circ}\)C (qualification) or \(-25\) to \(+55\,^{\circ}\)C (acceptance), with dwell times sufficient to achieve temperature stabilisation within \(\pm 2\,^{\circ}\)C. Typical cycle counts: 8 (acceptance), 100 (qualification). Cycling is performed in ambient air for unit-level tests (air cooling compensates for lack of radiation) and in vacuum for spacecraft-level tests.

docs.title: 9.9.1 Cryogenic Instrument Thermal Design
docs.text:
Cryogenic infrared and X-ray instruments present the most demanding thermal design challenges. The key principle is to minimise parasitic heat loads to the coldest stage through:

  • Passive cooling: L2, lunar trailing, or Sun-synchronous (with appropriate baffle) orbits allow large passive radiators to reach \(40\)–\(80\,\mathrm{K}\).

  • V-groove radiators: JWST uses three deployable V-groove radiators to achieve passive cooling of the telescope structure to \(\sim40\,\mathrm{K}\).

  • Thermal straps: braided aluminium or copper straps with low stiffness connect the cold stage to the cryocooler cold finger or passive radiator.

  • Multilayer insulation: cryogenic MLI with 30+ layers provides effective emittance \(\varepsilon^* < 0.005\).

docs.title: 9.9.2 Battery Thermal Management
docs.text:
Lithium-ion battery cells exhibit strong temperature sensitivity:

  • Optimal charge/discharge temperature: \(0\) to \(+40\,^{\circ}\)C

  • Charging below \(0\,^{\circ}\)C: lithium plating causes irreversible capacity loss

  • Storage at elevated temperature accelerates calendar aging (capacity fade)

  • Thermal runaway threshold: \(\sim 130\,^{\circ}\)C

  • Capacity recovery at low temperature: cells deliver \(\sim 50\%\) capacity at \(-20\,^{\circ}\)C vs. \(+20\,^{\circ}\)C

Battery thermal design must therefore maintain cells within \(0\) to \(+30\,^{\circ}\)C throughout the mission. This requires survival heaters (typically \(10\)–\(30\,\mathrm{W}\) per battery) for eclipse cold-soak and heat spreading/rejection in hot orbit.

docs.title: 9.10 Design Example: LEO Earth Observation Satellite Thermal Control
docs.text:
Consider a \(200\,\mathrm{kg}\) LEO Earth observation satellite in a \(600\,\mathrm{km}\) Sun-synchronous orbit. The satellite bus dissipates \(500\,\mathrm{W}\) in operational mode and \(100\,\mathrm{W}\) in safe mode. The radiator area required to reject the operational dissipation with a maximum panel temperature of \(+30\,^{\circ}\)C and an OSR cover (\(\varepsilon = 0.80\), \(\alpha_s = 0.07\)) is:

\[A_{\mathrm{rad}} = \frac{Q_{\mathrm{int}}}{\varepsilon \sigma T_{\mathrm{max}}^4 - \alpha_s S / 4} = \frac{500}{0.80 \times 5.67\times10^{-8} \times 303^4 - 0.07 \times 1361 / 4} \approx 1.35\,\mathrm{m^2}\tag{9.29}\]

This calculation ignores Earth IR and albedo inputs for brevity. The survival heater power to maintain the spacecraft above \(-15\,^{\circ}\)C during a \(35\%\) eclipse fraction with all equipment off (safe mode):

\[P_{\mathrm{survival}} = \varepsilon \sigma T_{\mathrm{survival}}^4 A_{\mathrm{rad}} - Q_{\mathrm{int,safe}} \approx 0.80 \times 5.67\times10^{-8} \times 258^4 \times 1.35 - 100 \approx 55\,\mathrm{W}\tag{9.30}\]

docs.title: 9.11 Summary
docs.text:
The thermal control system is a critical enabling subsystem that must be designed concurrently with the spacecraft structure, power, and attitude control from the earliest mission concept phase. The choice between passive-dominant and active-dominant thermal architectures is driven by the total internal dissipation, the mission orbit, and the temperature requirements of the payload.

Key design parameters are the thermo-optical properties \(\alpha_s\) and \(\varepsilon\) of all external surfaces, the effective emittance \(\varepsilon^*\) of MLI blankets, the heat pipe conductance sizing, and the heater power budget. The thermal mathematical model must be validated against thermal balance test data before flight predictions can be trusted.

Future trends include the increasing use of mechanically pumped loops and deployable radiators for high-power communications satellites (\(>20\,\mathrm{kW}\)), advanced variable conductance technologies for wide-range autonomy, and the development of sub-Kelvin refrigerators for next-generation quantum sensor and far-infrared astronomy missions (Gilmore 2002).
