docs.title: Chapter 10: On-Board Data Handling
docs.text:
Key Concepts in This Chapter

  • OBDH functions: data acquisition, command distribution, housekeeping telemetry, and payload data handling

  • Radiation-hardened and radiation-tolerant processor architectures for space

  • Memory technologies and error correction: EDAC, scrubbing, and Triple Modular Redundancy

  • Space data buses: MIL-STD-1553B, SpaceWire, and high-speed interfaces

  • CCSDS standards governing spacecraft data communications

  • Flight software design principles, RTOS selection, and autonomy/FDIR

  • On-board AI processing for next-generation payload autonomy

docs.title: 10.1 Introduction and System Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The On-Board Data Handling (OBDH) subsystem is the electronic nervous system of a spacecraft. It acquires measurement data from sensors distributed throughout the satellite, decodes and distributes commands received from the ground, maintains the spacecraft’s health through telemetry generation, manages on-board time, stores payload and housekeeping data, and executes the autonomous on-board software that controls every other subsystem (Wertz et al. 2011).

The OBDH architecture of a modern spacecraft can be understood as a layered hierarchy:

  1. Sensor/actuator layer: raw measurements from temperature sensors, current monitors, position encoders, and payload detectors; actuator interfaces to reaction wheels, heaters, and pyrotechnics.

  2. Remote Terminal Unit (RTU) layer: data concentrators that aggregate analogue and discrete measurements from the sensor layer and communicate digitally with the central computer via a data bus.

  3. On-Board Computer (OBC) layer: central processing unit that executes flight software, performs command decoding, schedules activities, and manages data flow.

  4. Mass memory layer: solid-state recorder or mass memory unit that stores payload science data pending downlink.

  5. Data bus layer: the communication backbone connecting all elements.

Figure 10.1. Representative OBDH block diagram for a medium-sized LEO Earth observation satellite, showing the SpaceWire backbone connecting the OBC, payload interface unit, mass memory unit, and remote terminal units.

docs.title: 10.2.1 Radiation Environment and Its Effects on Electronics
docs.text:
The space radiation environment consists of galactic cosmic rays (GCR), solar energetic particles (SEP), and trapped particles in the Van Allen belts. These produce several classes of radiation-induced failures in microelectronics:

  • Single Event Upset (SEU): a heavy ion or proton deposits sufficient charge along its track to flip a memory bit from 0 to 1 or vice versa (a “soft error”). The cross-section for SEU depends on the linear energy transfer (LET) of the particle and the critical charge \(Q_c\) of the cell. The SEU rate is:
\[R_{\mathrm{SEU}} = \int_{LET_c}^{\infty} \sigma(LET) \cdot \Phi(LET) \, d(LET)\tag{10.1}\]

where \(\sigma(LET)\) is the cell cross-section as a function of LET and \(\Phi(LET)\) is the differential particle fluence spectrum.

  • Single Event Latchup (SEL): an ion triggers a parasitic thyristor structure in CMOS logic, creating a low-impedance path from supply to ground. SEL is destructive unless power is cycled within milliseconds.

  • Total Ionising Dose (TID): cumulative ionisation in gate oxides shifts threshold voltages and degrades transistor gain. Expressed in Gray or rad(Si), typical TID limits are \(20\)–\(300\,\mathrm{krad(Si)}\) for radiation-hardened devices.

  • Displacement Damage: non-ionising energy loss (NIEL) from protons and neutrons creates crystal lattice defects, degrading minority carrier lifetime in bipolar transistors and CCDs.

docs.title: 10.2.2 Radiation-Hardened Processor Options
docs.text:
Table 10.1. Radiation-hardened and radiation-tolerant processor options for space applications. Performance figures are typical; exact values depend on operating frequency and configuration. Processor Architecture Frequency TID Power Heritage (MHz) (krad) (W) LEON3-FT (GR712RC) SPARC V8, dual-core 80 300 0.5 ESA, ATV, Galileo LEON4-FT (GR740) SPARC V8, quad-core 250 100 2.0 ExoMars, Hera RAD750 PowerPC 750 33–166 1000 5.0 MRO, Curiosity, Dawn RAD5545 PowerPC e6500, 4-core 600–1000 300 10.0 GPS III, GOES-R BAE MIPS R3000 MIPS R3000 20 1000 3.5 MSL entry descent Vorago VA10820 ARM Cortex-M0 116 1000 0.1 CubeSats Space Micro P50 ARM Cortex-A53 1000 100 2.5 Commercial LEO Xilinx Virtex-5QV Xilinx FPGA 400 (LUT) 1000 10–20 GOES-R, MMS

The LEON family of SPARC-V8 processors was developed by ESA/ESTEC and is now maintained by Cobham Gaisler. The GRLIB IP library provides a complete SoC platform including the LEON processor core, memory controllers, UART, SpaceWire controller, MIL-STD-1553 interface, and PCI. The LEON3-FT implements hardware fault-tolerance through:

  • Register file with parity and retry

  • Cache memory protected with EDAC

  • On-chip scrubbing controller

  • Processor lock-step with comparison

The RAD750 from BAE Systems is derived from the IBM PowerPC 750 and is manufactured using radiation-hardened silicon-on-insulator (SOI) process technology, giving TID immunity up to \(1\,\mathrm{Mrad(Si)}\). It has accumulated an exceptional heritage record: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Curiosity rover, Mars 2020 Perseverance, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, and many others.

docs.title: 10.2.3 FPGAs in Space
docs.text:
Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are used extensively in space for:

  • High-speed data routing and signal processing (where CPUs are too slow)

  • Custom peripheral controllers (SpaceWire routers, codec implementations)

  • Reconfigurable payload processing pipelines

The Xilinx Virtex-4QV and Virtex-5QV are radiation-hardened versions using configuration SRAM cells designed to be SEU-immune. The ProASIC3 from Microsemi uses a flash-based configuration memory that is inherently immune to SEU (since flash cells require erase voltage to change state), making it “zero configuration scrubbing” required.

For commercial/NewSpace missions with lower radiation requirements (LEO, \(<2\) years), Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) FPGAs (Xilinx Zynq, Intel/Altera Cyclone/Arria) are used with Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR) implemented in the FPGA fabric. In TMR, the logic is triplicated and a majority voter selects the output, tolerating a single SEU in any one copy:

\[F_{\mathrm{TMR}} = 3 F_{\mathrm{single}}^2 (1 - F_{\mathrm{single}}) + F_{\mathrm{single}}^3\tag{10.2}\]

where \(F_{\mathrm{single}}\) is the probability of failure for a single module over the mission period.

docs.title: 10.3.1 Error Detection and Correction (EDAC)
docs.text:
SRAM memories in space are susceptible to SEU-induced bit flips. The standard mitigation is Error Detection and Correction (EDAC) based on a Hamming code with Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection (SECDED). For a data word of \(k\) bits, the minimum number of parity check bits \(p\) satisfying the SECDED condition is:

\[2^p \geq k + p + 1\tag{10.3}\]

For \(k = 32\): \(p = 6\) (total codeword: 38 bits). For \(k = 64\): \(p = 7\) (total codeword: 71 bits). The parity check matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) defines the syndrome \(\mathbf{s}\):

\[\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{H} \, \mathbf{r}\tag{10.4}\]

where \(\mathbf{r}\) is the received codeword. A non-zero syndrome indicates an error; the syndrome value identifies the position of a single-bit error, which is then corrected by flipping that bit.

docs.title: 10.3.2 Memory Scrubbing
docs.text:
Even with EDAC, over time multiple SEUs may accumulate in the same word, eventually overwhelming the single-error correction capability. Memory scrubbing is the periodic re-reading and re-writing of memory to correct accumulated errors before they compound. The scrubbing rate must be set such that the probability of a second SEU in the same word between scrub passes remains negligible:

\[P_{\mathrm{double}} = \left( \lambda_{\mathrm{SEU}} \cdot \tau_{\mathrm{scrub}} \right)^2 / 2\tag{10.5}\]

where \(\lambda_{\mathrm{SEU}}\) is the per-word SEU rate and \(\tau_{\mathrm{scrub}}\) is the scrub interval. Typical scrub rates are \(0.1\)–\(1\,\mathrm{Hz}\) for program memory, \(0.01\)–\(0.1\,\mathrm{Hz}\) for mass memory.

docs.title: 10.3.3 Non-Volatile Memory
docs.text:
Non-volatile storage is required for:

  • Boot software (typically PROM or radiation-hardened EEPROM)

  • Non-volatile parameters (orbit ephemeris, attitude reference, mission timeline)

  • Payload science data (mass memory)

EEPROM (electrically erasable PROM) stores \(1\)–\(8\,\mathrm{Mbit}\) of configuration data with \(10^5\) erase/write cycles and \(>10\) year data retention. NAND flash provides \(>1\,\mathrm{Tbit/chip}\) density but requires wear-levelling algorithms and ECC to manage finite program/erase cycles (\(10^4\)–\(10^5\)) and ECC to handle multi-bit errors characteristic of NAND flash.

docs.title: 10.4.1 MIL-STD-1553B
docs.text:
MIL-STD-1553B is the dominant spacecraft data bus for command and housekeeping data. The bus architecture is:

  • Bus Controller (BC): one BC manages all transfers on the bus, polling Remote Terminals in turn.

  • Remote Terminals (RT): up to 31 RTs (each addressed 0–30), each representing a subsystem (ADCS, power, propulsion, etc.).

  • Bus Monitor (BM): passive listener for bus traffic logging.

  • Dual redundant bus: two physically independent twisted-shielded pairs (Bus A and Bus B); the BC switches to Bus B on failure detection.

Figure 10.2. MIL-STD-1553B dual redundant bus architecture. The Bus Controller (BC, implemented in the OBC) polls each Remote Terminal (RT) in a deterministic round-robin schedule. Coupling transformers at each stub connection provide electrical isolation.

Data encoding uses Manchester biphase-level encoding, providing inherent DC balance and clock recovery without a separate clock signal. Each 1553 word is 20 bits: 3 sync bits + 16 data bits + 1 parity bit. The bus operates at a fixed \(1\,\mathrm{Mbps}\) data rate with a maximum cable length of \(300\,\mathrm{m}\) at \(\leq 33\,\Omega/\mathrm{km}\) characteristic impedance.

A typical BC-to-RT command transfer consists of:

  1. BC transmits Command Word: RT address (5 bits) + T/R bit + subaddress (5 bits) + word count (5 bits)

  2. RT transmits Status Word after a response time of \(4\)–\(12\,\mu\mathrm{s}\)

  3. RT transmits \(1\)–\(32\) data words (if command was “Transmit”)

The total bus cycle time for 16 RTs each exchanging 32 words is \(\sim 5\,\mathrm{ms}\), giving an effective bus utilisation of \(200\,\mathrm{Hz}\) polling rate per RT. This is more than adequate for housekeeping data but insufficient for high-speed payload data.

docs.title: 10.4.2 SpaceWire
docs.text:
SpaceWire (ECSS-E-ST-50-12C, based on IEEE Std 1355) is a high-speed serial data bus designed for spacecraft payload data. Key characteristics:

  • Serial, full-duplex, point-to-point links (or via routers)

  • Low-voltage differential signalling (LVDS): \(\pm 200\,\mathrm{mV}\) differential, robust to EMC

  • Data rate: \(2\)–\(400\,\mathrm{Mbps}\) (auto-negotiated per link)

  • Packet-switched network: SpaceWire routers switch packets between ports

  • Character-level encoding: Data-Strobe (DS) encoding provides clock recovery

  • End-to-end error control via Error Control Codes (ECC) at the packet level

The SpaceWire character encoding transmits data and strobe signals on two LVDS pairs. The strobe signal \(S\) is defined as:

\[S_n = S_{n-1} \oplus D_n\tag{10.6}\]

where \(D_n\) is the current data bit. The receiver recovers the clock by XOR-ing data and strobe. This eliminates the need for a separate clock signal and provides inherent tolerance to skew between the signal pairs. SpaceWire networks are used as the payload data backbone on the Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, Sentinel-3, JUICE, BepiColombo, Solar Orbiter, and ExoMars missions.

docs.title: 10.4.3 CAN Bus and Low-Speed Interfaces
docs.text: The Controller Area Network (CAN) bus, operating at up to \(1\,\mathrm{Mbps}\) with inherent multi-master arbitration and error detection, is increasingly used in small satellites (\(<100\,\mathrm{kg}\)) where the lower mass and cost compared to 1553 are attractive. I2C (up to \(3.4\,\mathrm{Mbps}\)) and SPI (up to \(25\,\mathrm{Mbps}\)) are used for board-level sensor interfaces (temperature sensors, ADC/DAC converters, gyroscopes on the same PCB as the OBC).

docs.title: 10.5 CCSDS Standards for Space Data Systems
docs.text:
The Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) develops internationally agreed standards for space data communications, adopted by ESA, NASA, JAXA, ISRO, CNSA, and all major space agencies. The key standards form a layered protocol architecture:

Table 10.2. Key CCSDS standards and their application in spacecraft OBDH design. CCSDS Standard Short Name Function CCSDS 132.0-B-2 TM Space Data Link Telemetry framing: Virtual Channels, FECF, Frame Header CCSDS 232.0-B-3 TC Space Data Link Telecommand framing: CLTU, Frame Error Control CCSDS 131.0-B-3 TM Synchronization Frame sync, pseudo-randomisation CCSDS 401.0-B-29 Radio Frequency/Modulation TM/TC modulation standards CCSDS 133.0-B-1 Space Packet Packet structure: Primary Header + User Data Field CCSDS 727.0-B-4 CFDP File delivery: reliable transfer, segmentation, error recovery CCSDS 122.0-B-1 Image Data Compression Lossless image compression for EO data CCSDS 123.0-B-2 Hyperspectral Compression Near-lossless hyperspectral data compression CCSDS 350.0-G-3 Security Overview CCSDS Space Data Link Security (SDLS) framework

docs.title: 10.5.1 Space Packet Structure
docs.text:
The CCSDS Space Packet (CCSDS 133.0-B-1) is the fundamental data unit used in spacecraft telemetry. The packet structure is:

Table 10.3. CCSDS Space Packet primary header field structure (6 octets total). Field Content Bits Value/Range Version Number Always 000 3 0 Packet Type 0 = TM, 1 = TC 1 0 or 1 Secondary Header Flag 1 if secondary header present 1 0 or 1 APID (Application ID) Source/destination identifier 11 0–2047 Sequence Flags 11 = standalone packet 2 01, 10, 11 Packet Sequence Count Rolling counter per APID 14 0–16383 Packet Data Length Total packet length \(-7\) (octets) 16 0–65535 Secondary Header (optional) variable APID-specific User Data Field variable Science / HK data

Packets are multiplexed into Transfer Frames by the TM Space Data Link layer. Each Transfer Frame carries a fixed-length payload of \(\leq 65536\) octets, with a mandatory 6-octet frame primary header (spacecraft ID, virtual channel ID, frame counter) and optional Frame Error Control Field (FECF, CRC-16-CCITT). Multiple Virtual Channels (VCs) within one physical link allow multiplexing of science, housekeeping, and playback data streams.

docs.title: 10.5.2 CCSDS File Delivery Protocol (CFDP)
docs.text:
CFDP (CCSDS 727.0-B-4) provides reliable file transfer over lossy space links. Two classes of service exist:

  • Class 1 (Unreliable): no acknowledgement, used for low-priority downlink

  • Class 2 (Reliable): positive/negative acknowledgement, automatic retransmission of lost segments, used for critical command files and software uploads

CFDP handles segmentation of large files into Protocol Data Units (PDUs) that fit within the available Transfer Frame data field, managing reassembly autonomously at the receiving end. It also provides file checksum verification and directory listing services.

docs.title: 10.6.1 Real-Time Operating System Selection
docs.text:
The flight software executes on a Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) that provides:

  • Deterministic task scheduling with bounded worst-case execution time (WCET)

  • Priority-based preemption (higher-priority tasks immediately preempt lower)

  • Semaphores, mutexes, and message queues for inter-task communication

  • Memory protection (optionally via MMU)

  • POSIX-compatible API for portability

Table 10.4. RTOS options used in spacecraft flight software, with their key characteristics and mission heritage. RTOS Licence Heritage Notes VxWorks (Wind River) Commercial ISS, Hubble, MRO, Curiosity, many GEO DO-178C certified, POSIX RTEMS Open source (BSD) ESA: Rosetta, Mars Express, BepiColombo Free, POSIX, active community LynxOS-178 Commercial Military satellites DO-178C Level A FreeRTOS MIT open source CubeSats, university missions Lightweight, large ecosystem INTEGRITY (GHS) Commercial Various defence missions High-assurance, POSIX Nucleus RTOS Commercial Small satellites Low footprint

docs.title: 10.6.2 Scheduling Theory
docs.text:
Flight software tasks have hard real-time deadlines. Rate Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) assigns fixed priorities based on task period: shorter period = higher priority. The schedulability condition for \(n\) tasks is:

\[U = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{C_i}{T_i} \leq n \left( 2^{1/n} - 1 \right)\tag{10.7}\]

where \(C_i\) is the worst-case execution time (WCET) and \(T_i\) is the period of task \(i\). As \(n \to \infty\), the bound converges to \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\). Earliest Deadline First (EDF) is an optimal dynamic scheduler that achieves full processor utilisation (\(U \leq 1\)) but has more complex implementation and less predictable behaviour under overload.

docs.title: 10.6.3 Software Development Standards
docs.text:
Space flight software is developed to rigorous standards:

  • ECSS-E-ST-40C : ESA software engineering standard, covering software life cycle, planning, requirements, design, testing, and documentation.

  • NASA NPR 7150.2: NASA software engineering requirements, defining software classification (Class A through D) by criticality.

  • MISRA-C:2012: a subset of ISO C with 225 coding rules eliminating undefined behaviour and common error patterns. Applied to safety-critical software.

  • DO-178C: aviation software certification standard increasingly applied by analogy to spacecraft software for highest assurance levels.

Software complexity is managed through the Architecture Framework and the concept of software partitioning: functionally independent modules (FDIR monitor, attitude control law, command decoder) execute in separate protected address spaces, preventing a bug in one from corrupting another.

docs.title: 10.7 Autonomy and Failure Detection, Isolation, and Recovery
10.7.1 FDIR Hierarchy
docs.text:
FDIR is structured in levels of increasing severity:

  1. Level 0 – Local FDIR: hardware-level protection (current limiters, watchdog timers, redundancy switching). Response time: \(\mu\)s–ms.

  2. Level 1 – Unit FDIR: unit-level self-tests and resets. Response time: ms–s.

  3. Level 2 – Mode FDIR: OBC-executed function checks; transitions between nominal and degraded operational modes. Response time: 1–60 s.

  4. Level 3 – Safe Mode FDIR: autonomous entry into Safe Mode triggered by critical anomalies. Response time: \(<30\,\mathrm{s}\).

Safe Mode entry is triggered when any of the following conditions are detected:

  • Attitude error exceeding threshold (e.g., \(>10^{\circ}\) from Sun-pointing): risk of solar array depowering or thermal damage

  • Battery state of charge (SoC) below critical threshold (e.g., \(<30\%\)): risk of deep discharge and permanent damage

  • Critical bus voltage out of range

  • Communication loss for more than a specified number of orbits

  • OBC hardware watchdog timer expiry

In Safe Mode, the spacecraft achieves a minimum viable configuration: solar arrays oriented toward the Sun via magnetorquers or Sun-search manoeuvre, non-essential loads powered off, beacon telemetry transmitted on omni-directional antenna at a slow, robust downlink rate (\(\leq 2\,\mathrm{kbps}\)), and the ground notified to re-establish contact.

docs.title: 10.7.2 Watchdog Timer
docs.text:
The watchdog timer is a hardware counter that counts down from a preset value (\(\sim 1\)–\(30\,\mathrm{s}\)). If the flight software fails to “kick” the watchdog within the timeout period (indicating software has hung or entered an infinite loop), the timer reaches zero and asserts a hardware reset signal to the OBC. The reset vector then reloads the boot software from non-volatile memory and restarts the system.

Proper watchdog design requires that the “kick” be performed only after completing a health check of critical software tasks (not simply in an interrupt service routine), to ensure the kick reflects genuine software liveness.

docs.title: 10.8 Payload Data Handling and Mass Memory
10.8.1 Mass Memory Sizing
docs.text:
The on-board mass memory must store payload data accumulated during the orbit arc where no ground contact is available, until the next downlink pass. The memory requirement is:

\[M_{\mathrm{mem}} = R_{\mathrm{payload}} \cdot t_{\mathrm{store}} \cdot C_{\mathrm{margin}} + M_{\mathrm{HK}}\tag{10.8}\]

where \(R_{\mathrm{payload}}\) is the payload data rate (bits/s), \(t_{\mathrm{store}}\) is the maximum storage interval between downlinks, and \(C_{\mathrm{margin}} \geq 1.25\) is a design margin factor. For a Sentinel-2A type multi-spectral imager generating \(450\,\mathrm{Gbits/orbit}\) with 2 orbits between downlinks:

\[M_{\mathrm{mem}} \approx 450 \times 2 \times 1.25 = 1125\,\mathrm{Gbits} \approx 140\,\mathrm{GB}\tag{10.9}\]

Typical modern EO satellite mass memories range from 256 GB to 2 TB, implemented with radiation-tolerant NAND flash arrays in a Reed-Solomon or LDPC ECC-protected configuration.

docs.title: 10.8.2 On-Board Data Compression
docs.text:
On-board compression reduces downlink volume and thus ground station contact time requirements:

  • CCSDS 122.0-B-1 Lossless: based on a 2D discrete wavelet transform with adaptive entropy coding, achieving compression ratios of \(1.5\)–\(3\times\) for typical Earth imagery with no information loss. Suitable for scientific data where radiometric accuracy is essential.

  • JPEG-2000 Lossy: wavelet-based with quantisation; compression ratios of \(5\)–\(20\times\) at acceptable image quality degradation. Used for browse products and non-scientific commercial imagery.

  • CCSDS 123.0-B-2: near-lossless hyperspectral data compression, exploiting spatial and spectral correlation, achieving \(3\)–\(10\times\) compression.

docs.title: 10.9 On-Board AI Processing
docs.text:
The increasing computational demands of autonomous on-board processing—object detection, change detection, cloud screening, anomaly detection—have driven the development of dedicated AI inference accelerators for space:

Table 10.5. On-board AI processing hardware options for spacecraft applications. Processor Architecture Performance Power Status (TOPS) (W) Intel Myriad X (MA2485) 16\(\times\) SHAVE VPU 1.0 1.0 COTS, flown Ubotica CogniSAT-XE1 ARM + Myriad X 1.0 3.0 NewSpace product NVIDIA Jetson Nano 128-core Maxwell GPU 0.5 5.0 COTS (low TID) Xilinx Versal ACAP ARM + AI Engine 2.5 20 COTS with TMR Space Micro Proton 200k ARM + FPGA 0.5 10 Rad-tolerant PHI COTS (ESA study) Myriad 2 hardened 0.5 2.0 In development

The Intel Myriad X has been demonstrated on several commercial Earth observation CubeSats (Ubotica onboard the ESA PhiSat-1 mission, launched 2020) performing on-board cloud screening using a convolutional neural network (CNN) to eliminate cloud-contaminated scenes before downlink, reducing wasted downlink capacity by \(\sim 50\%\) (Giuffrida et al. 2020).

docs.title: 10.10 OBDH System Budgets and Typical Parameters
docs.text: Table 10.6. Typical OBDH subsystem mass and power budgets for different spacecraft classes. Spacecraft Class OBC Mass OBC Power Memory Example (kg) (W) (GB) 3U CubeSat 0.05–0.1 0.5–2 4–16 ISIS IOBC, GomSpace NanoCom 6U–12U CubeSat 0.1–0.3 1–5 16–128 SpaceCube Mini, Gomspace Small satellite (50–200 kg) 0.5–2 3–10 64–512 Astrobus S, SSTL 100 Medium satellite (200 kg–1 t) 2–5 10–25 256–2000 Sentinel-1, -2, -3 Large GEO (>3 t) 5–15 20–50 32–256 Eurostar E3000, Boeing 702 Deep space (planetary) 3–8 10–30 8–64 Curiosity (RAD750)

docs.title: 10.11 Design Example: Copernicus Sentinel-1 OBDH Architecture
docs.text:
The Copernicus Sentinel-1 SAR satellite employs a dual-string OBDH architecture for full cold redundancy. The main elements are:

  • OBC: Dual LEON3-FT processors (GR712RC), operating at 80 MHz, with 64 Mbyte SRAM (EDAC-protected) and 4 Mbyte EEPROM for boot software.

  • Data handling backbone: SpaceWire network at 200 Mbps connecting the OBC, SAR Instrument Control Unit (ICU), Mass Memory Unit (MMU), TT&C transponder interface, and ADCS computer.

  • Mass Memory Unit: 1.7 Tbits solid-state NAND flash recorder for SAR Level-0 data.

  • Housekeeping bus: MIL-STD-1553B connecting 18 remote terminal units for platform housekeeping.

  • Flight software: RTEMS RTOS with ECSS-E-ST-40C compliant software, \(\sim\)800 kLOC including FDIR, ADCS control laws, and CCSDS protocol stacks.

The SAR instrument generates raw data at approximately \(1.2\,\mathrm{Gbps}\) during imaging windows. This data is written to the MMU in real time by a dedicated SAR data processing unit, independent of the main OBC, which manages the SpaceWire data routing through a custom 4-port SpaceWire router.

docs.title: 10.12 Summary
docs.text:
The OBDH subsystem integrates the computational intelligence of the spacecraft, bridging sensor data acquisition, command management, autonomous operations, and payload data handling. The radiation environment imposes fundamental constraints on processor selection, memory protection, and software design that distinguish space computing from terrestrial embedded systems.

The convergence of high-performance COTS processors, TMR-protected FPGAs, and AI inference accelerators is transforming on-board data handling capabilities, enabling spacecraft to perform increasingly sophisticated on-board science analysis and autonomous decision-making that reduces dependence on continuous ground contact. This trend toward edge computing in orbit is a defining technological shift of the 2020s in spacecraft engineering.

docs.text:
Key Concepts in This Chapter

docs.title: 11.1 Introduction and System Functions
docs.text:
The Telemetry, Tracking and Command (TT&C) system is the communication bridge between a spacecraft and its ground segment. It serves four fundamental functions:

  1. Telemetry (TM): downlink of spacecraft housekeeping data (subsystem status, temperatures, voltages, currents, ADCS measurements) and, in some architectures, payload science data. This allows ground operators to monitor spacecraft health continuously.

  2. Tracking: determination of the spacecraft’s position and velocity through ranging (distance measurement) and Doppler (radial velocity measurement). This data feeds the orbit determination process.

  3. Command (TC): uplink of operator commands from the ground, decoded on-board, and executed by the relevant subsystems. Commands may be immediate or time-tagged for future execution.

  4. Ranging: generation of a precise time-of-flight measurement enabling orbit reconstruction and manoeuvre verification.

The TT&C system operates throughout the entire mission life, from separation detection after launch vehicle separation through nominal operations to end-of-life disposal. It must function reliably even when the spacecraft attitude is unknown (as during LEOP or after a safe mode entry) (Wertz et al. 2011; Pratt et al. 2003; Roddy 2006).

docs.title: 11.2 Frequency Band Selection for TT&C
docs.text:
Table 11.1. ITU frequency allocations for spacecraft TT&C and their characteristics. All frequency values are approximate; exact allocations depend on ITU Radio Regulations and national/regional modifications. Band Uplink (MHz) Downlink (MHz) Typical Use Key Characteristic UHF 400–401 435–438 LEO beacons, CubeSats Omni-directional, robust S-band 2025–2120 2200–2290 LEO/GEO TT&C, LEOP Workhorse TT&C band X-band TC 7190–7235 — Deep space uplink High gain needed X-band TM — 8025–8500 EO data downlink, deep space TM High bandwidth Ka-band 27.0–27.5 GHz 25.5–27.0 GHz High-rate TT&C, intersat Rain attenuation impact

S-band (\(2\)–\(4\,\mathrm{GHz}\)) is the most widely used TT&C band for LEO and GEO missions. It offers a good balance between:

  • Antenna size: a \(\lambda/4\) monopole at \(2.2\,\mathrm{GHz}\) is \(34\,\mathrm{mm}\) long, small enough for omnidirectional coverage.

  • Atmospheric losses: rain and cloud attenuation at S-band is \(<0.5\,\mathrm{dB}\) for \(99.9\%\) of the year at most locations.

  • Transponder maturity: S-band transponders with heritage going back to Sputnik are available from multiple vendors.

For deep space missions beyond \(3\times10^6\,\mathrm{km}\), X-band is preferred for its higher antenna gain at manageable antenna sizes (\(3\)–\(5\,\mathrm{m}\) HGA provides 45–50 dBi at X-band).

docs.title: 11.3 Transponder Architecture
docs.text:
The spacecraft transponder implements both the uplink receiver and downlink transmitter in a single unit, with the critical coherent turnaround function for ranging. The block diagram consists of:

Uplink receiver chain:

  1. Low-Noise Amplifier (LNA): amplifies the received RF signal with minimum noise figure (\(NF = 0.5\)–\(2\,\mathrm{dB}\))

  2. Bandpass filter: rejects out-of-band interference

  3. Downconverter: mixes RF carrier to intermediate frequency (IF) using a local oscillator referenced to the on-board frequency reference

  4. IF amplifier and automatic gain control (AGC)

  5. Demodulator: extracts the baseband data (PCM/PSK subcarrier demodulation)

  6. Decoder: CCSDS TC Space Data Link Protocol frame synchronisation and CLTU decoding

  7. Command decoder: parses decoded frame into individual telecommands for distribution

Coherent turnaround (ranging): The transponder generates a phase-coherent downlink carrier by multiplying the received uplink carrier frequency by a fixed rational number (the turnaround ratio \(k\)):

\[f_{\mathrm{DL}} = k \cdot f_{\mathrm{UL}}\tag{11.1}\]

For S-band, the standard turnaround ratio is \(k = 240/221\) (uplink \(\approx 2.1\,\mathrm{GHz}\), downlink \(\approx 2.3\,\mathrm{GHz}\)). For X-band, \(k = 880/749\) or \(k = 240/221\) depending on the allocation. This coherent relationship allows the ranging tone or PN code applied on the uplink to be retrieved on the downlink with a precisely known and constant delay.

Downlink transmitter chain:

  1. Frequency synthesiser: generates downlink RF carrier coherent with uplink

  2. BPSK/QPSK modulator: modulates TM data onto the carrier

  3. Driver amplifier

  4. Solid State Power Amplifier (SSPA) or TWTA: final power amplification (\(1\)–\(20\,\mathrm{W}\) typical for TT&C)

  5. Bandpass filter (harmonic rejection)

  6. Switch to antenna selection (main/redundant)

Figure 11.1. Coherent S-band TT&C transponder block diagram. The phase-locked loop (PLL) coherently regenerates the downlink carrier from the uplink, enabling two-way Doppler and ranging measurements. The ranging tone or PN code passes transparently through the transponder.

docs.title: 11.4.1 Two-Way Ranging Principle
docs.text:
Two-way ranging measures the round-trip light time (RTLT) from which the spacecraft range is derived:

\[\rho = \frac{c \cdot \mathrm{RTLT}}{2}\tag{11.2}\]

The process consists of:

  1. Ground station transmits a ranging signal (tone or PN code) modulated onto the uplink carrier.

  2. Transponder coherently retransmits the ranging signal on the downlink with the known turnaround delay.

  3. Ground station correlates the received downlink ranging signal with the transmitted reference, measuring RTLT.

  4. Range computed: \(\rho = c \cdot \mathrm{RTLT}/2\), correcting for the transponder’s internal turnaround delay (typically measured pre-launch).

Corrections applied to the raw ranging measurement include:

  • Ionospheric delay: \(\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{iono}} \propto \mathrm{TEC}/f^2\) (significant at S-band, \(\sim 1\)–\(10\,\mathrm{m}\))

  • Tropospheric delay: \(\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{tropo}} \approx 2.3\,\mathrm{m}\) (zenith, dry component) + water vapour term

  • Relativistic corrections: Sagnac effect, gravitational frequency shift

The one-sigma ranging accuracy achievable is:

\[\sigma_\rho = \frac{c}{2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot f_{\mathrm{range}} \cdot \sqrt{2 P_{\mathrm{range}} T / N_0}}\tag{11.3}\]

For a tone ranging system with a \(f_{\mathrm{range}} = 1\,\mathrm{MHz}\) highest-frequency tone and \(P/N_0 = 50\,\mathrm{dB\text{-}Hz}\), accuracy of \(\sigma_\rho \approx 1\)–\(5\,\mathrm{m}\) is achievable.

docs.title: 11.4.2 Pseudo-Noise Ranging
docs.text:
CCSDS-standardised PN ranging (CCSDS 414.1-B-2) uses a binary pseudo-random sequence modulated onto the uplink. The PN code has two critical properties:

  • Autocorrelation: the code’s autocorrelation function (ACF) has a sharp peak at zero delay and low sidelobes, enabling precise timing.

  • Unambiguous range: the code period \(T_{\mathrm{code}}\) must be longer than the round-trip light time to the target, avoiding range ambiguity.

CCSDS defines two code classes:

  • Class A (Rosette code, component code length \(N_c = 2\)): recommended for near-Earth missions (\(\leq 10^6\,\mathrm{km}\)). Unambiguous range: \(\sim 2 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{km}\).

  • Class B (T4B code): for deep space (\(> 10^6\,\mathrm{km}\)). Unambiguous range: \(\sim 10^9\,\mathrm{km}\).

docs.title: 11.4.3 Unified S-Band System
docs.text: The Unified S-Band (USB) system, originally developed for the Apollo programme, combines TM, TC, and ranging on a single S-band carrier. Telemetry is modulated as a PCM/PM subcarrier (\(f_{\mathrm{sc}} = 1.024\) MHz for wideband TM), command is modulated as a separate subcarrier, and ranging tones are injected simultaneously. The coherent transponder turnaround preserves the phase relationships of all three modulation components.

docs.title: 11.5 Doppler Tracking and Orbit Determination
docs.text:
When the spacecraft has a radial velocity component \(v_r\) relative to the ground station, the received frequency is Doppler-shifted. For the two-way case (ground transmits \(f_0\), spacecraft returns coherently at \(k \cdot f_0\), ground receives \(f_r\)):

\[f_r \approx k \cdot f_0 \cdot \frac{1 + 2 v_r / c}{1} \approx k \cdot f_0 \left(1 + \frac{2 v_r}{c} \right)\tag{11.4}\]

The two-way Doppler shift is therefore:

\[\Delta f = f_r - k \cdot f_0 = \frac{2 k f_0 v_r}{c}\tag{11.5}\]

The radial velocity is recovered as:

\[v_r = \frac{c \Delta f}{2 k f_0}\tag{11.6}\]

For a LEO spacecraft at \(v_{\mathrm{orbital}} = 7.6\,\mathrm{km/s}\) and \(k = 240/221 \approx 1.086\), the peak two-way Doppler shift at S-band (\(f_0 = 2.1\,\mathrm{GHz}\) uplink) is:

\[\Delta f_{\max} = \frac{2 \times 1.086 \times 2.1\times10^9 \times 7600}{3\times10^8} \approx 116\,\mathrm{kHz}\tag{11.7}\]

Ground-based orbit determination uses a least-squares batch estimator or Kalman filter to fit a dynamical model to tracking data (range \(+\) Doppler from multiple ground stations). The orbit solution improves as tracking arc length increases. A 3-station pass set covering \(> 30^{\circ}\) of orbital arc typically achieves position accuracy of \(10\)–\(50\,\mathrm{m}\) for LEO (RSS), dominated by atmospheric delay uncertainties.

docs.title: 11.6 TT&C Link Budget
docs.text:
The TT&C link budget evaluates whether the signal-to-noise ratio at the receiver is adequate for reliable demodulation. The fundamental link budget equation in decibels is:

\[E_b/N_0 = P_T + G_T - L_{\mathrm{space}} - L_{\mathrm{atm}} + G_R - k_B - R_{\mathrm{bit}}\tag{11.8}\]

where:

  • \(P_T\) = transmit power (dBW)

  • \(G_T\) = transmit antenna gain (dBi)

  • \(L_{\mathrm{space}} = 20\log_{10}(4\pi d/\lambda)\) = free-space path loss (dB)

  • \(L_{\mathrm{atm}}\) = atmospheric losses (dB, rain + gas absorption)

  • \(G_R\) = receive antenna gain (dBi)

  • \(k_B = -228.6\,\mathrm{dBW/K/Hz}\) = Boltzmann constant in dB

  • \(R_{\mathrm{bit}}\) = data rate (dBbps)

  • \(N_{\mathrm{sys}}\) = system noise temperature (dBK, \(T_{\mathrm{sys}} = T_{\mathrm{ant}} + T_{\mathrm{LNA}} + T_{\mathrm{feed}} + …\))

Table 11.2. Representative TT&C link budget for S-band downlink from a LEO satellite at \(600\,\mathrm{km}\) altitude to a \(5\,\mathrm{m}\) parabolic ground station antenna. Minimum elevation angle: \(5^{\circ}\) (worst case). Parameter Value Unit Spacecraft transmitter Transmit power (SSPA) \(+33.0\) dBm (2 W) Cable/connector losses (S/C side) \(-1.0\) dB Transmit antenna gain (hemi-coverage, \(5^{\circ}\) elev) \(+3.0\) dBi Spacecraft EIRP \(+35.0\) dBm Propagation Free-space path loss (600 km, \(5^{\circ}\) elev, 2.25 GHz) \(-161.5\) dB Atmospheric losses (S-band, low elevation) \(-0.5\) dB Pointing losses (ground antenna) \(-0.5\) dB Polarisation mismatch loss \(-0.3\) dB Total propagation loss \(-162.8\) dB Ground station receiver Ground antenna gain (\(D = 5\,\mathrm{m}\), \(\eta = 0.6\), 2.25 GHz) \(+38.5\) dBi LNA noise temperature \(T_{\mathrm{LNA}} = 30\,\mathrm{K}\), \(NF = 0.4\,\mathrm{dB}\) System noise temperature \(T_{\mathrm{sys}} = 80\,\mathrm{K}\), \(G/T = 17.0\,\mathrm{dB/K}\) Link performance Received \(C/N_0\) \(+72.2\) dBHz TM data rate (BPSK, rate-1/2 conv. code) \(\leq 32\,\mathrm{kbps}\) — \(E_b/N_0\) at 32 kbps \(+26.6\) dB Required \(E_b/N_0\) (BER \(10^{-5}\), BPSK, Viterbi) \(+4.3\) dB Link margin \(+22.3\) dB

The generous link margin of \(22\,\mathrm{dB}\) shown in Table 11.2 confirms the TT&C link is robust. In practice, TT&C links are designed with \(>6\,\mathrm{dB}\) margin at worst-case geometry (lowest elevation angle) to accommodate unpredicted losses, attitude errors, and antenna pattern nulls.

docs.title: 11.7.1 Omnidirectional and Low-Gain Antennas
docs.text:
Full spherical coverage is required for LEOP and safe mode, where the spacecraft attitude is undefined or in the process of being established. Omnidirectional coverage is achieved with:

  • Monopole/dipole: half-wave dipole gives \(G = 2.15\,\mathrm{dBi}\) with toroidal pattern, nulls along the axis. Two orthogonal dipoles cover the full sphere.

  • Cavity-backed slot: flush-mounted in the spacecraft panel, \(G = 3\)–\(5\,\mathrm{dBi}\), hemispherical coverage per unit.

  • Patch antenna: low-profile, \(G = 6\)–\(8\,\mathrm{dBi}\) over a \(\pm60^{\circ}\) half-angle cone, commonly used in pairs on opposite faces for full coverage.

  • Horn antenna: for downlink TM on GEO (\(G = 15\)–\(20\,\mathrm{dBi}\), covering the full Earth disk from GEO requires \(\theta_{3\mathrm{dB}} \approx 18^{\circ}\)).

For deep space missions (MRO, Voyager, New Horizons), a High-Gain Antenna (HGA) with \(G = 42\)–\(47\,\mathrm{dBi}\) is required to overcome path losses at AU-scale distances, supplemented by a Low-Gain Antenna (LGA) for near-Earth contingency operations.

docs.title: 11.8 Launch and Early Orbit Phase Operations
11.8.1 LEOP Timeline
docs.text:
LEOP represents the most critical operational period of the mission. The typical LEO LEOP sequence proceeds as:

  1. T = 0: Separation: pyrotechnic separation nuts release, springs separate spacecraft from upper stage. Separation switch triggers on-board autonomous sequence.

  2. T = \(+5\) s: On-board software starts. Beacon transmission begins autonomously on TT&C transmitter (omnidirectional antenna, \(1\,\mathrm{kbps}\), no encryption).

  3. T = \(+5\) to \(+20\) min: First ground station contact (typically a station under the launch orbit track). Ground acquires beacon, establishes TM/TC link.

  4. T = \(+20\) min: First TM packet received. Spacecraft health check performed: battery SoC, temperature, attitude mode.

  5. T = \(+30\) to \(+60\) min: Solar array deployment commanded. Current increase on solar array output confirms deployment.

  6. T = \(+1\) to \(+4\) h: Attitude initialisation: magnetometer-based coarse Sun acquisition, followed by Sun sensor-based fine Sun pointing. Power positive confirmed.

  7. T = \(+4\) to \(+24\) h: Orbit determination with tracking data from multiple stations. Manoeuvre planning for orbit correction if needed.

  8. T = \(+24\) to \(+72\) h: In-orbit check-out (IOCO) begins. Subsystem activation and verification sequence. Payload switch-on (if no outgassing/thermal conditioning required).

  9. T = \(+3\) to \(+30\) days: Commissioning phase. End-to-end performance verification, calibration, transition to nominal operations.

Figure 11.2. Typical LEOP timeline for a LEO satellite. Ground station contact windows (shaded bars) provide telecommand opportunities. The first 24 h are the most critical, requiring 24/7 ground staffing and contingency command sequences prepared for each anomaly scenario.

docs.title: 11.8.2 Safe Mode
docs.text:
Safe Mode (also called Survival Mode or Emergency Mode) is an autonomous spacecraft configuration entered when a critical anomaly is detected that the on-board FDIR cannot resolve at a lower level. From a TT&C perspective, safe mode operation requires:

  • Transmission on omnidirectional antenna (not directional HGA) to ensure contact regardless of attitude

  • Reduced, robust downlink rate (\(\leq 4\,\mathrm{kbps}\) BPSK) with forward error correction to maximise link margin

  • Periodic beacon transmission even without ground command, to enable ground station acquisition without prior knowledge of spacecraft state

  • Automatic uplink search: transponder scans across uplink frequency uncertainties if frequency drift has occurred

  • Minimum housekeeping telemetry downlink (power, temperature, attitude error, FDIR event log)

docs.title: 11.9.1 Command Uplink Chain
docs.text:
Commands are uplinked as a CCSDS TC Transfer Frame encapsulated in a Communications Link Transmission Unit (CLTU). The CLTU encoding provides robust error detection:

\[\mathrm{CLTU} = \underbrace{10101010…10101011}_{\text{Start Sequence (16 bits)}} \; \underbrace{(\mathrm{TC\,frame} + \mathrm{EDAC})}_{\text{$n$ code blocks of 64 bits}} \; \underbrace{C8… FEh}_{\text{Tail Sequence (8 octets)}}\tag{11.9}\]

Each 64-bit code block consists of 56 data bits and an 8-bit BCH code providing single-error correction and double-error detection within the block. A command rejected by the on-board decoder (due to CLTU decode error, authentication failure, or address mismatch) generates a Command Reject Acceptance Report downlinked as a TM packet.

docs.title: 11.9.2 Command Priority and Sequencing
docs.text:
Commands are classified by priority:

  1. Critical commands: one-time commands with irreversible effects (pyrotechnic firing, antenna deployment, mode change to safe mode). These require additional safeguards: separate arm/fire sequence, time window, count check.

  2. Operational commands: routine operational commands (payload power, attitude mode, downlink rate). Executed immediately or at specified time-tag.

  3. Low-priority commands: parameter updates, table uploads, maintenance commands. May be queued and executed during ground contact.

Time-tagged commands (TTC) are stored on-board in a command timeline with absolute on-board time tags. The on-board time correlation with UTC is maintained via periodic time correlation messages uplinked during ground contact.

docs.title: 11.10 Command Authentication and Security
docs.text:
The threat of unauthorised command injection (spoofing) is a serious concern, particularly for high-value missions. CCSDS Space Data Link Security (SDLS, CCSDS 355.0-B-1) defines a security protocol for authenticating and/or encrypting TC frames at the Space Data Link layer.

The standard supports two security services:

  1. Authentication Only: a Message Authentication Code (MAC) is appended to each TC frame. The ground computes the MAC using AES-256 CMAC with the current session key; the spacecraft verifies it before executing commands.

  2. Encryption + Authentication: TC frame payload is AES-256 encrypted and MACed. Protects against both spoofing and interception of sensitive command content.

The MAC computation for a TC frame of \(n\) octets using AES-CMAC is:

\[\mathrm{MAC} = \mathrm{AES\text{-}CMAC}(K_{\mathrm{session}}, \mathrm{TC\,Frame}[0:n-1])\tag{11.10}\]

Replay attack prevention is achieved by including a monotonically increasing frame sequence number in the authenticated portion; the spacecraft rejects frames whose sequence number is not greater than the last accepted frame.

Key management requires periodic key rotation. New session keys are uplinked encrypted under a long-term Key Encryption Key (KEK) pre-loaded at launch.

docs.title: 11.11 Deep Space Network
docs.text:
The NASA/JPL Deep Space Network (DSN) operates three ground station complexes at approximately \(120^{\circ}\) longitude separation to provide continuous Earth rotation coverage:

  • Goldstone (GDSCC), California, USA (\(116.8^{\circ}\) W)

  • Madrid (MDSCC), Spain (\(15.5^{\circ}\) W)

  • Canberra (CDSCC), Australia (\(148.9^{\circ}\) E)

Each complex operates multiple antenna apertures:

  • \(70\,\mathrm{m}\) antenna (DSS-14, DSS-63, DSS-43): gain \(\sim74\,\mathrm{dBi}\) at X-band, \(G/T = 52\,\mathrm{dB/K}\). Reserved for critical deep space operations.

  • \(34\,\mathrm{m}\) BWG (Beam Waveguide) antennas: gain \(\sim68\,\mathrm{dBi}\) at X-band. Used for routine mission support.

  • \(34\,\mathrm{m}\) HEF (High Efficiency) antennas.

Table 11.3. DSN performance summary for X-band operations (typical values, current capability). Parameter 70 m 34 m BWG Unit Receive frequency 8.4 8.4 GHz Receive gain 74.5 68.0 dBi System noise temperature (\(T_{\mathrm{sys}}\)) 25 20 K \(G/T\) 59.5 53.0 dB/K Transmit frequency 7.2 7.2 GHz Transmit power (max) 400 20–400 kW EIRP (max) \(\sim 126\) \(\sim 120\) dBW Supported data rates (deep space) 0.01–6000 0.01–6000 kbps

At interplanetary distances, the free-space path loss is enormous. For Voyager 1 at \(\sim 23\,\mathrm{AU}\) transmitting \(20\,\mathrm{W}\) at X-band with a \(3.7\,\mathrm{m}\) HGA (\(\sim 48\,\mathrm{dBi}\)), the received signal power at Earth’s DSN 70 m antenna is approximately \(-160\,\mathrm{dBW}\) (\(10^{-16}\,\mathrm{W}\)), requiring the full sensitivity of the DSN receiver and turbo-coded modulation to achieve a data rate of \(\sim 160\,\mathrm{bps}\).

docs.title: 11.12 Commercial Ground Station Networks
docs.text:
The emergence of commercial ground-as-a-service (GaaS) offerings has transformed TT&C operations for commercial and small satellite operators:

  • AWS Ground Station (Amazon): network of ground stations operated by Amazon, accessible via API with pay-per-use pricing. Supports S-band and X-band. Data delivered directly to AWS cloud for processing.

  • Microsoft Azure Orbital: similar service by Microsoft, integrated with Azure cloud.

  • KSAT (Kongsberg Satellite Services): the world’s largest commercial ground station network, with \(>200\) antennas at \(>24\) sites including polar stations (Svalbard, Troll) providing \(>10\) contacts/day for polar LEO orbits.

  • SSC Universal Space Network (USN): \(11\) stations worldwide.

  • Leaf Space: \(8\) stations, focused on small satellites and NewSpace.

The economics of commercial ground stations have enabled small satellite operators to avoid the capital expenditure of building their own ground infrastructure (\(>\)EUR 1M per station), instead paying per-contact fees of EUR 50–500.

docs.title: 11.13 TT&C for CubeSats
docs.text:
CubeSats typically use UHF (437–438 MHz) for TT&C, leveraging:

  • Small antennas: a \(\lambda/4\) monopole at 437 MHz is \(17\,\mathrm{cm}\) long. Deployable monopoles or dipoles provide \(\sim 0\,\mathrm{dBi}\) gain.

  • Amateur satellite band: the IARU-coordinated 435–438 MHz band is allocated to Amateur Satellites, accessible to university and research missions.

  • AX.25 protocol: the packet radio protocol used by AMSAT and the amateur radio community since the 1980s, providing a simple data link layer with CRC error detection.

  • Amateur radio support: the international AMSAT network of volunteer stations can support telemetry reception, even without a dedicated mission ground station.

  • Link performance: at 437 MHz, 0.5 W transmit power (\(+27\,\mathrm{dBm}\)) from a CubeSat dipole antenna with a \(3\,\mathrm{m}\) yagi ground antenna (\(G = 14\,\mathrm{dBi}\)) at 600 km altitude gives \(C/N_0 \approx 65\,\mathrm{dBHz}\), sufficient for \(\leq 9600\,\mathrm{bps}\) AX.25 (AFSK or GMSK).

Modern CubeSat missions increasingly use S-band for primary downlink (up to \(40\,\mathrm{Mbps}\)) and retain UHF only as a backup TT&C channel.

docs.title: 11.14 Future Directions: Optical TT&C
docs.text:
Optical (laser) communications offer orders-of-magnitude improvement in bandwidth relative to RF at similar power and aperture size. NASA’s Laser Communications Relay Demonstration (LCRD), launched December 2021, demonstrates two-way optical communications at \(1.2\,\mathrm{Gbps}\) downlink via geosynchronous relay. The Lunar Laser Communication Demonstration (LLCD) achieved \(622\,\mathrm{Mbps}\) downlink from lunar orbit.

The optical link budget uses the same fundamental equation as RF but expressed differently:

\[P_R = P_T \cdot G_T \cdot L_{\mathrm{FSL}} \cdot G_R = P_T \cdot \left(\frac{\pi D_T}{\lambda \theta_D}\right)^2 \cdot \left(\frac{\lambda}{4\pi d}\right)^2 \cdot \left(\frac{\pi D_R^2}{4}\right) / A_r\tag{11.11}\]

where \(D_T\) is the transmit telescope diameter, \(\theta_D = 2.44 \lambda/D_T\) is the diffraction-limited beam divergence, \(D_R\) is the receive telescope diameter, and \(d\) is the range.

The primary challenge for optical TT&C is cloud blockage and atmospheric turbulence. Mitigation strategies include site diversity (multiple geographically separated ground receivers), adaptive optics (wavefront correction to compensate atmospheric distortion), and relay via GEO optical satellites above the cloud layer.

docs.title: 11.15 Summary
docs.text:
The TT&C subsystem is the indispensable communication thread between the spacecraft and the ground segment that must never be broken. Its design must prioritise robustness and coverage over performance, particularly during LEOP and safe mode operations. The fundamental physical constraints—free-space path loss, atmospheric effects, and antenna pattern coverage—drive the key design decisions of frequency band, power level, and antenna selection.

The revolution in commercial ground station services and the increasing adoption of standardised CCSDS protocols are dramatically reducing the cost and complexity of TT&C operations for new entrants to the space sector. Looking forward, the transition to optical communications will enable data rates measured in gigabits per second, fundamentally changing the balance between on-board storage and real-time downlink for science missions (Pratt et al. 2003; Roddy 2006).
