docs.title: Chapter 12: Radio Frequency Satellite Communications
docs.text:
Key Concepts: ITU frequency band allocation, free-space path loss, atmospheric propagation effects, transponder architecture, TWTA and SSPA amplifiers, frequency reuse, Shannon capacity, GEO and LEO link characteristics, digital transparent processors, interference analysis.

Radio frequency (RF) communications via satellite constitute one of the most transformative technologies of the modern era. Since Early Bird (Intelsat I) demonstrated the first commercial transatlantic television relay in 1965, satellite communications have grown into a global industry exceeding $280 billion annually (including services and hardware), providing connectivity for broadcast television, broadband internet, maritime and aviation communication, military command networks, and emergency services. This chapter presents the fundamental physical principles governing RF satellite links, the engineering of satellite transponder hardware, and the system-level design of GEO and LEO communication satellites.

docs.title: 12.1 Why Satellite Communications?
docs.text:
The fundamental geometric advantage of satellite communications derives from the altitude of operation. A geostationary satellite at 35,786 km altitude has a radio horizon that encompasses approximately one-third of the Earth’s surface from a single vantage point. Three GEO satellites at 120 longitudinal separation provide near-global coverage (excluding polar regions above approximately 75 latitude). This geometry provides several unique capabilities:

  • Broadcast and multicast: A single uplink transmission is received simultaneously by all terminals in the satellite’s footprint. Satellite is the only cost-effective solution for true broadcast to millions of simultaneous receivers.

  • Rural and remote coverage: Satellite reaches locations where terrestrial fiber or cellular infrastructure is economically infeasible – oil platforms, polar research stations, aircraft at 35,000 ft, ships in the Southern Ocean.

  • Mobility: Unlike point-to-point terrestrial links, satellite coverage follows wherever the antenna can see the sky.

  • Disaster recovery: Satellite infrastructure is independent of the terrestrial network; it functions when terrestrial networks are destroyed by earthquakes, floods, or conflict.

  • 24/7 availability: GEO satellites appear stationary from the ground, requiring no antenna tracking and providing continuous service without handover.

The geometric coverage footprint of a satellite at altitude \(h\) (km) above a spherical Earth of radius \(R_e = 6371\) km is characterized by the nadir half-angle \(\rho\) and the Earth central angle \(\lambda_0\):

\[\sin \rho = \frac{R_e}{R_e + h}, \quad \lambda_0 = 90^\circ - \rho - \varepsilon_{min}\tag{12.1}\]

where \(\varepsilon_{min}\) is the minimum elevation angle for acceptable link quality (typically 5–10 for GEO, 25–40 for LEO). For GEO (\(h = 35{,}786\) km), \(\rho = 8.68\degree{}\), and the Earth central angle coverage radius \(\lambda_0 = 76.3\degree{}\) (for \(\varepsilon_{min} = 5\degree{}\)), corresponding to 42% of Earth’s surface.

docs.title: 12.2 ITU Frequency Band Allocations
docs.text:
The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), through its Radio Regulations (Radio Regulations, 2020 edition), allocates specific frequency bands for satellite services. The primary services relevant to satellite communications are the Fixed Satellite Service (FSS), Broadcasting Satellite Service (BSS), Mobile Satellite Service (MSS), and the Earth Exploration Satellite Service (EESS) (Maral et al. 2009).

Table 12.1. ITU Frequency Bands for Satellite Communications Band Frequency Range Primary Satellite Use Key Characteristics L-band 1–2 GHz MSS (Iridium, Inmarsat, GPS) Low rain attn.; large antenna S-band 2–4 GHz MSS, feeder links, TT&C Low rain attn.; GPS L2 C-band 4–8 GHz FSS (4/6 GHz), VSAT Low rain, earth station bias X-band 8–12 GHz Military, EO data downlink Military priority Ku-band 12–18 GHz BSS (12 GHz), FSS uplink 14 GHz Small dish; rain fading Ka-band 26.5–40 GHz HTS, feeder links, O3b High rain fading; high capacity Q/V-band 33–75 GHz Feeder links, future HTS Heavy rain fade; tech. frontier EHF (W) 75–110 GHz Military (AEHF 44 GHz) Military anti-jam; experimental

The choice of operating frequency involves fundamental trade-offs between antenna size, rain attenuation, atmospheric noise, and available spectrum. Lower frequencies (L, S, C) suffer less rain attenuation and penetrate foliage but require larger antenna apertures (antenna gain scales as \((D/\lambda)^2\)). Higher frequencies (Ku, Ka, Q/V) offer more spectrum bandwidth and smaller user terminals but are increasingly affected by rain-induced signal attenuation.

The C-band allocation (3.7–4.2 GHz downlink, 5.925–6.425 GHz uplink) has been the primary commercial FSS band since the 1970s. The ITU revised the C-band lower boundary in Region 2 (Americas) to 3.98 GHz in 2020 as part of the FCC’s Flexible Use Order that auctioned 280 MHz (3.7–3.98 GHz) for terrestrial 5G, paying approximately $81 billion in auction proceeds.

docs.title: 12.3 Free-Space Path Loss
docs.text:
The free-space path loss (FSPL) is the fundamental propagation loss experienced by an isotropic radio wave expanding spherically from the transmitter. At range \(d\) from an isotropic transmitter, the power flux density (W/m\(^2\)) is:

\[S = \frac{P_t G_t}{4\pi d^2}\tag{12.2}\]

An isotropic receive antenna captures power proportional to its effective aperture \(A_{eff} = \lambda^2/(4\pi)\), giving the Friis transmission equation. The free-space path loss is:

\[L_{FS} = \left(\frac{4\pi d}{\lambda}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{4\pi d f}{c}\right)^2\tag{12.3}\]

In decibels:

\[\text{FSPL [dB]} = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi d}{\lambda}\right) = 20\log_{10}(d) + 20\log_{10}(f) + 92.45\tag{12.4}\]

where \(d\) is in km and \(f\) is in GHz (the constant 92.45 = \(20\log_{10}(4\pi \times 10^{-6}/c)\) absorbs unit conversions). For a GEO satellite at \(d = 35{,}786\) km and Ku-band at \(f = 12\) GHz:

\[\text{FSPL} = 20\log_{10}(35786) + 20\log_{10}(12) + 92.45 = 91.07 + 21.58 + 92.45 \approx 205.1\,\mathrm{dB}\tag{12.5}\]

This enormous free-space loss (over 200 dB) must be overcome by large antenna gains and high-power transmitters. At Ka-band (\(f = 30\) GHz, uplink), FSPL \(\approx 213\) dB. At L-band (\(f = 1.5\) GHz), FSPL \(\approx 187\) dB for GEO – illustrating why L-band mobile satellite services require very large satellites with powerful amplifiers to close the link to small handheld terminals (Roddy 2006).

docs.title: 12.4 Atmospheric Propagation Effects
docs.text: Real satellite links are not in free space; the troposphere, ionosphere, and neutral atmosphere introduce additional losses and degradations beyond the geometric FSPL (Pratt et al. 2003).

docs.title: 12.4.1 Rain Attenuation
docs.text:
Rain is the dominant atmospheric impairment for frequencies above \(\sim\)10 GHz. Rain droplets scatter and absorb microwave energy through mechanisms related to the dielectric properties of liquid water. The specific rain attenuation \(\gamma_R\) (dB/km) is modeled by the ITU-R P.838 power-law relationship:

\[\gamma_R = k R^\alpha \quad [\mathrm{dB/km}]\tag{12.6}\]

where \(R\) is the rain rate (mm/hr) and \(k\), \(\alpha\) are frequency and polarization-dependent coefficients tabulated in ITU-R P.838-3. At 12 GHz (Ku downlink): \(k_H = 0.0188\), \(\alpha_H = 1.217\); at 30 GHz (Ka uplink): \(k_H = 0.187\), \(\alpha_H = 1.021\).

The total rain path attenuation \(A\) (dB) depends on the effective rain path length through the rain cell:

\[A = \gamma_R \cdot L_{eff} = \gamma_R \cdot L_s \cdot r\tag{12.7}\]

where \(L_s\) is the slant path length through rain (\(L_s = (h_R - h_s)/\sin\varepsilon\) for rain height \(h_R\) above mean sea level, station altitude \(h_s\), and elevation angle \(\varepsilon\)) and \(r\) is a rain path reduction factor accounting for the non-uniform horizontal extent of rain cells (ITU-R P.618-13 procedure). At 12 GHz and \(0.01\)% annual exceedance (99.99% availability), \(A_{0.01}\) is typically 2–4 dB for temperate climates and 10–15 dB for tropical regions. At Ka-band (30 GHz), rain attenuation is 4–7\(\times\) larger in dB, driving the need for adaptive coding and modulation in Ka-band systems.

docs.title: 12.4.2 Gaseous Absorption
docs.text:
Atmospheric gases (principally O\(_2\) and H\(_2\)O) absorb microwave energy at specific resonance frequencies. Oxygen has a strong absorption band centered at 60 GHz (making terrestrial 60 GHz links useful for spectrum reuse/security since the signal cannot propagate far) and a secondary resonance at 118.7 GHz. Water vapor has lines at 22.3 GHz, 183.3 GHz, and 325 GHz.

For satellite links at elevation angles \(> 10\degree{}\), zenith gaseous absorption at:

  • C-band (6 GHz): \(\sim\)0.03 dB (negligible)

  • Ku-band (14 GHz): \(\sim\)0.07 dB (negligible)

  • Ka-band (30 GHz): \(\sim\)0.10 dB (small but non-negligible near 22.3 GHz water vapor line)

  • Q-band (50 GHz): \(\sim\)0.5–1 dB (significant; varies strongly with humidity)

docs.title: 12.4.3 Ionospheric Effects
docs.text:
The ionosphere (60–1000 km altitude) contains free electrons that affect radio waves below \(\sim\)3 GHz through:

  • Faraday rotation: The polarization plane of linearly polarized waves rotates by angle \(\Omega \propto f^{-2}\) as the wave propagates through the ionosphere’s electron content (total electron content, TEC, in TEC units). At L-band (1.5 GHz), Faraday rotation can reach tens of degrees during geomagnetic storms, which is why circular polarization is standard for L-band satellite services.

  • Group delay and dispersion: Ionospheric electrons introduce a frequency-dependent group delay \(\tau_{iono} \propto \text{TEC}/f^2\) that must be calibrated in navigation systems (GPS dual-frequency correction).

  • Scintillation: Electron density irregularities in the equatorial ionosphere (between \(\pm\)20 magnetic latitude) and at auroral zones cause rapid amplitude and phase fluctuations (scintillation), particularly severe at frequencies \(<\) 3 GHz and during high solar activity (solar cycle 25, peak expected 2025, is active).

docs.title: 12.4.4 Tropospheric Scintillation
docs.text:
Even in clear weather, turbulent mixing in the troposphere creates refractive index fluctuations that cause amplitude and phase scintillation on satellite links. The Tatarski model gives scintillation variance:

\[\sigma_\chi^2 = 0.527 k^{7/6} L^{11/6} C_n^2\tag{12.8}\]

where \(k = 2\pi/\lambda\) is the wavenumber, \(L\) is the turbulence path length, and \(C_n^2\) is the refractive index structure constant (typically \(10^{-16}\)–\(10^{-14}\) m\(^{-2/3}\) in the lower troposphere). Tropospheric scintillation is most severe at low elevation angles (\(< 10\degree{}\)) and can reach 2–3 dB peak-to-peak at Ku-band for equatorial sites.

docs.title: 12.5 Transponder Architecture
docs.text: A satellite transponder receives an uplink signal, amplifies it, shifts it in frequency (or processes it digitally), and retransmits it as a downlink. The classical “bent-pipe” (frequency-converting) transponder architecture consists of the following functional stages (Maral et al. 2009; Pratt et al. 2003):

docs.title: 12.5.1 Receive Chain
docs.text:
1. Receive antenna: Large reflector dish (1.5–3 m for C/Ku-band GEO) focuses energy from the uplink coverage zone onto the feed horn or array feed.

  2. Input Multiplexer (IMUX): Contiguous bandpass filters divide the received spectrum into individual transponder channels. Each transponder occupies a channel bandwidth of 27 MHz (standard) to 500 MHz (wideband) depending on frequency plan.

  3. Low Noise Amplifier (LNA): The first amplification stage must minimize added noise since it directly sets the system noise temperature. Satellite LNAs use InP HEMT (indium phosphide high electron mobility transistor) or GaAs HEMT technology, achieving noise temperatures of 50–80 K (noise figures 0.7–1.1 dB) at ambient temperature operation in the spacecraft thermal environment.

  4. Frequency Conversion: A local oscillator (LO) and mixer downconvert the uplink frequency (e.g., 14 GHz Ku-band uplink) to the transmit frequency (e.g., 12 GHz Ku-band downlink) using heterodyne mixing: \(f_{down} = f_{up} - f_{LO}\) (or \(f_{up} + f_{LO}\) for upconversion). GEO satellites typically use a frequency plan with a fixed offset (e.g., Ku FSS: 14 GHz up, 11.7 GHz down, \(\Delta f = 2.3\) GHz).

docs.title: 12.5.2 High-Power Amplifiers
docs.text:
The transmit amplifier is the most power-consuming and thermally critical component of the transponder:

Traveling Wave Tube Amplifier (TWTA): A vacuum electron device where a pencil-like electron beam (from a thermionic electron gun) travels in close proximity to a helical slow-wave structure (SWS) carrying the RF signal. The phase velocity of the RF wave is reduced by the helix to match the electron beam velocity, enabling continuous energy transfer from the beam to the wave. Key features:

  • Gain: 40–60 dB over a wide bandwidth (\(>\) octave).

  • Output power: 20–300 W per TWT at C, Ku, Ka, EHF bands.

  • Efficiency: Without collector energy recovery, 20–35%. With a depressed multi-stage collector (3–5 stages recovering energy from electrons exiting the helix at different velocities), efficiency rises to 50–70%.

  • AM/AM and AM/PM nonlinearity: The TWT transfer characteristic is nonlinear near saturation. AM/AM distortion means output amplitude does not increase linearly with input; AM/PM conversion means output phase varies with input amplitude. For a single carrier, the TWT can be operated near saturation for maximum efficiency. For multi-carrier operation (multiple transponders sharing one TWT, or OFDM), back-off is required to reduce intermodulation distortion.

  • Output Back-Off (OBO): The multi-carrier output power must be backed off from saturation by OBO = IBO \(-\) gain compression (OBO \(\approx\) IBO + 5 dB for a Saleh model TWT). Typical OBO for multi-carrier is 3–7 dB, reducing effective power but ensuring acceptable \(C/I\) ratios.

The complete TWTA unit includes the TWT, Electronic Power Conditioner (EPC, which provides regulated high voltages of 3–10 kV for the cathode, collector, helix, and focus electrodes), and thermal interface. A 120 W Ka-band TWTA (e.g., Tesat, L3Harris, Communications & Power Industries CPI) operates at approximately 50% efficiency, dissipating 120 W of waste heat into the spacecraft thermal control system.

Solid-State Power Amplifier (SSPA): GaN (gallium nitride) HEMT transistors operating as power amplifiers offer an increasingly competitive alternative to TWTAs, particularly at lower frequencies and power levels:

  • GaN HEMT provides breakdown voltage of 100+ V (versus 15–20 V for GaAs), enabling high power density.

  • Power Added Efficiency (PAE) of 40–45% at Ku-band, 35–40% at Ka-band.

  • Single chip output power: 10 W at Ku-band, 5 W at Ka-band (2023 state of art), scalable by power combining.

  • No vacuum device: eliminates filament heater power, aging mechanisms, and high-voltage power supply complexity.

  • Better reliability in radiation environment: GaN is radiation-hard to \(> 1\) Mrad total ionizing dose.

  • Disadvantages: lower single-device power than TWT; power combining requires careful impedance and phase matching; thermal management of high power density chip.

For CubeSats and small satellites, GaN SSPAs are exclusively used (at power levels of 2–10 W). For large GEO satellites requiring 100–300 W per transponder at Ku and Ka-band, TWTAs remain the dominant choice due to their combination of high power and high efficiency.

Table 12.2. TWTA versus SSPA Comparison for Satellite Transponders Parameter TWTA (GaN collector) GaN SSPA Output power (single unit) 20–300 W 5–30 W (chip); 50–150 W (combined) PAE / efficiency 50–70% (w/ mult. collector) 35–45% Bandwidth Octave+ 10–30% relative Linearity (OIP3) Moderate Better (Class A/AB) Mass \(\sim\)2–4 kg \(\sim\)0.5–2 kg Radiation tolerance Moderate (vacuum device) High (GaN) Operating frequency DC–100 GHz DC–100 GHz Heritage Excellent (60+ years) Growing (2000+) Cost Higher (precision vacuum device) Lower (semiconductor) Typical application GEO high-power Ku/Ka LEO, small GEO, all Ka \(<\)30 W

docs.title: 12.6 Frequency Reuse Techniques
docs.text: The transponder bandwidth available to a GEO satellite is fixed by the ITU frequency plan (e.g., 500 MHz at C-band, 500 MHz at Ku-band, 2 GHz at Ka-band). To increase capacity beyond what a single global beam can support, frequency reuse multiplies spectral efficiency (Pratt et al. 2003):

docs.title: 12.6.1 Spatial Isolation (Spot Beams)
docs.text:
A satellite antenna with a narrow beam (spot beam) illuminates a small geographic area. The same frequency band can be reused in a distant spot beam without mutual interference, provided the antenna isolation between the two spots exceeds the required carrier-to-interference ratio (\(C/I\), typically 15–25 dB). Phased array antennas or multi-beam reflectors with cluster feeds (the “aplanatic lens” design used by Hughes Network Systems) can produce 50–1000 spot beams, each reusing the full frequency plan.

ViaSat-1 (2011) produced 72 Ka-band spot beams over North America, each reusing the same 500 MHz, for a total spectrum utilization of 72 \(\times\) 500 MHz and aggregate capacity of 140 Gbps. ViaSat-3 (2023) aims for \(>\) 1 Tbps using over 1000 spot beams per satellite.

docs.title: 12.6.2 Polarization Reuse
docs.text: Two orthogonal polarizations (right-hand circular polarization RHCP and left-hand circular polarization LHCP, or horizontal H and vertical V linear polarization) can occupy the same frequency band simultaneously if the cross-polarization isolation (XPI) exceeds the \(C/I\) requirement. GEO satellites typically achieve 33–40 dB XPI from their main reflector, and even the atmospheric cross-polarization discrimination (XPD) loss of 2–5 dB at Ku-band in rain still leaves adequate margin.

docs.title: 12.6.3 Four-Color Reuse Pattern
docs.text: Combining spatial and polarization reuse, the “4-color” frequency plan uses two frequency sub-bands and two polarizations (2\(f \times\) 2\(p\)), providing four color regions that can be reused across non-adjacent spot beams. Each spot beam uses only 25% of the total available bandwidth but, with aggressive spatial reuse across many spot beams, the overall capacity scales with the number of beams.

docs.title: 12.7 Shannon Capacity and Spectral Efficiency
docs.text:
The Shannon-Hartley theorem establishes the theoretical maximum data rate over a band-limited channel with additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN):

\[C = B \log_2\!\left(1 + \frac{S}{N}\right) = B \log_2\!\left(1 + \text{SNR}\right) \quad [\mathrm{bit/s}]\tag{12.9}\]

where \(B\) is the channel bandwidth (Hz) and SNR is the linear signal-to-noise ratio. The spectral efficiency \(\eta = C/B\) (bit/s/Hz) is:

\[\eta = \log_2(1 + \text{SNR}) \quad [\mathrm{bit/s/Hz}]\tag{12.10}\]

Modern DVB-S2X modulations approach within 1–2 dB of the Shannon limit. For a typical Ka-band transponder with 500 MHz bandwidth and 15 dB SNR (\(\eta \approx 5\) bit/s/Hz):

\[C = 500 \times 10^6 \times \log_2(1 + 31.6) \approx 500 \times 10^6 \times 5 = 2.5\,\mathrm{Gbps}\tag{12.11}\]

High-Throughput Satellites (HTS) aggregate this across hundreds of spot beams. EchoStar Jupiter-3 (2023), with 500 MHz per beam and 108 Ka-band spot beams using 4-color reuse (effective \(108/4 \times 500\) MHz = 13.5 GHz of spectrum), achieves approximately 500 Gbps aggregate capacity.

docs.title: 12.8 GEO Link Characteristics
docs.text:
The geostationary orbit (GEO) at 35,786 km provides unique and favorable link characteristics for many applications (Maral et al. 2009):

  • Coverage: \(\pm\)75 latitude (approximately) from a single satellite. Fixed elevation angle from any given Earth terminal (no tracking required for fixed VSAT or dish).

  • Propagation delay: The one-way propagation delay is \(d/c = 35{,}786{,}000 / 299{,}792{,}458 \approx 119\) ms for the subsatellite point. At non-subsatellite points (slant range up to \(\sim\)42,000 km for \(\varepsilon = 5\degree{}\)), the delay reaches 140 ms. Round-trip time (RTT) is approximately 240–280 ms. For a complete satellite hop (user terminal – satellite – hub – network – hub – satellite – user terminal), the total latency is approximately 550–600 ms.

  • Doppler shift: GEO satellites appear stationary (residual Doppler \(< 0.001\) Hz/s drift from orbital perturbations, effectively zero). No Doppler compensation is required.

  • Solar eclipse: GEO satellites experience eclipse (Earth’s shadow) for up to 70 minutes per day around equinoxes (March and September), requiring battery storage sized for the eclipse duration at full power.

  • Sun outage: Twice per year, the Sun passes within the receive antenna’s beamwidth as seen from the ground station, causing an outage lasting 5–30 minutes (broader beam = longer outage).

docs.title: 12.9 LEO Link Characteristics
docs.text: Low Earth orbit satellites (300–2000 km altitude) present fundamentally different link engineering challenges compared to GEO (Maral et al. 2009):

docs.title: 12.9.1 Doppler Shift
docs.text:
A LEO satellite at 550 km altitude orbits at \(v = \sqrt{\mu/r} = \sqrt{3.986 \times 10^{14} / (6{,}921{,}000)} \approx 7583\) m/s. The Doppler shift experienced by a ground terminal varies from \(+f_0 v/c\) (satellite approaching) to \(-f_0 v/c\) (satellite receding):

\[\Delta f = f_0 \frac{v \cos\theta}{c}\tag{12.12}\]

where \(\theta\) is the angle between the satellite velocity vector and the direction to the ground terminal. The maximum Doppler shift occurs at \(\theta = 0\) (horizon, directly ahead/behind), giving:

\[\Delta f_{max} = f_0 \frac{v}{c} = f_0 \frac{7583}{3 \times 10^8}\tag{12.13}\]

At L-band (\(f_0 = 1.5\) GHz): \(\Delta f_{max} = 1.5 \times 10^9 \times 7583 / (3 \times 10^8) \approx \pm 37.9\) kHz. For Starlink at Ku-band (\(f_0 = 12\) GHz): \(\Delta f_{max} \approx \pm 303\) kHz. The Doppler rate (rate of change) is maximum at zenith pass and can reach several kHz/s at L-band. User terminals must implement either frequency pre-compensation (shifting the transmit frequency based on predicted satellite ephemeris) or fast Doppler tracking receivers.

docs.title: 12.9.2 Handover
docs.text: A 550 km altitude satellite (Starlink altitude) is visible for a maximum of approximately \(2 \times \sqrt{(R_e + h)^2 - R_e^2}/v \approx 6.3\) minutes. Constellation operation requires seamless handover between satellites (and between beams within a satellite) as the satellite crosses the sky. The NTN (Non-Terrestrial Network) specifications in 3GPP Release 17 standardize procedures for LEO Doppler pre-compensation, timing advance, and handover execution within the NR (New Radio) frame structure (Digital Video Broadcasting (DVB); Second Generation Framing Structure, Channel Coding and Modulation Systems for Broadcasting, Interactive Services, News Gathering and Other Broadband Satellite Applications (DVB-S2) 2014).

docs.title: 12.9.3 Propagation Delay
docs.text: At 550 km altitude and 40 elevation, the slant range is approximately 750 km, giving one-way delay of 2.5 ms. This is dramatically lower than GEO’s 250 ms and makes LEO satellite broadband competitive with terrestrial broadband for latency-sensitive applications (video conferencing, gaming, real-time control). Starlink’s stated latency target is \(<\)20 ms (including ground processing), achieved in practice at 20–50 ms.

docs.title: 12.10 Digital Transparent Processor
docs.text:
Traditional analog bent-pipe transponders retransmit whatever signal they receive, without on-board signal processing. Digital Transparent Processors (DTPs), also called digital channelizers or on-board processors, perform on-board signal processing at the transponder level:

  • Digitization: The received signal is digitized (typically 8–12 bits ADC at 500 MHz sampling rate) after the LNA and downconversion.

  • Channelization: A digital filter bank (FFT-based or polyphase filter bank) separates the wideband digitized signal into many narrowband channels (e.g., 200 channels of 5 MHz each from 1 GHz of total bandwidth).

  • Beam switching matrix: Each narrowband channel can be routed to any downlink beam independently, enabling real-time flexible beam assignment without hardware changes. This is the key feature enabling software-defined satellites.

  • Beam hopping: In time-division beam hopping, the full transponder power is directed to one beam for a short time slot (e.g., 1 ms), then switched to the next beam. Each beam receives power proportional to its demand, enabling flexible capacity allocation across the coverage area. BeamHopping is standardized in DVB-S2X Annex E.

  • TDMA scheduling: The on-board DTP implements burst scheduling for the return link (user-to-satellite) in TDMA or MF-TDMA schemes.

The Intelsat Intelsat Epic NG satellites (starting with IS-39, 2019) and Eutelsat Quantum (2021) feature DTPs enabling software-reconfigurable coverage and capacity. Eutelsat Quantum’s DTP (from Airbus/Cobham) supports fully flexible bandwidth-on-demand across 8 active beams. The O3b mPOWER satellites (SES, launched 2022–2023) use full on-board processing for beam-by-beam capacity allocation across 4 Tbps aggregate capacity.

docs.title: 12.11 Interference Analysis
docs.text: Satellite communication systems must manage interference from multiple sources (Maral et al. 2009):

docs.title: 12.11.1 Adjacent Satellite Interference
docs.text:
At C and Ku bands, geostationary satellites are spaced as close as 2 in longitude (reduced from 3 after 2000 ITU decisions for Ku-band). The receive antenna’s sidelobe level toward the adjacent satellite at 2 angular separation determines the adjacent satellite interference (ASI):

\[\frac{C}{I_{adj}} = G(\theta_0) - G(\theta_{adj}) + \frac{EIRP_{sat}}{EIRP_{adj}}\tag{12.14}\]

where \(G(\theta_0)\) is the main beam gain and \(G(\theta_{adj})\) is the sidelobe gain toward the adjacent satellite (typically 15–25 dBi for a 0.6–1.8 m dish at Ku-band with 2 separation). The ITU minimum isolation standard for earth station antennas at Ku-band is \(G(\theta) \leq 32 - 25\log\theta\) (dBi) for \(1\degree{} \leq \theta \leq 48\degree{}\) – the reference radiation pattern (RRP).

docs.title: 12.11.2 Carrier-to-Interference Ratio
docs.text:
The total noise-plus-interference experienced at the satellite or earth terminal is characterized by the carrier-to-noise-plus-interference ratio (C/(N+I)):

\[\frac{C}{N+I} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{C/N_{thermal}} + \frac{1}{C/I_{adj}} + \frac{1}{C/I_{xpol}} + \frac{1}{C/I_{inter}}}\tag{12.15}\]

Frequency coordination between operators (ITU-R S-series Recommendations, S.728, S.1062, S.1503) governs the regulatory process for resolving interference disputes between networks filing at the ITU.

docs.title: 12.12 Summary
docs.text:
RF satellite communications exploit the geometric vantage of orbital altitude to provide global coverage, broadcast capability, and mobility services impossible with terrestrial infrastructure. The interplay between frequency selection, propagation effects (free-space path loss, rain attenuation, ionospheric effects), and hardware performance (LNA noise temperature, TWTA/SSPA efficiency, antenna gain) is captured in the link budget (Chapter 13). Shannon’s capacity theorem sets the theoretical ceiling that modern DVB-S2X and adaptive coding and modulation schemes approach to within 2 dB. The evolution from analog bent-pipe transponders to software-defined satellites with digital transparent processors and beam hopping represents the current frontier of commercial GEO satellite capability, while LEO constellations with phased array user terminals redefine the latency and mobility possibilities of satellite broadband (Maral et al. 2009; Roddy 2006; Pratt et al. 2003).

Key Equations:

  • FSPL: \(L_{FS}[\mathrm{dB}] = 20\log(d[\mathrm{km}]) + 20\log(f[\mathrm{GHz}]) + 92.45\)

  • GEO at 12 GHz: FSPL \(\approx\) 205 dB; GEO one-way delay \(\approx\) 119 ms

  • Rain attenuation: \(\gamma_R = kR^\alpha\) [dB/km] (ITU-R P.838)

  • Shannon: \(C = B\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR})\) [bit/s]

  • LEO Doppler: \(\Delta f_{max} = f_0 v/c \approx \pm 38\) kHz at L-band (550 km)

docs.title: Chapter 13: Satellite Link Budget Analysis
docs.text: Key Concepts: Effective Isotropic Radiated Power (EIRP), Free Space Path Loss (FSPL), Figure of Merit (\(G/T\)), Carrier-to-Noise Ratio (\(C/N\)), \(E_b/N_0\), System Noise Temperature, Atmospheric Attenuation, Rain Fade Margin, Adaptive Coding and Modulation (ACM), DVB-S2X.

docs.title: 13.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The satellite link budget is the fundamental accounting tool of satellite communications engineering. It is a systematic, end-to-end tabulation of all the gains and losses that a signal experiences as it propagates from a transmitter, through the space environment, to a receiver. The result of a link budget calculation is a carrier-to-noise ratio or energy-per-bit-to-noise-density ratio (\(E_b/N_0\)) at the demodulator input, which is then compared against the threshold required to achieve the target bit error rate (BER) (Pratt et al. 2003; Roddy 2006).

The philosophy of link budget engineering is to account for every decibel. In a resource- constrained satellite system—where every watt of transmit power, every centimeter of antenna aperture, and every kilogram of spacecraft mass comes at extraordinary cost— understanding the precise signal budget is essential. Link margins of even a fraction of a decibel can represent millions of dollars of spacecraft hardware or years of system lifetime.

This chapter develops the link budget from first principles. We begin with the transmitter and systematically account for each element of the propagation path: antenna gain, free-space spreading loss, atmospheric attenuation, noise contributions, and receiver figure of merit. We conclude with complete worked examples for Ku-band GEO links, high-throughput satellite (HTS) spot beam systems, LEO broadband (Starlink-style), inter-satellite links (ISL), and optical links.

docs.title: 13.2 Transmitter and Effective Isotropic Radiated Power
13.2.1 Transmit Power and Antenna Gain
docs.text:
The first element of any link budget is the transmitter. A satellite or earth station transmitter produces a radio-frequency signal at power \(P_t\) (Watts). This power is fed to a transmit antenna through a feed network, which may introduce insertion loss \(L_f\) (expressed as a ratio \(\geq 1\), i.e., a loss). The antenna concentrates energy in a preferred direction characterized by its directional gain \(G_t\) (dimensionless ratio relative to an isotropic radiator).

The Effective Isotropic Radiated Power (EIRP) is defined as the product of the net power delivered to the antenna and the antenna gain in the direction of the target:

\[\mathrm{EIRP} = \frac{P_t}{L_f} \cdot G_t \quad [\mathrm{W}]\tag{13.1}\]

Converting to the decibel domain, which is standard practice in link budgeting:

\[\mathrm{EIRP} \;[\mathrm{dBW}] = P_t \;[\mathrm{dBW}] + G_t \;[\mathrm{dBi}] - L_f \;[\mathrm{dB}]\tag{13.2}\]

where dBi denotes decibels relative to an isotropic antenna. The EIRP represents the power that would need to be transmitted by an isotropic source to produce the same power flux density at the receiver as the actual directional transmitter.

docs.title: 13.2.2 Aperture Antenna Gain
docs.text:
For a uniformly illuminated circular aperture of diameter \(D\), the gain at wavelength \(\lambda\) is:

\[G_t = \eta_a \left(\frac{\pi D}{\lambda}\right)^2\tag{13.3}\]

where \(\eta_a\) is the aperture efficiency (typically 0.55–0.70 for parabolic reflectors). In decibels:

\[G_t \;[\mathrm{dBi}] = 10 \log_{10}(\eta_a) + 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\pi D}{\lambda}\right)\tag{13.4}\]

The half-power beamwidth (HPBW) of a circular aperture antenna is approximately:

\[\theta_{\mathrm{HPBW}} \approx \frac{70\lambda}{D} \quad [\mathrm{degrees}]\tag{13.5}\]

This inverse relationship between gain and beamwidth is fundamental: narrow beams provide high gain but stringent pointing requirements.

docs.title: 13.3 Free Space Path Loss
docs.text:
Once the signal leaves the transmit antenna, it spreads in all directions according to the inverse square law. The free space path loss (FSPL) represents the geometric spreading of the wavefront as it propagates from the transmitter at distance \(d\) with no atmospheric effects.

The power flux density \(S\) at distance \(d\) from an isotropic source of power \(P\) is:

\[S = \frac{P}{4\pi d^2} \quad [\mathrm{W/m^2}]\tag{13.6}\]

A receive antenna with effective area \(A_{\mathrm{eff}} = \lambda^2 G_r / (4\pi)\) intercepts power:

\[P_r = S \cdot A_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{P \cdot G_r \lambda^2}{(4\pi d)^2}\tag{13.7}\]

This is the Friis transmission equation. The FSPL is defined as the ratio of transmitted to received power for isotropic antennas (\(G_t = G_r = 1\)):

\[\mathrm{FSPL} = \left(\frac{4\pi d}{\lambda}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{4\pi d f}{c}\right)^2\tag{13.8}\]

In decibels:

\[\mathrm{FSPL} \;[\mathrm{dB}] = 20\log_{10}(4\pi) + 20\log_{10}(d) + 20\log_{10}(f) - 20\log_{10}(c)\tag{13.9}\] \[\boxed{\mathrm{FSPL} \;[\mathrm{dB}] = 92.45 + 20\log_{10}(d \;[\mathrm{km}]) + 20\log_{10}(f \;[\mathrm{GHz}])}\tag{13.10}\]

For a GEO satellite at \(d = 35{,}786\) km and \(f = 11.7\) GHz:

\[\mathrm{FSPL} = 92.45 + 20\log_{10}(35{,}786) + 20\log_{10}(11.7) = 92.45 + 91.07 + 21.36 = 205.5 \;\mathrm{dB}\tag{13.11}\]

This enormous loss—over 205 dB—is the dominant term in any GEO link budget and explains why satellite receivers require extremely low noise figures and large antennas.

docs.title: 13.4 Received Signal Power
docs.text:
The received signal power in decibels is:

\[P_r \;[\mathrm{dBW}] = \mathrm{EIRP} - \mathrm{FSPL} + G_r - L_{\mathrm{misc}} \;[\mathrm{dB}]\tag{13.12}\]

where \(L_{\mathrm{misc}}\) encompasses all additional losses:

\[L_{\mathrm{misc}} = L_{\mathrm{atm}} + L_{\mathrm{rain}} + L_{\mathrm{pol}} + L_{\mathrm{point}} + L_{\mathrm{feed,rx}} \;[\mathrm{dB}]\tag{13.13}\]

  • \(L_{\mathrm{atm}}\): gaseous absorption (water vapor + oxygen)

  • \(L_{\mathrm{rain}}\): rain attenuation (dominant impairment at Ku/Ka-band)

  • \(L_{\mathrm{pol}}\): polarization mismatch loss (0–3 dB, typically 0.1–0.5 dB)

  • \(L_{\mathrm{point}}\): antenna pointing error loss

  • \(L_{\mathrm{feed,rx}}\): receive feed and waveguide losses

docs.title: 13.5 Noise Power and System Noise Temperature
13.5.1 Fundamental Noise Concepts
docs.text:
Thermal noise is the fundamental limit to receiver sensitivity. The available noise power from a resistor at physical temperature \(T\) in bandwidth \(B\) is given by the Nyquist formula:

\[N = k T_s B \quad [\mathrm{W}]\tag{13.14}\]

where \(k = 1.3806 \times 10^{-23}\) J/K is Boltzmann’s constant (equivalently \(k = -228.6\) dBW/K/Hz), \(T_s\) is the system noise temperature in Kelvin, and \(B\) is the noise bandwidth in Hz. In decibels:

\[N \;[\mathrm{dBW}] = k \;[\mathrm{dBW/K/Hz}] + 10\log_{10}(T_s) + 10\log_{10}(B)\tag{13.15}\] \[N \;[\mathrm{dBW}] = -228.6 + 10\log_{10}(T_s \;[\mathrm{K}]) + 10\log_{10}(B \;[\mathrm{Hz}])\tag{13.16}\]

docs.title: 13.5.2 Cascaded Noise Figure and System Noise Temperature
docs.text:
A receive chain consists of multiple components in cascade: antenna, feed waveguide, low-noise amplifier (LNA), bandpass filter, downconverter, IF amplifier, and modem. Each component contributes noise characterized by its noise figure \(F_n = T_n/290 + 1\) where \(T_n\) is the equivalent noise temperature of the component.

The Friis formula for cascaded noise temperature gives the system noise temperature referred to the antenna output terminal:

\[T_{\mathrm{sys}} = T_{\mathrm{ant}} + T_{\mathrm{feed}} + \frac{T_{\mathrm{LNA}}}{G_{\mathrm{feed}}} + \frac{T_2}{G_{\mathrm{feed}} G_{\mathrm{LNA}}} + \frac{T_3}{G_{\mathrm{feed}} G_{\mathrm{LNA}} G_2} + \cdots\tag{13.17}\]

where \(G_{\mathrm{feed}} = 1/L_f < 1\) for a lossy feed (loss = gain < 1). A lossy passive component at physical temperature \(T_{\mathrm{phys}}\) contributes noise temperature:

\[T_{\mathrm{comp}} = (L - 1) T_{\mathrm{phys}} \quad [K]\tag{13.18}\]

where \(L > 1\) is the component loss ratio. The practical implication is that the LNA must come first in the receive chain to minimize the noise temperature contribution of subsequent (noisier) stages.

docs.title: 13.5.3 Antenna Noise Temperature
docs.text:
The antenna noise temperature \(T_{\mathrm{ant}}\) depends on what the antenna “sees”: the physical temperature of materials in its field of view, weighted by the antenna pattern. Three contributions are important:

  1. Sky (cosmic) background: At frequencies above 3 GHz the cosmic microwave background contributes \(T_{\mathrm{cmb}} = 2.73\) K. Galactic emission adds a frequency-dependent term: \(T_{\mathrm{gal}} \approx 25 (f/408\,\mathrm{MHz})^{-2.75}\) K.

  2. Atmospheric emission: The atmosphere emits thermal noise that couples into the antenna’s main beam. By the reciprocity of Kirchhoff’s law, atmospheric opacity \(\alpha_{\mathrm{atm}}\) at physical temperature \(T_{\mathrm{atm}} \approx 270\) K contributes:

    \[T_{\mathrm{sky}} = T_{\mathrm{atm}}(1 - e^{-\tau/\sin\varepsilon}) + T_{\mathrm{cmb}} e^{-\tau/\sin\varepsilon}\tag{13.19}\]

    where \(\tau\) is the zenith opacity and \(\varepsilon\) is the elevation angle.

  3. Ground spillover: Sidelobe and spillover radiation that couples to the warm ground (\(T_{\mathrm{gnd}} \approx 290\) K). For a well-designed earth station antenna: \(T_{\mathrm{spill}} \approx \eta_{\mathrm{spill}} \cdot 290\) K with \(\eta_{\mathrm{spill}} < 0.01\) for high-quality antennas.

Typical system noise temperatures for earth station receivers:

  • C-band (4 GHz) with LNA: \(T_{\mathrm{sys}} \approx 50\)–80 K

  • Ku-band (11–12 GHz) with LNA: \(T_{\mathrm{sys}} \approx 100\)–150 K

  • Ka-band (20 GHz) with LNA: \(T_{\mathrm{sys}} \approx 200\)–400 K (atmospheric contribution increases)

docs.title: 13.6 Figure of Merit and Carrier-to-Noise Ratio
13.6.1 Figure of Merit G/T
docs.text:
The receive antenna gain \(G_r\) and system noise temperature \(T_{\mathrm{sys}}\) always appear together in the link budget. Their ratio, the figure of merit \(G/T\), completely characterizes the receive system quality independent of bandwidth:

\[\frac{G}{T} \;[\mathrm{dBK^{-1}}] = G_r \;[\mathrm{dBi}] - 10\log_{10}(T_{\mathrm{sys}} \;[\mathrm{K}])\tag{13.20}\]

docs.title: 13.6.2 Carrier-to-Noise Ratio
docs.text:
The carrier-to-noise ratio (CNR or \(C/N\)) is the ratio of received signal power to noise power in the receiver bandwidth \(B\). Combining all previous equations:

\[\boxed{\frac{C}{N} \;[\mathrm{dB}] = \mathrm{EIRP} - \mathrm{FSPL} + \frac{G}{T} - k - 10\log_{10}(B) - L_{\mathrm{misc}}}\tag{13.21}\]

The carrier-to-noise density \(C/N_0\) eliminates the bandwidth dependence, making it a fundamental figure of system performance:

\[\frac{C}{N_0} \;[\mathrm{dB\cdot Hz}] = \mathrm{EIRP} + \frac{G}{T} - \mathrm{FSPL} - k - L_{\mathrm{misc}}\tag{13.22}\]

where \(k = -228.6\) dBW/K/Hz. \(C/N_0\) is the standard metric used in satellite system specifications as it is independent of the modulation bandwidth.

docs.title: 13.6.3 Energy per Bit to Noise Density
docs.text:
For digital communications, the key performance metric is the energy-per-bit to noise density ratio \(E_b/N_0\), which relates directly to the BER through modulation-specific expressions:

\[\frac{E_b}{N_0} \;[\mathrm{dB}] = \frac{C}{N_0} \;[\mathrm{dB\cdot Hz}] - 10\log_{10}(R_b \;[\mathrm{bits/s}])\tag{13.23}\]

where \(R_b\) is the information bit rate after channel decoding. For a QPSK signal at \(R_s = 36\) Msps with rate-3/4 coding, the information bit rate is: \(R_b = 2 \times (3/4) \times 36\times10^6 = 54\) Mbps.

docs.title: 13.7 BER Performance of Satellite Modulation Schemes
13.7.1 Phase-Shift Keying
docs.text:
For BPSK, the exact BER expression is:

\[\mathrm{BER}_{\mathrm{BPSK}} = Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2E_b}{N_0}}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{E_b}{N_0}}\right)\tag{13.24}\]

QPSK achieves the same BER vs \(E_b/N_0\) performance as BPSK but with twice the spectral efficiency (2 bits/symbol vs. 1 bit/symbol):

\[\mathrm{BER}_{\mathrm{QPSK}} = Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2E_b}{N_0}}\right)\tag{13.25}\]

For 8-PSK with Gray coding, the BER approximation is:

\[\mathrm{BER}_{\mathrm{8PSK}} \approx \frac{2}{3}\,Q\!\left(\sqrt{2 \cdot 3 \cdot \frac{E_b}{N_0}} \cdot \sin\frac{\pi}{8}\right)\tag{13.26}\]

where the factor \(\log_2(8) = 3\) accounts for bits-per-symbol. 8-PSK requires approximately 4 dB more \(E_b/N_0\) than QPSK at BER \(= 10^{-6}\).

docs.title: 13.7.2 Amplitude and Phase Shift Keying for Nonlinear Channels
docs.text:
The DVB-S2 standard introduced 16-APSK and 32-APSK, which are optimized for operation through a nonlinear TWTA transponder at near-saturation. The 16-APSK constellation uses two rings: 4 inner points at radius \(r_1\) and 12 outer points at radius \(r_2\), with ring ratio \(\gamma = r_2/r_1 = 2.57\) (for code rate 3/4 per DVB-S2 specification).

The 32-APSK uses three rings: 4 + 12 + 16 points. The constellation was designed using optimization over a nonlinear channel model (Saleh model for TWTA) to maximize minimum Euclidean distance in the presence of AM/AM and AM/PM conversion.

docs.title: 13.8.1 Gaseous Absorption
docs.text:
The primary gaseous absorbers in the microwave region are water vapor (centered near 22.2 GHz and 183 GHz) and molecular oxygen (60 GHz and 118.7 GHz). The ITU-R P.676 model provides the specific attenuation coefficients \(\gamma_o\) (dry air) and \(\gamma_w\) (water vapor) in dB/km. Total zenith gaseous attenuation:

\[A_{\mathrm{gas}} = \frac{\gamma_o h_o + \gamma_w h_w}{\sin\varepsilon} \quad [\mathrm{dB}]\tag{13.27}\]

where \(h_o \approx 6\) km and \(h_w \approx 2\) km are equivalent scale heights, and \(\varepsilon\) is elevation angle. At Ku-band (12 GHz) and \(\varepsilon = 30\degree\), \(A_{\mathrm{gas}} \approx 0.3\) dB; at Ka-band (20 GHz), \(A_{\mathrm{gas}} \approx 0.5\)–1.5 dB.

docs.title: 13.8.2 Cloud and Water Vapor Attenuation
docs.text:
Cloud liquid water content \(W\) [g/m\(^3\)] contributes specific attenuation:

\[\gamma_c = K_l W \quad [\mathrm{dB/km}]\tag{13.28}\]

where \(K_l\) is the mass absorption coefficient (temperature-dependent, approximately \(K_l \approx 0.06\) dB/(g/m\(^3\)) at 11 GHz). The ITU-R P.840 model provides global cloud statistics. Cloud attenuation at Ku-band typically ranges 0.1–2 dB.

docs.title: 13.8.3 Rain Attenuation
docs.text:
Rain attenuation is the dominant propagation impairment at Ku-band and above. Rain drops absorb and scatter electromagnetic energy. The specific attenuation of rain is modeled as:

\[\gamma_R = a R^b \quad [\mathrm{dB/km}]\tag{13.29}\]

where \(R\) [mm/hr] is the rain rate and \(a\), \(b\) are frequency- and polarization-dependent coefficients from ITU-R P.838. At 12 GHz: \(a = 0.0168\), \(b = 1.217\) (horizontal polarization). At 20 GHz: \(a = 0.0751\), \(b = 1.099\).

The ITU-R P.618 rain attenuation prediction method gives the effective rain path length as:

\[d_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{(h_R - h_s) / \sin\varepsilon}{1 + 0.78\sqrt{\gamma_R L_s / f} - 0.38(1-e^{-2L_s})}\tag{13.30}\]

where \(h_R\) is the rain height, \(h_s\) is the earth station height above MSL, \(\varepsilon\) is the elevation angle, and \(L_s\) is the slant path through rain. Total rain attenuation:

\[A_{0.01} = \gamma_R \cdot d_{\mathrm{eff}} \quad [\mathrm{dB}]\tag{13.31}\]

This gives the attenuation exceeded 0.01% of the time (i.e., exceeded for 52.6 minutes/year). For other percentages \(p\) (in range 0.001–5%):

\[A_p = A_{0.01} \cdot \left(\frac{p}{0.01}\right)^{-(0.655 + 0.033\ln p - 0.045\ln A_{0.01})}\tag{13.32}\] Table 13.1. Typical rain attenuation at Ku-band (12 GHz, 30elevation, Temperate Europe) Availability [%] Time Exceeded [min/year] Attenuation [dB] 99.0 5,256 \(\sim\)1.5 99.5 2,628 \(\sim\)2.5 99.9 526 \(\sim\)5.0 99.95 263 \(\sim\)7.0 99.99 52.6 \(\sim\)10.5 99.999 5.26 \(\sim\)16.0

docs.title: 13.9.1 Antenna Pointing Loss
docs.text:
For a Gaussian beam approximation to the antenna pattern, the gain reduction due to pointing error \(\theta_e\) (smaller than the half-power beamwidth) is:

\[L_{\mathrm{point}} = 12 \left(\frac{\theta_e}{\theta_{\mathrm{HPBW}}}\right)^2 \quad [\mathrm{dB}]\tag{13.33}\]

Earth station antennas with servo tracking achieve \(\theta_e < 0.01\degree\) for Ku-band, giving \(L_{\mathrm{point}} < 0.1\) dB. Fixed VSAT antennas may have \(L_{\mathrm{point}} \approx 0.3\)–0.5 dB if not precisely aligned.

docs.title: 13.9.2 Polarization Loss
docs.text:
Polarization mismatch loss occurs when the transmit and receive polarization states are not perfectly matched. For linear polarization with angle offset \(\psi\):

\[L_{\mathrm{pol}} = -20\log_{10}(\cos\psi) \quad [\mathrm{dB}]\tag{13.34}\]

Faraday rotation in the ionosphere can rotate the polarization angle by 0–30at L-band and by less than 1at Ku-band. For circular polarization, Faraday rotation causes no loss, which is why circular polarization is preferred for lower-frequency systems.

docs.title: 13.10 Combined Uplink and Downlink Budget
docs.text:
For a bent-pipe (non-regenerative) satellite transponder, the satellite receives the uplink signal with noise, amplifies the signal-plus-noise, and retransmits it. The downlink adds further noise. The overall \(C/N\) is:

\[\left(\frac{C}{N}\right)_{\mathrm{total}}^{-1} = \left(\frac{C}{N}\right)_{\mathrm{uplink}}^{-1} + \left(\frac{C}{N}\right)_{\mathrm{downlink}}^{-1} + \left(\frac{C}{N}\right)_{\mathrm{intermod}}^{-1}\tag{13.35}\]

The intermodulation term \((C/N)_{\mathrm{intermod}}\) arises from nonlinear distortion in the TWTA when multiple carriers share a transponder. It is minimized by operating the TWTA 3–6 dB below saturation (input backoff, IBO).

For a regenerative (on-board processing) satellite, the uplink and downlink are independent:

\[\mathrm{BER}_{\mathrm{total}} \approx \mathrm{BER}_{\mathrm{uplink}} + \mathrm{BER}_{\mathrm{downlink}}\tag{13.36}\]

(for small BER values). Regenerative payloads completely decouple the uplink and downlink budgets.

docs.title: 13.11.1 System Parameters
docs.text:
We analyze a standard Ku-band GEO communication system with the following parameters:

Uplink (Earth station to satellite):

  • Earth station transmit power: \(P_t = 100\) W = 20 dBW

  • Earth station antenna diameter: \(D = 3\) m, \(\eta_a = 0.65\), at \(f_u = 14.0\) GHz (\(\lambda_u = 21.4\) mm)

  • Earth station antenna gain: \(G_t = 10\log_{10}(0.65 \cdot (\pi \cdot 3/0.0214)^2) = 52.5\) dBi

  • Earth station EIRP: \(52.5 + 20 - 0.5 = 72.0\) dBW

  • Satellite orbit: GEO at 36,000 km

  • FSPL at 14 GHz, 36,000 km: \(92.45 + 91.12 + 22.92 = 206.5\) dB

  • Satellite \(G/T = -1.0\) dBK\(^{-1}\) (includes feed loss and LNA noise figure 1.5 dB)

  • Atmospheric losses: \(A_{\mathrm{gas}} = 0.35\) dB, rain fade margin analysis below

Uplink \(C/N_0\):

\[\frac{C}{N_0}\bigg|_{\mathrm{UL}} = 72.0 - 206.5 + (-1.0) - (-228.6) - 0.35 = 92.75 \;\mathrm{dB\cdot Hz}\tag{13.37}\]

Downlink (satellite to earth station):

  • Satellite EIRP: 52 dBW (includes 20W HPA at 13 dBW, 40 dBi spot beam antenna, minus 1 dB losses)

  • Downlink frequency: \(f_d = 11.7\) GHz (\(\lambda_d = 25.6\) mm)

  • FSPL at 11.7 GHz, 36,000 km: \(92.45 + 91.12 + 21.36 = 204.9\) dB

  • Earth station receive dish: \(D_r = 0.75\) m, \(\eta_r = 0.65\)

  • Earth station receive gain: \(G_r = 10\log_{10}(0.65 \cdot (\pi \cdot 0.75/0.0256)^2) = 39.2\) dBi

  • Earth station LNA noise figure: \(F = 0.8\) dB, \(T_{\mathrm{LNA}} = 54\) K

  • Sky noise temperature at 30elevation: \(T_{\mathrm{sky}} = 35\) K

  • System noise temperature: \(T_{\mathrm{sys}} = 35 + 5 + 54 \approx 94\) K = 19.7 dBK

  • Earth station \(G/T = 39.2 - 19.7 = 19.5\) dBK\(^{-1}\)

  • Atmospheric losses: 0.3 dB (clear sky)

Downlink \(C/N_0\):

\[\frac{C}{N_0}\bigg|_{\mathrm{DL}} = 52.0 - 204.9 + 19.5 - (-228.6) - 0.3 = 94.9 \;\mathrm{dB\cdot Hz}\tag{13.38}\]

Overall \(C/N_0\):

\[\frac{C}{N_0}\bigg|_{\mathrm{total}} = -10\log_{10}\!\left(10^{-92.75/10} + 10^{-94.9/10}\right) = 91.3 \;\mathrm{dB\cdot Hz}\tag{13.39}\]

docs.title: 13.11.2 Required E_b/N₀ for QPSK at BER = 10⁻8
docs.text:
For QPSK with rate-1/2 LDPC coding (DVB-S2 QPSK 1/2), the threshold \(E_b/N_0\) for BER \(= 10^{-8}\) is approximately 3.3 dB (from AWGN performance curves including implementation loss of 0.3 dB).

Information bit rate: \(R_b = 2 \times (1/2) \times R_s = R_s\). For \(R_s = 36\) Msps: \(R_b = 36\) Mbps; \(10\log_{10}(36\times10^6) = 75.6\) dB.

\[\frac{E_b}{N_0}\bigg|_{\mathrm{total}} = 91.3 - 75.6 = 15.7 \;\mathrm{dB}\tag{13.40}\]

Link margin = \(15.7 - 3.3 = 12.4\) dB. This substantial margin accommodates rain fade: at Ku-band in temperate Europe, 99.9% availability requires approximately 5 dB of rain fade margin, leaving an additional 7.4 dB of implementation margin.

Table 13.2. Complete Ku-band GEO Link Budget Summary Parameter Uplink Downlink Frequency [GHz] 14.0 11.7 Transmit power [dBW] 20.0 13.0 Transmit antenna gain [dBi] 52.5 40.0 Feed/cable losses [dB] 0.5 1.0 EIRP [dBW] 72.0 52.0 Free space path loss [dB] 206.5 204.9 Atmospheric loss [dB] 0.35 0.3 Receive antenna gain [dBi] 24.0\(^a\) 39.2 System noise temperature [dBK] 24.8\(^a\) 19.7 \(G/T\) [dBK\(^{-1}\)] \(-\)1.0 19.5 Boltzmann’s constant [dBW/K/Hz] \(-\)228.6 \(-\)228.6 \(C/N_0\) [dB\(\cdot\)Hz] 92.75 94.9 Bit rate [dBHz] 75.6 (36 Mbps) \(E_b/N_0\) [dB] 17.15 19.3 Overall \(E_b/N_0\) [dB] 15.7 Required \(E_b/N_0\) [dB] 3.3 (QPSK 1/2) Link margin [dB] 12.4 \(^a\) Satellite receive antenna and noise temperature.

docs.title: 13.12 DVB-S2X Adaptive Coding and Modulation
docs.text:
The DVB-S2X standard (ETSI EN 302 307-2) extends DVB-S2 with higher-order modulation formats and finer code rate granularity. Adaptive Coding and Modulation (ACM) dynamically selects the modcod based on real-time link conditions, maximizing throughput under varying propagation. The link budget must therefore be computed for the nominal (clear sky) condition and separately for the edge-of-coverage and rain fade conditions.
