docs.title: 13.13 High-Throughput Satellite Link Budget
docs.text:
High-throughput satellites (HTS) achieve terabit-level aggregate throughput through aggressive frequency reuse. A system with \(N_b\) beams, frequency reuse factor \(F_r\), and transponder bandwidth \(B_t\) has aggregate bandwidth:

\[B_{\mathrm{total}} = N_b \cdot B_t / F_r \quad [\mathrm{Hz}]\tag{13.41}\]

The spectral efficiency \(\eta_s\) [bits/s/Hz] depends on the modcod and the carrier-to- interference ratio (CIR) from co-frequency beams. Adjacent beam interference (ABI) adds to the noise budget:

\[\left(\frac{C}{N+I}\right)^{-1} = \left(\frac{C}{N}\right)^{-1} + \left(\frac{C}{I}\right)^{-1}\tag{13.42}\]

For a 4-color frequency reuse plan, adjacent beams use different frequencies, giving \(C/I \approx 20\)–25 dB. With \(C/N = 14\) dB and \(C/I = 22\) dB, \(C/(N+I) \approx 13.4\) dB.

Viasat-3 (launched 2023) exemplifies state-of-the-art HTS design: approximately 1 Tbps aggregate capacity over 500+ spot beams, each 200–400 MHz wide at Ka-band, with 4-color reuse, adaptive coding, and beam hopping.

docs.title: 13.14 LEO Broadband Link Budget
docs.text:
LEO broadband constellations such as Starlink (SpaceX) and OneWeb operate at altitude \(h \approx 550\) km. The much shorter path dramatically reduces free space loss:

\[\mathrm{FSPL}_{\mathrm{LEO}} = 92.45 + 20\log_{10}(550) + 20\log_{10}(14) = 92.45 + 54.8 + 22.9 = 170.1 \;\mathrm{dB}\tag{13.43}\]

Compare with GEO: \(\Delta\mathrm{FSPL} = 206.5 - 170.1 = 36.4\) dB improvement. This allows much smaller user terminals (flat-panel phased arrays rather than 0.75–1.2 m dishes).

At minimum elevation angle \(\varepsilon = 25\degree\), the slant range increases to:

\[d = \sqrt{(R_e + h)^2 - R_e^2\cos^2\varepsilon} - R_e\sin\varepsilon = 1{,}000 \;\mathrm{km} \quad (\varepsilon=25\degree)\tag{13.44}\] \[\mathrm{FSPL}_{25\degree} = 92.45 + 20\log_{10}(1000) + 20\log_{10}(14) = 92.45 + 60 + 22.9 = 175.4 \;\mathrm{dB}\tag{13.45}\]

Additional 5.3 dB compared to zenith. The Starlink user terminal (Generation 2) uses a 480-element Ku-band phased array (approximately 0.5 m \(\times\) 0.3 m flat panel) with electronically steered beam tracking the satellite across the sky. Typical downlink performance: \(\geq 100\) Mbps with latency \(\leq 45\) ms.

docs.title: 13.15 Inter-Satellite Link Budget
docs.text:
Inter-satellite links (ISL) operate in a benign environment: no atmosphere, no rain, no ionospheric effects. However, the distances can be significant. For adjacent orbital plane ISLs at 550 km altitude, separation \(\approx 1{,}500\) km.

V-band ISL at 60 GHz, separation 1,500 km:

\[\mathrm{FSPL}_{\mathrm{ISL}} = 92.45 + 20\log_{10}(1500) + 20\log_{10}(60) = 92.45 + 63.5 + 35.6 = 191.6 \;\mathrm{dB}\tag{13.46}\]

With 25 dBi gain antennas (each side) and 0 dBW transmit power, the received power is: \(P_r = 0 + 25 - 191.6 + 25 = -141.6\) dBW. With \(T_{\mathrm{sys}} = 500\) K (space environment), \(C/N_0 = -141.6 + 228.6 - 27.0 = 60.0\) dB\(\cdot\)Hz for 10 Gbps (\(R_b = 100\) dBHz): \(E_b/N_0 = 60 - 100 = -40\) dB — insufficient. Therefore ISL links use higher EIRP (e.g., 40 dBW satellite EIRP with high-gain directional antenna).

For Starlink optical ISL (1550 nm, 1 W transmit, 10 cm aperture):

\[\mathrm{FSPL}_{\mathrm{opt}} = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi R}{\lambda}\right) = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi \cdot 1.5\times10^6}{1.55\times10^{-6}}\right) = 262 \;\mathrm{dB}\tag{13.47}\]

With about 106 dBi optical gain each side (ideal aperture, \(G = (\pi D/\lambda)^2\)) and 0 dBW transmit, \(P_r = 0 + 106 - 262 + 106 = -50\) dBW (about \(-20\) dBm) before pointing and implementation losses, which can support multi-Gbps coherent links.

docs.title: 13.16 Link Margin Philosophy and Availability
docs.text:
The link margin is the difference between the available \(C/N\) and the required \(C/N\) for the target BER:

\[M_{\mathrm{link}} = (C/N)_{\mathrm{available}} - (C/N)_{\mathrm{required}} \quad [\mathrm{dB}]\tag{13.48}\]

The required margin \(M_{\mathrm{req}}\) must account for:

  1. Rain fade margin \(M_{\mathrm{rain}}\): The attenuation not exceeded for the required availability percentage (e.g., 99.9% \(\rightarrow\) 5 dB at Ku-band in Europe).

  2. Pointing loss margin \(M_{\mathrm{point}} \approx 0.3\)–0.5 dB: Variability in earth station alignment due to thermal deformation, wind loading, and tracking jitter.

  3. Implementation margin \(M_{\mathrm{impl}} \approx 0.5\)–1.0 dB: Allows for deviation from ideal AWGN performance due to phase noise, frequency error, filter distortion, and A/D converter quantization.

  4. Interference margin \(M_{\mathrm{int}} \approx 0.5\)–2.0 dB: Allowance for adjacent satellite interference (ASI) and co-channel interference.

  5. Aging/end-of-life margin \(M_{\mathrm{EOL}} \approx 1\)–3 dB: Accounts for solar cell degradation and TWT cathode emission reduction over a 15-year mission life.

Total required margin: \(M_{\mathrm{req}} = M_{\mathrm{rain}} + M_{\mathrm{point}} + M_{\mathrm{impl}} + M_{\mathrm{int}} + M_{\mathrm{EOL}}\)

For a 99.9% Ku-band link in central Europe: \(M_{\mathrm{req}} = 5.0 + 0.4 + 0.8 + 1.0 + 2.0 = 9.2\) dB.

docs.title: 13.17 Satellite Capacity and Spectral Efficiency
docs.text:
The Shannon channel capacity provides the theoretical upper bound:

\[C = B \log_2\!\left(1 + \frac{S}{N}\right) \quad [\mathrm{bits/s}]\tag{13.49}\]

A satellite transponder with bandwidth \(B = 500\) MHz and operating at \(C/N = 20\) dB (SNR linear = 100) has theoretical capacity \(C = 500 \times 10^6 \times \log_2(101) \approx 3.3\) Gbps. Modern DVB-S2X with 256APSK 3/4 achieves 5.84 bits/s/Hz spectral efficiency, approaching Shannon limit to within 2–3 dB in ideal AWGN conditions.

Aggregate HTS throughput:

\[\Gamma_{\mathrm{total}} = N_b \cdot B_{\mathrm{beam}} \cdot \eta_s \cdot (1 - \mathrm{FEC overhead}) \quad [\mathrm{bits/s}]\tag{13.50}\]

For a system with \(N_b = 300\) beams, \(B_{\mathrm{beam}} = 500\) MHz, \(\eta_s = 3.0\) bits/s/Hz: \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{total}} = 300 \times 500\times10^6 \times 3.0 = 450\) Gbps aggregate throughput.

docs.title: 13.18 Summary
docs.text:
This chapter has derived the satellite link budget from electromagnetic first principles and applied it to representative GEO, HTS, LEO, ISL, and optical communication scenarios. The key equations governing link budget analysis are:

  1. EIRP [dBW] = \(P_t\) [dBW] + \(G_t\) [dBi] \(-\) \(L_f\) [dB]

  2. FSPL [dB] = \(92.45 + 20\log_{10}(d[\mathrm{km}]) + 20\log_{10}(f[\mathrm{GHz}])\)

  3. \(C/N_0\) [dBHz] = EIRP + \(G/T\) \(-\) FSPL \(-\) \(k\) \(-\) \(L_{\mathrm{misc}}\)

  4. \(E_b/N_0\) [dB] = \(C/N_0\) \(-\) \(10\log_{10}(R_b)\)

  5. \((C/N)_{\mathrm{total}}^{-1} = (C/N)_{\mathrm{UL}}^{-1} + (C/N)_{\mathrm{DL}}^{-1}\) (for bent-pipe)

The DVB-S2X ACM framework allows dynamic modcod selection, optimizing throughput under varying propagation conditions. Modern HTS systems approach terabit aggregate throughput through spatial frequency reuse, and LEO constellations exploit the shorter propagation path to deliver broadband services with consumer-grade user terminals.

Link Budget Design Rules of Thumb:

  • Every 3 dB of path loss requires doubling the transmit power or quadrupling the antenna area.

  • The LNA noise figure dominates: a 1 dB improvement in LNA noise figure directly improves \(G/T\) by 1 dB.

  • LEO offers \(\sim\)36 dB lower free space path loss than GEO at same frequency.

  • At Ka-band, rain attenuation can exceed 20 dB for 0.01% exceedance in tropical regions.

  • DVB-S2X ACM can recover 8–12 dB of link margin in clear sky, trading margin for throughput.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. Calculate the FSPL at 20 GHz for a path distance of 37,000 km. What is the FSPL at 30 GHz for the same path? What is the difference in dB and how is this related to the frequency ratio?

  2. A Ku-band earth station uses a 1.2 m antenna with 65% efficiency. Calculate (a) the receive antenna gain at 11.7 GHz, (b) the half-power beamwidth, and (c) the \(G/T\) if the system noise temperature is 120 K.

  3. Using the ITU-R P.618 procedure, estimate the rain attenuation exceeded 0.1% of the time for a terminal in Singapore (tropical, rain rate \(R_{0.01} = 145\) mm/hr) at 20 GHz and 30elevation angle.

  4. For the worked example in Section 13.11, compute the BER for the nominal (clear sky) condition. What rain fade (in dB) can be tolerated before the BER exceeds \(10^{-6}\) for QPSK 1/2 LDPC coding?

  5. A Ka-band HTS spot beam has EIRP = 65 dBW, the receive terminal has \(G/T = 20\) dBK\(^{-1}\), slant path distance is 37,000 km, and gaseous attenuation is 1.0 dB. Find \(C/N_0\) and determine the maximum achievable spectral efficiency assuming the DVB-S2X modcod table (Table 13.3).

docs.title: Chapter 14: Satellite Antenna Systems
docs.text: Key Concepts: Antenna gain and directivity, aperture efficiency, parabolic reflector systems, phased array antennas, active electronically scanned arrays (AESA), deployable mesh reflectors, digital beamforming (DBF), multi-beam antennas, polarization diversity.

docs.title: 14.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The antenna is the interface between the guided electromagnetic wave within the satellite or earth station hardware and the radiated field propagating through space. In the link budget, the antenna appears twice: as the transmit gain \(G_t\) multiplying the transmitter power to produce EIRP, and as the receive gain \(G_r\) in the figure of merit \(G/T\). Consequently, antenna performance has a one-to-one impact on link margin in decibels, making antenna engineering one of the highest-leverage disciplines in satellite system design.

Modern satellite missions impose extraordinarily demanding antenna requirements: 0.5 m diameter antennas on CubeSats that must provide regional coverage, 22 m deployable reflectors on mobile satellite service (MSS) spacecraft, 1,000-element active phased arrays for LEO broadband user terminals, and multi-beam antennas generating hundreds of spot beams from a single GEO spacecraft. This chapter addresses all of these, developing the underlying physics before describing each antenna type in detail.

docs.title: 14.2.1 Gain, Directivity, and Efficiency
docs.text:
An antenna’s directivity \(D\) is defined as the ratio of the radiation intensity \(U(\theta,\phi)\) in the direction of maximum radiation to the average radiation intensity over all directions:

\[D = \frac{4\pi U_{\max}}{P_{\mathrm{rad}}} = \frac{4\pi U_{\max}}{\oint U(\theta,\phi)\,d\Omega}\tag{14.1}\]

The gain \(G\) incorporates the antenna radiation efficiency \(\eta_r\) (accounting for ohmic and dielectric losses):

\[G = \eta_r \cdot D\tag{14.2}\]

For an aperture antenna, directivity and gain are related to the physical aperture area \(A\) and aperture efficiency \(\eta_a\) through:

\[G = \eta_a \cdot \frac{4\pi A}{\lambda^2}\tag{14.3}\]

The aperture efficiency \(\eta_a\) is the product of several sub-efficiency factors:

\[\eta_a = \eta_{\mathrm{ill}} \cdot \eta_{\mathrm{spill}} \cdot \eta_{\mathrm{phase}} \cdot \eta_{\mathrm{block}} \cdot \eta_{\mathrm{surface}} \cdot \eta_{\mathrm{pol}}\tag{14.4}\]

  • \(\eta_{\mathrm{ill}}\): illumination efficiency — accounts for non-uniform amplitude taper across the aperture (ranges from 0.75 to 1.0 for typical tapers; 1.0 for uniform illumination)

  • \(\eta_{\mathrm{spill}}\): spillover efficiency — fraction of feed radiation intercepted by the reflector (typically 0.85–0.95)

  • \(\eta_{\mathrm{phase}}\): phase efficiency — reduction due to phase error across aperture (defocus, surface distortion)

  • \(\eta_{\mathrm{block}}\): blockage efficiency — reduction due to the feed/subreflector shadowing the main aperture (0 for offset-fed systems, 0.95–0.99 for prime focus)

  • \(\eta_{\mathrm{surface}}\): Ruze surface efficiency — \(\eta_{\mathrm{surface}} = \exp[-(4\pi\epsilon/\lambda)^2]\) where \(\epsilon\) is the RMS surface error

  • \(\eta_{\mathrm{pol}}\): polarization efficiency — loss due to cross-polarized radiation

Typical overall aperture efficiency for a well-designed parabolic reflector: \(\eta_a \approx 0.55\)–\(0.70\).

docs.title: 14.2.2 Half-Power Beamwidth and Sidelobe Levels
docs.text:
The half-power beamwidth (HPBW) of a circular aperture of diameter \(D\) is approximately:

\[\theta_{\mathrm{HPBW}} \approx \frac{70\lambda}{D} \quad [\mathrm{degrees}]\tag{14.5}\]

This expression holds for \(-10\) dB edge taper illumination, which is a common design target. For a rectangular aperture with dimensions \(a \times b\):

\[\theta_{\mathrm{HPBW,a}} \approx \frac{51\lambda}{a}\quad [\mathrm{deg}], \qquad \theta_{\mathrm{HPBW,b}} \approx \frac{51\lambda}{b}\quad [\mathrm{deg}]\tag{14.6}\]

The first sidelobe level of a uniformly illuminated aperture is \(-13.3\) dBc. Tapering the aperture illumination (e.g., Taylor distribution) reduces sidelobes at the cost of reduced gain and wider main beam. A \(-25\) dB Taylor taper reduces sidelobes to \(-25\) dBc but increases beamwidth by approximately 30%.

Table 14.1. Gain versus Aperture Diameter at Selected Frequencies (\(\eta_a = 0.60\)) Diameter [m] Freq. \(\lambda\) [mm] Gain [dBi] HPBW [deg] Application 0.30 11.7 GHz 25.6 32.5 5.96 VSAT (small) 0.60 11.7 GHz 25.6 38.6 2.98 VSAT (medium) 0.75 11.7 GHz 25.6 40.3 2.39 Consumer DTH 1.20 11.7 GHz 25.6 44.2 1.49 Professional VSAT 2.40 14.0 GHz 21.4 51.0 0.62 Medium hub station 4.50 14.0 GHz 21.4 57.0 0.33 Major earth station 0.60 30.0 GHz 10.0 44.6 1.17 Ka-band VSAT 22.00 1.6 GHz 187.5 48.3 0.60 MSS (deployable)

docs.title: 14.2.3 Polarization
docs.text:
Satellite antennas can transmit and receive linear polarization (horizontal or vertical, or \(\pm 45\degree\)) or circular polarization (left-hand or right-hand, LHCP/RHCP). Key polarization metrics include:

  • Cross-polarization discrimination (XPD): ratio of co-polarized to cross-polarized gain in the main beam direction. Required \(\mathrm{XPD} \geq 30\) dB for dual-polarization frequency reuse systems.

  • Axial ratio (AR): for circular polarization, the ratio of major to minor axes of the polarization ellipse. AR = 1 (0 dB) for perfect circular polarization. The power loss due to axial ratio mismatch is:

    \[L_{\mathrm{AR}} = \frac{(AR_t \cdot AR_r + 1)^2 + (AR_t - AR_r)^2}{(AR_t^2 + 1)(AR_r^2 + 1)} \quad [\mathrm{ratio}]\tag{14.7}\]

  • Faraday rotation: At L-band, the ionosphere rotates linear polarization by \(\Delta\phi \approx 40.3 \cdot \mathrm{TEC} / f^2\) [rad], where TEC is the total electron content (typically 1–100 TECU). At 1.5 GHz with 30 TECU: \(\Delta\phi \approx 35\degree\), necessitating circular polarization for robust operation.

docs.title: 14.3 Horn Antennas
docs.text:
Horn antennas are the workhorses of satellite TT&C (telemetry, tracking, and command) systems and the primary feeds for reflector antennas. A conical corrugated horn is the preferred feed design because it produces a circularly symmetric, low-sidelobe radiation pattern with excellent polarization purity. The corrugations (grooves cut into the inner wall perpendicular to the propagation axis) force the boundary conditions to support the \(\mathrm{HE}_{11}\) hybrid mode rather than the \(\mathrm{TE}_{11}\) fundamental mode, suppressing asymmetric sidelobes and cross-polarization.

The far-field radiation pattern of a corrugated horn with aperture radius \(a\) and half-flare angle \(\psi\) can be expressed using Gaussian beam optics as:

\[E(\rho,z) = E_0 \frac{w_0}{w(z)} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\rho^2}{w^2(z)}\right) \exp\!\left(-j\!\left[kz + k\frac{\rho^2}{2R(z)} - \arctan\!\frac{z}{z_R}\right]\right)\tag{14.8}\]

where \(w_0\) is the beam waist radius, \(w(z) = w_0\sqrt{1 + (z/z_R)^2}\) is the beam radius at distance \(z\), \(R(z) = z[1 + (z_R/z)^2]\) is the wavefront radius of curvature, and \(z_R = \pi w_0^2/\lambda\) is the Rayleigh range.

Potter horns (step-discontinuity horns) use a simple diameter step transition to generate the \(\mathrm{TM}_{11}\) mode and combine it with \(\mathrm{TE}_{11}\) to produce a similar symmetric pattern to corrugated horns, with lower fabrication complexity.

docs.title: 14.4.1 Prime Focus Parabolic Reflector
docs.text:
The parabolic reflector focuses a plane wave incident from the direction of the parabola axis onto a single point (the focus). Equivalently, radiation from the focus reflects into a plane wave. The parabola equation in polar coordinates from the focus is:

\[r = \frac{2f}{1 + \cos\theta} = \frac{f}{\cos^2(\theta/2)}\tag{14.9}\]

where \(f\) is the focal length and \(\theta\) is measured from the parabola axis. The \(f/D\) ratio governs the illumination angle \(\psi_0\):

\[\tan\!\left(\frac{\psi_0}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{4(f/D)}\tag{14.10}\]

For \(f/D = 0.4\) (common for satellite antennas), \(\psi_0 = 64\degree\). The feed must illuminate the reflector within \(\pm\psi_0\) while spilling minimal power outside this angle.

Prime focus designs suffer aperture blockage from the feed structure, reducing gain and increasing sidelobe levels. Aperture blockage efficiency for a feed support of diameter \(d_s\) in an aperture of diameter \(D\):

\[\eta_{\mathrm{block}} \approx \left(1 - \frac{d_s^2}{D^2}\right)^2\tag{14.11}\]

docs.title: 14.4.2 Offset-Fed Parabolic Reflector
docs.text: The offset-fed reflector displaces the feed from the axis of the parent parabola, so the feed and feed support structure are moved outside the projected aperture. This eliminates aperture blockage completely (\(\eta_{\mathrm{block}} = 1\)), typically improving gain by 0.5–1.0 dB and dramatically reducing sidelobe levels. The trade-off is structural asymmetry and the generation of cross-polarized radiation, which must be compensated by the feed. Offset reflectors are standard for Ku-band direct-to-home (DTH) receive antennas and for satellite transmit antennas where high gain and low cross-polarization are required simultaneously.

docs.title: 14.4.3 Cassegrain and Gregorian Dual-Reflector Systems
docs.text:
Figure 14.1. Geometry of Cassegrain (left) and Gregorian (right) dual-reflector antenna systems. The Cassegrain uses a convex hyperboloidal subreflector; the Gregorian uses a concave ellipsoidal subreflector located beyond the prime focus.

The Cassegrain system places a convex hyperboloidal subreflector between the feed and the main paraboloidal reflector. The two foci of the hyperboloid coincide: one with the feed phase center and the other with the focal point of the paraboloid. This arrangement allows the feed to be located at the vertex of the main reflector, shortening the feed transmission line and improving overall system efficiency for large antennas.

The Gregorian system uses a concave ellipsoidal subreflector located beyond the prime focus. This allows more physical clearance between the feed and subreflector, accommodating larger feed assemblies. The Gregorian geometry is preferred when a large feed cluster is required (e.g., for multi-beam antenna feeds), or when shaping both reflectors to achieve specific far-field coverage patterns.

For shaped-beam satellites, both reflectors are numerically optimized using methods such as physical optics (PO) and physical theory of diffraction (PTD) to produce prescribed coverage footprints with minimum EIRP variation across a service region. Commercial software (GRASP from TICRA) is the industry standard for such reflector synthesis.

docs.title: 14.5 Shaped Reflector Antennas for Coverage Optimization
docs.text:
A shaped beam antenna produces a radiation pattern whose gain contour closely matches the boundary of a specified service zone—e.g., the continental United States, Europe, or a country. This maximizes EIRP toward the intended service area while minimizing radiation toward interference-sensitive adjacent regions.

The far-field pattern of a reflector antenna is related to the aperture field distribution \(E_a(x',y')\) by the Fourier transform:

\[E(\theta,\phi) = \iint_A E_a(x',y') \exp\!\left[j k (x'\sin\theta\cos\phi + y'\sin\theta\sin\phi)\right] dx'\,dy'\tag{14.12}\]

Reflector shaping adjusts the surface curvature (equivalently, the phase of \(E_a\)) to redistribute energy in the far field. The inverse problem—finding the reflector surface that produces a desired pattern—is solved iteratively using physical optics methods.

docs.title: 14.6.1 Array Factor and Beam Steering
docs.text:
A linear array of \(N\) elements, uniformly spaced by \(d\), with complex weights \(w_n = a_n e^{j\psi_n}\) (amplitude \(a_n\), phase \(\psi_n\)), produces an array factor:

\[\mathrm{AF}(\theta) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} w_n \exp[j n k d \sin\theta]\tag{14.13}\]

where \(k = 2\pi/\lambda\) is the free-space wavenumber. To steer the main beam to angle \(\theta_0\), a progressive phase shift is applied:

\[\psi_n = -n k d \sin\theta_0\tag{14.14}\]

For a 2D rectangular array of \(N_x \times N_y\) elements with spacings \(d_x\) and \(d_y\):

\[\mathrm{AF}(\theta,\phi) = \sum_{m=0}^{N_x-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N_y-1} w_{mn} \exp\!\left[j(mkd_x\sin\theta\cos\phi + nkd_y\sin\theta\sin\phi)\right]\tag{14.15}\]

docs.title: 14.6.2 Grating Lobes and Element Spacing
docs.text:
Grating lobes are spurious main-lobe replicas that appear at angles where the progressive phase shift produces constructive interference in an unintended direction. For a linear array, grating lobes occur at:

\[\sin\theta_g = \sin\theta_0 \pm \frac{m\lambda}{d}, \quad m = 1, 2, 3, …\tag{14.16}\]

To prevent grating lobes within real space (\(|\sin\theta| \leq 1\)) for all scan angles \(|\theta_0| \leq \theta_{\max}\):

\[d \leq \frac{\lambda}{1 + |\sin\theta_{\max}|}\tag{14.17}\]

For a maximum scan angle of \(\theta_{\max} = 60\degree\) (typical for LEO user terminals): \(d \leq \lambda / 1.866 \approx 0.54\lambda\). Standard element spacing is \(d = \lambda/2\), which prevents grating lobes for scan to \(\pm 90\degree\).

docs.title: 14.6.3 Scan Loss
docs.text:
The gain of a phased array decreases as the beam is scanned away from broadside. For an element pattern with \(\cos^q\theta\) directivity (commonly \(q = 1\) for patch elements, \(q = 1.5\) for dipoles over a ground plane), the array gain at scan angle \(\theta_0\) is:

\[G(\theta_0) = G_{\mathrm{broadside}} \cdot \cos^q\theta_0\tag{14.18}\]

For \(q = 1\): scan to \(60\degree\) incurs \(10\log_{10}(\cos 60\degree) = -3\) dB scan loss. Practical phased array designs for satellite user terminals accept up to \(-4\) dB scan loss at \(60\degree\) scan (corresponding to \(25\degree\) elevation angle when the satellite is overhead at \(55\degree\) elevation and the terminal tracks).

docs.title: 14.7.1 T/R Module Architecture
docs.text:
An AESA integrates a transmit/receive (T/R) module at each radiating element, or at each subarray of 4–16 elements. A complete T/R module contains:

  • Transmit path: Driver amplifier \(\rightarrow\) Power amplifier (PA) \(\rightarrow\) Phase shifter \(\rightarrow\) Attenuator \(\rightarrow\) Antenna element

  • Receive path: Antenna element \(\rightarrow\) Low-noise amplifier (LNA) \(\rightarrow\) Phase shifter \(\rightarrow\) Attenuator \(\rightarrow\) Combiner

  • Control: DC/DC converter, thermal management, digital control interface (SPI/I2C)

For a satellite user terminal T/R module at Ku-band:

  • LNA noise figure: 1.5–2.0 dB at 10.7–12.7 GHz

  • PA output power: 23–27 dBm per element

  • Phase shifter resolution: 5 or 6 bits (11.25or 5.625steps)

  • Attenuator range: 0–31.5 dB in 0.5 dB steps (6-bit)

  • MMIC technology: GaAs pHEMT for LNA, GaN HEMT for PA

docs.title: 14.7.2 MMIC Technology
docs.text:
Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuits (MMICs) fabricate all active and passive components on a single semiconductor die using semiconductor process technology:

  • GaAs pHEMT: Noise figure 0.5–1.5 dB at 10–18 GHz; electron mobility \(\mu_e \approx 8{,}500\) cm\(^2\)/V\(\cdot\)s; standard for receive-side LNAs.

  • GaN HEMT: Breakdown voltage \(>100\) V; power density 5–10 W/mm vs. 0.5–1.0 W/mm for GaAs; preferred for high-power transmit modules; noise figure 1.5–2.5 dB.

  • SiGe BiCMOS: Lower cost than III-V compounds; integrated digital control; noise figure 2–4 dB at Ku-band; used in consumer-grade satellite terminals (Starlink, OneWeb, flat panel designs targeting sub-$1000 terminal cost).

  • InP HEMT: Highest frequency capability (\(f_T > 600\) GHz); noise figure \(< 0.3\) dB at millimeter-wave; used in ground-based very high-performance receivers.

docs.title: 14.7.3 Thermal Management
docs.text:
The PA dissipated power in an AESA is:

\[P_{\mathrm{diss}} = P_{\mathrm{DC}} - P_{\mathrm{RF,out}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{RF,out}}}{\mathrm{PAE}} - P_{\mathrm{RF,out}} = P_{\mathrm{RF,out}}\left(\frac{1 - \mathrm{PAE}}{\mathrm{PAE}}\right)\tag{14.19}\]

where PAE is power added efficiency (typically 20–40% for Ku-band GaN PAs). For a 1000-element array with 100 mW per element and 30% PAE: \(P_{\mathrm{diss}} = 100 \times 1000 \times (0.7/0.3) = 233\) W total dissipated power, requiring conductive thermal management to a cold plate or radiator.

docs.title: 14.8 Multi-Beam Antennas
docs.text:
A multi-beam antenna (MBA) generates multiple simultaneous spot beams from a single large reflector, using a cluster of feeds at or near the focal plane. Each feed illuminates the full reflector aperture and produces a spot beam pointing in the direction determined by the feed’s offset from the reflector focal point. The angular offset \(\Delta\theta\) of the beam from boresight is related to the feed lateral displacement \(\Delta s\) from focus by:

\[\Delta\theta \approx \frac{\Delta s}{f} \quad [\mathrm{rad}]\tag{14.20}\]

For an HTS with \(f = 1.5\) m and beam spacing of \(0.3\degree\) (\(\approx 5.2\) mrad): \(\Delta s \approx 5.2 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.5 = 7.8\) mm between feed centers.

The fundamental limit to MBA performance is that each feed subtends a significant portion of the reflector (since the feeds fill the focal plane rather than a single focal point), degrading gain and increasing spillover. The maximum number of beams that can be efficiently served from a single reflector is roughly:

\[N_{\mathrm{beam,max}} \approx \left(\frac{D}{2\lambda f/D}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{D^2}{2\lambda f}\right)^2\tag{14.21}\]

In practice, 100–300 beams from a single reflector are achievable in HTS designs, with beam efficiency (ratio of in-beam to total radiated power) of 80–90%.

docs.title: 14.8.1 Beam Hopping
docs.text: Beam hopping is a time-division approach where the satellite illuminates different beams at different time slots within a frame. A single active power channel is shared across many beams, with the beam selection controlled by a high-speed switch matrix or digital beamformer. This approach is efficient when traffic demand is highly non-uniform across beams, as the dwell time per beam can be adapted to demand. DVB-S2X includes physical layer support for beam hopping through the Super-Frame structure.

docs.title: 14.9 Deployable Antenna Systems
docs.text: Large deployable antennas enable mobile satellite services at L- and S-band, where wavelengths are large (150–300 mm) and small antenna gain would result in extremely low EIRP. A 1 dBi gain omnidirectional handset antenna on a mobile phone can close an L-band satellite link only with a very large satellite antenna.

docs.title: 14.9.1 Mesh Reflector Antennas
docs.text:
The AstroMesh reflector (developed by Northrop Grumman, formerly TRW) is the most widely deployed large deployable mesh reflector in commercial satellite service. Key features:

  • Reflective mesh: gold-plated molybdenum wire, mesh density optimized to achieve \(<10\%\) RF transmission (reflectivity \(> 0.9\))

  • Maximum demonstrated diameter: 22 m (Inmarsat-4 satellites, L-band at 1.5/1.6 GHz)

  • Surface accuracy: RMS \(\leq 1\) mm (suitable for L-band and lower S-band)

  • Stowed volume: fits within 1.5 m diameter envelope for launch vehicle shroud compatibility

  • Deployment: driven by spring-loaded booms and tensioned cable network

  • Gain at 1.6 GHz with 12 m diameter: \(G = 10\log_{10}(0.40 \times (\pi \times 12/0.1875)^2) \approx 48\) dBi

Viasat-3, launched in 2023, uses a large deployable reflector at Ka-band (20/30 GHz) with approximately 6 m diameter and surface accuracy \(\approx 0.1\) mm RMS required to achieve \(\eta_{\mathrm{surface}} > 0.9\) at 30 GHz (\(\lambda = 10\) mm, Ruze criterion: surface error \(< \lambda/16 \approx 0.6\) mm RMS).

docs.title: 14.9.2 Wrap-Rib Reflectors
docs.text: Wrap-rib reflectors use a set of ribs that wrap around a central hub in the stowed configuration and spring out to support the mesh surface when deployed. This approach is simpler mechanically than AstroMesh for smaller apertures (3–6 m diameter) and was used on early MSS satellites including the Intelsat VI series.

docs.title: 14.9.3 Inflatable Reflectors
docs.text: Inflatable antenna concepts use pressurized membrane structures. The IRMA (Inflatable Reflector Membrane Antenna) design uses a rigid foam-supported membrane inflated to maintain parabolic shape. These concepts are attractive for their exceptionally high stowage efficiency but have seen limited flight heritage due to leak concerns and susceptibility to micrometeorite damage.

docs.title: 14.10 Flat Panel Phased Array User Terminals
docs.text: The emergence of LEO broadband constellations has driven unprecedented commercial interest in flat-panel phased array terminals. These electronically steered antennas eliminate the mechanical gimbal required for tracking a moving satellite, providing faster acquisition and higher reliability at lower cost in mass production.

docs.title: 14.10.1 Starlink User Terminal (Generation 2)
docs.text:
The SpaceX Starlink Generation 2 user terminal (“Flat High Performance” model) provides:

  • Physical dimensions: approximately 0.59 m \(\times\) 0.38 m (wide rectangular aperture)

  • Operating band: Ku-band receive (10.7–12.7 GHz), Ka-band transmit (14.0–14.5 GHz)

  • Approximate element count: 1,500–2,000 elements

  • Maximum downlink throughput: \(\geq 200\) Mbps

  • Transmit EIRP: \(\approx 46\) dBW

  • Receive \(G/T\): \(\approx 13\) dB/K

  • Scan range: \(\pm 75\degree\) from boresight (full sky hemisphere coverage)

  • Power consumption: 50–75 W during operation

  • Form factor: weatherproof, tiltable mount with 5–35recommended mounting angle

Mass production has driven terminal cost below $500 (subsidized), with per-unit manufacturing cost targets of $200–$300 as volume scales to millions of units, enabled primarily by the transition to SiGe BiCMOS T/R modules fabricated in standard CMOS foundries (GlobalFoundries, TSMC 65 nm and below).

docs.title: 14.10.2 OneWeb and Competitive Designs
docs.text: The OneWeb terminal (Kymeta FlatSat derivative and Hughes concept) uses a similar electronically steered aperture at Ku-band. The Intelsat/SES flat-panel terminal products for aero and maritime applications use separate transmit and receive apertures to avoid the complexity of a duplex T/R module. The maritime market, with higher terminal price tolerance, adopted electronically steered antennas earlier than residential markets.

docs.title: 14.11 Digital Beamforming
docs.text:
Digital beamforming (DBF) replaces the analog phase shifters and combiners of a classical phased array with digital processing. Each receive element (or subarray) has its own analog-to-digital converter (ADC), and beamforming weights are applied in the digital domain:

\[y_k[n] = \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} w_m^{(k)*} \cdot x_m[n]\tag{14.22}\]

where \(y_k[n]\) is the \(k\)-th beam output, \(x_m[n]\) is the digitized signal from element \(m\), and \(w_m^{(k)}\) are the complex beamforming weights for beam \(k\). DBF enables:

  1. Simultaneous formation of \(K\) independent beams, each with arbitrary pointing, tapering, and null placement

  2. Null steering to suppress interference from specific directions

  3. Adaptive beamforming: MVDR (Minimum Variance Distortionless Response) weights:

    \[\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{MVDR}} = \frac{\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{a}(\theta_0)}{\mathbf{a}^H(\theta_0)\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{a}(\theta_0)}\tag{14.23}\]

    where \(\mathbf{R}\) is the received signal covariance matrix and \(\mathbf{a}(\theta_0)\) is the array steering vector.

  4. Software-defined beam shapes without hardware reconfiguration

  5. On-board massive MIMO processing for multi-user spatial multiplexing

The SES Quantum satellite (Airbus Defence & Space, launched 2021) employs a fully software-defined payload with digital beamforming, allowing the beam shapes, pointing, and frequency allocation to be reprogrammed in orbit via ground command—a paradigm shift from the fixed hardware of conventional GEO satellites.

docs.title: 14.12.1 Far-Field Test Range
docs.text:
Classical antenna gain measurement requires the transmitting antenna to be in the far field of the antenna under test (AUT). The far-field distance (Fraunhofer distance) is:

\[R_{\mathrm{ff}} = \frac{2D^2}{\lambda}\tag{14.24}\]

For a 3 m antenna at 14 GHz (\(\lambda = 21.4\) mm): \(R_{\mathrm{ff}} = 2(3)^2/0.0214 = 840\) m. This requires either an outdoor range (susceptible to multipath and weather) or an impractically large anechoic chamber.

docs.title: 14.12.2 Compact Antenna Test Range (CATR)
docs.text:
A CATR uses a precision-machined parabolic or dual-reflector system to convert the spherical wave from a nearby feed into a collimated plane wave at the AUT location, effectively simulating the far field at a distance of only a few meters. Typical CATR specifications:

  • Quiet zone diameter: 0.5–3 m

  • Amplitude taper in quiet zone: \(< 0.5\) dB

  • Phase variation in quiet zone: \(< 5\degree\)

  • Frequency range: 1–110 GHz

  • Required measurement room length: approximately \(R_{\mathrm{ff}}/10\) to \(R_{\mathrm{ff}}/50\)

docs.title: 14.12.3 Near-Field Measurement
docs.text: Near-field measurement systems scan a probe antenna across a planar, cylindrical, or spherical surface close to the AUT and transform the measured near-field data to the far field via the Fourier transform relationship (planar near field) or wave expansion coefficients (spherical near field). Spherical near-field scanning is the gold standard for satellite antenna characterization, providing the full 4\(\pi\) steradian pattern.

docs.title: 14.13 Feed Network Design
docs.text:
The feed network distributes RF power from the transmitter to the array elements (transmit) or combines signals from elements to the receiver (receive). The choice of feed network technology depends on frequency, loss budget, and complexity:

  • Waveguide: Lowest loss (0.01–0.05 dB/m at Ku-band), used for satellite transmit feeds and high-power applications; mass penalty is significant.

  • Microstrip: Compact, low cost, easily integrated with MMIC; higher loss (0.1–1.0 dB/m at Ku-band); suitable for element-level distribution in compact arrays.

  • Butler matrix: An \(N \times N\) passive beamforming network producing \(N\) orthogonal beams from \(N\) ports, using only 90hybrid couplers and fixed phase shifters. A \(4\times 4\) Butler matrix uses 4 hybrids and 2 crossovers, producing 4 beams at fixed angles \(\theta = \pm\arcsin(1/(2N)) = \pm 14.5\degree\) and \(\pm 48.6\degree\) for \(N=4\), \(d=\lambda/2\).

  • Blass matrix: A general multiple-beam forming network using directional couplers along transmission line buses; allows arbitrary beam positions but is lossy and complex.

  • Rotman lens: A true-time-delay beamforming lens for broadband (squint-free) operation; achieves equal path lengths for multiple beam ports; naturally suited to wideband waveforms and UWB radar.

docs.title: 14.14 On-Board Array Calibration
docs.text:
Active phased arrays require periodic amplitude and phase calibration to correct for thermal drift, component aging, and manufacturing variations. Satellite-based calibration approaches include:

  1. Mutual coupling injection: A signal injected at one element couples to adjacent elements via the mutual coupling of the array and can be used to measure relative amplitude/phase.

  2. Pilot signal injection: Known calibration tones are injected at dedicated calibration ports and measured at the receive port after passing through the array manifold.

  3. Over-the-air calibration: Ground-based reference stations transmit known signals that are received by all elements; comparison with expected phase fronts yields element-level calibration corrections.

  4. Self-calibration using natural sources: Radio stars (Cassiopeia A, Cygnus A) serve as known amplitude/phase reference sources for large aperture arrays.

Calibration accuracy requirements are driven by the sidelobe level target: to achieve \(-30\) dBc sidelobes, amplitude calibration must be within \(\pm 0.5\) dB RMS and phase calibration within \(\pm 5\degree\) RMS across the array.

docs.title: 14.15.1 VSAT Dish Antennas
docs.text: Very Small Aperture Terminal (VSAT) dishes range from 0.6 m (Ku-band receive) to 2.4 m (enterprise hub stations). Mechanical construction uses stamped aluminum or fiberglass panels assembled to a parabolic contour, achieving surface accuracy of 0.5–1.0 mm RMS for Ku-band operation. The pointing alignment is typically performed manually using a signal strength meter, with \(\pm 0.2\degree\) accuracy achievable by a trained installer.

docs.title: 14.15.2 Maritime and Aeronautical Stabilized Platforms
docs.text: Maritime and aeronautical satellite terminals must maintain pointing to the satellite despite vehicle motion. A gyro-stabilized two-axis mount (azimuth + elevation) or three-axis mount (azimuth + elevation + cross-elevation) decouples the antenna from platform motion. Platform rate sensors (fiber-optic or ring laser gyroscopes) measure angular rate, and servo drives counteract motion to maintain pointing within \(< 0.1\degree\) in elevation and azimuth. For Ku-band with HPBW \(\approx 3\degree\) (1.2 m dish), this keeps the antenna within \(<3\%\) of peak gain at all times.

docs.title: 14.16 Summary
docs.text:
Satellite antenna engineering encompasses an extraordinary range of technologies, from simple horn feeds to electronically steered arrays with thousands of active elements. The fundamental tradeoff—high gain requires large aperture, which requires either a large mechanical structure or many active elements—drives the technology choices for each application.

Key design relationships:

  • Gain: \(G = \eta_a (\pi D/\lambda)^2\) — doubles with aperture area, increases \(\times 4\) with frequency doubling at same aperture

  • HPBW: \(\theta \approx 70\lambda/D\) — narrows proportionally with aperture at fixed wavelength

  • Phased array element spacing: \(d \leq \lambda/2\) to suppress grating lobes

  • Far-field distance: \(R_{\mathrm{ff}} = 2D^2/\lambda\) — limits antenna range measurement

  • Scan loss for planar array: \(\propto \cos\theta\) per element, totaling \(\sim\)3 dB at 60scan

Emerging trends include mass-produced SiGe flat-panel arrays for LEO broadband user terminals, software-defined beams using on-board DBF, and deployable mesh reflectors at Ka-band with sub-millimeter surface accuracy.

Summary of Key Antenna Relationships:

\[\begin{align*} G &= \eta_a \left(\frac{\pi D}{\lambda}\right)^2 && \text{(aperture gain)} \\ \theta_{\mathrm{HPBW}} &\approx 70\lambda/D \quad [\mathrm{deg}] && \text{(circular aperture)} \\ R_{\mathrm{ff}} &= 2D^2/\lambda && \text{(far-field distance)} \\ d &\leq \lambda/2 && \text{(no grating lobes, full scan)} \\ G(\theta_0) &= G_0 \cos^q\theta_0 && \text{(phased array scan loss)} \end{align*}\]

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. A parabolic reflector antenna has diameter \(D = 2.4\) m and operates at 14 GHz. Calculate: (a) the aperture area, (b) the theoretical maximum gain (\(\eta_a = 1\)), (c) the actual gain with \(\eta_a = 0.63\), and (d) the half-power beamwidth.

  2. An offset-fed parabolic reflector has a parent parabola with \(f/D_{\mathrm{parent}} = 0.45\). Explain why the offset configuration eliminates aperture blockage and describe the two main performance benefits. What new challenge does the offset geometry introduce regarding polarization?

  3. A linear phased array has 64 elements at \(d = \lambda/2\) spacing operating at 12 GHz. The beam is scanned to \(\theta_0 = 45\degree\). Calculate: (a) the required progressive phase shift between adjacent elements, (b) the grating lobe location (confirm there is no grating lobe within real space), and (c) the scan loss assuming \(\cos^1\theta\) element pattern.

  4. An AstroMesh deployable reflector has a diameter of 12 m and operates at 1.6 GHz. Using the Ruze equation, calculate the maximum permissible RMS surface error to maintain \(\eta_{\mathrm{surface}} \geq 0.90\). Compare this to the RMS surface error required at 20 GHz for the same efficiency.

  5. Calculate the total dissipated DC power in a 1024-element Ku-band AESA user terminal where each PA element delivers 50 mW RF output with 28% power added efficiency. Include the LNA DC power (5 mW per element) and phase shifter power (1 mW per element) and estimate the required thermal management area if the panel temperature must remain below \(70\degree\)C in a \(+40\degree\)C ambient with a heat flux limit of 0.5 W/cm\(^2\).

docs.title: Chapter 15: Digital Signal Processing for Satellites
docs.text: Chapter Objectives This chapter covers the principles and implementation of digital signal processing (DSP) systems for satellite communications. Topics include software-defined radio architectures, digital filtering, modulation and coding, spread spectrum techniques, OFDM, interference mitigation, on-board processing, beamforming, and compressed sensing for Earth observation.

docs.title: 15.1 Introduction to Space DSP
docs.text:
Digital signal processing has become the cornerstone of modern satellite communication systems. The transition from analog to digital processing has fundamentally transformed how satellites generate, transmit, receive, and exploit signals. Space-grade DSP systems must satisfy a demanding set of requirements that differ substantially from terrestrial implementations: they must operate reliably under intense radiation exposure, within tight power and mass budgets, and across temperature extremes ranging from \(-180^\circ\)C to \(+150^\circ\)C in the thermal cycling environment of low Earth orbit.

The evolution of space DSP follows closely the advances in VLSI technology and EDA tools. Early satellites relied on fixed-function analog circuits; modern spacecraft incorporate reprogrammable FPGAs and radiation-hardened digital signal processors capable of executing trillions of operations per second. This flexibility enables satellites to be reconfigured on-orbit to serve new missions, adapt to changing interference environments, or correct design errors discovered after launch.

Key performance metrics for space DSP hardware include:

  • Radiation tolerance: Total ionizing dose (TID) up to 100 krad(Si) for GEO missions, single-event latch-up (SEL) immunity, and single-event upset (SEU) mitigation through triple-module redundancy (TMR) or EDAC.

  • Power efficiency: Operations per watt (GOPS/W) is critical; space-grade FPGAs achieve 10–100\(\times\) lower efficiency than commercial parts but maintain functionality under radiation.

  • Processing throughput: Wideband channelizers may require processing bandwidths of 500 MHz to 4 GHz, demanding real-time throughput of \(10^{10}\)–\(10^{12}\) operations per second.

  • Latency: Interactive voice and video applications over satellite require end-to-end latencies below 280 ms (ITU-T G.114 recommendation), placing tight bounds on codec and processing delays.

Radiation Effects on DSP Hardware Cosmic rays and trapped belt protons can flip bits in SRAM-based FPGAs, causing single-event upsets (SEUs). Mitigation strategies include configuration scrubbing (reading and rewriting the FPGA bitstream every 10–100 ms), TMR for critical logic, and EDAC-protected memory. Flash-based FPGAs (Microsemi SmartFusion2) are inherently SEU-immune in the configuration memory but require careful attention to combinational logic. Radiation-hardened ASICs offer the highest TID tolerance (up to 1 Mrad) but lack in-orbit reprogrammability.

docs.title: 15.2 Software-Defined Radio Architecture
docs.text: Software-defined radio (SDR) replaces traditional fixed-function analog hardware with a combination of wideband RF front-end hardware and flexible digital processing. In an ideal SDR, the analog-to-digital converter (ADC) is placed as close to the antenna as possible, and all signal processing—filtering, demodulation, decoding—is performed in software running on a reconfigurable digital platform.

docs.title: 15.2.1 SDR Block Diagram
docs.text:
A typical space SDR receiver chain consists of:

  1. Antenna: Aperture-coupled patch, horn, or reflector providing \(G/T\) performance.

  2. Low-Noise Amplifier (LNA): Sets system noise figure; GaAs pHEMT achieves \(N_F < 0.5\) dB at 20 GHz.

  3. Bandpass Filter (BPF): Preselect filter suppresses out-of-band interference and LNA noise before mixing.

  4. Downconverter: Heterodyne or direct-conversion architecture; dual-conversion preferred for image rejection.

  5. Variable Gain Amplifier (VGA): Automatic gain control (AGC) maintains ADC input level across dynamic range.

  6. ADC: Nyquist or bandpass sampling; 12–16 bits at 100 MS/s to 10 GS/s.

  7. FPGA/DSP: Channelization, demodulation, decoding, and output formatting.

Figure 15.1. Generic software-defined radio (SDR) receiver architecture for satellite applications. The analog RF chain downconverts the received signal to baseband or intermediate frequency before the ADC, after which all processing is performed digitally on an FPGA or DSP processor.

docs.title: 15.2.2 ADC and DAC Specifications
docs.text:
The ADC is the critical interface between the analog RF world and the digital processing domain. Key performance parameters include:

Effective Number of Bits (ENOB): The ENOB characterizes the true dynamic range of the ADC accounting for noise and distortion:

\[\text{ENOB} = \frac{\text{SINAD} - 1.76}{6.02}\tag{15.1}\]

where SINAD is the signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio in dB. A 16-bit ADC typically achieves ENOB of 12–14 bits due to thermal noise and nonlinearity.

Spurious-Free Dynamic Range (SFDR): The ratio between the fundamental signal and the largest spurious component. Space ADCs must achieve SFDR \(>\) 70 dBc to avoid interference from harmonics and intermodulation products.

Nyquist Criterion: The sampling frequency must satisfy:

\[f_s \geq 2 B_{\text{signal}}\tag{15.2}\]

For bandpass sampling (undersampling), signals centered at \(f_c\) with bandwidth \(B\) can be sampled at \(f_s \geq 2B\) if \(f_c\) falls in the appropriate Nyquist zone, enabling lower-cost ADCs to process high-frequency IF signals without a full downconversion stage.

Representative space-qualified ADC devices include the Analog Devices AD9208 (14-bit, 3 GSPS) and the e2v EV10AQ190 (10-bit, 10 GSPS quad-channel), both available in radiation-tolerant variants certified to 100 krad(Si).

docs.title: 15.2.3 Programmable Hardware Platforms
docs.text:
Modern space SDR systems employ a range of programmable processing platforms:

  • Xilinx (AMD) Virtex UltraScale+: The XQRVU37P space-grade variant offers 2.35M logic cells, 12 Gbps GTH transceivers, and HBM2 memory. Operating at 600 MHz, it can process 4 GHz instantaneous bandwidth with polyphase filter banks. TID rating: 100 krad(Si); SEU cross-section: \(< 10^{-8}\) cm\(^2\)/device.

  • NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier: Commercial-grade Jetson modules are used in low-Earth orbit missions (ISS experiments, LEO Earth observation) for machine learning inference at 32 TOPS with 30 W power envelope. Software TMR and shielding mitigate SEU.

  • Microchip RTG4: Flash-based FPGA, 150 krad TID, 4M gates, SEU-immune configuration memory, used in deep-space and GEO missions requiring extreme reliability. Available in CCGA624 hermetic ceramic package.

  • NXP QorIQ T2080: Radiation-tolerant PowerPC processor for housekeeping and protocol processing alongside FPGA-based waveform engines.

docs.title: 15.3 Digital Filtering
docs.text: Digital filters are the fundamental building blocks of every DSP system. In satellite communications, filters perform channel selection, noise reduction, pulse shaping, and signal conditioning for subsequent processing stages.

docs.title: 15.3.1 FIR Filters
docs.text:
A finite impulse response (FIR) filter of order \(N\) is characterized by the transfer function:

\[H(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} b_k\, z^{-k}\tag{15.3}\]

where \(b_k\) are the filter coefficients and \(z^{-k}\) represents a delay of \(k\) samples. The frequency response is obtained by evaluating on the unit circle (\(z = e^{j\omega}\)):

\[H\!\left(e^{j\omega}\right) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} b_k\, e^{-j\omega k}\tag{15.4}\]

FIR filters offer two critical advantages for satellite systems: linear phase (all frequency components experience identical group delay, eliminating phase distortion) and inherent stability (no feedback, so all poles are at the origin).

The Parks-McClellan/Remez exchange algorithm provides the optimal equiripple FIR filter design. Given specifications for passband ripple \(\delta_p\), stopband attenuation \(\delta_s\), passband edge \(\omega_p\), and stopband edge \(\omega_s\), the algorithm minimizes the maximum weighted Chebyshev approximation error:

\[\min_{\{b_k\}} \max_{\omega \in \mathcal{F}} W(\omega) \left| H_d(\omega) - H\!\left(e^{j\omega}\right) \right|\tag{15.5}\]

where \(\mathcal{F}\) is the union of passband and stopband frequency bands, \(H_d(\omega)\) is the desired response, and \(W(\omega)\) is a frequency-dependent weighting function.

FIR Filter Length Estimation A useful rule of thumb for estimating FIR filter tap count \(N\) is the Harris approximation: \(N \approx -20\log_{10}(\delta_s \delta_p) / (14.6\, \Delta f)\), where \(\Delta f\) is the normalized transition bandwidth. For 60 dB stopband attenuation with 1% transition bandwidth, this gives \(N \approx 400\) taps. Root-raised-cosine (RRC) pulse shaping filters for QPSK typically use 32–64 taps at 4 samples per symbol.

docs.title: 15.3.2 IIR Filters
docs.text:
Infinite impulse response (IIR) filters use feedback to achieve steep roll-off with fewer coefficients than equivalent FIR designs. The general IIR transfer function is:

\[H(z) = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k\, z^{-k}}{1 + \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{N} a_k\, z^{-k}}\tag{15.6}\]

Butterworth filters provide maximally flat magnitude response in the passband with no ripple, at the cost of a moderate roll-off rate. The magnitude squared response of an \(N\)-th order Butterworth filter is:

\[|H(j\Omega)|^2 = \frac{1}{1 + \left(\Omega/\Omega_c\right)^{2N}}\tag{15.7}\]

Chebyshev Type I filters equiripple in the passband and monotone in the stopband, achieving steeper roll-off than Butterworth for the same filter order. The magnitude response:

\[|H(j\Omega)|^2 = \frac{1}{1 + \varepsilon^2 T_N^2(\Omega/\Omega_c)}\tag{15.8}\]

where \(T_N(\cdot)\) is the \(N\)-th Chebyshev polynomial and \(\varepsilon\) controls passband ripple.

IIR filters are preferred where computational resources are limited (e.g., analog channel pre-select filters digitally implemented), but require careful attention to coefficient quantization sensitivity and potential limit cycle oscillations.

docs.title: 15.3.3 Polyphase Filter Banks for Channelization
docs.text:
A polyphase filter bank (PFB) efficiently divides a wideband signal into \(M\) narrowband channels simultaneously. It is the workhorse of satellite on-board channelizers and digital multi-beam receivers. The computational efficiency arises from commuting the downsampling operation before the subfilter computations.

For an \(M\)-channel filter bank, the \(k\)-th polyphase component of the prototype lowpass filter \(H(z)\) with transfer function \(\sum_n h[n] z^{-n}\) is defined as:

\[E_k(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} h[nM + k]\, z^{-n}, \quad k = 0, 1, …, M-1\tag{15.9}\]

The analysis filter bank applies an \(M\)-point IFFT to the polyphase outputs, producing \(M\) simultaneously filtered and \(M\)-fold downsampled channels. Computational complexity is \(O(M \log_2 M)\) multiply-accumulate operations per input sample, compared to \(O(M \cdot N_{\rm filt})\) for \(M\) independent filters where \(N_{\rm filt}\) is the prototype filter length.

Overlapped PFBs (with oversampling factor \(K/M > 1\)) provide superior stopband rejection and reduced inter-channel interference, at the cost of additional computation. The Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+ can implement a 64-channel oversampled PFB operating at 2 GHz input sample rate using approximately 30% of available DSP48E2 slices.

docs.title: 15.4 Modulation and Demodulation
docs.text: Satellite modulation schemes must balance spectral efficiency against power efficiency, since satellite amplifier power and available downlink spectrum are both constrained resources.

docs.title: 15.4.1 Phase-Shift Keying Modulations
docs.text:
BPSK (Binary Phase-Shift Keying): Modulates one bit per symbol onto two phases \(\{0^\circ, 180^\circ\}\). The bit error rate over an AWGN channel is:

\[P_b^{\text{BPSK}} = Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2E_b}{N_0}}\right)\tag{15.10}\]

where \(Q(x) = \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{erfc}(x/\sqrt{2})\) is the Q-function and \(E_b/N_0\) is the energy per bit to noise density ratio.

QPSK (Quadrature Phase-Shift Keying): Two bits per symbol, four phases \(\{45^\circ, 135^\circ, 225^\circ, 315^\circ\}\). The BER in AWGN is identical to BPSK when plotted against \(E_b/N_0\), but achieves double the spectral efficiency (2 b/s/Hz ideal).

8PSK: Three bits per symbol on eight equally spaced phases. The Gray-coded BER:

\[P_b^{\text{8PSK}} \approx \frac{2}{3}\, Q\!\left(\sqrt{6\, \frac{E_b}{N_0}} \sin\frac{\pi}{8}\right)\tag{15.11}\]

16APSK and 32APSK: Amplitude-and-phase-shift keying constellations optimized for nonlinear satellite channels operating near HPA saturation. The 16APSK constellation consists of 4 points on an inner ring of radius \(r_1\) and 12 points on an outer ring of radius \(r_2\), with the ratio \(r_2/r_1 = 2.57\) optimized for the DVB-S2 standard. The 32APSK uses three rings. These constellations support spectral efficiencies up to 4.99 b/s/Hz in DVB-S2X.

docs.title: 15.4.2 Matched Filter Receiver
docs.text:
The optimal receiver for maximizing SNR in AWGN is the matched filter. For a transmitted pulse \(s(t)\), the matched filter impulse response is \(h(t) = s(T - t)\) (time-reversed and delayed replica). At the sampling instant, the output SNR is:

\[\mathrm{SNR}_{\text{MF}} = \frac{2 E_s}{N_0}\tag{15.12}\]

where \(E_s\) is the symbol energy and \(N_0/2\) is the two-sided noise power spectral density. The matched filter is equivalently implemented as a correlator receiver that integrates the product of the received signal with a local replica of the transmitted pulse.

docs.title: 15.4.3 Timing and Carrier Recovery
docs.text:
Mueller-Müller Timing Recovery: A decision-directed timing error detector (TED) widely used in satellite modems. The timing error is estimated as:

\[\varepsilon[n] = \hat{a}[n-1] \cdot y[n] - \hat{a}[n] \cdot y[n-1]\tag{15.13}\]

where \(y[n]\) is the current sample at the nominal sampling instant, \(y[n-1]\) is the previous sample, and \(\hat{a}[n]\) are data decisions from the slicer. The TED output drives a numerically controlled oscillator (NCO) through a loop filter to adjust the sampling phase.

Costas Loop (Carrier Phase Recovery): A second-order PLL variant that tracks the carrier phase of a suppressed-carrier modulation such as BPSK or QPSK. The phase error detector output for QPSK is:

\[e_\phi = I \cdot \operatorname{sgn}(Q) - Q \cdot \operatorname{sgn}(I)\tag{15.14}\]

The PLL loop bandwidth \(B_L\) is chosen as a compromise between phase noise tracking ability (favoring wider \(B_L\)) and noise performance (favoring narrower \(B_L\)), typically 0.1–1% of the symbol rate \(R_s\).

docs.title: 15.5 Channel Coding
docs.text: Channel coding adds structured redundancy to the transmitted data, enabling the receiver to detect and correct bit errors introduced by the channel. Modern satellite systems employ powerful codes operating within 1–2 dB of the Shannon capacity limit.

docs.title: 15.5.1 Convolutional Codes
docs.text:
A rate \(R = 1/2\), constraint length \(K = 7\) convolutional encoder is the historical standard for satellite communications (used in GPS, CCSDS heritage missions). The encoder contains \(K - 1 = 6\) memory elements with generator polynomials (octal) \(g_1 = 171_8\) and \(g_2 = 133_8\).

The free distance \(d_{\text{free}} = 10\) determines the asymptotic bit error probability:

\[P_b \leq \frac{1}{k} \sum_{d=d_{\text{free}}}^{\infty} w_d \cdot P_d\tag{15.15}\]

where \(w_d\) is the input weight of error events at Hamming distance \(d\) and \(P_d\) is the pairwise error probability. Viterbi decoding (maximum likelihood sequence estimation) achieves a coding gain of approximately 5–6 dB at \(P_b = 10^{-5}\) versus uncoded BPSK over an AWGN channel.

docs.title: 15.5.2 Turbo Codes
docs.text:
Turbo codes (Berrou et al., 1993) use parallel concatenated convolutional codes (PCCC) with iterative decoding. The encoder consists of two recursive systematic convolutional (RSC) encoders separated by a pseudo-random interleaver of length \(N\). The iterative decoder exchanges extrinsic soft information (log-likelihood ratios, LLRs) between two BCJR (MAP) decoders:

\[L(u_k \,|\, \mathbf{r}) = \log \frac{P(u_k = +1 \,|\, \mathbf{r})}{P(u_k = -1 \,|\, \mathbf{r})} = L_a(u_k) + L_e(u_k)\tag{15.16}\]

where \(L_a\) is the a priori LLR and \(L_e\) is the extrinsic LLR from the other decoder. The 3GPP Release 8 LTE turbo code (rate 1/3, block lengths 40–6144 bits) achieves within 0.5 dB of Shannon for block lengths exceeding 1000 bits at \(P_b = 10^{-4}\).

docs.title: 15.5.3 LDPC Codes
docs.text:
Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, invented by Gallager (1962) and rediscovered by MacKay (1996), are defined by a sparse parity-check matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) with roughly \(d_c\) ones per column and \(d_v\) ones per row (the Tanner graph). The belief propagation (sum-product) algorithm iterates check-to-variable and variable-to-check messages:

\[\mu_{c \to v} = 2 \tanh^{-1}\!\left( \prod_{v' \in \mathcal{N}(c) \setminus v} \tanh\!\left(\frac{\mu_{v' \to c}}{2}\right) \right)\tag{15.17}\]

The DVB-S2 standard specifies 28 LDPC codes with rates from 1/4 to 9/10 and block lengths of 16200 (short) or 64800 (normal) bits. These codes achieve BER “waterfall” regions 0.5–2.0 dB from the Shannon limit, enabling the aggressive spectral efficiencies required for high-throughput satellite (HTS) systems operating at hundreds of Gbps aggregate capacity.

docs.title: 15.5.4 Polar Codes
docs.text:
Polar codes (Arıkan, 2009) are the first family of codes proven to achieve the symmetric capacity of binary-input discrete memoryless channels with an explicit construction and low-complexity encoding and decoding. The key idea is channel polarization: applying an \(N = 2^n\)-point butterfly transform creates \(N\) synthetic channels, some approaching noiseless and others approaching pure noise. Data bits are placed on the reliable channels; “frozen” bits (set to 0 or known values) occupy the unreliable channels.

The successive cancellation (SC) decoder operates with complexity \(O(N \log N)\). The successive cancellation list (SCL) decoder with list size \(L = 8\), optionally augmented with a cyclic redundancy check (CRC-aided SCL), achieves performance exceeding turbo codes at short block lengths (200–1000 bits). Polar codes are adopted in 5G NR for control channels (PBCH, PDCCH) and are under evaluation for future satellite uplink standards.

docs.title: 15.5.5 Reed-Solomon Codes
docs.text:
RS(255, 239) is a widely used outer code in concatenated coding schemes (inner convolutional or LDPC + outer RS). The code operates on 8-bit symbols over GF(\(2^8\)), correcting up to \(t = 8\) symbol errors per 255-symbol block. The minimum Hamming distance is \(d_{\min} = 2t + 1 = 17\). RS codes are particularly effective against burst errors and are specified in CCSDS 101.0-B for space data link protocols. The concatenated RS(255,239) \(+\) rate-1/2 convolutional code was standard in the Voyager deep-space missions, achieving approximately 8 dB combined coding gain.
