docs.title: 15.6 Spread Spectrum
docs.text: Spread spectrum techniques deliberately expand the transmitted signal bandwidth far beyond the minimum required for the information rate. This provides resistance to narrowband jamming, low probability of intercept (LPI), multiple access capability (CDMA), and accurate two-way ranging.

docs.title: 15.6.1 Direct Sequence Spread Spectrum (DSSS)
docs.text:
In DSSS, the data signal \(d(t)\) is multiplied by a pseudorandom noise (PN) code \(c(t)\) running at the chip rate \(R_c \gg R_b\) (data bit rate). The transmitted signal is:

\[s(t) = \sqrt{2P}\; d(t)\; c(t) \cos(2\pi f_c t)\tag{15.18}\]

The processing gain (PG), which equals the jamming margin in a barrage jamming scenario, is:

\[\mathrm{PG} = \frac{B_{\text{SS}}}{B_{\text{data}}} = \frac{R_c}{R_b}\tag{15.19}\]

A GPS L1 C/A signal with \(R_c = 1.023\) Mcps and \(R_b = 50\) bps achieves \(\mathrm{PG} = 43.1\) dB. The anti-jamming margin (J/S margin) for reliable reception is:

\[\left.\frac{J}{S}\right|_{\text{max}} = \mathrm{PG} - \left(\frac{E_b}{N_0}\right)_{\text{req}}\tag{15.20}\]

For GPS C/A with \(\mathrm{PG} = 43\) dB and \((E_b/N_0)_{\text{req}} = 10\) dB, the maximum tolerable jamming-to-signal ratio is 33 dB (a factor of 2000:1 in power).

docs.title: 15.6.2 GPS Signal Structure
docs.text:
The GPS L1 C/A signal (1575.42 MHz) employs Gold codes of length 1023 chips at 1.023 Mcps, with code repeat period of 1 ms. Gold codes are constructed from two maximal-length sequences (m-sequences) of length \(2^{10} - 1\) via modulo-2 addition with varying delays, yielding 1025 codes with bounded cross-correlation: \(|R_{xy}(\tau)| \leq 65/1023 \approx -23.9\) dB for any offset.

The GPS L5 signal (1176.45 MHz) uses a 10.23 Mcps chip rate with longer codes (\(2^{10230} - 1\)), providing 10 dB more processing gain and improved multipath rejection compared to L1 C/A. Military M-code at 10.23 Mcps with classified PRN sequences provides an additional 20 dB of anti-jam margin over C/A code, enabled by a higher-gain antenna (directional controlled reception pattern antenna, CRPA) and advanced receiver tracking.

docs.title: 15.6.3 Frequency-Hopping Spread Spectrum (FHSS)
docs.text:
In FHSS, the carrier frequency hops across \(N\) channels according to a pseudorandom sequence. During each dwell time \(T_d\), a narrowband signal occupies one frequency channel. The hopping rate \(f_h = 1/T_d\) determines resistance to follower jamming: a fast hopper with \(f_h > 10^3\) hops/s prevents the jammer from measuring the frequency and retransmitting before the next hop occurs.

The processing gain for FHSS against partial-band jamming across fraction \(\rho\) of the band is:

\[\mathrm{PG}_{\text{FHSS}} = 10\log_{10}(N)\; \text{dB}\tag{15.21}\]

Military FHSS systems (HAVE QUICK UHF radio, SINCGARS VHF) hop over 25 kHz channels covering 30 MHz bandwidth, giving PG \(= 30\) dB. CDMA systems exploit orthogonal Gold codes among users in the same bandwidth, with each user recovering its signal via the processing gain while treating other users’ signals as noise (interference-limited).

docs.title: 15.7 OFDM Systems
docs.text: Orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) divides the wideband channel into \(N\) narrowband orthogonal subcarriers, each experiencing nearly flat fading over its symbol duration. OFDM is the modulation of choice for broadband wireless (LTE, 5G, Wi-Fi) and is increasingly considered for satellite systems despite unique challenges posed by LEO Doppler shifts and HPA nonlinearity.

docs.title: 15.7.1 OFDM Fundamentals
docs.text:
The OFDM baseband signal over one symbol duration \(T_s\) is:

\[s(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} X_k\, e^{j2\pi k\,\Delta f\, t}, \quad 0 \leq t < T_s\tag{15.22}\]

where \(\Delta f = 1/T_s\) ensures subcarrier orthogonality: \(\int_0^{T_s} e^{j2\pi k \Delta f t} e^{-j2\pi l \Delta f t}\,dt = 0\) for \(k \neq l\). The modulator implements this as an \(N\)-point IDFT, and the demodulator as an \(N\)-point DFT.

The cyclic prefix (CP) of length \(N_{CP}\) samples (duration \(T_{CP} = N_{CP}/f_s\)) is prepended to each symbol. The CP must satisfy \(T_{CP} \geq \tau_{\max}\) (maximum channel delay spread) to eliminate inter-symbol interference. It converts linear convolution with the channel into circular convolution, enabling simple per-subcarrier one-tap equalization. The spectral efficiency reduction from CP overhead is:

\[\eta_{\text{CP}} = \frac{N}{N + N_{CP}} = \frac{T_s}{T_s + T_{CP}}\tag{15.23}\]

docs.title: 15.7.2 PAPR and Crest Factor Reduction
docs.text:
A critical disadvantage of OFDM is its high Peak-to-Average Power Ratio (PAPR). With \(N\) subcarriers, when all add coherently, the PAPR can reach \(10\log_{10}(N)\) dB. For satellite HPA operation, high PAPR forces the amplifier to operate far from saturation (large output back-off, OBO), directly reducing DC-to-RF power efficiency, which is a critical resource on a satellite.

Crest factor reduction (CFR) techniques include:

  • Clipping and filtering: Hard clip at threshold \(A\), then filter to restore spectral mask. Introduces a clipping noise floor that limits achievable EVM.

  • Active constellation extension (ACE): Move outer constellation points outward to cancel time-domain peaks while maintaining the spectral mask.

  • Tone reservation: Reserve a subset of subcarriers exclusively for a PAPR reduction peak-canceling waveform (no data on reserved tones).

  • Selected mapping (SLM): Multiply the frequency-domain block by \(U\) independent phase rotation vectors, select the variant with minimum PAPR for transmission, and signal the index to the receiver as side information.

docs.title: 15.7.3 DVB-T2 and Satellite OFDM Parameters
docs.text:
The DVB-T2 standard (terrestrial broadcast) employs OFDM with a 32K FFT mode (\(N = 32768\) subcarriers), subcarrier spacing \(\Delta f = 279\) Hz in an 8 MHz channel, and a maximum CP duration of \(1/4 \times T_s \approx 896\) µ s, providing immunity to multipath delays up to 532 km (far beyond the physical requirement but enabling large single-frequency network areas). For 8 MHz channels, the maximum CP is approximately 6.7 ms.

For satellite applications (DVB-SH, S2X extensions), OFDM faces the challenge of large Doppler shifts from LEO platforms. A LEO satellite at 550 km altitude moving at 7.6 km/s relative to a ground station produces a carrier Doppler shift of:

\[f_D = \frac{v_r}{c} f_c \approx \frac{7600}{3\times 10^8} \times 20 \times 10^9 \approx 507 \text{ kHz}\tag{15.24}\]

at Ka-band (20 GHz). This frequency offset, if not pre-compensated, can destroy subcarrier orthogonality for the narrow subcarrier spacings used in terrestrial OFDM. Solutions include Doppler pre-compensation at the satellite feeder or terminal, and DFT-spread OFDM (SC-FDMA) which is inherently more robust to frequency offsets.

docs.title: 15.8 Interference Mitigation
docs.text: Satellite systems must cope with interference from co-channel satellites, adjacent satellites, terrestrial systems sharing spectrum (MSS/FSS spectrum sharing), and intentional jamming. Digital signal processing provides powerful tools for interference detection, characterization, and cancellation.

docs.title: 15.8.1 Adaptive Equalization
docs.text:
The LMS (Least Mean Squares) adaptive algorithm updates the equalizer tap weight vector \(\mathbf{w}[n]\) to minimize the mean squared error between filter output and a reference signal:

\[\mathbf{w}[n+1] = \mathbf{w}[n] + \mu\, e[n]\, \mathbf{x}^*[n]\tag{15.25}\]

where \(e[n] = d[n] - \mathbf{w}^H[n]\mathbf{x}[n]\) is the error signal, \(d[n]\) is the desired reference (known training symbol or slicer decision), \(\mathbf{x}[n]\) is the input tap vector, and \(\mu\) is the step size. Convergence requires \(0 < \mu < 1/(N\sigma_x^2)\).

The RLS (Recursive Least Squares) algorithm achieves faster convergence (typically \(2N\) iterations vs. \(>10N\) for LMS) at \(O(N^2)\) computational cost:

\[\begin{align*} \mathbf{k}[n] &= \frac{\lambda^{-1} \mathbf{P}[n-1] \mathbf{x}[n]}{1 + \lambda^{-1} \mathbf{x}^H[n] \mathbf{P}[n-1] \mathbf{x}[n]} \\ \mathbf{w}[n] &= \mathbf{w}[n-1] + \mathbf{k}[n]\, e^*[n] \end{align*}\]

where \(\lambda \in (0,1]\) is a forgetting factor that controls the tracking-variance tradeoff and \(\mathbf{P}[n]\) is the regularized inverse correlation matrix estimate.

docs.title: 15.8.2 Decision Feedback Equalizer
docs.text: The decision feedback equalizer (DFE) consists of a forward filter (FFF) that processes the received signal and a feedback filter (FBF) that subtracts intersymbol interference from previously decoded symbols. The DFE avoids noise enhancement in the forward filter at the cost of error propagation: a decision error in the feedback path corrupts several subsequent symbol decisions. DFEs are effective for frequency-selective satellite channels produced by adjacent beam interference or multipath in non-geostationary orbits.

docs.title: 15.8.3 Successive and Parallel Interference Cancellation
docs.text:
In multi-user satellite systems (CDMA or NOMA uplink), interference cancellation improves achievable throughput:

SIC (Successive Interference Cancellation): Decode users in order of decreasing received SNR. After successfully decoding user \(k\), re-encode and subtract its contribution from the received signal before decoding user \(k+1\). SIC achieves any point on the AWGN MAC capacity region boundary and is optimal for two-user channels.

PIC (Parallel Interference Cancellation): All users are decoded simultaneously using tentative hard or soft decisions. Each successive iteration refines estimates by subtracting the multi-user interference reconstructed from other users’ tentative decisions. PIC converges in fewer satellite round-trip delays than SIC but requires multiple iterations, each introducing processing delay.

docs.title: 15.8.4 GNSS Interference Detection and Mitigation
docs.text:
GNSS receivers are particularly vulnerable to narrowband jamming (both intentional and unintentional from LTE/5G signals in adjacent or harmonically related bands). Detection and mitigation methods include:

  • AGC monitoring: A sudden decrease in AGC gain indicates a strong wideband interference signal saturating the ADC input.

  • Spectral excision: FFT-based detection of spectral peaks above the noise floor, followed by replacing the affected bins with zero or noise-floor values.

  • Adaptive notch filter: An IIR notch filter with time-varying center frequency tracks and suppresses narrowband continuous wave (CW) interferers. The notch frequency is estimated via the LMS algorithm applied to a prediction error filter.

  • STAP: Space-Time Adaptive Processing with a controlled reception pattern antenna (CRPA) array forms spatial nulls toward jammers while maintaining gain toward GNSS satellites, achieving \(> 30\) dB of jamming suppression.

docs.title: 15.9 On-Board Processing Satellites
docs.text: On-board processing (OBP) transponders demodulate, decode, switch, recode, and remodulate signals in space, as opposed to transparent (bent-pipe) transponders that simply amplify and frequency-translate the uplink signal to the downlink without signal regeneration.

docs.title: 15.9.1 Regenerative Transponders vs. Transparent
docs.text:
The key advantages of regenerative (OBP) transponders are:

  • Interference isolation: Uplink interference is not forwarded to the downlink; only decoded data bits are retransmitted, eliminating interference sources that would otherwise enter the downlink.

  • Noise threshold reset: Uplink \(C/N\) and downlink \(C/N\) are treated independently; the overall link margin is not degraded by cascading both noise contributions.

  • On-board switching: Digital crosspoint switch matrices route traffic between beams and transponders without requiring ground-based switching hubs.

  • Bandwidth flexibility: Digital channelizers can be reconfigured to reallocate spectral bandwidth among beams in response to changing traffic demand.

  • On-board ACM: Adaptive coding and modulation decisions can be made based on uplink channel quality measurements, independent of the downlink ACM selection.

docs.title: 15.9.2 Digital Channelizer Architecture
docs.text: A digital channelizer divides the wideband transponder receive band into \(M\) narrowband sub-channels using a polyphase filter bank followed by an \(M\)-point FFT. Representative parameters for HTS missions: \(M = 50\)–\(500\) channels of 36–250 MHz each, from a 500 MHz–4 GHz input band. Output sub-channels feed a digital crosspoint switch that connects any input sub-channel to any beam output. The switch matrix for \(B\) beams and \(M\) channels is an \(M \times B\) non-blocking router implemented in FPGA.

docs.title: 15.9.3 Notable OBP Missions
docs.text:
• Eutelsat KA-SAT (2010): First high-throughput GEO satellite with a fully digital on-board processor. 82 spot beams, 500 MHz channelizer implemented in a 1.4-billion transistor custom ASIC, 70 Gbps aggregate capacity.

  • ViaSat-3 (2023): Approximately 1 Tbps capacity GEO satellite with extensive OBP for flexible beam connectivity, on-demand frequency reuse, and interference mitigation.

  • SkyTerra-1 (2010): L-band MSS satellite with OBP for CDMA uplink demodulation/recode, enabling direct service to handheld terminals without requiring regenerative ground gateways.

docs.title: 15.10 Beamforming and Spatial Processing
docs.text: Phased array antennas combined with digital beamforming (DBF) enable a satellite to simultaneously form multiple narrow, high-gain beams pointed at different ground locations, with independent control of beam shape, pointing, sidelobe level, and null placement.

docs.title: 15.10.1 Digital Beamforming Fundamentals
docs.text:
For an \(N\)-element array with element positions \(\mathbf{r}_n\), the array response (steering) vector to a signal arriving from direction \(\hat{\mathbf{s}}\) at wavelength \(\lambda\) is:

\[\mathbf{a}(\hat{\mathbf{s}}) = \left[ e^{j\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\mathbf{r}_1^T \hat{\mathbf{s}}},\; e^{j\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\mathbf{r}_2^T \hat{\mathbf{s}}}, …, e^{j\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\mathbf{r}_N^T \hat{\mathbf{s}}} \right]^T\tag{15.28}\]

The beamformer output is \(y = \mathbf{w}^H \mathbf{x}\), where \(\mathbf{x}\) is the received signal vector. The conventional (delay-and-sum) beamformer uses \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{a}(\hat{\mathbf{s}}_0)/N\), which maximizes the array gain toward the desired direction \(\hat{\mathbf{s}}_0\) but cannot place nulls on interferers.

docs.title: 15.10.2 MVDR Beamformer
docs.text:
The Minimum Variance Distortionless Response (MVDR) or Capon beamformer minimizes the total output power subject to a unity gain constraint in the desired direction:

\[\mathbf{w}_{\text{MVDR}} = \frac{\mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{a}}{\mathbf{a}^H \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{a}}\tag{15.29}\]

where \(\mathbf{R} = E[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^H] + \sigma_n^2 \mathbf{I}\) is the regularized spatial covariance matrix. The MVDR beamformer automatically places nulls at interference sources while maintaining unity gain in the desired direction, achieving 30–40 dB of jammer suppression with an 8-element array. In practice, \(\mathbf{R}\) is estimated from training data snapshots: \(\hat{\mathbf{R}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbf{x}[k]\mathbf{x}^H[k]\).

docs.title: 15.10.3 DOA Estimation: MUSIC and ESPRIT
docs.text:
MUSIC (Multiple Signal Classification): Exploits the eigendecomposition of \(\mathbf{R}\). The noise subspace \(\mathbf{E}_n\) is spanned by the \(N - d\) eigenvectors corresponding to the smallest (noise) eigenvalues, and is orthogonal to the signal subspace. The MUSIC spatial pseudospectrum is:

\[P_{\text{MUSIC}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{\mathbf{a}^H(\theta)\, \mathbf{E}_n \mathbf{E}_n^H\, \mathbf{a}(\theta)}\tag{15.30}\]

DOA estimates are the \(d\) sharpest peaks of \(P_{\text{MUSIC}}(\theta)\), with resolution capability exceeding the Rayleigh beamwidth when SNR is sufficient.

ESPRIT (Estimation of Signal Parameters via Rotational Invariance Techniques) avoids the peak search by exploiting the rotational invariance property of two identically translated sub-arrays, providing closed-form DOA estimates at lower computational cost.

docs.title: 15.10.4 MIMO Space-Time Block Codes
docs.text:
The Alamouti 2\(\times\)1 space-time block code achieves full transmit diversity order 2 with coding rate 1 symbol per channel use, using two transmit antennas. Over two consecutive symbol periods, the \(2 \times 2\) space-time transmission matrix is:

\[\mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix} s_1 & s_2 \\ -s_2^* & s_1^* \end{bmatrix}\tag{15.31}\]

where column \(t\) represents the transmitted vector at time slot \(t\). The receiver decouples \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) using simple linear combining without requiring channel state information at the transmitter. The diversity gain substantially improves BER at the same SNR compared to single-antenna transmission, particularly important for non-line-of-sight LEO-to-ground links experiencing fast fading due to platform vibration and antenna pointing jitter.

docs.title: 15.11 Compressed Sensing for Earth Observation
docs.text: Earth observation satellites generate enormous data volumes: a hyperspectral imager with 200 spectral bands at 30 m spatial resolution covering a 100 km swath at 7 km/s produces over 100 Gbps of raw pixel data. Compressed sensing (CS) enables sub-Nyquist sampling and sparse signal reconstruction, dramatically reducing on-board data storage and downlink bandwidth requirements.

docs.title: 15.11.1 Sparsity and the CS Framework
docs.text:
A signal \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^N\) is said to be \(K\)-sparse in a basis \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) if it can be represented as:

\[\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\, \boldsymbol{\alpha}, \quad \|\boldsymbol{\alpha}\|_0 = K \ll N\tag{15.32}\]

where \(\|\cdot\|_0\) counts non-zero entries (the \(\ell_0\) “norm”). Hyperspectral images are highly compressible in the wavelet or DCT domain, with 90% of signal energy concentrated in fewer than 10% of the transform coefficients.

The CS measurement process takes \(M \ll N\) incoherent linear measurements:

\[\mathbf{y} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}\, \mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}\, \boldsymbol{\Psi}\, \boldsymbol{\alpha} = \mathbf{A}\, \boldsymbol{\alpha}\tag{15.33}\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\Phi} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\) is the measurement matrix (random Gaussian or Bernoulli entries ensure incoherence with high probability). Recovery of \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) from \(\mathbf{y}\) when \(M < N\) requires that the sensing matrix \(\mathbf{A} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) satisfies the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) of order \(2K\):

\[(1 - \delta_{2K}) \|\boldsymbol{\alpha}\|_2^2 \leq \|\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\|_2^2 \leq (1 + \delta_{2K}) \|\boldsymbol{\alpha}\|_2^2\tag{15.34}\]

for all \(2K\)-sparse \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\). The sufficient condition for stable recovery is \(\delta_{2K} < \sqrt{2} - 1 \approx 0.414\).

docs.title: 15.11.2 Reconstruction Algorithms
docs.text:
OMP (Orthogonal Matching Pursuit): Greedy algorithm that iteratively selects the column of \(\mathbf{A}\) most correlated with the current residual, then orthogonally projects the residual onto the selected support set. Complexity \(O(KMN)\) per reconstruction, requiring \(K\) iterations. Suitable for FPGA implementation with small \(K\).

LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator): Convex \(\ell_1\) relaxation of the combinatorial \(\ell_0\) minimization problem:

\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\alpha}\|_2^2 + \lambda \|\boldsymbol{\alpha}\|_1\tag{15.35}\]

Solved efficiently via ADMM, ISTA/FISTA (fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding), or interior-point methods. The regularization parameter \(\lambda\) balances fidelity and sparsity.

docs.title: 15.11.3 On-Board Implementation and Standards
docs.text:
For a hyperspectral imager achieving 10:1 compression ratio (\(M/N = 0.1\)), the on-board CS processor computes the \(M \times N\) matrix-vector product in real time before the downlink buffer. The total on-board multiply-accumulate rate is \(M \times N \times f_{\rm pixel}\), feasible on an FPGA consuming \(< 5\) W for 100 Mpixel/s throughput.

The CCSDS 122.0-B-2 image data compression standard specifies a lossless and near-lossless wavelet-based compression algorithm (DWT + bit-plane coding) suitable for hardware implementation on FPGAs. Compression ratios of 4:1 (lossless progressive) to 20:1 (near-lossless) are achievable with \(< 1\) W for 100 Mpixel/s. The CCSDS 123.0-B standard extends this to multispectral and hyperspectral data, exploiting inter-band spectral correlations.

Key Performance Summary: Space DSP A well-designed satellite DSP system should achieve:

  • SDR flexibility: \(> 500\) MHz instantaneous bandwidth with 12-bit ENOB ADC

  • Channel coding: LDPC DVB-S2 within 0.5–2.0 dB of Shannon limit

  • Spread spectrum: Processing gain \(> 43\) dB for GPS L1 C/A (anti-jam margin \(> 33\) dB)

  • Beamforming: MVDR adaptive nulling achieving \(> 30\) dB interference suppression

  • On-board processing: 50–500 channel polyphase channelizer with flexible routing

  • Compressed sensing: 10:1 hyperspectral compression within 3 dB SNR of original

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter has surveyed the complete landscape of digital signal processing for satellite systems. Software-defined radio architectures leverage space-qualified FPGAs and radiation-tolerant ADCs to achieve the flexibility required for multi-mission satellites operating across diverse frequency bands and waveform standards. Advanced channel coding—LDPC, turbo, and polar codes—has enabled satellite links to approach the Shannon capacity limit, driving increases in spectral efficiency that are essential for economically viable high-throughput satellite systems. Spread spectrum techniques provide anti-jamming protection and precision ranging for navigation and military applications. OFDM enables high-spectral-efficiency broadband services, with Doppler pre-compensation addressing the unique challenges of LEO platforms. On-board processing regenerative transponders isolate link budgets, improve interference management, and enable intelligent traffic routing. Adaptive beamforming using MVDR and related algorithms provides spatial interference rejection of 30–40 dB. Finally, compressed sensing offers a mathematically principled framework for reducing data volumes from Earth observation payloads, enabling higher-bandwidth science with constrained downlink capacity.

docs.title: Chapter 16: Optical Satellite Communications
docs.text: Chapter Objectives This chapter presents the physics, engineering, and operational aspects of free-space optical (FSO) communications for satellite systems. Topics include atmospheric propagation, adaptive optics, pointing-acquisition-tracking (PAT), optical link budgets, modulation and detection schemes, laser sources, inter-satellite links, and demonstrated missions from LLCD to TBIRD and the Starlink optical ISL network.

docs.title: 16.1 Introduction to Free-Space Optical Communications
docs.text:
Free-space optical (FSO) communications represents a paradigm shift in satellite data transmission, offering data rates of 1–1000 Gbps using narrow laser beams that are thousands of times more spectrum-efficient than conventional radio frequency (RF) links. The fundamental advantage of optical wavelengths (typically 780 nm, 1064 nm, or 1550 nm) over RF is the dramatically reduced beam divergence: for a 10 cm aperture at 1550 nm, the diffraction-limited half-angle divergence is \(\theta_{\rm div} \approx 19~\mu\)rad, compared to several degrees for a comparable RF aperture. This narrows the beam to deliver essentially all transmitted power within a small illuminated spot at the receiver, enabling extraordinary link efficiency.

FSO satellite links face challenges absent in terrestrial fiber: atmospheric turbulence introduces intensity fluctuations (scintillation) and beam wander; clouds block the link entirely; and the sub-microradian pointing accuracy requirement demands sophisticated acquisition and tracking systems. Despite these challenges, the success of missions including LLCD (2013), LCRD (2021), and TBIRD (2022) has validated FSO technology for operational satellite communications.

Key technical drivers motivating optical satellite links include:

  • Bandwidth: Optical carrier frequencies near \(2 \times 10^{14}\) Hz offer 200 THz of potential bandwidth, vastly exceeding the total allocated RF satellite spectrum.

  • Mass and power: A 1 Gbps optical terminal weighing 1–5 kg replaces an RF system at hundreds of kilograms; the narrow beam eliminates the need for large dish antennas.

  • Licensing-free operation: Optical wavelengths are unregulated by the ITU Radio Regulations, eliminating spectrum coordination delays.

  • Security: The narrow beam (\(< 1\) mrad) is inherently difficult to intercept without detection, providing physical-layer security that supplements encryption.

  • Interference immunity: Optical links are immune to RF interference and electronic warfare, providing resilience in contested environments.

docs.title: 16.2.1 Received Power and Link Equation
docs.text:
The received optical power in a space-to-space FSO link (above the atmosphere) is governed by a form analogous to the RF Friis transmission equation. For a transmitter with power \(P_t\), transmit aperture diameter \(D_t\), receive aperture diameter \(D_r\), link distance \(d\), and wavelength \(\lambda\), the received power is:

\[P_r = P_t\, \eta_t\, \eta_r\, \left(\frac{D_t D_r}{4 d\,\lambda}\right)^2 \cdot L_{\rm point}\tag{16.1}\]

where \(\eta_t\) and \(\eta_r\) are transmit and receive optics efficiency (typically 0.7–0.9 each), and \(L_{\rm point}\) is the pointing loss factor. This expression assumes diffraction-limited operation of both apertures. The geometric loss (free-space path loss) dominates for space-to-space links, scaling as \(1/d^2\), identical to RF free-space loss but with the beam diffraction efficiency factor \((\lambda/D)^2\) replacing the RF wavelength factor.

The transmit telescope gain relative to an isotropic radiator is:

\[G_t = \eta_t \left(\frac{\pi D_t}{\lambda}\right)^2\tag{16.2}\]

and the half-angle diffraction-limited beam divergence (to the \(1/e^2\) intensity radius) is:

\[\theta_{\rm div} = \frac{2.44\,\lambda}{D_t}\tag{16.3}\]

For a 10 cm aperture at 1550 nm, \(\theta_{\rm div} \approx 37.8~\mu\)rad \((7.8~\text{arcsec})\).

docs.title: 16.2.2 Atmospheric Transmission
docs.text:
For ground-to-space links passing through the atmosphere, the Beer-Lambert law gives the atmospheric transmission at zenith angle \(\zeta\):

\[T_{\rm atm} = \exp\!\left(-\sigma_{\rm ext}(\lambda)\, L_{\rm eff}\right) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\tau(\lambda)}{\cos\zeta}\right)\tag{16.4}\]

where \(\sigma_{\rm ext}(\lambda)\) is the wavelength-dependent extinction coefficient (sum of absorption and scattering), \(L_{\rm eff}\) is the effective atmospheric path length, and \(\tau(\lambda)\) is the vertical optical depth. At 1550 nm in clear sky at zenith, \(\tau \approx 0.05\), giving \(T_{\rm atm} \approx 0.95\). Absorption bands at 940 nm, 1140 nm, and 1380 nm must be avoided; the 1550 nm window benefits from minimal absorption by water vapor and \(\rm O_2\).

docs.title: 16.3.1 Atmospheric Turbulence
docs.text:
Turbulent mixing of air masses with different temperatures creates refractive index fluctuations \(n(\mathbf{r},t) = n_0 + n_1(\mathbf{r},t)\), where \(n_1 \ll n_0 \approx 1\). These fluctuations distort the optical wavefront, causing beam spreading, beam wander, and intensity scintillation at the receiver.

The strength of turbulence is characterized by the refractive index structure constant \(C_n^2\) (units of m\(^{-2/3}\)), which ranges from \(10^{-17}\) m\(^{-2/3}\) (weak, high altitude) to \(10^{-13}\) m\(^{-2/3}\) (strong, near ground). For a horizontal path of length \(L\) at constant turbulence strength, the Rytov variance (log-intensity variance for a plane wave) is:

\[\sigma_R^2 = 1.23\, C_n^2\, k^{7/6}\, L^{11/6}\tag{16.5}\]

where \(k = 2\pi/\lambda\) is the optical wavenumber. The turbulence regime is classified as:

  • Weak: \(\sigma_R^2 < 0.3\) — perturbative treatment valid, scintillation index \(\sigma_I^2 \approx \sigma_R^2\).

  • Moderate: \(0.3 < \sigma_R^2 < 5\) — multiple scattering effects, saturation begins.

  • Strong: \(\sigma_R^2 > 5\) — saturation regime, \(\sigma_I^2 \to 1\) (Rayleigh distribution).

For a vertical path from ground to a LEO satellite at 500 km, the integrated \(C_n^2\) path (Kolmogorov model) gives \(\sigma_R^2 \approx 0.1\)–\(0.5\) at 1550 nm for typical mid-latitude sites, placing most ground-to-space links in the weak-to-moderate turbulence regime.

docs.title: 16.3.2 Coherence Parameters
docs.text:
The Fried parameter \(r_0\) characterizes the spatial coherence of the wavefront:

\[r_0 = \left[ 0.423\, k^2 \sec\zeta \int_0^H C_n^2(h)\, dh \right]^{-3/5}\tag{16.6}\]

Typical values: \(r_0 = 2\)–\(20\) cm at visible wavelengths at good astronomical sites (Mauna Kea, La Palma). Larger apertures (\(D > r_0\)) collect more power but with distorted wavefronts, requiring adaptive optics for coherent detection.

The coherence time \(\tau_0 = r_0 / \bar{v}\), where \(\bar{v}\) is the effective wind velocity, characterizes how rapidly the wavefront changes. Typical values \(\tau_0 = 1\)–\(10\) ms impose requirements on the adaptive optics bandwidth.

docs.title: 16.3.3 Cloud Blockage
docs.text: Clouds completely block optical links, with blockage probability varying strongly with geographic location and season. Good astronomical sites (high altitude, subtropical, or polar): 5–20% cloud blockage annually. Poor mid-latitude sites: 40–60%. Site diversity (two or more ground stations separated by 100–200 km) reduces joint outage probability to the product of individual probabilities (assuming statistical independence of cloud cover at separated sites).

docs.title: 16.4 Adaptive Optics
docs.text: Adaptive optics (AO) systems measure and correct atmospheric wavefront distortions in real time, enabling diffraction-limited performance with large-aperture ground telescopes despite turbulence.

docs.title: 16.4.1 Shack-Hartmann Wavefront Sensor
docs.text:
The Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor (SHWFS) divides the incoming wavefront into \(N_{\rm sub} \times N_{\rm sub}\) subapertures using a lenslet array. Each lenslet focuses light from its subaperture onto a CCD detector, and the centroid displacement of the focal spot relative to the reference position is proportional to the local wavefront slope:

\[s_{x,i} = \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}\bigg|_{\rm subaperture~i} \cdot \frac{d_{\rm sub}}{2}\tag{16.7}\]

where \(d_{\rm sub}\) is the subaperture diameter and \(\phi\) is the wavefront phase. The collection of slope measurements \(\mathbf{s}\) is related to the actuator commands \(\mathbf{u}\) via the interaction matrix \(\mathbf{G}\): \(\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{G}\mathbf{u}\), inverted to give \(\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{G}^+\mathbf{s}\) (pseudoinverse).

docs.title: 16.4.2 Deformable Mirror
docs.text:
The deformable mirror (DM) is controlled by \(N_{\rm act}\) piezoelectric, electrostatic, or MEMS actuators. Each actuator deforms the mirror surface according to an influence function \(F_i(\mathbf{r})\) such that the corrected surface is:

\[W_{\rm DM}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\rm act}} u_i\, F_i(\mathbf{r})\tag{16.8}\]

Commercial DMs for FSO: Boston Micromachines Multi-DM (140 actuators, \(\pm3.5~\mu\)m stroke, MEMS-based), ALPAO DM97 (97 voice-coil actuators, \(> 80~\mu\)m stroke). Closed-loop AO bandwidth of \(> 100\) Hz is required to track the evolving wavefront within the coherence time \(\tau_0\).

docs.title: 16.4.3 Strehl Ratio and Performance Metric
docs.text:
The Strehl ratio \(S\) quantifies AO performance as the ratio of the actual on-axis intensity to the diffraction-limited (unaberrated) intensity:

\[S = \exp\!\left(-\left(\frac{2\pi\, \sigma_\phi}{\lambda}\right)^2\right)\tag{16.9}\]

where \(\sigma_\phi\) is the rms residual wavefront error after AO correction. The Maréchal approximation, valid for \(\sigma_\phi < \lambda/14\), gives:

\[S \approx 1 - \left(\frac{2\pi\, \sigma_\phi}{\lambda}\right)^2\tag{16.10}\]

A well-corrected AO system achieves \(S > 0.8\) (Strehl criterion for “diffraction-limited”), corresponding to \(\sigma_\phi < \lambda/14\) rms. Tip-tilt correction alone (second-order AO) recovers \(\sim 70\)% of the Strehl, while higher-order correction (\(> 100\) modes) is needed for high \(D/r_0\) ratios.

docs.title: 16.5 Pointing, Acquisition, and Tracking
docs.text: Successful establishment of an FSO link requires three phases: acquisition (finding the remote terminal), pointing (aligning the beam), and tracking (maintaining alignment during relative motion). The PAT system is often the most technically challenging subsystem of an optical communication terminal.

docs.title: 16.5.1 PAT System Architecture
docs.text: Figure 16.1. Block diagram of a satellite optical PAT (Pointing, Acquisition, and Tracking) system. The coarse gimbal provides \(\pm 45^\circ\) pointing range using star tracker and IMU attitude references; the fine steering mirror (FSM) provides high-bandwidth fine correction; acquisition uses spiral scanning until the beacon is detected.

docs.title: 16.5.2 Pointing Loss Budget
docs.text:
The total pointing error \(\sigma_\theta\) consists of contributions from platform jitter (mechanical vibrations, thermal gradients), residual tracking error (finite control bandwidth), and thermal structural drift. The pointing-induced power loss is:

\[L_{\rm point} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{8\,\sigma_\theta^2}{\theta_{\rm div}^2}\right)\tag{16.11}\]

For a beam divergence \(\theta_{\rm div} = 40~\mu\)rad and pointing error \(\sigma_\theta = 1~\mu\)rad, the pointing loss is \(L_{\rm point} = \exp(-8/1600) \approx -0.022\) dB, negligible. For \(\sigma_\theta = 10~\mu\)rad with the same divergence, the loss rises to 2.2 dB.

The TBIRD terminal (NASA, 2022) demonstrated \(< 1~\mu\)rad pointing accuracy for a 10 cm aperture on a LEO satellite, achieving 200 Gbps.

docs.title: 16.5.3 Acquisition Scan Patterns
docs.text:
During acquisition, the pointing direction of one terminal is uncertain within an uncertainty cone of half-angle \(\sigma_{\rm unc}\) (typically 1–10 mrad from attitude reference uncertainty). A spiral scan pattern systematically covers the uncertainty area:

\[\begin{align*} \theta(t) &= \omega_s t \\ r(t) &= v_s t \end{align*}\]

where \(\omega_s\) and \(v_s\) are the angular velocity and radial velocity. The acquisition time is bounded by \(T_{\rm acq} \leq \pi \sigma_{\rm unc}^2 / (\theta_{\rm div} \cdot v_s)\). Track loop bandwidth: 1–10 kHz, providing rejection of platform vibrations up to the loop bandwidth with \(> 20\) dB attenuation.

docs.title: 16.6.1 Complete Link Equation
docs.text:
Combining all factors, the received power for a ground-to-space uplink is:

\[P_r = P_t \cdot G_t \cdot T_{ m atm} \cdot L_{ m geom} \cdot A_r \cdot \eta_r \cdot L_{ m point} \cdot L_{ m AO} ag{16.14}\]

where \(G_t = \eta_t(\pi D_t/\lambda)^2\) is the transmit telescope gain, \(L_{ m geom} = (\lambda/(4\pi d))^2\) is the free-space geometric loss, \(A_r = \pi(D_r/2)^2\) is the receive aperture area, \(L_{ m AO}\) accounts for residual wavefront error and is equivalent to the Strehl ratio.

The signal-to-noise ratio for a direct-detection (photodiode) receiver in the quantum noise limited regime is:

\[\mathrm{SNR} = rac{P_r}{2\, h u\, B \left(1 + ar{n}_{ m th} ight)} ag{16.15}\]

where \(h u\) is the photon energy (\(h u = 1.28 imes 10^{-19}\) J at 1550 nm), \(B\) is the receiver electrical bandwidth, and \( ar{n}_{ m th}\) is the mean thermal photon number (negligible at 1550 nm, \(< 0.01\) at room temperature). For coherent detection (homodyne), the SNR is 3 dB higher for the same received power.

Table 16.1. Representative optical link budget for a LEO-to-ground downlink at 1550 nm. Satellite altitude 550 km, elevation angle \(30^\circ\), link range \(d = 1100\) km. Parameter Value Unit / dB Transmit laser power \(P_t\) 1.0 W +30.0 dBm Transmit aperture \(D_t\) 10 cm — Transmit telescope gain \(G_t\) \(\eta_t(\pi D_t/\lambda)^2\) +108.1 dB Transmit optics efficiency \(\eta_t\) 0.80 \(-\)0.97 dB Free-space geometric loss \(L_{ m geom}\) \(({\lambda}/{4\pi d})^2\) \(-\)283.9 dB Atmospheric transmission (clear) 0.85 \(-\)0.71 dB Pointing loss \(L_{ m point}\) \(e^{-8(1/40)^2}\) \(-\)0.09 dB Receive aperture area (1 m) 0.785 m\(^2\) +118.9 dBcm\(^2\) Receive optics efficiency \(\eta_r\) 0.80 \(-\)0.97 dB Received power \(P_r\) (clear sky) \(\mathbf{-29.6}\) dBm Detector sensitivity (BER \(10^{-6}\), DPSK) \(-\)43.0 dBm Link margin (clear sky) \(\mathbf{+13.4}\) dB Atmospheric transmission (thin cloud) 0.30 \(-\)5.2 dB Link margin (thin cloud) \(\mathbf{+8.2}\) dB

docs.title: 16.7.1 On-Off Keying (OOK)
docs.text:
OOK is the simplest optical modulation: the laser is switched on for “1” and off (or dimmed) for “0.” The spectral efficiency is 1 b/s/Hz (ideal), and the bit error rate for direct detection with intensity noise is:

\[P_b^{\rm OOK} = \frac{1}{2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\bar{n}_s}{2}\right)\tag{16.16}\]

where \(\bar{n}_s\) is the mean signal photon count per bit for a “1” symbol.

docs.title: 16.7.2 Pulse Position Modulation (PPM)
docs.text:
\(M\)-ary PPM encodes \(\log_2 M\) bits by placing a single optical pulse in one of \(M\) time slots within a frame. The slot error probability for a Poisson detector is:

\[P_{\rm slot} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\bar{K}_s}{M}\right)\tag{16.17}\]

where \(\bar{K}_s\) is the mean signal photon count per symbol. PPM is used in deep-space optical links (LLCD: 16-PPM) where the received photon rate is extremely low (\(< 1\) photon/bit at lunar distances) and power efficiency is paramount.

docs.title: 16.7.3 Differential Phase-Shift Keying (DPSK)
docs.text: DPSK encodes data in the phase difference between consecutive pulses rather than the absolute phase, eliminating the need for a coherent phase reference. DPSK achieves approximately 3 dB better receiver sensitivity than OOK at the same bit error rate. Using a Mach-Zehnder delay interferometer (MZDI) as the demodulator, the differential phase is converted to intensity difference before photodetection.

docs.title: 16.7.4 Coherent QPSK
docs.text:
Coherent detection with a local oscillator (LO) laser is shot-noise limited and achieves the highest possible spectral efficiency. For QPSK coherent detection:

\[P_b^{\rm QPSK} = Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2\eta_{\rm opt}\, P_r}{h\nu\, B}}\right)\tag{16.18}\]

where \(\eta_{\rm opt}\) is the quantum efficiency of the receiver. TBIRD (2022) achieved 200 Gbps using coherent QPSK at 1550 nm with a 10 cm aperture in LEO.

docs.title: 16.7.5 Photon-Counting Detection
docs.text:
For very low light levels (deep space, or photon-efficient PPM links), photon-counting detectors offer the highest sensitivity:

Avalanche Photodiode (APD): The APD achieves internal gain \(M\) through impact ionization. The excess noise factor is:

\[F = k\, M + \left(2 - \frac{1}{M}\right)(1-k)\tag{16.19}\]

where \(k\) is the ionization ratio (\(k \approx 0.02\) for Si, \(k \approx 0.4\) for InGaAs). Si APDs at 800 nm achieve \(M \approx 100\) with \(F \approx 3\) dB excess noise; InGaAs APDs at 1550 nm achieve \(M \approx 10\)–\(30\) with \(F \approx 5\)–8 dB.

Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detector (SNSPD): Cryogenic detectors (operating at 0.8–3 K) using a superconducting NbN or WSi nanowire. Performance: detection efficiency \(> 93\)% at 1550 nm, timing jitter \(< 50\) ps, dark count rate \(< 1\) cps, maximum count rate \(> 100\) Mcps. SNSPDs are used in LLCD and LCRD ground terminals for single-photon-level sensitivity.

docs.title: 16.8.1 Wavelength Selection
docs.text:
The choice of operating wavelength involves tradeoffs among atmospheric transmission, detector technology, laser technology, and eye safety regulations:

  • 1550 nm: Eye-safe (cornea and lens absorb, retina protected); EDFA amplifiers provide 30 dB gain with \(< 5\) dB noise figure; telecom-grade components available; InGaAs detectors and coherent receivers well-developed.

  • 1064 nm: High-power Nd:YAG and Yb-fiber lasers; Si APDs have higher quantum efficiency than at 1550 nm; shorter wavelength gives smaller diffraction divergence for given aperture, reducing geometric loss.

  • 780 nm / 850 nm: Si APD peak sensitivity; Rb atomic transition at 780 nm can serve as absolute frequency reference for clock applications; higher Rayleigh scattering limits low-elevation-angle links.

docs.title: 16.8.2 Laser Types
docs.text:
Nd:YAG DPSS (1064 nm): Diode-pumped solid-state Nd:YAG lasers provide output powers of 0.5–10 W with high beam quality (\(M^2 < 1.1\)) and good frequency stability. Used in early MLCD and LLCD demonstrations.

Er-doped Fiber Amplifier (EDFA, 1530–1570 nm): A master oscillator power amplifier (MOPA) architecture combines a narrow-linewidth distributed feedback (DFB) laser seed with an EDFA booster to produce 0.5–2 W of amplified output. EDFA gain bandwidth covers the entire C-band; noise figure 4–5 dB typical. The MOPA architecture allows the modulation to be applied to the low-power seed laser, then amplified without distortion.

Semiconductor Laser Diode: Single-mode DFB lasers at 780 nm or 850 nm offer compactness and direct modulation at rates up to 40 GHz but are limited to \(\leq 100\) mW single-mode power; arrays can reach watts. InGaAsP/InP DFB lasers at 1310 nm or 1550 nm are the workhorses of coherent optical communications.

For coherent detection, the laser linewidth must satisfy \(\Delta\nu_{\rm LW} \ll B_{\rm symbol}\) to prevent phase noise from dominating receiver performance. For QPSK at 10 Gbaud, the combined transmitter-LO linewidth must be \(< 1\) MHz; for 64-QAM, \(< 100\) kHz. ECL (external cavity laser) and DFB+fiber Bragg grating lasers achieve linewidths of 1–100 kHz.

docs.title: 16.9.1 LLCD: Lunar Laser Communication Demonstration
docs.text:
LLCD (2013) flew aboard NASA’s LADEE spacecraft in lunar orbit, demonstrating optical communications from the Moon for the first time. Key achievements:

  • 622 Mbps downlink: DPSK modulation, 0.5 W transmitted, 15 cm telescope on spacecraft.

  • 20 Mbps uplink: From three ground stations (White Sands NM, Tenerife Spain, Table Mountain CA) with 1 m receive apertures.

  • Error-free reception: At lunar distance (385,000 km), a factor of \(\sim\!5\times\) improvement over the best RF link from lunar distance demonstrated to that point.

  • PPM format: 16-slot PPM with rate-1/2 LDPC coding for power efficiency.

docs.title: 16.9.2 LCRD: Laser Communications Relay Demonstration
docs.text: LCRD (launched December 2021 on STPSat-6 into GEO) is NASA’s first two-way optical relay demonstration. Operating at 1.2 Gbps bidirectional, LCRD relays data between two ground stations at White Sands and Table Mountain, demonstrating the relay concept for future TDRSS optical replacement. LCRD remains operational as of 2025.

docs.title: 16.9.3 TBIRD: TeraByte InfraRed Delivery
docs.text:
TBIRD (2022) on the PathFinder Technology Demonstrator-3 (PTD-3) CubeSat in LEO achieved 200 Gbps—the highest data rate ever demonstrated in a space optical communication link—using:

  • Coherent QPSK modulation at 200 Gbaud equivalent

  • 10 cm aperture telescope on the 12U CubeSat

  • 0.72 m ground telescope at White Sands Missile Range

  • Sub-microradian (\(< 1~\mu\)rad) pointing performance

  • 1550 nm EDFA-based MOPA transmitter

The 200 Gbps rate enables transfer of terabytes of data per satellite pass, with implications for high-volume Earth observation data downlink.

docs.title: 16.9.4 EDRS Space Data Highway
docs.text:
The European Data Relay System (EDRS), operated by Airbus and ESA, provides a commercial optical ISL service between GEO relay satellites (EDRS-A at 9\(^\circ\)E, EDRS-C at 3\(^\circ\)E) and LEO satellites including Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2. Each ISL uses the Tesat Laser Communication Terminal (LCT):

  • 1.8 Gbps full-duplex at 1064 nm (BPSK coherent)

  • 13.5 cm Cassegrain telescope

  • Acquisition time \(< 20\) s from cold start

  • Pointing accuracy \(< 0.3~\mu\)rad RMS

  • Maximum ISL range 45,000 km (LEO-to-GEO)

docs.title: 16.10.1 ISL Geometry and Link Parameters
docs.text:
Inter-satellite links (ISL) eliminate atmospheric effects, operating in vacuum where the link is purely geometric. Key ISL geometries:

  • LEO-LEO (in-plane): Separation 1000–5000 km; relative velocity \(< 0.5\) km/s (same orbital plane); Doppler shift \(< 1\) GHz; high-rate links (100 Gbps) feasible with \(< 5\) cm apertures.

  • LEO-LEO (cross-plane): High relative velocity at low latitudes causes link disruption; Starlink disables cross-plane links at latitudes \(> 65^\circ\).

  • GEO-GEO: Separation up to 70,000 km (full-ring GEO); Doppler nearly zero; large geometric loss requires larger apertures (\(\geq 20\) cm).

  • LEO-GEO: Separation 35,000–45,000 km; significant relative motion; EDRS architecture uses GEO relay to store and forward from LEO to ground.

docs.title: 16.10.2 Starlink Optical ISL
docs.text:
SpaceX Starlink Generation 2 satellites incorporate four optical ISL terminals per satellite: two in-plane (fore and aft) and two cross-plane (left and right). The ISL network enables routing of user traffic through the satellite mesh without requiring ground relay stations, substantially reducing latency for transoceanic routes.

Key parameters (estimated from available disclosures):

  • Wavelength: 1550 nm (eye-safe, telecom-compatible)

  • Data rate: \(\sim 100\) Gbps per ISL link

  • Aperture: \(\sim 5\) cm (consistent with Tesat LCT heritage)

  • Network topology: Mesh routing using modified BGP-like protocol

  • Latency advantage: FSO propagation at \(c = 3\times10^8\) m/s vs. fiber at \(c/n_{\rm fiber} \approx 2\times10^8\) m/s, giving 33% lower propagation delay.

The latency advantage for a transoceanic route (London to New York, 5570 km great circle) via Starlink ISL is approximately:

\[\Delta t = \frac{d}{c_{\rm fiber}} - \frac{d_{\rm ISL}}{c} = \frac{5570}{2 \times 10^5} - \frac{6100}{3 \times 10^5} \approx 7.4 \text{ ms}\tag{16.20}\]

(accounting for the longer ISL path through LEO orbits at \(\sim 550\) km altitude).

docs.title: 16.11.1 Ground Terminal Design
docs.text:
Optical ground station (OGS) telescopes for satellite communication use designs adapted from astronomical telescope mounts with additions for optical communications:

  • Aperture: 0.4–4 m diameter; 1 m is typical for operational stations; larger apertures reduce terminal count needed for the same link availability.

  • Mount: Alt-azimuth tracking with slew rates \(> 10^\circ\)/s and tracking accuracy \(< 1~\mu\)rad with additional fine steering mirror.

  • Vibration isolation: Active and passive isolation to suppress building HVAC and traffic vibrations to \(< 1~\mu\)rad pointing residual.

  • Dome/enclosure: Fast-opening shutters (\(< 5\) s) for responsive tasking; active ventilation to minimize dome seeing (local turbulence from temperature gradients).

docs.title: 16.11.2 Site Diversity and Cloud Outage Statistics
docs.text:
Cloud outage statistics at candidate optical ground station sites:

Table 16.3. Optical ground station cloud outage statistics for candidate sites. Joint outage probability computed assuming statistical independence (conservative for sites \(> 300\) km apart during stratiform cloud events; correlated for cyclonic weather). Site Elevation (m) Annual Outage (%) Summer (%) Winter (%) Mauna Kea, Hawaii 4205 8 5 12 La Palma, Canary Is. 2396 12 7 18 Atacama, Chile 5000 5 3 8 White Sands, NM 1200 22 30 15 Tenerife OGS (ESA) 2393 15 10 22 Singapore 10 55 52 58 Central Europe (avg) 300 62 55 70

For a two-site diversity network with outage probabilities \(P_1\) and \(P_2\), the joint outage probability (both sites blocked simultaneously) is:

\[P_{\rm joint} \approx P_1 \cdot P_2 \cdot (1 + \rho_{12})^{1/2}\tag{16.21}\]

where \(\rho_{12}\) is the temporal cross-correlation between outage events (0 for independent, 1 for fully correlated). For Mauna Kea and La Palma (hemispheric separation): joint outage \(\approx 8\% \times 12\% = 0.96\%\), achieving \(> 99\%\) availability, meeting most service level agreements.

docs.title: 16.11.3 UAV and High-Altitude Platform Relay
docs.text:
For locations with persistent cloud cover, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) relay platforms or high-altitude pseudo-satellites (HAPS) at 20 km altitude (above 95% of cloud cover) can serve as optical relay nodes, converting between FSO and ground-level RF or fiber links. Solar-powered HAPS (Airbus Zephyr, Boeing PHASA-35) with 24-hour endurance at 20 km can position above cloud systems for days at a time, providing FSO connectivity to otherwise inaccessible ground networks.

Optical Link Design Guidelines Key rules of thumb for optical satellite link design:

  • Beam divergence: \(\theta_{\rm div} = 2.44\,\lambda/D_t\) (Airy disk first null)

  • Pointing accuracy: \(\sigma_\theta < \theta_{\rm div}/10\) for \(< 0.5\) dB pointing loss

  • Site diversity: Two sites \(> 200\) km apart reduces cloud outage from 40% to \(< 4\%\)

  • Detector technology: SNSPD for \(< 1\) photon/bit sensitivity; APD for intermediate; PIN for \(> 1000\) photons/bit

  • 1550 nm is the preferred wavelength for satellite-to-ground links (eye-safe, EDFA-compatible, mature component ecosystem)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Optical satellite communications has advanced from theoretical proposal to operational infrastructure in the decade following LLCD’s 2013 lunar demonstration. The 200 Gbps achievement of TBIRD (2022) marks a 300-fold increase over LLCD’s 622 Mbps in just nine years. The key enabling technologies—coherent modulation, EDFA power amplifiers, fast PAT systems achieving sub-microradian pointing, and adaptive optics for ground terminals—are sufficiently mature for operational deployment. The Starlink optical ISL network and EDRS Space Data Highway represent the first commercial-scale deployments. The fundamental advantages of FSO—orders of magnitude more bandwidth than RF, mass and power efficiency, and licensing-free operation—ensure that optical communications will play an increasingly central role in future satellite constellations, particularly for high-throughput broadband, inter-satellite routing, and deep-space missions.

docs.title: Chapter 17: Earth Observation and Remote Sensing
docs.text: Chapter Overview Earth observation (EO) from space has transformed our ability to monitor and understand the planet at global scale with consistent, repeatable measurements. This chapter provides a comprehensive treatment of the physical principles underlying remote sensing, the design and characterization of optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) sensors, interferometric and polarimetric analysis techniques, hyperspectral and thermal imaging, and the rapidly growing commercial EO sector. Algorithms for geophysical parameter retrieval, artificial intelligence applications, and major archival data systems are also addressed.

docs.title: 17.1 Fundamentals of Remote Sensing Physics
docs.text: Remote sensing is the science of acquiring information about an object or phenomenon without direct physical contact, exploiting the interaction of electromagnetic radiation (EMR) with matter. From a satellite platform, the atmosphere, land surface, ocean, and cryosphere all interact with incoming solar radiation and emit their own thermal radiation in ways that carry unique geophysical signatures.

docs.title: 17.1.1 Electromagnetic Radiation and the Solar Spectrum
docs.text:
The Sun approximates a blackbody at \(T_\odot \approx 5778\) K. The spectral radiance of a blackbody is described by the Planck function:

\[B_\lambda(T) = \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5} \frac{1}{\exp\!\left(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}\right) - 1}\tag{17.1}\]

where \(h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\) J s is Planck’s constant, \(c = 2.998 \times 10^8\) m s\(^{-1}\) is the speed of light, \(k_B = 1.381 \times 10^{-23}\) J K\(^{-1}\) is the Boltzmann constant, \(\lambda\) is wavelength, and \(T\) is absolute temperature. The wavelength of peak emission is given by Wien’s displacement law:

\[\lambda_{\max} \cdot T = 2897.8\ \mu\text{m}\cdot\text{K}\tag{17.2}\]

For the Sun, \(\lambda_{\max} \approx 0.50\,\mu\)m (visible green), whereas for the Earth at \(T \approx 288\) K, \(\lambda_{\max} \approx 10\,\mu\)m (thermal infrared). This spectral separation forms the basis for distinguishing reflected solar radiation from thermally emitted radiation.

docs.title: 17.1.2 Surface Reflectance and Emittance
docs.text:
The bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) \(f_r(\theta_i, \phi_i; \theta_r, \phi_r)\) describes how surface reflectance varies with illumination and viewing geometry:

\[f_r(\theta_i, \phi_i; \theta_r, \phi_r) = \frac{dL_r(\theta_r, \phi_r)}{dE_i(\theta_i, \phi_i)}\tag{17.3}\]

where \(L_r\) is the reflected radiance and \(E_i\) is the incident irradiance. For operational remote sensing, the hemispherical-directional reflectance factor (HDRF) and bidirectional reflectance factor (BRF) are commonly used (Schaepman-Strub, G., Schaepman, M.E., Painter, T.H., Dangel, S., Martonchik, J.V. 2006). Surface reflectance \(\rho_s\) is retrieved from top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiance after atmospheric correction.

The surface energy balance links emittance to surface temperature via Kirchhoff’s law: at thermal equilibrium, emissivity \(\varepsilon_\lambda\) equals absorptivity \(\alpha_\lambda\):

\[L_\lambda^{\text{emit}} = \varepsilon_\lambda \cdot B_\lambda(T_s)\tag{17.4}\]

For most natural surfaces, \(\varepsilon_\lambda \approx 0.95\)–\(0.99\) in the 8–14 \(\mu\)m window.

docs.title: 17.2.1 Ground Sampling Distance
docs.text:
The ground sampling distance (GSD), which defines the smallest resolvable spatial element on the ground, is given by:

\[\text{GSD} = \frac{p \cdot H}{f}\tag{17.5}\]

where \(p\) is the detector element (pixel) size, \(H\) is the orbital altitude, and \(f\) is the effective focal length of the optical system. For a typical commercial satellite at \(H = 500\) km with \(p = 8\,\mu\)m and \(f = 12.9\) m (e.g., WorldView-3), GSD \(\approx 0.31\) m.

docs.title: 17.2.2 Diffraction Limit: Rayleigh Criterion
docs.text:
The angular resolution of a circular aperture of diameter \(D\) is limited by diffraction to:

\[\theta_{\min} = 1.22 \frac{\lambda}{D}\tag{17.6}\]

The corresponding ground resolution at nadir is \(\Delta x = \theta_{\min} \cdot H = 1.22 \lambda H / D\). For \(\lambda = 0.55\,\mu\)m, \(H = 500\) km, and \(D = 1.1\) m, \(\Delta x \approx 0.30\) m, consistent with the optical GSD of sub-metre commercial sensors.

docs.title: 17.2.3 Nyquist Sampling and MTF
docs.text:
To avoid aliasing, the Nyquist criterion requires that the detector sampling frequency exceed twice the optical cutoff frequency. The system modulation transfer function (MTF) combines contributions from the optics, detector, electronics, and platform motion:

\[\text{MTF}_{\text{sys}}(f) = \text{MTF}_{\text{opt}}(f) \cdot \text{MTF}_{\text{det}}(f) \cdot \text{MTF}_{\text{elec}}(f) \cdot \text{MTF}_{\text{motion}}(f)\tag{17.7}\]

A minimum MTF of 0.20 at Nyquist is a common specification for imaging satellites (Pagnutti, M., Ryan, R.E., Holekamp, K., et al. 2001).

docs.title: 17.3.1 Digital Number to Radiance Conversion
docs.text:
Raw sensor output is expressed in digital numbers (DN). Conversion to physical radiance units follows:

\[L = G \cdot \text{DN} + B\tag{17.8}\]

where \(G\) is the absolute gain (W m\(^{-2}\) sr\(^{-1}\) \(\mu\)m\(^{-1}\) DN\(^{-1}\)) and \(B\) is the offset, determined from pre-launch and in-orbit calibration. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at reference radiance \(L_{\text{ref}}\) is:

\[\text{SNR} = \frac{L_{\text{ref}}}{L_{\text{NE}\Delta L}}\tag{17.9}\]

where \(L_{\text{NE}\Delta L}\) is the noise-equivalent change in radiance. Typical specifications: Landsat 9 OLI SNR \(>\) 200:1 at reference radiance; WorldView-3 SNR \(\approx\) 100:1.

docs.title: 17.3.2 Calibration Methods
docs.text: Pre-launch calibration uses integrating spheres and flat-field sources to characterize gain, offset, linearity, and inter-channel uniformity. Vicarious calibration uses ground truth measurements at pseudo-invariant calibration sites (PICS) such as Railroad Valley Playa (Nevada, USA), La Crau (France), and Algodones Dunes (California) (Thome, K.J. 2001). Cross-calibration exploits simultaneous or near-simultaneous imaging of the same target by two sensors in compatible spectral bands. Solar diffuser on-board calibration (e.g., Landsat 9 OLI, Sentinel-2 MSI) illuminates the detector array with a known solar-illuminated panel.

docs.title: 17.4.1 Landsat 9: OLI-2 and TIRS-2
docs.text: Landsat 9, launched in September 2021, carries the Operational Land Imager-2 (OLI-2) and Thermal Infrared Sensor-2 (TIRS-2). OLI-2 covers 9 spectral bands (0.43–2.29 \(\mu\)m) at 30 m GSD with a 185 km swath, and includes a panchromatic band at 15 m GSD. TIRS-2 provides two thermal bands (10.6 \(\mu\)m and 12.0 \(\mu\)m) at 100 m resolution. The 16-day repeat cycle is halved to 8 days when combined with Landsat 8. The archive, extending back to 1972 with earlier Landsat missions, provides an unparalleled 50+ year record of land surface change (Wulder, M.A., Roy, D.P., Radeloff, V.C., et al. 2022).

docs.title: 17.4.2 Sentinel-2 MSI
docs.text: The European Space Agency Sentinel-2 mission comprises two satellites (2A launched 2015, 2B launched 2017), each carrying a Multi-Spectral Instrument (MSI) with 13 bands ranging from 443 nm to 2190 nm. Spatial resolutions of 10 m (visible and near-infrared), 20 m (red-edge and SWIR), and 60 m (atmospheric correction bands) are achieved with a 290 km swath. With 2A and 2B combined, the revisit time at mid-latitudes is 5 days. Open data policy and high spatial/temporal resolution have made Sentinel-2 the workhorse of operational land monitoring in Europe (Drusch, M., Del Bello, U., Carlier, S., et al. 2012).

docs.title: 17.4.3 Planet Dove and SkySat
docs.text: Planet Labs operates the world’s largest constellation of Earth observation satellites, with over 200 Dove 3U CubeSats (each \(\sim\)5 kg) providing daily global coverage at 3–5 m GSD. Each Dove carries a 4-band (RGB + NIR) imager; newer SuperDove satellites extend to 8 bands. Planet’s SkySat constellation (21 satellites, \(\sim\)100 kg each) provides 50 cm pan, 1 m multispectral imagery with same-day revisit over major cities (Safyan, M. 2020).

docs.title: 17.4.4 Commercial Very-High-Resolution (VHR) Sensors
docs.text: WorldView-3 (Maxar, 2014) achieves 0.31 m panchromatic GSD and 1.24 m in 8 multispectral bands at 617 km altitude, with 16 SWIR bands (3.7 m) and 12 CAVIS atmospheric compensation bands. Pleiades HR 1A and 1B (Airbus DS) offer 0.5 m pan and 2 m multi with a 20 km swath, enabling stereo DEMs at 1 m vertical accuracy. Gaofen-7 (CNSA, 2019) delivers 0.65 m stereo optical imagery combined with a laser altimeter, enabling 1:10,000 scale topographic mapping.

docs.title: 17.5.1 Radar Equation
docs.text:
The received power for a monostatic radar (transmitter and receiver co-located) is given by the radar range equation:

\[P_r = \frac{P_t G_t G_r \lambda^2 \sigma}{(4\pi)^3 R^4}\tag{17.10}\]

where \(P_t\) is transmitted power, \(G_t\) and \(G_r\) are transmit and receive antenna gains, \(\lambda\) is wavelength, \(\sigma\) is target radar cross-section (RCS) in m\(^2\), and \(R\) is slant range. For distributed targets (extended scenes), the RCS is expressed via the backscattering coefficient:

\[\sigma^0 = \frac{\sigma}{A} \quad [\text{m}^2/\text{m}^2]\tag{17.11}\]

In decibels: \(\sigma^0_{\text{dB}} = 10 \log_{10}(\sigma^0)\). Typical values range from \(-30\) dB (calm sea) to \(+5\) dB (urban corner reflectors).

docs.title: 17.5.2 SAR Image Formation: Range and Azimuth Processing
docs.text:
A SAR transmits linear frequency-modulated (LFM) chirp pulses with bandwidth \(B_r\) over pulse duration \(\tau_p\). The chirp rate is \(k_r = B_r / \tau_p\). Pulse compression (matched filtering) in range achieves range resolution:

\[\delta r = \frac{c}{2 B_r}\tag{17.12}\]

For Sentinel-1 IW mode with \(B_r = 56\) MHz, \(\delta r \approx 2.7\) m in slant range. In azimuth, the satellite motion synthesizes a long aperture of length \(L_a = \lambda R / D_a\) (where \(D_a\) is the physical antenna length). In stripmap operation, in which the antenna beam is held at a fixed pointing angle, this achieves the azimuth resolution:

\[\delta az = \frac{D_a}{2}\tag{17.13}\]

Notably, for stripmap SAR the azimuth resolution is independent of range and wavelength, determined solely by the physical antenna length (this does not hold for radar in general, nor for the scanning modes below). For Sentinel-1 with \(D_a = 12.3\) m the stripmap limit is \(\delta az \approx 6.1\) m; the wide-swath TOPS (IW) mode scans the beam in azimuth to cover a wider swath and therefore gives a coarser azimuth resolution of about 20 m.

docs.title: 17.5.3 Noise Equivalent Sigma Zero (NESZ)
docs.text:
The NESZ quantifies the minimum detectable \(\sigma^0\) and is the figure of merit for SAR sensitivity:

\[\text{NESZ} = \frac{(4\pi)^3 R^3 v_s k_B T_s F B_n}{P_t \bar{G}^2 \lambda^3 c_0 \tau_p f_{\text{PRF}} N_l}\tag{17.14}\]

where \(v_s\) is satellite velocity, \(T_s\) is system noise temperature, \(F\) is noise figure, \(B_n\) is noise bandwidth, \(f_{\text{PRF}}\) is pulse repetition frequency, and \(N_l\) accounts for system losses (Curlander and McDonough 1991). Typical NESZ values: Sentinel-1 IW \(\approx -22\) dB, ICEYE \(\approx -18\) dB.

docs.title: 17.6.1 TOPSAR: Terrain Observation by Progressive Scan
docs.text: TOPSAR, employed by Sentinel-1 in Interferometric Wide (IW) mode, is an evolution of ScanSAR that steers the beam electronically in azimuth from aft to fore during each burst. This progressive scan ensures uniform scene illumination and eliminates the scalloping artefact present in traditional ScanSAR. The IW mode acquires 3 sub-swaths (IW1, IW2, IW3), each with 9 burst images, achieving 250 km total swath at \(5 \times 20\) m spatial resolution in Single Look Complex (SLC) format (De Zan, F., Guarnieri, A.M. 2006).

docs.title: 17.6.2 Spotlight Mode
docs.text: In spotlight mode, the antenna beam is steered to illuminate a fixed scene continuously as the satellite passes, increasing the synthetic aperture length and thus azimuth resolution. TerraSAR-X achieves \(\delta az = 0.25\) m and \(\delta rg = 0.25\) m in High Resolution Spotlight (HS) mode, with scene sizes of \(\sim5 \times 5\) km (Moreira et al. 2013). ICEYE X-series SAR CubeSats achieve 0.5 m Spotlight resolution from a \(\sim 100\) kg platform.

docs.title: 17.7.1 Scattering Matrix
docs.text:
A fully polarimetric (quad-pol) SAR measures the complete \(2\times 2\) complex scattering matrix:

\[\mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix} S_{HH} & S_{HV} \\ S_{VH} & S_{VV} \end{bmatrix}\tag{17.15}\]

where subscripts denote transmit/receive polarization (H: horizontal, V: vertical). For reciprocal media, \(S_{HV} = S_{VH}\). The Pauli decomposition expresses the scattering vector as:

\[\mathbf{k}_P = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} S_{HH} + S_{VV} \\ S_{HH} - S_{VV} \\ 2S_{HV} \end{bmatrix}\tag{17.16}\]

The three components correspond to odd-bounce (sphere/flat surface), even-bounce (dihedral), and volume (random) scattering mechanisms, which are directly mapped to RGB in Pauli false-colour composites.

docs.title: 17.7.2 Coherency Matrix and Decompositions
docs.text:
The \(3\times3\) Hermitian coherency matrix is \(\mathbf{T} = \langle \mathbf{k}_P \mathbf{k}_P^{*T} \rangle\) (ensemble-averaged). The Cloude–Pottier eigendecomposition (Cloude, S.R., Pottier, E. 1997) yields:

\[\mathbf{T} = \sum_{i=1}^{3} \lambda_i \mathbf{e}_i \mathbf{e}_i^{*T}\tag{17.17}\]

Key parameters extracted are:

  • Entropy: \(H = -\sum_{i=1}^{3} p_i \log_3 p_i\), \(p_i = \lambda_i / \sum_j \lambda_j\) (\(0 \le H \le 1\))

  • Anisotropy: \(A = (\lambda_2 - \lambda_3)/(\lambda_2 + \lambda_3)\)

  • Mean scattering angle: \(\bar{\alpha} = \sum_{i} p_i \alpha_i\)

The \(H/\alpha\) plane partitions targets into 8 scattering classes (surface, volume, double-bounce dominance regimes) with wide application in land-cover and sea-ice classification. The Freeman–Durden three-component decomposition separates \(\sigma^0\) into surface scattering (\(P_s\)), double-bounce (\(P_d\)), and volume (\(P_v\)) contributions (Freeman, A., Durden, S.L. 1998).

docs.title: 17.8.1 Interferometric Phase
docs.text:
When two SAR images acquired from slightly different positions (or times) are combined, the interferometric phase contains information about path length difference \(\Delta R\):

\[\Delta\phi = \frac{4\pi}{\lambda} \Delta R\tag{17.18}\]

For Earth observation, \(\Delta R\) arises from topography (used to generate DEMs) and surface displacement (used in deformation mapping):

\[\Delta\phi_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{\frac{4\pi}{\lambda} \frac{B_\perp}{R\sin\theta} \Delta h}_{\text{topographic}} + \underbrace{\frac{4\pi}{\lambda} d_{\text{LOS}}}_{\text{displacement}} + \phi_{\text{atm}} + \phi_{\text{noise}}\tag{17.19}\]

where \(B_\perp\) is the perpendicular baseline, \(\theta\) is the look angle, \(\Delta h\) is height relative to the reference DEM, and \(d_{\text{LOS}}\) is displacement in the line-of-sight (LOS) direction. The height of ambiguity (one fringe = one \(2\pi\) phase cycle) is:

\[h_a = \frac{\lambda R \sin\theta}{2 B_\perp}\tag{17.20}\]

docs.title: 17.8.2 Coherence
docs.text:
Interferometric coherence is a measure of phase quality:

\[|\gamma| = \frac{\left|\langle s_1 s_2^* \rangle\right|}{\sqrt{\langle |s_1|^2 \rangle \langle |s_2|^2 \rangle}}, \quad 0 \le |\gamma| \le 1\tag{17.21}\]

Coherence degrades with temporal decorrelation (vegetation growth, snow, soil moisture change), geometric decorrelation (\(B_\perp > B_{\perp,\text{crit}}\)), volumetric decorrelation, and thermal noise. For reliable phase unwrapping, \(|\gamma| > 0.25\) is typically required.

docs.title: 17.8.3 Time-Series InSAR
docs.text:
Single-pair InSAR is limited by atmospheric phase noise (\(\sim 1\)–\(10\) cm of apparent displacement). Time-series methods exploit large stacks of interferograms to separate deformation from atmospheric signals and noise (Berardino, P., Fornaro, G., Lanari, R., Sansosti, E. 2002).

SBAS (Small Baseline Subsets): Forms interferograms with short spatial and temporal baselines to maximize coherence and solves for the displacement time-series using singular value decomposition (SVD):

\[\mathbf{B}\mathbf{v} = \boldsymbol{\Delta\phi}\tag{17.22}\]

where \(\mathbf{B}\) is the design matrix encoding temporal baselines and \(\mathbf{v}\) is the velocity vector.

PSInSAR (Permanent Scatterers): Identifies phase-stable scatterers (PS, typically buildings, rock outcrops) that maintain coherence over many years, enabling mm/year subsidence measurement in urban environments (Ferretti, A., Prati, C., Rocca, F. 2001). StaMPS and MintPy are widely used open-source implementations.

Applications of time-series InSAR include: urban subsidence (Mexico City \(>400\) mm/year), mining-induced deformation, earthquake cycle (interseismic, coseismic, postseismic), volcanic inflation/deflation (mm-cm scale), glacier flow velocity, and permafrost thaw settlement.

docs.title: 17.9 Hyperspectral Remote Sensing
docs.text:
Hyperspectral sensors acquire images in hundreds of contiguous narrow spectral bands (typical bandwidth 5–10 nm), enabling spectroscopic identification of surface materials. The data cube \(I(x, y, \lambda)\) contains full spectral information at each pixel.

Table 17.3. Major spaceborne hyperspectral sensors. Sensor Platform Bands Range (nm) GSD (m) Swath (km) PRISMA HYC ASI 237 400–2505 30 30 EnMAP VNIR+SWIR DLR 228 420–2450 30 30 EMIT NASA/ISS 384 380–2500 60 75 DESIS DLR/ISS 235 400–1000 30 30 HyperScout-2 ESA 45 400–1000 100 220

docs.title: 17.9.1 Spectral Unmixing
docs.text:
At 30 m spatial resolution, most pixels are mixed, containing contributions from multiple pure materials (endmembers). Linear mixing model:

\[\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\alpha} + \mathbf{n}, \quad \sum_{k=1}^{K} \alpha_k = 1, \quad \alpha_k \ge 0\tag{17.23}\]

where \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^B\) is the measured spectrum, \(\mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{B\times K}\) is the endmember matrix, \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) are fractional abundances, and \(\mathbf{n}\) is noise. Endmember extraction algorithms include N-FINDR (maximum simplex volume), Vertex Component Analysis (VCA), and ICE (Iterated Constrained Endmembers). EMIT (Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation) aboard the ISS has mapped surface mineralogy globally, quantifying dust source regions for radiative forcing studies (Green, R.O., et al. 2022).

docs.title: 17.10 Thermal Remote Sensing
docs.text:
Thermal infrared (TIR) remote sensing exploits the 8–14 \(\mu\)m atmospheric window. Surface temperature retrieval requires separation of emissivity from temperature (the temperature/emissivity separation problem). The split-window algorithm exploits the differential absorption in two adjacent TIR channels (e.g., MODIS bands 31 and 32 at 11 \(\mu\)m and 12 \(\mu\)m):

\[T_s = a_0 + a_1 T_{11} + a_2 (T_{11} - T_{12}) + a_3 (T_{11} - T_{12})^2\tag{17.24}\]

where \(T_{11}\) and \(T_{12}\) are brightness temperatures at 11 \(\mu\)m and 12 \(\mu\)m, and \(a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3\) are regression coefficients dependent on emissivity and water vapour (Wan, Z., Dozier, J. 1996). The ECOSTRESS instrument on the ISS (5 TIR bands, 70 m GSD) provides evapotranspiration and plant temperature stress measurements at sub-field scale.

docs.title: 17.11.1 Vegetation Indices
docs.text:
Vegetation indices exploit the contrast between chlorophyll absorption in the red and the leaf scattering plateau in the near-infrared. The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is:

\[\text{NDVI} = \frac{\rho_{\text{NIR}} - \rho_{\text{Red}}}{\rho_{\text{NIR}} + \rho_{\text{Red}}}, \quad -1 \le \text{NDVI} \le 1\tag{17.25}\]

The Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) reduces background and atmospheric sensitivity:

\[\text{EVI} = G \cdot \frac{\rho_{\text{NIR}} - \rho_{\text{Red}}}{\rho_{\text{NIR}} + C_1 \rho_{\text{Red}} - C_2 \rho_{\text{Blue}} + L}\tag{17.26}\]

with \(G = 2.5\), \(C_1 = 6\), \(C_2 = 7.5\), \(L = 1\). The Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) for wildfire burned area mapping uses SWIR:

\[\text{NBR} = \frac{\rho_{\text{NIR}} - \rho_{\text{SWIR},2200}}{\rho_{\text{NIR}} + \rho_{\text{SWIR},2200}}\tag{17.27}\]

docs.title: 17.11.2 Ocean Color and Chlorophyll Retrieval
docs.text:
Ocean color remote sensing retrieves phytoplankton chlorophyll-\(a\) concentration from the water-leaving radiance ratio. The OC3M algorithm (MODIS operational) uses:

\[\log_{10}[\text{Chl-}a] = a_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{4} a_i \left(\log_{10} R_{rs}\right)^i\tag{17.28}\]

where \(R_{rs} = \max(R_{rs}(443), R_{rs}(488)) / R_{rs}(547)\) is the blue-to-green band ratio of remote sensing reflectance and \(a_i\) are polynomial coefficients (O’Reilly, J.E., et al. 1998). The PACE satellite (2024) with the OCI hyperspectral imager enables phytoplankton functional type (PFT) mapping.

docs.title: 17.12 Commercial Earth Observation Sector
docs.text:
The commercial EO sector has undergone a revolution driven by miniaturization, rideshare launch, and New Space economics. Key operators and their capabilities include:

Planet: 200+ Dove CubeSats provide daily global coverage at 3–5 m GSD; 21 SkySats at 50 cm. Planet Data API provides access to \(>10\) million scenes.

Maxar Technologies (WorldView constellation): VHR optical imagery at 0.3–0.5 m, licensed through US Government NextView/EnhancedView programs and commercial APIs (SecureWatch).

Airbus Defence & Space: Pleiades 1A/1B (0.5 m) and Pleiades Neo (0.3 m) for tasked VHR; SPOT-6/7 (1.5 m) for wide-area monitoring.

ICEYE: Finland-based SAR constellation of \(>30\) X-band SAR satellites (2019–2024), achieving 1 m Spotlight resolution from 100 kg microsatellites. All-weather, 24/7 capability; focus on maritime, flood, and change detection (Ignatenko, V., et al. 2020).

Capella Space: US-based X-band SAR constellation (0.5 m Spotlight); OMEGA mode for moving target indication.

BlackSky: Tasked multispectral constellation (0.9 m GSD) with analytics platform.

Satellogic: \(>30\) hyperspectral satellites at 1 m resolution.

docs.title: 17.13.1 Deep Learning for Classification and Detection
docs.text:
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for EO image analysis. U-Net, originally developed for biomedical segmentation, is widely applied to land cover, building, and road segmentation:

\[\hat{\mathbf{y}} = f_\theta(\mathbf{X}), \quad \mathcal{L} = -\sum_i \left[y_i \log\hat{y}_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{y}_i)\right]\tag{17.29}\]

Object detection architectures (RetinaNet, YOLO, Faster R-CNN) are deployed for ship, aircraft, and vehicle detection in optical VHR imagery. Change detection using Siamese networks:

\[d(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) = \|f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1) - f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)\|_2\tag{17.30}\]

where \(f_\theta\) is a shared encoder branch and \(d\) is the feature-space change magnitude.

docs.title: 17.13.2 Foundation Models for EO
docs.text: The Prithvi geospatial foundation model (NASA + IBM, 2023) is a Vision Transformer (ViT) pre-trained on 1 million+ Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) patches using masked autoencoding. SatCLIP and DeCUR apply contrastive learning for multi-modal (optical + SAR) representation alignment (Reed, C.J., et al. 2023). These models enable few-shot adaptation to new downstream tasks (e.g., flood mapping, crop type classification) with \(<100\) labelled examples.
