docs.title: 17.15 Summary
docs.text:
This chapter has surveyed the breadth of spaceborne Earth observation technology, from fundamental radiation physics to state-of-the-art AI-driven analysis pipelines. Key themes include:

  • Remote sensing retrieval begins with the Planck function and surface radiative transfer; calibration bridges raw DN values to physical radiance and ultimately to geophysical parameters.

  • Optical sensors have achieved sub-metre GSD commercially, with daily global revisit enabled by CubeSat constellations.

  • SAR provides all-weather, day-night imaging with capabilities ranging from 0.25 m Spotlight to 500 km ScanSAR swaths.

  • PolSAR and InSAR extract physical scattering mechanisms and millimetre-precision deformation fields.

  • Hyperspectral and thermal sensors enable material identification and temperature mapping at global scale.

  • Commercial New Space operators have democratized EO data access; AI/ML has transformed information extraction workflows.

  • Open data archives (ESA Copernicus, USGS EarthExplorer, NASA Earthdata) support scientific research and operational applications worldwide.

docs.title: Chapter 18: Global Navigation Satellite Systems
docs.text: Chapter Overview Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) are space-based radio positioning services that have become foundational infrastructure for transportation, surveying, telecommunications, scientific research, and national security. This chapter presents the physics of satellite ranging, signal structure and error modelling, the four global constellations (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou), regional systems, augmentation architectures, high-precision techniques (RTK, PPP), timing services, and the growing landscape of jamming and spoofing threats.

docs.title: 18.1.1 Pseudorange Measurement
docs.text:
A GNSS receiver estimates the signal travel time \(\Delta t\) from satellite to receiver and computes a pseudorange:

\[\rho = c\,(\hat{t}_u - \hat{t}_s) = \|\mathbf{r}_u - \mathbf{r}_s\| + c(\delta t_u - \delta t_s) + I + T + \varepsilon\tag{18.1}\]

where \(c = 2.998 \times 10^8\) m s\(^{-1}\) is the speed of light, \(\hat{t}_u\) and \(\hat{t}_s\) are receiver and satellite clock readings, \(\delta t_u\) and \(\delta t_s\) are their respective clock errors relative to GNSS system time, \(I\) and \(T\) are ionospheric and tropospheric delays, and \(\varepsilon\) encompasses multipath and receiver noise. The geometric range is \(\|\mathbf{r}_u - \mathbf{r}_s\|\), the Euclidean distance between the unknown receiver position \(\mathbf{r}_u\) and the known satellite position \(\mathbf{r}_s\).

docs.title: 18.1.2 Position Solution: Linearisation and Least Squares
docs.text:
Four unknowns exist: \(x_u, y_u, z_u\) (receiver position in ECEF) and \(\delta t_u\) (receiver clock bias). With \(n \ge 4\) pseudorange observations, the system is linearised about an approximate solution \(\mathbf{r}_0\):

\[\delta\rho_k = \mathbf{h}_k \cdot \delta\mathbf{x} - c\,\delta t_u + \nu_k, \quad k = 1,…,n\tag{18.2}\]

where \(\mathbf{h}_k = -(\mathbf{r}_s^k - \mathbf{r}_0)/\|\mathbf{r}_s^k - \mathbf{r}_0\|\) is the unit vector from the approximate position to satellite \(k\) and \(\delta\mathbf{x}\) is the correction to be estimated. In matrix form:

\[\mathbf{H}\,\delta\mathbf{x} = \delta\boldsymbol{\rho}, \quad \hat{\delta\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{H}^T \mathbf{H})^{-1} \mathbf{H}^T \delta\boldsymbol{\rho}\tag{18.3}\]

docs.title: 18.1.3 Dilution of Precision
docs.text:
The covariance of the position/time solution is \(\mathbf{Q} = \sigma_{\rho}^2 (\mathbf{H}^T \mathbf{H})^{-1}\). Dilution of Precision (DOP) factors quantify the geometric amplification of ranging error:

\[\text{PDOP} = \sqrt{Q_{xx} + Q_{yy} + Q_{zz}}, \quad \text{HDOP} = \sqrt{Q_{xx} + Q_{yy}}, \quad \text{VDOP} = \sqrt{Q_{zz}}\tag{18.4}\] \[\sigma_{\text{pos}} = \text{PDOP} \cdot \sigma_{\text{URE}}\tag{18.5}\]

Optimal satellite geometry (satellites spread uniformly across the sky) yields PDOP \(\approx 1.5\). PDOP \(>6\) is considered poor. The User Range Error (URE) for GPS SPS is specified at \(<2.9\) m (95%) (Department of Defense 2020).

docs.title: 18.2.1 Constellation Configuration
docs.text:
The GPS constellation (Block IIR/IIR-M/IIF/III) consists of a minimum of 24 operational satellites (plus 3–6 active spares) in 6 orbital planes (\(\Delta\Omega = 60\degree{}\) spacing) with 4 satellites per plane:

  • Orbital altitude: 20,200 km (semi-major axis \(a = 26,560\) km)

  • Inclination: \(55\degree{}\)

  • Period: 11 h 58 min (approximately 2 sidereal revolutions/day)

  • Ground repeat: sidereal day (geometry repeats daily, 4-min earlier)

docs.title: 18.2.2 GPS Signal Structure
docs.text:
GPS signals are generated by a master oscillator at \(f_0 = 10.23\) MHz. All signal frequencies are coherent multiples:

\[f_{L1} = 154 f_0 = 1575.42\,\text{MHz}, \quad f_{L2} = 120 f_0 = 1227.60\,\text{MHz}, \quad f_{L5} = 115 f_0 = 1176.45\,\text{MHz}\tag{18.6}\] Table 18.1. GPS signal characteristics by frequency band. Signal Frequency (MHz) Code Chip Rate (Mcps) Modulation L1 C/A 1575.42 Gold code (PRN), 1023 chips 1.023 BPSK-R(1) L1 P(Y) 1575.42 P-code (encrypted Y) 10.23 BPSK-R(10) L1C 1575.42 BOC(1,1) + TMBOC 1.023/10.23 TMBOC L2C (CM+CL) 1227.60 767 + 75372 chips 0.5115 BPSK-R(0.5) L5 (I5+Q5) 1176.45 Neumann–Hofman 10.23 BPSK-R(10) M-code L1, L2 Classified 5.115 BOC(10,5)

The L1 C/A code repeats every 1 ms (1023 chips at 1.023 Mcps). Each satellite uses a unique PRN code (Gold code), enabling code-division multiple access (CDMA). The navigation message (50 bps on L1 C/A) contains broadcast ephemeris parameters, satellite clock corrections (polynomial coefficients \(a_{f0}, a_{f1}, a_{f2}\)), ionospheric model (Klobuchar coefficients \(\alpha_i, \beta_i\)), and almanac.

docs.title: 18.2.3 Navigation Message and Broadcast Ephemeris
docs.text:
Satellite positions are computed from Keplerian elements plus 9 perturbation parameters:

\[\mathbf{r}_s = f\!\left(a, e, i_0, \Omega_0, \omega, M_0, \dot{n}, \dot{i}, \dot{\Omega}, C_{uc}, C_{us}, C_{rc}, C_{rs}, C_{ic}, C_{is}\right)\tag{18.7}\]

Satellite clock error is modelled as:

\[\delta t_s = a_{f0} + a_{f1}(t - t_{oc}) + a_{f2}(t - t_{oc})^2 + \Delta t_{rel}\tag{18.8}\]

The relativistic correction \(\Delta t_{rel} = -\frac{2\sqrt{\mu a}}{c^2} e \sin E\) (\(\approx \pm 70\) ns) accounts for the eccentricity-dependent radial motion.

docs.title: 18.3.1 Ionospheric Delay
docs.text:
The ionosphere (60–1000 km altitude) introduces a dispersive delay proportional to the total electron content (TEC) along the signal path:

\[I = \frac{40.3}{\nu^2} \cdot \text{TEC} \quad [\text{m}]\tag{18.9}\]

where \(\nu\) is the signal frequency in Hz and TEC is in TEC units (1 TECU \(= 10^{16}\) el m\(^{-2}\)). Typical TEC values: 5–30 TECU, giving \(I_{L1} \approx 1\)–\(15\) m. For dual-frequency receivers, the ionosphere-free (IF) combination eliminates the first-order term:

\[\rho_{IF} = \frac{f_1^2 \rho_1 - f_2^2 \rho_2}{f_1^2 - f_2^2}\tag{18.10}\]

Single-frequency users apply the Klobuchar broadcast model which corrects \(\approx 50\%\) of the ionospheric error.

docs.title: 18.3.2 Tropospheric Delay
docs.text:
The neutral atmosphere delay is non-dispersive (same for all GNSS frequencies). Total tropospheric delay at zenith is approximately 2.3 m (dry component 2.1 m, wet component 0.1–0.4 m). The mapping function \(m(\varepsilon)\) scales zenith delay to elevation angle \(\varepsilon\):

\[T(\varepsilon) = m(\varepsilon) \cdot T_z^{\text{dry}} + m_w(\varepsilon) \cdot T_z^{\text{wet}}\tag{18.11}\]

The Saastamoinen zenith dry delay model (Saastamoinen, J. 1973):

\[T_z^{\text{dry}} = \frac{0.0022768 \, P_0}{1 - 0.00266\cos 2\phi - 0.00028 H} \quad [\text{m}]\tag{18.12}\]

where \(P_0\) is surface pressure (hPa), \(\phi\) is latitude, and \(H\) is height (km).

docs.title: 18.3.3 Relativistic Effects
docs.text:
Two relativistic effects apply to GPS clocks (Ashby, N. 2003):

  1. Special relativity (time dilation): Satellite clock runs \(-7.2\,\mu\)s/day slow due to orbital velocity (\(v_s \approx 3.87\) km/s).

  2. General relativity (gravitational blue shift): Satellite clock runs \(+45.9\,\mu\)s/day fast due to lower gravitational potential at 20,200 km.

Net effect: \(+38.4\,\mu\)s/day. GPS clocks are factory-offset to \(f_0^* = f_0 \times (1 - 4.464 \times 10^{-10})\) to cancel this.

docs.title: 18.3.4 Error Budget Summary
docs.text: Table 18.2. Representative GPS SPS pseudorange error budget (1\(\sigma\), single frequency L1 C/A). Error Source Typical Value (m) Mitigation Satellite clock (broadcast) 0.5–1.0 Broadcast corrections Satellite orbit (broadcast) 1.0–2.0 Broadcast ephemeris Ionosphere (Klobuchar) 2.0–5.0 Dual freq or model Troposphere (model) 0.5–1.0 Saastamoinen model Multipath 0.5–5.0 Choke ring, CRPA Receiver noise 0.1–1.0 Code smoothing Typical UERE (RMS) 3–8 —

docs.title: 18.4.1 Galileo
docs.text:
Galileo is the European Union’s civil GNSS, operated by the EU Agency for the Space Programme (EUSPA). As of 2024, 28 satellites are operational in 3 MEO orbital planes:

  • Altitude: 23,222 km; Inclination: \(56\degree{}\); Period: \(\sim 14\) h 4 min

  • Frequencies: E1 (1575.42 MHz, interoperable with GPS L1), E5a (1176.45 MHz \(=\) L5), E5b (1207.14 MHz), E6 (1278.75 MHz)

Galileo services: Open Service (OS, free), Commercial Service (CS, authenticated high-accuracy), Public Regulated Service (PRS, encrypted, government), Safety-of-Life (SoL), SAR/Galileo (MEOSAR Galileo contribution). Navigation Message Authentication (OSNMA) is a unique security feature providing open-service signal authentication to resist spoofing (Fernandez-Hernandez, I., et al. 2016).

docs.title: 18.4.2 GLONASS
docs.text:
Russia’s GLONASS constellation uses frequency-division multiple access (FDMA) for its legacy signals, in which each satellite transmits on its own frequency channel \(k\) (the channel numbers are re-used by antipodal satellites):

\[f_{L1,k} = 1602 + k \times 0.5625\,\text{MHz}, \quad k = -7, …, +6\tag{18.13}\] \[f_{L2,k} = 1246 + k \times 0.4375\,\text{MHz}\tag{18.14}\]

Code-division (CDMA) signals were added with the modernized GLONASS-K satellites: the first GLONASS-K1 satellite, launched in 2011, introduced the L3OC signal at 1202.025 MHz, and the later GLONASS-K2 generation adds CDMA signals on L1 and L2 as well, interoperable with other constellations. The constellation consists of 24 satellites in 3 orbital planes at 64.8 inclination and 19,100 km altitude.

docs.title: 18.4.3 BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS-3)
docs.text:
BeiDou-3 (fully operational 2020) is China’s global GNSS with a unique mixed-orbit architecture:

  • 24 MEO (Walker 24/3/1 at 21,528 km, 55) + 3 IGSO (35,786 km inclined geosynchronous) + 3 GEO (35,786 km, 80E, 110.5E, 140E)

  • Frequencies: B1C (1575.42 MHz, compatible with L1/E1), B2a (1176.45 MHz, compatible with L5), B2b (1207.14 MHz), B3I (1268.52 MHz)

BDS-3 innovations: global Short Message Communication (SMC) via L-band, Precise Point Positioning service (PPP-B2b, 0.1 m level in China), satellite-based search and rescue (MEOSAR), and global coverage including polar regions via MEO satellites (Yang, Y., et al. 2019).

docs.title: 18.4.4 Regional Systems
docs.text:
QZSS (Quasi-Zenith Satellite System, Japan): 4 operational satellites (1 GEO + 3 QZSS orbit, 44N/S inclination) providing GPS augmentation over Japan and Asia-Oceania with \(>3\) satellites at high elevation simultaneously. L1C/A, L1C, L2C, L5, LEX (L6) signals.

NavIC/IRNSS (India): 7-satellite constellation (3 GEO + 4 IGSO) covering India and 1500 km surroundings. L5 (1176.45 MHz) and S-band (2492.028 MHz) dual-frequency.

docs.title: 18.5.1 Differential GNSS
docs.text:
A reference station with precisely known coordinates computes pseudorange corrections:

\[\Delta\rho_k = \rho_k^{\text{true}} - \rho_k^{\text{measured}} = c(\delta t_s - \delta t_u) - I_k - T_k - \varepsilon_k\tag{18.15}\]

These corrections are broadcast to rover receivers, which subtract them from their own measurements. Errors correlated in space and time (satellite clock, orbit, ionosphere for short baselines \(<\) 50 km) are largely cancelled, achieving sub-metre accuracy in code-differential mode and centimetre accuracy with carrier-phase.

docs.title: 18.5.2 Satellite-Based Augmentation Systems (SBAS)
docs.text:
SBAS provides integrity and differential corrections via GEO satellite broadcasts:

Table 18.3. SBAS operational systems and coverage (2024). System Region GEO Satellites LPV-200 Capability WAAS North America 3 (Inmarsat, ANIK) Yes EGNOS Europe 3 (Inmarsat, SES) Yes MSAS Japan 2 (MTSAT) Limited GAGAN India 2 (GSAT) Yes SDCM Russia 2 (Luch-5) No BDSBAS China 3 (BDS GEO) No

SBAS broadcasts fast corrections (FCs, for satellite clock errors, updated every 6 s), slow corrections (LTCs, for orbit errors, updated every 120 s), and integrity parameters (User Differential Range Error, UDRE; Grid Ionospheric Vertical Error, GIVE). LPV-200 (Localizer Performance with Vertical guidance, 200 ft DA) requires \(\sigma_{\text{VPL}} < 35\) m and horizontal protection level \(< 40\) m (RTCA 2022).

docs.title: 18.6.1 Carrier-Phase Measurement
docs.text:
The carrier-phase measurement on frequency \(j\) is:

\[\phi_j = rac{f_j}{c} \|\mathbf{r}_u - \mathbf{r}_s\| - f_j \delta t_u + f_j \delta t_s + N_j - rac{I_j}{\lambda_j} + rac{T_j}{\lambda_j} + \varepsilon_\phi ag{18.16}\]

where \(N_j\) is the integer ambiguity (cycles). Differencing between satellites (single difference) and between receivers (double difference) eliminates receiver and satellite clock errors:

\[ abla\Delta\phi_j^{pq} = rac{f_j}{c} abla\Delta\|\mathbf{r}\| + abla\Delta N_j^{pq} + ext{residuals} ag{18.17}\]

docs.title: 18.6.2 Integer Ambiguity Resolution: LAMBDA Method
docs.text:
The Least-squares AMBiguity Decorrelation Adjustment (LAMBDA) method (Teunissen, P.J.G. 1995) solves the integer least-squares problem:

\[\hat{\mathbf{N}} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{N} \in \mathbb{Z}^n} (\hat{\mathbf{N}}_{\text{float}} - \mathbf{N})^T \mathbf{Q}_{\hat{N}}^{-1} (\hat{\mathbf{N}}_{\text{float}} - \mathbf{N})\tag{18.18}\]

The float solution \(\hat{\mathbf{N}}_{\text{float}}\) is obtained from standard LS; LAMBDA decorrelates the ambiguity covariance matrix \(\mathbf{Q}_{\hat{N}}\) using an integer transformation \(\mathbf{Z}\) (\(|\det \mathbf{Z}| = 1\)), then applies sequential conditional least-squares. The fix is validated using the ratio test:

\[r = \frac{||\hat{\mathbf{N}}_{\text{float}} - \hat{\mathbf{N}}_2||_{\mathbf{Q}}^2}{||\hat{\mathbf{N}}_{\text{float}} - \hat{\mathbf{N}}_1||_{\mathbf{Q}}^2} > r_{\text{threshold}}\tag{18.19}\]

where \(\hat{\mathbf{N}}_1\) is the best and \(\hat{\mathbf{N}}_2\) the second-best integer candidate. A ratio threshold of 3 is commonly used. A confirmed integer fix enables cm-level positioning. RTK baseline limitation: ionospheric decorrelation limits reliable ambiguity resolution to \(\sim 10\)–30 km in standard RTK; Network RTK (NRTK) extends to \(\sim 50\) km using interpolated corrections from a reference station network.

docs.title: 18.7.1 PPP Observation Model
docs.text:
PPP uses precise satellite orbits and clocks from an analysis centre (e.g., IGS) instead of broadcast ephemerides, along with dual-frequency measurements to eliminate ionospheric delay:

\[\rho_{IF} = \rho_{\text{geom}} + c\,\delta t_u + T + \varepsilon_{\rho}\tag{18.20}\] \[\lambda_{IF} \phi_{IF} = \rho_{\text{geom}} + c\,\delta t_u + T + \lambda_{IF} N_{IF} + \varepsilon_\phi\tag{18.21}\]

IGS product accuracy:

  • Final orbits: 2.5 cm (delay: 12–18 days)

  • Rapid orbits: 5 cm (delay: 17 h)

  • Ultra-rapid (predicted): 10–15 cm (delay: real-time)

  • Final clocks: 0.075 ns (5-min sampling)

docs.title: 18.7.2 PPP Convergence and PPP-RTK
docs.text: Traditional PPP requires 20–45 min to converge to centimetre-level precision as the receiver clock, troposphere, and ambiguity parameters are absorbed into the float solution. Integer PPP (PPP-AR) uses satellite phase bias products to recover integer ambiguities, reducing convergence by 30–50% (Ge et al. 2008). PPP-RTK augments PPP with network-derived ionospheric corrections, enabling convergence in \(<5\) min. Commercial implementations: Trimble RTX, TerraStar, GNSS+1, Point One Navigation Atlas.

docs.title: 18.8 GNSS Timing Services
docs.text: GNSS provides time transfer at the sub-nanosecond level, underpinning telecommunications, financial systems, power grid synchronization, and scientific timekeeping.

docs.title: 18.8.1 Atomic Clocks in GNSS Satellites
docs.text:
Table 18.4. Atomic frequency standards used in GNSS satellites. Satellite Clock Type Stability Drift Accuracy GPS Block IIF Rb + Cs \(10^{-14}\)/day \(<1\) ns/day \(<2\) ns GPS Block III Rb (RAFS) \(10^{-15}\)/day \(<1\) ns/day \(<2\) ns Galileo PHM (passive H-maser) \(10^{-15}\)/day \(<0.45\) ns/day \(<2\) ns GLONASS-M Cs + Rb \(5\times10^{-14}\)/day 5 ns/day \(<5\) ns BDS-3 MEO Rb + PHM \(10^{-15}\)/day 1 ns/day \(<2.5\) ns

The Galileo Passive Hydrogen Maser (PHM) achieves 1 ps per day frequency stability, the most stable clock ever flown in a navigation satellite (Rochat, P., Droz, F., Wang, Q., Froidevaux, S. 2012). GPS SPS time is specified at \(<30\) ns from UTC(USNO) at 95%.

docs.title: 18.8.2 Two-Way Satellite Time Transfer (TWSTT)
docs.text: TWSTT achieves \(< 1\) ns accuracy by simultaneously transmitting and receiving timing signals through the satellite, cancelling common-path delays. It is the primary method for comparing national atomic timescales contributing to TAI.

docs.title: 18.9.1 Jamming Vulnerability and Analysis
docs.text:
GNSS signals arrive at Earth’s surface at approximately \(-130\) dBm (L1 C/A), some 20 dB below the thermal noise floor of a typical receiver (\(-110\) dBm). The processing gain of spread-spectrum code acquisition is:

\[G_p = 10 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{B_{\text{spread}}}{B_{\text{data}}}\right) = 10 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{1.023 \times 10^6}{50}\right) \approx 43\,\text{dB}\tag{18.22}\]

The effective jamming range (for a ground jammer of power \(P_J\) and gain \(G_J\) that overloads the receiver) is:

\[R_J = \left(\frac{P_J G_J}{P_s G_r (J/S)_{\min}}\right)^{1/2} \cdot \frac{\lambda}{4\pi}\tag{18.23}\]

A 1 W omni-directional L-band jammer can disrupt civilian GPS receivers within \(\sim 15\) km radius. Military solutions include:

  • Controlled Radiation Pattern Antenna (CRPA): 7-element array steers nulls toward jammers; \(25\)–\(40\) dB null depth.

  • GPS M-code: BOC(10,5) modulation with 100\(\times\) higher effective power spectral density; encrypted; broadcast from spot-beam regional military satellites for up to 20 dB additional J/S margin.

docs.title: 18.9.2 Spoofing and Authentication
docs.text:
GNSS spoofing generates counterfeit signals to mislead the receiver into computing a false position or time. The Galileo OSNMA (Open Service Navigation Message Authentication) (Fernandez-Hernandez, I., et al. 2016) uses TESLA-based delayed key disclosure to authenticate the navigation message:

\[\text{MAC}_k = H_{\text{HMAC-SHA256}}\!\left(K_k, \text{NavData}_k\right)\tag{18.24}\]

Keys are disclosed with a delay, preventing replay. Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM) detects measurement outliers using a \(\chi^2\) test on the pseudorange residuals. Advanced RAIM (ARAIM) supports Horizontal and Vertical navigation down to LPV-200 precision approach using multi-constellation.

docs.title: 18.10 Multi-Constellation Multi-Frequency (MCMF) Positioning
docs.text:
Modern GNSS receivers track all four global constellations plus regional systems, observing 40–80 satellites simultaneously. Benefits include:

  1. Improved DOP (more satellites \(\Rightarrow\) better geometry \(\Rightarrow\) lower PDOP).

  2. Higher redundancy for integrity (RAIM availability).

  3. Improved performance in urban canyons and challenging environments.

  4. Faster PPP convergence with triple-frequency observations.

The triple-frequency extra-wide-lane ambiguity (EWL, \(\lambda \approx 5.86\) m) resolves almost instantaneously, bootstrapping narrow-lane (NL, \(\lambda \approx 10.7\) cm) integer resolution within one epoch in ideal conditions.

docs.title: 18.11.1 Assisted GNSS (A-GNSS)
docs.text: A-GNSS accelerates receiver time-to-first-fix (TTFF) by providing satellite ephemeris, approximate position, and time via a cellular or WiFi network, reducing the need to demodulate the 12.5-minute navigation message (TTFF: cold start 30–50 s \(\to\) A-GNSS \(<2\) s).

docs.title: 18.11.2 GNSS/IMU Sensor Fusion
docs.text:
An Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) provides dead-reckoning between GNSS fixes. The extended Kalman filter (EKF) state vector in a loosely-coupled architecture:

\[\mathbf{x} = [\delta\mathbf{r}, \delta\mathbf{v}, \boldsymbol{\psi}, \mathbf{b}_a, \mathbf{b}_g]^T\tag{18.25}\]

where \(\delta\mathbf{r}\), \(\delta\mathbf{v}\), \(\boldsymbol{\psi}\) are position, velocity, and attitude errors, and \(\mathbf{b}_a\), \(\mathbf{b}_g\) are accelerometer and gyroscope biases. Tightly coupled integration uses raw pseudoranges and Doppler as observations, maintaining position output even with \(<4\) visible satellites.

docs.title: 18.11.3 5G-Based Positioning
docs.text:
3GPP Release 16/17 defines radio positioning methods for NR (5G New Radio) (3GPP 2022):

  • DL-TDOA: Downlink Time Difference of Arrival (requires synchronised gNBs, \(\sim 1\)–3 m horizontal).

  • AoD: Angle of Departure using massive MIMO beamforming (\(\sim 1\) m).

  • GNSS hybrid: Combining 5G DL-TDOA with GNSS for \(<0.3\) m (horizontal) in good conditions.

docs.title: 18.12 GNSS Interference and Security Incidents
docs.text: GNSS jamming incidents have proliferated globally: North Korea operates ground-based jammers (Haeju, Kaesong) that have disrupted aviation and maritime navigation in South Korea. GPS jamming in the Baltic Sea region (attributed to Russian electronic warfare) has been reported continuously since 2022, affecting civilian aviation in Finland, Estonia, and Poland. GNSS spoofing of maritime vessels in the Black Sea and Persian Gulf has been documented, where ships reported false positions displaced by tens of kilometres. The Viasat KA-SAT cyber attack (February 2022), which disrupted satellite internet across Europe, demonstrated that ground segment vulnerabilities can cascade to navigation (Viasat Inc. 2022).

docs.title: 18.13 Summary
docs.text:
GNSS is a complex system-of-systems spanning space, control, and user segments across four global constellations and multiple regional systems. Key takeaways:

  • The pseudorange observation model links satellite and receiver positions through ranging codes; 4+ measurements resolve the 3D position and receiver clock bias.

  • Error sources (ionosphere, troposphere, multipath) require careful modelling and mitigation; dual-frequency measurements eliminate the dominant ionospheric error.

  • Differential techniques (RTK, PPP) reduce errors to cm or mm level by exploiting carrier-phase ambiguity resolution.

  • SBAS and ARAIM provide integrity assurance for safety-critical aviation applications.

  • GNSS timing underpins global telecommunications, finance, and scientific timekeeping.

  • Jamming and spoofing pose growing threats; signal authentication (OSNMA), antenna nulling (CRPA), and sensor fusion provide resilience.

docs.title: Chapter 19: Communication Satellites and Services
docs.text: Communication satellites represent the largest commercial segment of the space industry, enabling global telecommunications, broadcasting, broadband internet, and maritime and aeronautical connectivity. From the first experimental TELSTAR 1 (1962) to today’s high-throughput satellites (HTS) delivering hundreds of gigabits per second, the evolution of satellite communications has been driven by advances in transponder technology, antenna design, modulation schemes, and orbital architectures. This chapter presents the engineering principles underlying GEO communication satellite design, transponder performance, frequency reuse strategies, HTS architectures, direct broadcast satellite systems, VSAT networks, and emerging LEO broadband constellations (Maral et al. 2009; Pratt, T., Bostian, C., Allnutt, J. 2002; Elbert, B.R. 2008).

docs.title: 19.1.1 Historical Development and Major Operators
docs.text:
Geostationary Earth orbit (GEO) at approximately 35,786 km altitude remains the dominant orbit for commercial communication satellites because a single satellite provides continuous coverage of nearly one-third of Earth’s surface. The concept was proposed by Arthur C. Clarke in 1945, and the first operational GEO communication satellite, INTELSAT I (Early Bird), was launched in 1965 providing 240 telephone circuits or one television channel across the Atlantic.

By 2025, several hundred operational GEO communication satellites occupy the Clarke belt, operated by companies including Intelsat, SES, Eutelsat, Inmarsat, ViaSat, Hughes Network Systems, and numerous national operators. The geostationary arc is managed through International Telecommunication Union (ITU) coordination to avoid interference between co-frequency satellites.

Key Operators and Fleets (2025)

  • Intelsat: C-band/Ku-band global coverage, Galaxy/Intelsat Epic series (Intelsat was acquired by SES in 2025)

  • SES: GEO and MEO (O3b) satellites, Astra/NSS/SES series, SES-17 HTS

  • Eutelsat: GEO satellites plus the OneWeb LEO constellation, Ku/Ka-band, Konnect series HTS

  • ViaSat: ViaSat-1/2/3 Ka-band HTS, focus on broadband

  • Hughes: EchoStar/Jupiter series HTS, HughesNet service

  • Inmarsat: L/Ka-band mobile satcom, BGAN/GX fleet

docs.title: 19.1.2 Spacecraft Bus Architecture
docs.text:
A modern GEO communication satellite comprises two primary elements: the satellite bus (platform) providing structural support, power, attitude control, propulsion, thermal management, and telemetry; and the payload (communications mission equipment) comprising transponders, antennas, and associated electronics.

Typical mass ranges from 2,000 kg to 7,000 kg at launch (including \(\sim\)40–50% propellant), with end-of-life (EOL) dry mass between 1,000 and 3,000 kg. Solar array power at BOL ranges from 5 kW (small satellites) to 25 kW or more for large HTS platforms. Design lifetime is typically 15–18 years, limited primarily by propellant consumption for station-keeping and battery degradation.

The spacecraft must maintain geostationary position within \(\pm0.05^\circ\) to \(\pm0.1^\circ\) in both longitude (east-west) and latitude (north-south). Station-keeping maneuvers consume approximately 42 m/s per year for north-south and 2 m/s per year for east-west control, yielding a total \(\Delta v\) budget of approximately \(650\)–\(700\) m/s over 15 years.

\[\Delta v_{\mathrm{total}} \approx \left(\dot{v}_{NS} + \dot{v}_{EW}\right) \times T_{\mathrm{life}}\tag{19.1}\]

where \(\dot{v}_{NS} \approx 42\) m/s/yr and \(\dot{v}_{EW} \approx 2\) m/s/yr for a near-circular GEO orbit.

docs.title: 19.1.3 Major Platform Families
docs.text:
Leading spacecraft manufacturers offer standardized bus platforms that reduce cost and schedule risk. Key platforms include:

Table 19.1. Major GEO Communication Satellite Bus Platforms Platform Manufacturer BOL Power (kW) Payload (kg) Examples 702HP Boeing 12–25 1,100 WGS, Intelsat 29e BSS-702MP Boeing 8–16 900 SES-12, AsiaSat 9 A2100 Lockheed Martin 5–18 1,200 XIPS-25, GDStar Spacebus 4000 Thales Alenia 8–18 800 Astra 2E, Inmarsat 5 Eurostar-3000 Airbus DS 10–22 1,100 Eutelsat 65WA LS-1300 SSL/MDA 5–25 1,300 SES-17, ViaSat-2 Star-2 Orbital ATK 4–10 400 Nimiq, AMC GX-500 Gilat/generic 4–8 300 ChinaSat series

docs.title: 19.2.1 Bent-Pipe Transponder Architecture
docs.text:
The classic bent-pipe (or transparent) transponder receives uplink signals, frequency-converts them to the downlink band, amplifies them, and retransmits without on-board signal processing. A standard C-band transponder chain consists of:

  1. Receive antenna (uplink 5.925–6.425 GHz)

  2. Low-noise amplifier (LNA) — typical noise figure 1.5–2.5 dB

  3. Input multiplexer (IMUX) — channelizes the broadband received signal

  4. Frequency converter (upconverter/downconverter) — translates to downlink band (3.7–4.2 GHz)

  5. High-power amplifier (HPA) — TWTA or SSPA

  6. Output multiplexer (OMUX) — recombines channels

  7. Transmit antenna (downlink)

For Ku-band, uplink is 14.0–14.5 GHz and downlink is 10.95–12.75 GHz. For Ka-band, uplink is 27.5–31.0 GHz and downlink is 17.7–21.2 GHz (FSS) or 18.3–18.8 GHz (BSS uplink 17.3–17.8 GHz).

docs.title: 19.2.2 Traveling Wave Tube Amplifiers (TWTA)
docs.text:
The Traveling Wave Tube Amplifier remains the dominant HPA technology for GEO communication satellites due to its high power efficiency at microwave frequencies. A TWTA comprises an electron gun, a helix slow-wave structure, and a collector. The electron beam interacts with the RF signal propagating along the helix, achieving gain through velocity modulation and energy transfer.

Key performance parameters:

  • Saturated output power: 40–300 W per tube (Ku-band), up to 500 W (C-band)

  • Small-signal gain: 40–55 dB

  • DC-to-RF efficiency: 65–75% at saturation (depressed collector designs)

  • Operating bandwidth: 500 MHz (typical transponder)

  • AM/AM conversion: nonlinear gain compression

  • AM/PM conversion: phase shift as function of drive level

The TWTA output back-off (OBO) and input back-off (IBO) characterize operating point relative to saturation:

\[\mathrm{OBO} = P_{\mathrm{sat}} - P_{\mathrm{out}} \quad [\mathrm{dB}]\tag{19.2}\] \[\mathrm{IBO} = P_{\mathrm{in,sat}} - P_{\mathrm{in}} \quad [\mathrm{dB}]\tag{19.3}\]

For multi-carrier operation (MCPC or FDMA), the amplifier must operate at substantial back-off (typically 5–8 dB OBO) to limit intermodulation distortion (IMD). The third-order intercept point (OIP3) relates to IM3 product levels:

\[\mathrm{IM3} = 2(P_{\mathrm{OIP3}} - P_{\mathrm{out}}) \quad [\mathrm{dBc}]\tag{19.4}\]

Linearizers preceding the TWT reduce AM/AM and AM/PM distortion, enabling operation 2–3 dB closer to saturation while maintaining acceptable IM levels. Pre-distortion linearizers are analog or digital circuits that apply the inverse of the TWTA nonlinearity.

docs.title: 19.2.3 Solid-State Power Amplifiers (SSPA)
docs.text:
SSPAs based on Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) or Gallium Nitride (GaN) pseudomorphic high-electron-mobility transistors (pHEMTs) are increasingly used for lower-power applications and HTS spot beam amplifiers. Advantages over TWTAs:

  • Higher reliability (no moving parts, no high-voltage electron gun)

  • Lower power supply voltage requirements

  • Better linearity without back-off (GaN devices)

  • Suitable for per-beam amplification in multibeam payloads

GaN SSPAs achieve 40–60% power-added efficiency (PAE) at Ku/Ka-band, compared to 65–75% for optimized TWTAs with depressed collectors. Typical SSPA output powers range from 2–20 W for spot beam applications.

\[\eta_{\mathrm{PAE}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{out}} - P_{\mathrm{in}}}{P_{\mathrm{DC}}} \times 100\%\tag{19.5}\]

docs.title: 19.2.4 Noise Temperature and G/T
docs.text:
The satellite receive figure of merit \(G/T\) (dB/K) characterizes the uplink receive chain:

\[G/T = G_{\mathrm{rx}} - 10\log_{10}(T_{\mathrm{sys}}) \quad [\mathrm{dB/K}]\tag{19.6}\]

where \(G_{\mathrm{rx}}\) is the receive antenna gain (dBi) and the system noise temperature:

\[T_{\mathrm{sys}} = T_{\mathrm{ant}} + T_{\mathrm{LNA}} + \frac{T_{\mathrm{converter}}}{G_{\mathrm{LNA}}} + \cdots \quad [\mathrm{K}]\tag{19.7}\]

Typical GEO satellite \(G/T\) values range from \(-3\) to \(+8\) dB/K for global beams and \(+8\) to \(+20\) dB/K for high-gain spot beams.

docs.title: 19.3.1 Spatial Isolation
docs.text:
Frequency reuse through spatial beam separation allows the same frequency band to be used simultaneously by multiple beams serving different geographic areas. The carrier-to-interference ratio (C/I) arising from beam overlap must be sufficient for acceptable link performance.

For two cochannel beams separated by angle \(\theta\), the C/I is determined by the antenna discrimination pattern. For a parabolic reflector with Gaussian beam approximation:

\[\frac{C}{I} = \frac{G(\theta=0)}{G(\theta_{\mathrm{sep}})} = \exp\!\left(\frac{2.77 \theta_{\mathrm{sep}}^2}{\theta_{3\mathrm{dB}}^2}\right)\tag{19.8}\]

where \(\theta_{3\mathrm{dB}}\) is the half-power beamwidth. Practical multibeam designs target \(C/I > 25\) dB for QPSK and \(C/I > 30\) dB for higher-order modulations such as 8PSK or 16APSK.

The antenna discrimination between spot beams is typically 25–35 dB for beams separated by 2–3 beamwidths, enabling 4-color or even 2-color frequency reuse schemes.

docs.title: 19.3.2 Polarization Reuse
docs.text:
Orthogonal polarizations (linear horizontal/vertical or left/right circular) provide an additional frequency reuse factor of 2. Cross-polarization isolation (XPI) must exceed 25–30 dB for acceptable interference levels. Rain depolarization in Ku and Ka bands degrades XPI, requiring fade margin or uplink power control (ULPC).

The overall frequency reuse factor combining spatial and polarization techniques:

\[F_{\mathrm{reuse}} = N_{\mathrm{beams}} \times N_{\mathrm{pol}} / N_{\mathrm{colors}}\tag{19.9}\]

For a 4-color scheme with 2 polarizations and 72 beams: \(F_{\mathrm{reuse}} = 72 \times 2 / 4 = 36\).

docs.title: 19.3.3 Interference Budget
docs.text:
The total interference budget in a multibeam system includes:

  • Co-channel interference (CCI): from other beams using the same frequency

  • Adjacent channel interference (ACI): from imperfect IMUX/OMUX filtering

  • Cross-polarization interference (XPI): from polarization leakage

  • Terrestrial interference: from co-frequency terrestrial systems (C-band)

The total \(C/(N+I)\) combining noise and interference:

\[\frac{C}{N+I} = \left[\frac{N_0}{C} + \frac{I_{\mathrm{total}}}{C}\right]^{-1}\tag{19.10}\]

docs.title: 19.4.1 HTS Design Principles
docs.text:
High-throughput satellites employ aggressive frequency reuse through large numbers of narrow spot beams, achieving system throughput 50–100 times greater than conventional wide-beam satellites for the same allocated spectrum. Key architectural features:

  • Multispot beam antenna: 50–500+ narrow beams (0.3\(^\circ\)–1\(^\circ\) diameter) covering the service area

  • Aggressive frequency reuse: same Ka-band spectrum reused 50–100+ times across the beam pattern

  • High EIRP per beam: 60–70 dBW per spot beam enables small user terminals

  • Gateway ground infrastructure: multiple large gateway stations aggregate traffic

  • On-board processing (OBP): some HTS use digital transparent processors for switching

docs.title: 19.4.2 Spot Beam Frequency Assignment
docs.text:
For a 4-color frequency reuse plan, the Ka-band user downlink (17.7–20.2 GHz, 2.5 GHz) is divided into 4 sub-bands of 625 MHz each, with 2 polarizations. Each color cell uses one sub-band/polarization combination. The frequency reuse factor:

\[F_r = \frac{N_{\mathrm{beams}}}{N_{\mathrm{colors}}} = \frac{500}{4} = 125\tag{19.11}\]

Total system capacity with 500 beams at 1 Gbps per beam:

\[C_{\mathrm{total}} = N_{\mathrm{beams}} \times C_{\mathrm{beam}} = 500 \times 1~\mathrm{Gbps} = 500~\mathrm{Gbps}\tag{19.12}\]

Spectral efficiency per beam depends on the modulation/coding scheme and operating \(E_b/N_0\). Modern HTS with adaptive coding and modulation (ACM) achieve 3–5 bit/s/Hz, yielding per-beam capacities of 1.5–3 Gbps over 500–600 MHz.

docs.title: 19.4.3 Gateway Architecture
docs.text:
HTS gateways connect the satellite spot beams to the terrestrial internet backbone. Each gateway serves multiple spot beams, with the gateway transmitting uplink on dedicated gateway beams (feeder links) separate from the user link beams. Typical gateway characteristics:

  • Antenna diameter: 4.5–13 m for Ka-band feeder links

  • Uplink EIRP: 80–90 dBW (high-power amplifiers 200–2000 W)

  • Site diversity (2–4 sites per gateway cluster) to mitigate rain fade

  • Aggregate gateway throughput: 10–50 Gbps per gateway cluster

  • Number of gateways: 8–50 per HTS system

Smart gateway diversity switches traffic between diverse gateway sites when one site experiences heavy rain fade, maintaining link availability without user-link degradation.

docs.title: 19.4.4 Major HTS Systems
docs.text: Table 19.2. Major High-Throughput Satellite Systems Satellite Operator Band Beams Throughput Launch ViaSat-1 ViaSat Ka 72 140 Gbps 2011 ViaSat-2 ViaSat Ka 120+ 300 Gbps 2017 ViaSat-3 (Amer) ViaSat Ka 1000+ 1 Tbps 2023 SES-17 SES Ka 200 200 Gbps 2021 Konnect VHTS Eutelsat Ka 260 500 Gbps 2023 Jupiter-3 Hughes/EchoStar Ka 500+ 500 Gbps 2023 Intelsat Epic Intelsat C/Ku/Ka 80+ 60 Gbps 2016–2017 BSAT-4b BSAT Ka 8 40 Gbps 2020 Hylas-4 Avanti Ka 66 40 Gbps 2018

docs.title: SES-17
docs.text: SES-17, launched in October 2021 on Ariane 5 ECA, is a 200 Gbps Ka-band HTS built on the Thales Alenia Space Spacebus Neo platform. Key features include a fully digital transparent processor (DTP) enabling flexible frequency and power allocation across 200 spot beams serving the Americas and Atlantic Ocean region. The satellite targets aviation connectivity (inflight entertainment) and maritime services.

docs.title: ViaSat-3
docs.text: The ViaSat-3 constellation (3 satellites in GEO) aims to deliver 1 Tbps capacity per satellite using a massive array of narrow spot beams and 4-color frequency reuse. ViaSat-3 F1 (Americas) was launched in April 2023 on Falcon Heavy, but an antenna reflector deployment anomaly reduced its capacity well below the design value. The architecture uses advanced reflector antennas with 1,000+ beams.

docs.title: 19.4.5 Multibeam Antenna Design
docs.text:
Multibeam antennas for HTS employ either:

  1. Multiple feed array reflector (MFAR): single large reflector illuminated by an array of feed horns, each producing a separate beam. Economic but limited flexibility.

  2. Direct radiating array (DRA): planar phased array producing beams electronically, maximum flexibility.

  3. Multiple reflectors: 2–4 separate reflectors each handling a subset of beams.

The beamwidth of a circular aperture of diameter \(D\) at wavelength \(\lambda\):

\[\theta_{3\mathrm{dB}} \approx \frac{70\lambda}{D} \quad [\mathrm{degrees}]\tag{19.13}\]

For a 2.8 m reflector at Ka-band (20 GHz, \(\lambda = 15\) mm):

\[\theta_{3\mathrm{dB}} \approx \frac{70 \times 0.015}{2.8} \approx 0.375^\circ\tag{19.14}\]

A \(0.375^\circ\) beam covers approximately \(220 \times 220\) km at GEO, suitable for regional HTS coverage.

docs.title: 19.5.1 DBS Architecture and Regulatory Framework
docs.text:
Direct broadcast satellite (DBS) services transmit high-power Ku or Ka-band signals directly to consumer dish antennas of 45–90 cm diameter. DBS satellites operate in the BSS (Broadcasting Satellite Service) frequency bands allocated by the ITU, with high EIRP (\(>\)55 dBW) enabling small consumer dishes.

Regulatory planning in ITU Region 2 (Americas) allocates specific orbital positions and frequency assignments to each country under the BSS plan (ITU Radio Regulations, Appendix 30). In Region 1 (Europe/Africa), the WARC-77 plan similarly coordinates orbital positions.

Major DBS systems include:

  • DirecTV (USA): 32\(^\circ\)W, 99\(^\circ\)W, 101\(^\circ\)W, 103\(^\circ\)W, 110\(^\circ\)W positions; Ku/Ka-band; \(>\)24 million subscribers

  • DISH Network (USA): 61.5\(^\circ\)W, 72.7\(^\circ\)W, 77\(^\circ\)W; Ku/Ka-band; EchoStar fleet

  • BSkyB/Sky UK: Astra 2 satellites at 28.2\(^\circ\)E; Ku-band; \(>\)11 million subscribers

  • Astra/SES (Europe): 19.2\(^\circ\)E (German-speaking market); Ku/Ka-band; 125+ million households

  • BSAT (Japan): BS orbital positions; 110\(^\circ\)E; 12.2–12.75 GHz

  • TeleSat (Canada): Anik satellites; Ku-band

docs.title: 19.5.2 DVB-S2 and DVB-S2X Standards
docs.text:
The Second Generation Digital Video Broadcasting via Satellite (DVB-S2) standard (ETSI EN 302 307) was published in 2005 and superseded the original DVB-S standard. DVB-S2X (extended) was published in 2014 (ETSI EN 302 307-2), introducing additional MODCODs and narrower roll-offs for improved spectral efficiency.

DVB-S2 key features:

  • Modulation: QPSK, 8PSK, 16APSK, 32APSK

  • Forward error correction (FEC): concatenated LDPC + BCH

  • LDPC code lengths: 64,800 bits (normal) or 16,200 bits (short)

  • Code rates: 1/4, 1/3, 2/5, 1/2, 3/5, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, 5/6, 8/9, 9/10

  • Roll-off: 0.20, 0.25, 0.35

  • Adaptive coding and modulation (ACM) mode: per-frame MODCOD selection

  • Spectral efficiency: 0.49–4.53 bit/s/Hz

DVB-S2X enhancements:

  • Additional modulations: 64APSK, 128APSK, 256APSK

  • Finer granularity code rates and additional MODCODs

  • Narrower roll-offs: 0.05, 0.10, 0.15 (5–15% improvement in spectral efficiency)

  • Super-frame structure for channel bonding and synchronization

  • Linear pre-compensation (LPC) for satellite nonlinearity

  • Extended bandwidth (500 MHz MCPC channels)

Table 19.3. DVB-S2/S2X Selected MODCOD Performance MODCOD Modulation Code Rate Spectral Eff. \(E_s/N_0\) (dB) QPSK 1/4 QPSK 1/4 0.49 \(-\)2.35 QPSK 1/3 QPSK 1/3 0.66 \(-\)1.24 QPSK 2/5 QPSK 2/5 0.79 \(-\)0.30 QPSK 1/2 QPSK 1/2 0.99 1.00 QPSK 3/5 QPSK 3/5 1.19 2.23 QPSK 2/3 QPSK 2/3 1.32 3.10 QPSK 3/4 QPSK 3/4 1.49 4.03 QPSK 5/6 QPSK 5/6 1.65 5.18 QPSK 9/10 QPSK 9/10 1.79 6.42 8PSK 3/5 8PSK 3/5 1.78 5.50 8PSK 2/3 8PSK 2/3 1.98 6.62 8PSK 3/4 8PSK 3/4 2.23 7.91 8PSK 5/6 8PSK 5/6 2.48 9.35 8PSK 9/10 8PSK 9/10 2.68 10.69 16APSK 2/3 16APSK 2/3 2.64 9.27 16APSK 3/4 16APSK 3/4 2.97 10.21 16APSK 4/5 16APSK 4/5 3.17 11.03 16APSK 5/6 16APSK 5/6 3.30 11.61 32APSK 3/4 32APSK 3/4 3.70 12.73 32APSK 4/5 32APSK 4/5 3.95 13.64 32APSK 5/6 32APSK 5/6 4.12 14.28 64APSK 5/6* 64APSK 5/6 4.94 16.05 256APSK* 256APSK 3/4 5.96 19.57 * DVB-S2X only. \(E_s/N_0\) at quasi-error-free (QEF): BER \(< 10^{-7}\)

docs.title: Adaptive Coding and Modulation
docs.text:
In ACM mode, the MODCOD is selected per-frame (or per-user in MIS mode) based on the instantaneous channel condition reported by the receiver. The spectral efficiency gain of ACM over constant coding and modulation (CCM):

\[\eta_{\mathrm{ACM}} = \frac{\sum_i f_i \eta_i}{\eta_{\mathrm{CCM}}}\tag{19.15}\]

where \(f_i\) is the fraction of time spent in MODCOD \(i\) and \(\eta_i\) is its spectral efficiency. ACM systems can achieve 20–50% throughput improvement over CCM in variable rain fade environments.

docs.title: 19.5.3 DTH Services: Encryption and Conditional Access
docs.text:
Direct-to-home (DTH) services use conditional access systems (CAS) to restrict viewing to authorized subscribers. The CAS comprises:

  • Subscriber Management System (SMS): manages subscriptions and entitlements

  • Conditional Access System (CAS): generates and distributes encrypted keys

  • Smart card or software CA: stores the decryption key hierarchy in the receiver

The DVB Common Scrambling Algorithm (DVB-CSA) or newer AES-128 based DVB-CSA3 encrypts MPEG transport streams at the PID level. The key hierarchy:

  1. Control word (CW): 64-bit key, changed every 10 s (crypto period)

  2. Service key: encrypts CW in entitlement control message (ECM)

  3. Operator key: protects entitlement management messages (EMM)

  4. Personal distribution key (PDK): subscriber-specific, stored in smart card

Major CAS providers include Nagravision (NagraVision 3), Irdeto, Viaccess-Orca, Conax, and CISCO VideoGuard. DirecTV uses DIRECTV’s NDS VideoGuard system.

docs.title: 19.5.4 Video Compression Standards
docs.text:
DTH services use standardized video compression to maximize the number of channels per transponder:

  • MPEG-2: 4–8 Mbps per SD channel; legacy standard, widely deployed

  • MPEG-4 AVC (H.264): 2–5 Mbps SD, 4–8 Mbps HD; 2\(\times\) MPEG-2 efficiency

  • HEVC (H.265): 2–4 Mbps HD, 8–15 Mbps UHD/4K; 2\(\times\) H.264 efficiency

  • AV1: open-source alternative to HEVC, similar compression ratio

A 36 MHz Ku-band transponder operating at QPSK 3/4 (DVB-S2) provides approximately 55 Mbps, accommodating:

  • 7–14 HD channels (MPEG-4, 4–8 Mbps each)

  • 3–7 UHD/4K channels (HEVC, 8–15 Mbps each)

docs.title: 19.6.1 VSAT System Architecture
docs.text:
Very Small Aperture Terminal (VSAT) networks provide two-way satellite communications using small (0.6–2.4 m) dish antennas at remote sites. Applications include corporate enterprise networks, rural broadband, ATM connectivity, point-of-sale terminals, and government/military communications.

Hub-and-spoke topology: A large hub station (3.7–7 m antenna) provides the network control point. Outbound (hub-to-VSAT) traffic uses a Time Division Multiplex (TDM) broadcast carrier. Inbound (VSAT-to-hub) traffic uses Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) or Multi-Frequency TDMA (MF-TDMA).

Mesh topology: VSATs communicate directly with each other through the satellite without hub intervention. Each VSAT requires higher EIRP and G/T. Suitable for point-to-point circuits and VoIP.

docs.title: 19.6.2 Return Link Multiple Access
docs.text:
TDMA assigns time slots to VSATs within a single shared carrier. TDMA burst rate is much higher than the average data rate, requiring burst buffers:

\[R_{\mathrm{burst}} = R_{\mathrm{avg}} \times \frac{T_{\mathrm{frame}}}{T_{\mathrm{slot}}}\tag{19.16}\]

MF-TDMA divides the return link bandwidth into multiple frequency sub-bands, each carrying TDMA bursts. VSATs may be assigned to different carriers depending on load. iDirect platforms (now ST Engineering iDirect) use MF-TDMA with SCPC fallback for high-demand sites.

Demand-Assigned Multiple Access (DAMA) dynamically assigns capacity in response to traffic demand, improving efficiency compared to Fixed Assignment Multiple Access (FAMA).

docs.title: 19.6.3 iDirect and HughesNet Platforms
docs.text:
iDirect (ST Engineering): Industry-leading VSAT platform using MF-TDMA return link, DVB-S2 ACM outbound. iQ platform adds DVB-S2X and supports HTS spot beam operation. Typical remote terminal: 0.76–1.2 m antenna, 1–4 W BUC.

HughesNet/Hughes EchoStar: JUPITER system uses Ka-band HTS (Jupiter-1 and Jupiter-3 satellites), proprietary waveform on return link, DVB-S2 forward link. Delivers consumer broadband at 25–100 Mbps receive rate. EchoStar XIX (Jupiter-2) provided 220 Gbps capacity.

docs.title: 19.7.1 Motivation: LEO vs GEO Latency
docs.text:
The fundamental limitation of GEO satellite systems for interactive broadband is the propagation delay. The one-way propagation time from ground to GEO satellite:

\[t_{\mathrm{GEO}} = \frac{d_{\mathrm{GEO}}}{c} = \frac{35{,}786~\mathrm{km}}{3 \times 10^5~\mathrm{km/s}} \approx 119~\mathrm{ms}\tag{19.17}\]

The round-trip time (RTT) for a GEO bent-pipe link (user-satellite-hub-satellite-user):

\[\mathrm{RTT}_{\mathrm{GEO}} \approx 4 \times 119~\mathrm{ms} = 476~\mathrm{ms} \quad \text{(+ processing)}\tag{19.18}\]

In practice, GEO satellite broadband exhibits RTT of 550–650 ms, severely impacting real-time applications (VoIP, gaming, video conferencing).

For a LEO constellation at 550 km altitude:

\[t_{\mathrm{LEO}} = \frac{550~\mathrm{km}}{c} \approx 1.8~\mathrm{ms}\tag{19.19}\]

With inter-satellite links (ISL) or ground gateway routing, Starlink achieves RTT of 20–50 ms, comparable to terrestrial broadband.

Table 19.4. LEO vs GEO Broadband Satellite Comparison Parameter GEO (ViaSat-3) LEO (Starlink) Orbital altitude 35,786 km 540–570 km One-way delay (zenith) \(\sim\)119 ms \(\sim\)2 ms RTT (typical) 550–650 ms 20–50 ms Satellites in service one or a few per region thousands Coverage per satellite about one third of the Earth a small cap, many satellites needed User terminal dish or flat panel electronically steered flat panel Free-space path loss (Ka, 20 GHz, zenith) 209.5 dB 173.3 dB

docs.title: 19.7.2 Starlink
docs.text:
SpaceX’s Starlink constellation, whose first production satellites were launched in 2019 and which began public beta service in 2020, is the most rapidly deployed satellite broadband system to date. Key technical parameters:

  • Orbital shells: 540 km (Gen1), 570 km (Gen1), 340 km (Gen2 planned)

  • Frequency: Ku-band (user link: 10.7–12.7 GHz downlink, 14.0–14.5 GHz uplink), Ka-band (gateway), E-band (backhaul)

  • Inter-satellite links (ISL): laser links on later Gen1 and on Gen2 satellites

  • User terminal: electronically steered phased array (flat panel)

  • Satellite mass: \(\sim\)260 kg (Gen1), \(\sim\)800 kg (Gen2)

  • Constellation size: 4,408 (Gen1 authorized) + 7,500 (Gen2 authorized); more than 7,000 in orbit in 2025

  • User performance: typically tens to a few hundred Mbps receive, with latency of a few tens of ms

  • Subscribers: several million (company statements, as of 2025)

docs.title: 19.7.3 OneWeb
docs.text:
OneWeb (now part of Eutelsat) completed its first-generation constellation of 648 satellites (about 650 in orbit with spares), planned in near-polar orbits at an altitude of about 1,200 km, providing Ku-band connectivity primarily for enterprise, government, and maritime customers. OneWeb uses gateway stations operated at teleports around the world.

Key characteristics:

  • Altitude: 1,200 km (higher than Starlink, lower latency than GEO)

  • Coverage: Polar-inclusive global coverage

  • Latency: higher propagation delay than at 550 km but far lower than GEO

  • User link: Ku-band; Gateway: Ka-band

  • Target markets: maritime, aviation, enterprise, government

docs.title: 19.7.4 Amazon Kuiper
docs.text: Amazon’s Project Kuiper (FCC license: 3,236 satellites at 590–630 km altitude) targets mass-market consumer broadband using Ka-band communications. Two prototype satellites were launched in October 2023 and the first production satellites in 2025.

docs.title: 19.8.1 Inmarsat BGAN and Fleet Systems
docs.text:
Inmarsat operates a global L-band network (1.5–1.6 GHz) using GEO satellites (I-4 and I-5 fleet) for mobile satellite services (MSS). The Broadband Global Area Network (BGAN) provides:

  • Up to 492 kbps streaming IP (land portable terminals)

  • Near-global coverage (excluding the polar regions)

  • ISDN circuits and voice services

  • Terminal sizes: laptop-sized (Inmarsat-C), briefcase (BGAN), maritime dome

Inmarsat Fleet Xpress (FX) combines L-band (Global Xpress via I-5 Ka-band) with a backup L-band link, providing multi-Mbps broadband to maritime vessels.

docs.title: 19.8.2 Inflight Connectivity (IFC)
docs.text:
Aviation satcom delivers in-flight broadband to commercial aircraft. Three main architectures:

  1. GEO Ku-band: ViaSat IFC uses Ku-band spot beams; Gogo 2Ku; speeds of the order of tens of Mbps per aircraft

  2. GEO Ka-band: ViaSat-3 Ka IFC; SES/O3b for short-haul routes; typically higher speeds per aircraft than Ku-band

  3. LEO: Starlink Aviation (introduced 2023) with low latency; electronically steered antenna (ESA)

Aircraft antennas must be low-profile aerodynamic radomes. Mechanically steered Ku-band antennas weigh 15–25 kg; flat-panel ESAs for LEO links weigh 10–15 kg with \(<\)25 mm height.

docs.title: 19.9 Satellite News Gathering and Professional Services
19.9.1 SNG Systems
docs.text:
Satellite News Gathering (SNG) refers to the use of portable/fly-away satellite uplink systems for live broadcast from remote locations. SNG systems typically employ:

  • Antenna: 0.9–2.4 m deployable offset-fed reflector

  • Uplink frequency: Ku-band (14.0–14.5 GHz) or C-band (5.925–6.425 GHz)

  • HPA: 25–400 W SSPA or TWTA

  • Video encoder: HEVC or H.264, 2–20 Mbps depending on quality

  • DVB-S2 modulation for satellite uplink

  • Setup time: 2–15 minutes

SCPC (Single Channel Per Carrier) provides dedicated bandwidth for each SNG link, while MCPC (Multiple Channels Per Carrier) multiplexes several feeds on a shared carrier, managed by a hub station.

docs.title: 19.9.2 SCPC vs MCPC
docs.text:
SCPC: Each carrier occupies a dedicated bandwidth slice of the transponder. Advantages: simple link, no hub required, low latency. Disadvantages: inefficient for bursty traffic, each carrier has overhead.

MCPC: Multiple program channels are statistically multiplexed (MPEG transport stream) on a single carrier. A headend multiplexer combines channels and outputs a single DVB carrier. Advantages: higher efficiency (statistical multiplexing gain 20–40%), easier management.

Statistical multiplexing gain:

\[G_{\mathrm{StatMux}} = \frac{N \cdot R_{\mathrm{peak}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{R}_i} \approx 1.2 \text{ to } 1.4\tag{19.20}\]

docs.title: 19.10.1 ITU Orbital Coordination
docs.text:
The ITU Radio Regulations govern satellite network coordination through two processes:

  1. Advance Publication Information (API): published up to 7 years (and at least 2 years) before the planned date of bringing the network into use, establishes the initial claim

  2. Coordination: Bilateral coordination between potentially interfering networks (for example, GSO networks within about \(6^\circ\) of each other)

  3. Notification: Filed with the ITU to record the frequency assignments in the Master International Frequency Register after coordination

For non-geostationary systems, the limits on equivalent power flux density (EPFD) in Article 22 of the Radio Regulations protect geostationary networks.

docs.title: 19.10.2 Carrier-to-Interference Calculations
docs.text:
The C/I from an interfering satellite at angular separation \(\Delta\phi\) from the desired satellite:

\[\frac{C}{I} = \frac{G_t(\phi_t)}{G_t(\Delta\phi)} \cdot \frac{P_t G_s}{P_i G_i} \cdot \frac{d_i^2}{d_s^2}\tag{19.21}\]

For GSO satellite spacing, the receive earth station antenna discrimination against an adjacent satellite at angle \(\Delta\phi\):

\[G(\Delta\phi) = 32 - 25\log_{10}(\Delta\phi) \quad \text{dBi, for } \Delta\phi > \phi_{\min}\tag{19.22}\]

where \(\phi_{\min} = 20\lambda/D\) (degrees) per ITU-R S.580.

docs.title: 19.10.3 HTS Capacity Economics
docs.text:
The commercial viability of HTS systems is driven by the cost per Gbps of capacity, which has fallen by large factors from the first HTS generation to the latest ones (published cost-per-bit figures differ between sources and are not quoted here).

An illustrative exponential model of the capacity cost trend is:

\[C_{\mathrm{capacity}}(t) \approx C_0 \cdot 10^{-\alpha(t-t_0)}\tag{19.23}\]

where, for example, \(\alpha = 0.08\) year\(^{-1}\) corresponds to about a 17% annual decline (an assumed value for illustration).

docs.title: 19.11 Summary
docs.text: Communication satellites remain the backbone of global telecommunications infrastructure, with GEO satellites providing broadcast, VSAT, and trunking services while HTS systems deliver broadband at costs approaching terrestrial alternatives. The DVB-S2X standard provides spectral efficiency from 0.49 to nearly 6 bit/s/Hz through adaptive coding and modulation. High-throughput satellites employing aggressive spot-beam frequency reuse deliver 100 Gbps to 1 Tbps of system capacity from a single GEO position. LEO broadband constellations (Starlink, OneWeb, Kuiper) address the latency limitation of GEO systems, achieving round-trip times of 20–50 ms compared to 550–650 ms for GEO. Maritime and aviation connectivity markets are growing rapidly as LEO systems enable high-bandwidth IFC at prices competitive with GEO solutions (Maral et al. 2009; Pratt, T., Bostian, C., Allnutt, J. 2002; Elbert, B.R. 2008).

docs.title: Chapter 20: Scientific Satellites and Space Observatories
20.1 Introduction to Space Science
docs.text:
Scientific satellites represent humanity’s most powerful tools for understanding the universe, Earth, and the space environment. By escaping the limitations imposed by the terrestrial atmosphere, space observatories access electromagnetic radiation across the entire spectrum—from radio waves through gamma rays—without attenuation or distortion. This capability has transformed astronomy, Earth science, heliophysics, and planetary science over the past six decades.

Scientific satellites fall into four primary categories: (1) astronomy and astrophysics observatories studying celestial objects and phenomena; (2) Earth science satellites monitoring our planet’s climate and surface systems; (3) space physics and heliophysics missions examining the Sun–Earth connection; and (4) planetary science spacecraft exploring other bodies in the Solar System.

The advantages of space-based observation are manifold. The atmosphere absorbs or distorts radiation across most of the electromagnetic spectrum, transmitting only visible light, near-infrared, and radio wavelengths through narrow “windows.” X-rays, ultraviolet, far-infrared, and gamma rays are entirely blocked at ground level. Even in transparent windows, atmospheric turbulence limits angular resolution to approximately 1 arcsecond for ground-based optical telescopes, compared with diffraction-limited performance achievable in space.

Microgravity enables instrument configurations impossible on the ground: deployable structures of arbitrary size, cryogenic cooling systems unencumbered by convection, and long-duration experiments requiring vibration isolation. The 24-hour observation window eliminates the day–night cycle, while orbital mechanics enables vantage points including the Sun–Earth Lagrange points, polar orbits for global Earth coverage, and interplanetary trajectories to every body in the Solar System.

Table 20.1 summarizes the major space observatories discussed in this chapter, spanning the full electromagnetic spectrum.

docs.title: 20.2.1 Hubble Space Telescope
docs.text:
The Hubble Space Telescope (HST) remains the most scientifically productive observatory ever built, having generated over 19,000 peer-reviewed publications since its launch on April 24, 1990, aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery. Its 2.4 m primary mirror operates in a circular orbit at 593 km altitude, completing one orbit every 95 minutes with a period of approximately 5,700 s.

HST employs a Ritchey–Chrétien optical design with focal ratio \(f/24\), producing an image scale of approximately 0.045 arcsec/pixel on the Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3). The fundamental angular resolution limit is given by the Rayleigh criterion:

\[\theta = 1.22 \frac{\lambda}{D}\tag{20.1}\]

where \(\theta\) is the angular resolution in radians, \(\lambda\) is the observation wavelength, and \(D\) is the telescope aperture diameter. At 500 nm wavelength with \(D = 2.4\) m:

\[\theta = 1.22 \times \frac{500 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}}{2.4\,\mathrm{m}} = 2.54 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{rad} \approx 0.052\,\mathrm{arcsec}\]

This diffraction-limited resolution is typically 20 times better than ground-based seeing-limited telescopes under good conditions. Expressed as a physical resolution on an object at distance \(d\):

\[s = d \cdot \theta = d \times 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}\]

At the distance of the Large Magellanic Cloud (50 kpc), HST resolves structures of \(\sim\)13 AU.

HST’s original spherical aberration, discovered after launch, resulted from a 2.2 \(\mu\)m error in the primary mirror figure introduced during polishing. The Corrective Optics Space Telescope Axial Replacement (COSTAR) installed during Servicing Mission 1 (SM1) in December 1993 added corrective optics restoring diffraction-limited performance. COSTAR was subsequently removed after instruments with built-in aberration correction replaced the original complement.

HST’s current instrument suite includes:

  • Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3): 200–1700 nm with a UV/optical UVIS channel (\(0.04\) arcsec/pixel, \(162”\times162”\) FOV) and NIR channel (\(0.13\) arcsec/pixel, \(123”\times136”\) FOV).

  • Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS): optimized for wide-field optical imaging, 0.05 arcsec/pixel, \(202”\times202”\) field in the Wide Field Channel.

  • Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS): UV spectroscopy at \(R=1000\)–\(24{,}000\), 115–320 nm, optimized for faint point sources with high throughput.

  • Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS): UV through near-IR spectroscopy and imaging, long-slit spectroscopy at \(R\) up to 200,000.

Five Space Shuttle servicing missions (SM1: 1993, SM2: 1997, SM3A: 1999, SM3B: 2002, SM4: 2009) replaced all instruments and upgraded hardware, extending HST’s operational life well into the 2030s. Scientific highlights span the breadth of astrophysics:

  • Hubble Deep Field (1995) and Ultra Deep Field (2004): Revealed thousands of galaxies in tiny sky patches, establishing galaxy number counts and demonstrating the universe’s large-scale structure.

  • Dark energy discovery (1998): HST observations of Type Ia supernovae contributed to the Nobel Prize-winning discovery of the universe’s accelerating expansion, requiring a cosmological constant or dark energy.

  • Hubble constant: \(H_0 = 73.0 \pm 1.0\) km s\(^{-1}\) Mpc\(^{-1}\) via Cepheid variable calibration—in \(>5\sigma\) tension with the Planck CMB value of 67.4 km s\(^{-1}\) Mpc\(^{-1}\).

  • Exoplanet atmospheres: Transmission spectroscopy detections of sodium, potassium, and water vapor in hot Jupiter atmospheres.

  • Stellar populations: Color-magnitude diagrams of globular clusters measuring stellar ages of 13.0–13.5 Gyr, consistent with the age of the universe.

docs.title: 20.2.2 James Webb Space Telescope
docs.text:
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched December 25, 2021, and delivering first science images in July 2022, is the largest and most complex space observatory ever built. Its 6.5 m primary mirror, composed of 18 hexagonal beryllium segments each coated with a thin layer (about 100 nm) of gold, provides a collecting area of 25.4 m\(^2\)—approximately 6.3 times that of HST in area.

JWST orbits the Sun–Earth \(L_2\) Lagrange point \(\sim\)1.5 million km from Earth. A five-layer Kapton/aluminium sunshield the size of a tennis court maintains the telescope cold side at \(\sim\)40 K (\(-233\,^\circ\)C), essential for infrared sensitivity. Wavefront error achieved in commissioning was 57–75 nm rms, far exceeding the \(\lambda/14\) requirement at 2 \(\mu\)m (\(\approx\)143 nm).

Each of the 18 primary mirror segments is 1.32 m across (flat-to-flat) and actuated with 7 degrees of freedom (three translation, three rotation, one radius of curvature adjustment) via cryogenic stepper motor actuators. The secondary mirror assembly is also actuated for fine alignment. Figure 20.1 shows the segment layout.

Figure 20.1. JWST primary mirror layout. The 18 hexagonal beryllium segments (C1 centre, A1–A6 inner ring, B1–B12 outer ring) together form a 6.5 m effective aperture. Each segment is individually actuated with seven degrees of freedom to achieve the required wavefront error of \(\lambda/14\) at 2 \(\mu\)m.

JWST’s four science instruments cover 0.6–28 \(\mu\)m:

  • NIRCam (0.6–5 \(\mu\)m): Primary imager with two \(2.2'\times2.2'\) modules, \(0.032”\)/pixel short-wavelength channel, \(0.065”\)/pixel long-wavelength.

  • NIRSpec (0.6–5.3 \(\mu\)m): Multi-object spectrograph with \(\sim\)250,000 individually programmable microshutters enabling \(>\)100 simultaneous spectra. Fixed slits and IFU modes available. Spectral resolution \(R = 100\), 1000, or 2700.

  • MIRI (5–28 \(\mu\)m): Mid-infrared imager, low-resolution spectrograph, and medium-resolution IFU. Cooled to 7 K by a dedicated JWST cryocooler (a closed-cycle helium Joule–Thomson cooler), providing sensitivity unattainable by any ground instrument in this band.

  • NIRISS (0.6–5 \(\mu\)m): Wide Field Slitless Spectrograph for exoplanet transits, aperture masking interferometry, and single-object slitless spectroscopy.

JWST sensitivity reaches \(\sim10^9\) times fainter than the naked eye, approximately 100 times more sensitive than HST in the infrared for extended sources. Key science results through early 2025 include: first unambiguous CO\(_2\) detection in an exoplanet atmosphere (WASP-39b, 4.3 \(\mu\)m, August 2022); SO\(_2\) photochemical detection in WASP-39b indicating active photochemistry; galaxy candidates at \(z > 13\) forming just 320 Myr after the Big Bang; resolved protoplanetary disk substructures in Taurus and Orion; Neptune ring detail; and the Enceladus water plume extending 9,600 km.

docs.title: 20.2.3 X-ray and Gamma-ray Observatories
docs.text:
X-ray and gamma-ray photons carry energies from \(\sim\)100 eV to tens of GeV, requiring specialized detection technologies. For X-ray energies below \(\sim\)10 keV, Wolter Type-I grazing-incidence optics (nested coaxial paraboloid–hyperboloid mirror pairs) focus photons by total external reflection at shallow grazing angles typically \(< 1^\circ\).

Chandra X-ray Observatory (launched July 1999): Achieves an unprecedented angular resolution of 0.5 arcsec in the 0.1–10 keV band using four nested Wolter I mirror pairs of total effective area \(\sim\)800 cm\(^2\) at 1 keV. The 10 m focal length feeds the Advanced CCD Imaging Spectrometer (ACIS-I and ACIS-S) for simultaneous imaging and spectroscopy, and the High Energy Transmission Grating Spectrometer (HETGS) achieving spectral resolution \(E/\Delta E \sim 1000\) at soft X-ray energies. Chandra operates in a highly elliptical orbit (\(\sim\)10,000–140,000 km) to spend most of its time above the radiation belts. Scientific achievements span AGN jets, dark matter in galaxy clusters, the equation of state of neutron stars, and starburst-driven galactic winds.

XMM-Newton (ESA, launched December 1999): Complements Chandra with much higher throughput (\(\sim\)4,300 cm\(^2\) at 1 keV from three mirror modules of 58 nested shells each) but coarser angular resolution (\(\sim\)6 arcsec). The European Photon Imaging Camera (EPIC) includes pn and two MOS CCD arrays, while the Reflection Grating Spectrometers (RGS) provide high-resolution spectroscopy from 0.35–2.5 keV at \(\lambda/\Delta\lambda \sim 200\)–500. An Optical Monitor images simultaneously with the X-ray instruments.

Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope (launched June 2008): Two instruments cover eight decades in energy. The Large Area Telescope (LAT) detects 20 MeV–300 GeV photons via electron–positron pair production in 18 layers of tungsten converter foils, tracked by silicon strip detectors and measured by a CsI calorimeter. The LAT’s 2.4 sr field of view enables full-sky survey every \(\sim\)3 hours. The Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) consists of 12 NaI (8–900 keV) and 2 BGO (0.2–40 MeV) detectors covering the full unocculted sky. Fermi discoveries include thousands of gamma-ray sources (4FGL catalog), the Fermi Bubbles (25,000 light-year lobes above/below the Galactic center), millisecond pulsar populations, and gamma-ray counterparts to gravitational wave events.

NuSTAR (Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array, launched June 2012): The first focusing hard X-ray telescope in orbit, operating at 3–79 keV using multilayer-coated Wolter I optics on a 10 m deployable mast. The multilayer coatings alternate tungsten and silicon layers with depths tuned to Bragg-reflect specific energies at specific grazing angles, enabling focus at energies 10–80\(\times\) higher than conventional soft X-ray mirrors. NuSTAR enables spin measurements of stellar-mass and supermassive black holes through broad iron K\(\alpha\) line profiles, radioactive isotope mapping in supernova remnants (\(^{44}\)Ti in Cas A), and census of obscured AGN.

docs.title: 20.2.4 ESA Gaia Astrometry Mission
docs.text:
Gaia, launched in December 2013, performs the most ambitious astrometry survey ever undertaken, measuring positions, parallaxes, proper motions, radial velocities, and photometry for over 1.5 billion Milky Way stars and Solar System objects.

The spacecraft employs a dual-field Korsch telescope design with two primary mirrors of \(1.45 \times 0.5\) m aperture separated by a 106.5 basic angle. This design enables simultaneous measurement of two sky regions separated by precisely this angle, enabling absolute parallax determination without reference to bright standard stars. The spacecraft rotates at 60 arcsec/s about an axis inclined 45 to the Sun direction, precessing to cover the full sky in \(\sim\)6 months. The focal plane array contains 106 CCDs totalling 938 Megapixels.

The trigonometric parallax \(p\) yields stellar distance in parsecs:

\[d\,[\text{pc}] = \frac{1}{p\,[\text{arcsec}]}\tag{20.4}\]

Gaia achieves parallax precision of \(\sim\)20 \(\mu\)arcsec (\(= 2\times10^{-5}\) arcsec) at \(G=15\) mag, corresponding to 1% distance uncertainty at 50 pc. For 1 kpc, the uncertainty is \(\sim\)20%. Proper motion precision matches the parallax precision in \(\mu\)as/yr.

Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3, June 2022) contains: astrometry and photometry for 1.47 billion sources; radial velocities for 33 million stars measured to \(\pm\)1 km/s; astrophysical parameters for 470 million objects; \(BP/RP\) spectra for 220 million sources; non-single-star orbital solutions for 800,000 systems; and 156,000 Solar System objects. Scientific highlights include mapping Milky Way spiral arms in 3D, discovering disrupted globular cluster stellar streams, detecting astrometric binary orbits including suspected black holes, and constraining the Galaxy’s dark matter halo shape.

docs.title: 20.3.1 Gravity and Geodesy: GRACE-FO
docs.text:
The Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-On (GRACE-FO), a joint NASA–GFZ project launched May 2018, consists of two identical spacecraft flying in formation \(\sim\)220 km apart in a 490 km near-circular orbit.

The primary measurement is microwave ranging between the two spacecraft. A K-band (24 GHz) and Ka-band (32 GHz) dual-frequency system measures inter-satellite range changes with \(\sim\)1 \(\mu\)m precision, equivalent to \(\lambda/1000\) in wavelength. As the satellite pair traverses regions of varying mass distribution beneath them, the leading satellite is gravitationally pulled ahead, then recedes as it passes overhead, encoding the gravity field anomaly as a range oscillation. The Laser Ranging Interferometer (LRI) demonstrated on GRACE-FO achieves \(\sim\)30 nm precision, roughly \(10\times\) better than the microwave system, paving the way for future missions.

Each gigaton (Gt = \(10^{12}\) kg) of ice mass loss corresponds to a global mean sea level rise of \(\sim\)2.78 \(\mu\)m. GRACE-FO measures Greenland’s \(-280\) Gt/yr loss, Antarctica’s \(-150\) Gt/yr loss, and mountain glacier contributions, together accounting for \(\sim\)2 mm/yr of the observed 3.7 mm/yr sea level rise.

Applications include: glacial mass balance (Greenland, Antarctica, mountain glaciers); groundwater depletion in major aquifers (India Indo-Gangetic Plain, California Central Valley, Ogallala Aquifer); ocean bottom pressure and ocean circulation; terrestrial water storage anomalies for drought and flood monitoring; and post-glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA) separating current cryospheric changes from ancient ice-age rebound.

docs.title: 20.3.2 Ice Topography: ICESat-2
docs.text:
ICESat-2 (Ice, Cloud, and land Elevation Satellite-2), launched September 2018, employs the Advanced Topographic Laser Altimeter System (ATLAS), a photon-counting green (532 nm) laser altimeter. The laser fires 20 \(\mu\)J pulses at 10 kHz, split by diffractive optics into six beams arranged as three pairs. Each pair spans 3.3 km cross-track; the two beams in each pair are separated by 90 m.

The photon-counting detector array uses single-photon avalanche detectors (SPADs) capable of timing individual returning photons to \(\sim\)300 ps (4.5 cm range equivalent). At an orbital velocity of 7 km/s and 10 kHz fire rate, along-track sample spacing is 0.7 m. When averaged over 100 m segments, ice sheet elevation precision reaches \(\sim\)3 mm. Applications include: Arctic and Antarctic ice sheet mass balance; sea ice freeboard from which thickness and volume are derived; forest canopy height for biomass estimation; shallow-water bathymetry (\(<\)40 m depth in clear water); and inland lake and river surface elevation for hydrological monitoring.

docs.title: 20.3.3 Atmosphere and Climate
docs.text:
OCO-2 and OCO-3: The Orbiting Carbon Observatory 2 (2014, 705 km sun-synchronous) and OCO-3 (2019, on ISS) use three-band grating spectrometers measuring reflected sunlight at 0.76 \(\mu\)m (O\(_2\) A-band, pressure calibration), 1.61 \(\mu\)m (CO\(_2\) weak absorption), and 2.06 \(\mu\)m (CO\(_2\) strong absorption). Column-averaged dry-air CO\(_2\) mole fraction (XCO\(_2\)) is retrieved with \(\sim\)0.5 ppm precision against a \(\sim\)420 ppm background. OCO-2 has captured the seasonal “breathing” of terrestrial ecosystems and anomalous CO\(_2\) releases from El Niño droughts and boreal forest fires.

SMAP (launched January 2015): The Soil Moisture Active Passive mission measures surface soil moisture (0–5 cm) at 40 km resolution via an L-band (1.4 GHz) radiometer with 3-day global revisit. The L-band penetrates moderate vegetation canopies, enabling retrievals of volumetric soil moisture to 0.04 m\(^3\)/m\(^3\) accuracy. Applications include drought early warning, flood inundation mapping, and agricultural yield forecasting.

TROPOMI on Sentinel-5P (launched October 2017): The TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument is a nadir push-broom hyperspectral spectrometer covering UV (270–320 nm), UV-VIS (305–400 nm), NIR (675–775 nm), and SWIR (2305–2385 nm) with a ground pixel of 5.5 km \(\times\) 3.5 km (7 km \(\times\) 3.5 km before August 2019). Daily global mapping at this resolution enables: NO\(_2\) column mapping for urban air quality; tropospheric and total ozone; SO\(_2\) from volcanic emissions and smelters; methane (CH\(_4\)) hotspots from oil/gas fields and landfills; CO from wildfires; and formaldehyde as a proxy for biogenic and pyrogenic VOC emissions.

GPM Core Observatory (launched February 2014): The Global Precipitation Measurement mission carries the Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar (DPR) at Ku-band (13.6 GHz) and Ka-band (35.5 GHz), measuring rainfall rate from 0.5 mm/hr to 300 mm/hr. The multi-frequency approach distinguishes rain and snow. A constellation of 10+ partner radiometers extends coverage to 65N–65S with 30-minute global revisit.

docs.title: 20.3.4 ESA Copernicus Sentinels
docs.text:
The Copernicus programme operates the Sentinel satellite series, providing free open-access data for European environmental and security services:

Sentinel-1 (\(C\)-band SAR, 5.4 GHz): Interferometric Wide Swath (IW) mode provides a 250 km swath at 5 m \(\times\) 20 m resolution with 6-day revisit (two satellites). Strip Map (SM) mode achieves 5 m resolution over 80 km. InSAR processing of repeat-pass pairs detects ground deformation at millimetre scale for earthquake, volcanic, and subsidence monitoring.

Sentinel-2 (MultiSpectral Instrument, MSI): 13 spectral bands from 443–2190 nm at 10 m (four visible/NIR), 20 m (six red-edge/SWIR), and 60 m (three atmospheric correction) spatial resolution. With two satellites, 5-day global revisit enables dense phenological time series. The Normalised Difference Vegetation Index NDVI \(= (R_{NIR} - R_{red})/(R_{NIR} + R_{red})\) is derived at 10 m for crop monitoring, land cover mapping, and deforestation detection.

Sentinel-3: Ocean and land mission carrying the Ocean and Land Colour Instrument (OLCI, 21 bands, 300 m, 1.7-day revisit), Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR, 9 channels, SST \(\pm\)0.3 K), and SAR Radar Altimeter (SRAL) for ocean topography and inland water surface height.

Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich: The Jason altimetry successor carries the Poseidon-4 Ku/C-band radar altimeter providing sea surface height with \(\sim\)2 cm precision. Continuous records since TOPEX/Poseidon (1992) document global mean sea level rise of \(3.7 \pm 0.5\) mm/yr with an accelerating trend.

docs.title: 20.4.1 Magnetospheric Missions
docs.text:
Van Allen Probes (RBSP, launched August 2012, decommissioned October 2019): Two spacecraft in highly elliptical orbits (\(600 \times 30{,}600\) km, 10.2 inclination) traversed the radiation belts four to six times per day. The Relativistic Electron-Proton Telescope (REPT) and Magnetic Electron-Ion Spectrometer (MagEIS) measured energetic particle fluxes from 20 keV to 100 MeV electrons. The Electric and Magnetic Field Instrument Suite and Integrated Science (EMFISIS) measured DC to 12 kHz plasma waves. Discoveries include a transient “third” radiation belt, ultra-relativistic acceleration via chorus wave resonance, and dramatic loss events during geomagnetic storms.

Cluster II (ESA, four spacecraft, launched 2000): Operating in a tetrahedral formation with separations adjustable from 100 km to 100,000 km, Cluster provides the only multi-spacecraft measurement of 3D plasma and field structures. The Fluxgate Magnetometer (FGM), WHISPER plasma wave antenna, CIS ion composition analyser, and STAFF search-coil provide comprehensive plasma diagnostics. All four spacecraft remain operational after 24+ years—an extraordinary mission lifetime.

Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS): NASA’s four MMS spacecraft (launched March 2015) target electron-scale magnetic reconnection with 10–160 km inter-spacecraft separations. The Fast Plasma Investigation (FPI) measures complete electron and ion distribution functions every 30 ms—fast enough to resolve the electron diffusion region where reconnection occurs. MMS directly measured the reconnection rate and confirmed theoretical predictions of electron demagnetisation in current sheets, resolving a 60-year-old fundamental plasma physics question.

docs.title: 20.4.2 Solar Missions
docs.text:
Parker Solar Probe (NASA, launched August 2018): Using seven Venus gravity assists to progressively lower its perihelion, Parker Solar Probe reached about 6.1 million km from the Sun’s centre (0.041 AU, within the solar corona) in December 2024 and achieved a heliocentric speed record of 690,000 km/h (192 km/s). The Thermal Protection System (TPS)—a 115 mm thick carbon composite foam sandwich—shields instruments from \(>\)1650C solar irradiance while maintaining instrument temperatures near ambient.

Parker’s four instrument suites include: FIELDS (electric and magnetic fields, plasma waves, quasi-thermal noise spectroscopy); WISPR (Wide-field Imager for Solar PRobe, white-light coronagraph images of coronal structures and CMEs); SWEAP (Solar Wind Electrons Alphas and Protons, electron/ion velocity distribution functions); and IS\(\odot\)IS (Integrated Science Investigation of the Sun, energetic particle spectra 20 keV–100 MeV).

Key results: direct measurement of the Alfvén critical surface location (the boundary where solar wind transitions from sub- to super-Alfvénic); discovery of ubiquitous magnetic “switchbacks” (reversals of field polarity); and first in-situ sampling of dust-free zone near the Sun.

Solar Orbiter (ESA/NASA, launched February 2020): Achieves 0.28 AU perihelion and, through gravity assists, latitudes up to 33 above the ecliptic—enabling the first images of solar polar regions. Six remote-sensing instruments (EUI high-resolution EUV imager, METIS coronagraph, PHI helioseismic photometer, SoloHI wide-field imager, SPICE UV spectrograph, STIX X-ray spectrometer) operate synergistically with four in-situ instruments (MAG, SWA, EPD, RPW) to connect solar wind source regions to local plasma measurements.

Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO): In geosynchronous-class orbit for continuous ground station visibility, SDO transmits \(\sim\)1.5 TB/day. The Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) images the full solar disk in 10 EUV channels every 12 s at 0.6 arcsec/pixel.
