docs.title: 27.11 CW Trajectory Diagram
docs.text:
Figure 27.1 illustrates a V-bar approach trajectory in the Clohessy-Wiltshire (Hill) frame, showing the natural drift and controlled hold-point approach.

Figure 27.1. Clohessy-Wiltshire frame V-bar approach trajectory for an OOS servicer rendezvous. The chaser traverses a series of hold points (HP1–HP4) spaced along the +\(y\) (V-bar) axis, executing impulsive \(\Delta v\) maneuvers at each hold point to counteract natural drift and advance to the next waypoint. The keep-out sphere (KOS, dashed red circle) defines the exclusion zone around the target within which entry requires positive ground authorization. A natural drift ellipse (dashed green) illustrates the trajectory a free-drifting chaser would follow without additional thrust.

docs.title: 27.12 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter 27 Key Takeaways

  • On-orbit servicing encompasses life extension (MEV), refueling (OSAM-1), inspection, relocation, and active debris removal—each imposing distinct rendezvous, manipulation, and interface requirements.

  • The Clohessy-Wiltshire equations govern relative motion for close proximity operations; V-bar glideslope and R-bar approaches provide the principal rendezvous corridors with distinct safety and propellant trade-offs.

  • Navigation sensor suites combine LIDAR (0.1-m range accuracy at 100 m), stereo vision (photogrammetric), relative GPS (\(\pm\)1 m in LEO), and CNN-based pose estimation (\(<\)1% error at 5 m) into layered architectures.

  • Commercial OOS missions (MEV-1/2, Astroscale ELSA-d, ClearSpace-1) have demonstrated or are demonstrating the full lifecycle from rendezvous to capture to life extension or deorbit in both GEO and LEO environments.

  • Impedance control with wrist force-torque sensing enables compliant manipulation for ORU exchange and propellant transfer without damaging either the manipulator or client hardware.

  • Propellant refueling economics are compelling: a $50–100M refueling mission providing 5-year life extension of a $300M GEO satellite delivers NPV-positive returns even at conservative revenue assumptions.

  • Interface standardization (RAFTI, CONFERS, ESA SDI) and regulatory clarification (ITU, FCC, COPUOS) are the two principal non-technical barriers to widespread OOS market adoption.

docs.title: Chapter 28: Space Debris and Long-Term Sustainability
docs.text:
“We are conducting a grand experiment in orbit: filling a finite commons with an ever-growing population of objects, some operational, many dead, all moving at velocities that turn a paint flake into a projectile. The experiment has no control group.”

The near-Earth space environment is increasingly congested with the detritus of six decades of human spaceflight. More than 34,000 objects larger than 10 cm are tracked by the United States Space Surveillance Network (SSN); statistical models indicate the presence of perhaps 900,000 objects in the 1–10 cm size range—too small to track reliably but large enough to cause catastrophic damage to a spacecraft—and over 128 million fragments smaller than 1 cm. The aggregate mass of all artificial objects in Earth orbit exceeds 9,400 metric tons. This environment has been shaped by a handful of catastrophic fragmentation events, by the accumulation of rocket upper stages and defunct satellites, and by the proliferation of operational constellations that increase both the collision risk and the mitigation challenge. The threat is not hypothetical: it was concretely realized on February 10, 2009, when Iridium 33 and the defunct Cosmos 2251 collided at 789 km altitude, producing 2296 trackable fragments and demonstrating that the Kessler syndrome—a self-sustaining collision cascade—is not a theoretical curiosity but an operational risk that is already unfolding in specific altitude bands. This chapter develops the physics of the debris environment, the engineering of impact protection, the mathematics of cascade dynamics, the technology of active debris removal, and the governance frameworks emerging to ensure the long-term sustainability of Earth orbit as a shared resource (Kessler and Cour-Palais 1978).

docs.title: 28.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Orbital debris is, in essence, a tragedy of the commons at 7.8 km/s. Each actor who launches into orbit gains exclusive use of the launched spacecraft but shares the increased collision risk with all other operators—a classic externality that the market, without regulation, systematically underweights. Debris mitigation guidelines, passivation requirements, deorbit timelines, and active debris removal are all instruments directed at correcting this externality: internalizing the cost of orbital pollution that each mission imposes on the shared orbital environment.

The problem is physically self-amplifying in a way that distinguishes it from most environmental challenges. Above a critical debris density threshold—estimated to have already been crossed in certain altitude bands near 800 km—the collision rate between existing objects exceeds the natural removal rate from atmospheric drag. Even if all launches ceased tomorrow, the debris population in these altitude bands would continue to grow through mutual collisions over decades to centuries. This insight, captured mathematically by Kessler and Cour-Palais in 1978 (Kessler and Cour-Palais 1978), defines the urgency of both mitigation and active removal.

The chapter proceeds as follows. Section 28.2 characterizes the current debris environment quantitatively. Section 28.3 covers hypervelocity impact physics and Whipple shield design. Section 28.4 develops the cascade dynamics mathematically. Section 28.5 reviews Space Situational Awareness (SSA) sensors, catalog maintenance, and conjunction assessment. Sections 28.6 and 28.7 address mitigation guidelines and active debris removal technologies. Section 28.8 covers the broader sustainability governance and economics framework.

docs.title: 28.2.1 Population Statistics
docs.text:
The US Space Surveillance Network (SSN) maintained by US Space Command tracks objects larger than approximately 10 cm in LEO and 1 m in GEO, cataloging their orbital elements (TLE format) and publishing the data publicly via the Space-Track.org portal. As of 2024, the SSN catalog contains approximately 34,000 objects. The European Space Agency’s MASTER-8 (Meteoroid and Space Debris Terrestrial Environment Reference) statistical model extends the population characterization to smaller sizes using fragment size distributions derived from ground-based and orbital measurements, calibrated against known fragmentation events. MASTER-8 estimates approximately 900,000 objects in the 1–10 cm size range (too small to track with current ground-based radar but large enough to cause catastrophic satellite damage on impact) and over 128 million fragments below 1 cm. The total mass of all artificial objects in orbit—including intact spacecraft, rocket bodies, and debris—exceeds 9,400 metric tons, of which operational satellites account for approximately 2,500 metric tons.

NASA’s ORDEM (Orbital Debris Engineering Model, version 3.2) provides flux estimates for orbital debris impact assessment:

\[\Phi(d, h, i) = \int_{h_\text{min}}^{h_\text{max}} \rho(h, i, d)\,V_\text{rel}(h,i)\,d h \quad [\text{m}^{-2}\,\text{yr}^{-1}]\tag{28.1}\]

where \(\rho\) is the spatial density of objects larger than diameter \(d\) at altitude \(h\) and inclination \(i\), and \(V_\text{rel}\) is the average relative velocity. At the ISS altitude (400 km) and inclination (51.6\(^\circ\)), the ORDEM 3.2 impact flux for 1-cm objects is approximately \(5 \times 10^{-5}\) m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)—meaning a 1-m\(^2\) exposed surface would experience a 1-cm object impact roughly every 20,000 years, but the ISS’s exposed critical surface area is orders of magnitude larger, making MMOD (Micrometeoroid and Orbital Debris) a persistent design driver.

docs.title: 28.2.2 Debris Sources
docs.text:
The orbital debris population arises from several distinct source categories, each with characteristic size distributions and altitude profiles:

  • Fragmentation events (the majority of objects): The largest debris source by object count. Explosions of spent rocket upper stages (aging propellant and battery deterioration, residual propellant detonation) and hypervelocity collisions between tracked objects generate clouds of fragments spanning the full size spectrum from meter-scale down to sub-millimeter. The Breeze-M upper stage (used on the Russian Proton) has been responsible for several fragmentation events, cumulatively adding hundreds of tracked objects.

  • Rocket bodies: Upper stages and mission adapters left in operational orbits represent the largest individual debris objects—typically 1,000–4,000 kg each. Their large collision cross-section makes them disproportionate contributors to the Kessler cascade risk; a collision involving a rocket body can produce a very large number of fragments.

  • Mission-related debris: Separation nuts, clamp bands, lens caps, shrouds, payload adapters, and other objects released intentionally during mission operations.

  • Defunct satellites: Approximately 3,000 non-operational satellites tracked in the SSN catalog, spanning from Vanguard 1 (1958) to recent commercial failures.

  • Sub-centimeter fragments: Paint flakes detached by UV and thermal cycling, multi-layer insulation (MLI) fragments from aging thermal blankets, and solid propellant slag particles—untrackable but cumulatively representing a significant hypervelocity flux on exposed surfaces.

docs.title: 28.2.3 Major Fragmentation Events
docs.text:
A small number of catastrophic events have dominated the growth of the tracked debris population:

Fengyun-1C ASAT Test (January 11, 2007).

China’s destruction of its defunct Fengyun-1C weather satellite at 863 km altitude using a kinetic kill vehicle created 3537 new trackable fragments—the largest single contribution to the SSN catalog from any event. At 863 km altitude, atmospheric drag is negligible: the fragments will remain in orbit for centuries to millennia, with the highest-altitude pieces (apogee \(>\)2000 km) effectively permanent. The test increased the collision probability for objects at 750–1000 km altitude by approximately 10% and drew worldwide diplomatic criticism that led China to announce a moratorium on further destructive ASAT testing.

Iridium 33 / Cosmos 2251 Collision (February 10, 2009).

At 789 km altitude over Siberia, the operational Iridium 33 communication satellite collided with the defunct Russian Cosmos 2251 military communication satellite at a closing velocity of approximately 11.7 km/s—the first accidental collision between two intact satellites in history. The collision generated 2296 trackable fragments (with tens of thousands of smaller untracked pieces) and remains the single largest increase in LEO collision risk from a non-deliberate event. The Iridium constellation was redesigned to include automatic collision avoidance capability for subsequent generations, but the debris cloud from the collision persists at an altitude where it will remain hazardous for decades.

USA-193 Intercept (February 2008).

The US Navy’s destruction of the malfunctioning USA-193 reconnaissance satellite at 247 km altitude produced fragments that largely decayed within weeks due to the low altitude, avoiding the long-term persistence that characterized the FY-1C event. The decision to intercept was publicly justified on hydrazine propellant risk grounds.

docs.title: 28.2.4 Spatial Distribution by Altitude
docs.text:
The debris spatial density is strongly altitude-dependent, reflecting both the history of launch activities and the varying atmospheric drag lifetimes at different altitudes:

  • LEO (200–2000 km): Peak debris spatial density at 750–900 km, elevated by the FY-1C and Iridium/Cosmos events. Atmospheric drag lifetimes at 750 km are approximately 200–400 years; at 400 km (ISS), less than 1 year. The Starlink, OneWeb, and Kuiper constellations operate at 340–550 km where 5-year deorbit is naturally achievable.

  • MEO (2000–35,786 km): Lower debris density but including GPS, GLONASS, and Galileo satellite rings. Radiation belt trapping of charged fragments and nuclear-powered satellites (RORSAT program) create additional hazards. The van Allen belts significantly increase radiation dose rates for objects at MEO altitudes.

  • GEO (35,786 km): A ring of roughly 1500 satellites (operational and defunct) plus the accumulated objects from 60 years of GEO operations. Unlike LEO, there is no natural removal mechanism at GEO; disposal to a graveyard orbit 300+ km above the GEO arc is required to remove objects from the active operational band.

docs.title: 28.3.1 Hypervelocity Impact Physics
docs.text:
Objects in LEO collide with spacecraft surfaces at average velocities of approximately 10 km/s (mean for LEO object vs. operational satellite at similar altitude and inclination) with maximum closing velocities of approximately 15 km/s for head-on collisions. At these velocities, the impact process is dominated by hydrodynamic phenomena rather than material strength: both impactor and target material behave as fluids during the initial impact, with the shock wave pressure far exceeding the material yield strength. A 1-cm aluminum sphere impacting a thin aluminum wall at 10 km/s creates a crater \(\sim\)5 cm in diameter and may penetrate walls up to 1 cm thick; behind a simple wall, it produces a debris cloud of thousands of fragments more destructive than the original impactor.

The threshold for catastrophic fragmentation of a satellite—defined as producing more mass in fragments than in the largest remaining piece—corresponds to a specific energy threshold:

\[\frac{E_k}{M_\text{target}} = \frac{m_p v_r^2}{2 M_\text{target}} \geq 40 \;\text{J/g} \quad \text{(for aluminum alloy targets)}\tag{28.2}\]

where \(m_p\) is the impactor mass, \(v_r\) is the relative velocity, and \(M_\text{target}\) is the target satellite mass. For a 1000-kg satellite at 10 km/s average impact velocity, catastrophic fragmentation requires an impactor of only \(m_p = 0.8\) kg—an object approximately 10 cm in diameter—demonstrating that untracked 10-cm objects represent a catastrophic threat to operational satellites.

docs.title: 28.3.2 Whipple Shield Design
docs.text:
The Whipple shield, invented by Fred Whipple in 1947, exploits the fact that a thin aluminum bumper plate vaporizes and disperses the impactor into a debris cloud whose energy is spread over a larger area, allowing a thinner rear wall to stop the dispersed fragments. The canonical penetration limit for the rear wall thickness \(t\) of a Whipple shield is given by the modified Cour-Palais equation:

\[t = 0.25\,m_p^{1/3}\,\frac{(v_r\cos\theta)^{2/3}}{\rho_B^{1/3}\,S_{cr}^{1/3}}\tag{28.3}\]

where \(m_p\) is the impactor mass (g), \(v_r\) is the relative velocity (km/s), \(\theta\) is the impact angle from normal, \(\rho_B\) is the bumper density (g/cm\(^3\)), and \(S_{cr}\) is the standoff distance between bumper and rear wall (cm). Doubling the standoff distance reduces the rear wall thickness requirement by a factor \(2^{-1/3} \approx 0.79\) (about 21%)—illustrating the importance of maximizing standoff within spacecraft volume constraints.

Modern ISS shielding employs multi-shock shields with multiple thin bumper layers of different materials:

  1. Outer aluminum 6061-T6 bumper (0.8–3.2 mm thick): vaporizes the impactor

  2. Intermediate Nextel AF-62 ceramic fabric + Kevlar layers: captures and disperses fragment cloud

  3. Inner aluminum or stuffed Whipple rear wall: final containment

Multi-shock shields stop larger projectiles at a given mass per unit area than a simple Whipple shield, which is why they are used on the more exposed parts of the ISS.

docs.title: 28.3.3 Impact Probability Analysis for ISS
docs.text:
The MMOD risk to the ISS is assessed using NASA’s BUMPER code, which integrates a debris flux model such as NASA’s ORDEM over the ISS surface geometry, accounting for orientation, shielding configuration, and module-specific critical area. The metric used is Probability of No Penetration (PNP):

\[\text{PNP} = \exp\!\left(-\Phi \cdot A_c \cdot \Delta t\right)\tag{28.4}\]

where \(\Phi\) is the integrated MMOD flux for penetrating objects (m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)), \(A_c\) is the total critical exposed area (m\(^2\)), and \(\Delta t\) is the exposure time (yr). NASA sets a demanding PNP requirement for crewed modules, which drives the adoption of multi-shock shielding for habitable volumes.

docs.title: 28.4.1 Kessler-Cour-Palais Theory
docs.text: Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais published a landmark 1978 paper (Kessler and Cour-Palais 1978) demonstrating that, for a sufficiently dense debris population, the collision rate between objects exceeds the natural removal rate, initiating a self-sustaining cascade. The key insight is that the number of fragments produced by a collision grows with the colliding mass (in the NASA Standard Breakup Model the number of fragments larger than a given size scales with the mass raised to the power 0.75); if these new fragments have shorter atmospheric drag lifetimes they are removed, but if they orbit at altitudes where lifetimes exceed the orbital period by large factors, they persist to participate in further collisions.

docs.title: 28.4.2 Collision Rate Equation
docs.text:
The pairwise collision rate in an orbital shell of volume \(V_\text{total}\), object count \(N\), average collision cross-section \(\sigma = \pi(r_1 + r_2)^2\), and average relative velocity \(V_\text{rel}\) is:

\[R_c = \frac{1}{2}\frac{N^2}{V_\text{total}}\,\sigma\,V_\text{rel}\tag{28.5}\]

The factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\) avoids double-counting pairwise collisions. For an illustrative case, the 750–900 km altitude band (where FY-1C and Iridium/Cosmos debris is concentrated), with \(N \approx 5000\) tracked objects, an assumed average cross-section \(\sigma \approx 1\) m\(^2\), \(V_\text{rel} = 10\) km/s and \(V_\text{total} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{12}\) km\(^3\), gives \(R_c \approx 0.003\) collisions per year—roughly one collision every 300 years among the tracked objects alone. Smaller untracked objects add many more potential collisions, mostly non-catastrophic, and detailed models give higher rates in the most crowded altitude bands.

docs.title: 28.4.3 Critical Density and Cascade Threshold
docs.text:
The critical spatial density \(\rho_\text{cr}\) at which the collision rate \(R_c\) equals the natural removal rate \(R_d = N/\tau_d\) (where \(\tau_d\) is the atmospheric drag lifetime) is:

\[\rho_\text{cr} = \frac{N_\text{cr}}{V_\text{total}} = \frac{2}{\sigma\,V_\text{rel}\,\tau_d\,f}\tag{28.6}\]

where \(f\) is the fragmentation coefficient (fragments produced per collision exceeding the critical threshold). At 900 km altitude, the estimated critical density is approximately \(N_\text{cr} \approx 10^{-8}\) km\(^{-3}\), corresponding to roughly 500 objects larger than 10 cm in the 750–1000 km shell. Long-term evolution modeling using NASA’s LEGEND (LEO-to-GEO Environment Debris) Monte Carlo simulation indicates that this density is already exceeded in some altitude sub-bands when untracked objects are included, and that long-term projections show continued growth of the debris population in LEO without active debris removal, even with good compliance with mitigation guidelines.

The LEGEND model further quantifies the Active Debris Removal (ADR) requirement: removing of the order of 5–10 large objects per year (preferably intact rocket bodies or defunct satellites with large collision cross-sections) from the 800–900 km altitude band is sufficient to stabilize the population at approximately current levels—a conclusion that has driven the development of commercial ADR missions.

docs.title: 28.5.1 US Space Surveillance Network
docs.text:
The US Space Surveillance Network comprises more than 30 sensor sites worldwide, combining dedicated space surveillance radars and telescopes with sensors tasked from other primary missions. Key SSN sensors include:

  • Eglin AFB AN/FPS-85 (Florida): A UHF phased array radar, a long-serving sensor of the network for tracking satellites in low Earth orbit.

  • Ground-based Electro-Optical Deep Space Surveillance (GEODSS): One-meter aperture telescopes at Diego Garcia (Indian Ocean), Maui (Hawaii), and Socorro (New Mexico) provide deep-space (GEO and above) optical surveillance.

  • Globus II (Vardø, Norway): An X-band tracking radar in Norway, used for space object tracking and characterization, including radar cross-section (RCS) estimation.

  • Space Fence (Kwajalein Atoll, Marshall Islands; declared operational in 2020): An S-band phased array radar with separate transmit and receive arrays. It can detect and track much smaller objects in LEO than the older radars it supplements (down to a few centimetres), and is expected to add many thousands of new objects to the catalog.

docs.title: 28.5.2 Commercial Space Situational Awareness
docs.text:
A growing commercial SSA ecosystem supplements government sensors with higher revisit rates, specialized capabilities, and data products sold to satellite operators:

  • LeoLabs: Operates a network of phased array radars, including sites at Poker Flat (Alaska), Midland (Texas), New Zealand, Costa Rica and the Azores, and sells tracking data and conjunction assessment services to satellite operators and agencies.

  • ExoAnalytic Solutions: Operates a network of over 300 optical telescopes worldwide, including 25-cm aperture stations optimized for GEO and MEO surveillance. Provides commercial data products for GEO conjunction assessment, object characterization, and satellite health monitoring.

  • Slingshot Aerospace: Provides space traffic analytics and conjunction assessment products using a fusion of government and commercial sensor data, with a focus on automated conjunction screening for constellation operators.

docs.title: 28.5.3 Conjunction Assessment
docs.text:
The US Space Command 18th Space Control Squadron (18 SPCS, formerly 18th Space Control Squadron) provides conjunction assessment services to all satellite operators through the public portal space-track.org, screening all cataloged objects against each other and issuing Conjunction Data Messages (CDMs) when the probability of collision \(P_c\) exceeds notification thresholds.

The probability of collision is computed using the Alfano formulation that integrates the combined position-covariance probability density function over the hard-body region—a disk of radius \(r_1 + r_2\) (sum of the objects’ radii) in the plane of closest approach:

\[P_c = \int\!\!\int_{\text{hard-body}} p_\text{combined}(x, y)\,dx\,dy\tag{28.7}\]

where \(p_\text{combined}(x,y)\) is the 2D Gaussian probability density in the miss-plane formed by the combined position error covariance of both objects. The standard maneuver threshold recommended by IADC and NASA is \(P_c > 10^{-4}\), above which a conjunction warrants serious consideration of an avoidance maneuver. The ISS executes approximately 25–30 avoidance maneuvers per year against debris conjunctions.

A critical limitation of current conjunction assessment is TLE accuracy: Two-Line Element sets have typical 1\(\sigma\) position errors of 1–2 km at epoch, growing to 10 km or more after 5 days of propagation. This large uncertainty dominates \(P_c\) calculations and drives many false-positive high-\(P_c\) alerts that do not materialize as actual close approaches. Improved orbital element sources (Laser ranging, commercial GNSS on satellites, commercial radar tracking) would substantially reduce uncertainty and improve maneuver decision quality.

docs.title: 28.5.4 Orbit Determination Accuracy
docs.text: Ranging techniques vary enormously in accuracy: TLEs based on radar tracking have position uncertainties of 1 km at epoch; satellite laser ranging (SLR) achieves better than 1-cm ranging accuracy for retro-reflector-equipped satellites; VLBI (Very Long Baseline Interferometry) provides sub-centimeter angular positioning for radio-emitting satellites. The dramatic accuracy difference between TLE-based and high-precision orbit determination drives ongoing advocacy for broader deployment of laser reflectors on active satellites and for exchange of high-accuracy ephemeris data among operators.

docs.title: 28.6.1 IADC Mitigation Guidelines
docs.text:
The Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee (IADC), comprising 13 national space agencies, published the internationally recognized debris mitigation guidelines that form the basis of national and international regulation. The key provisions are (IADC 2007):

  1. 25-year deorbit rule: Objects in LEO at altitudes below 2000 km should complete reentry within 25 years of mission completion. This was the industry standard from 2002 until the FCC adopted a 5-year requirement for US-licensed satellites in 2022.

  2. GEO graveyard orbit: GEO objects should be moved to a disposal orbit at least 300 km above the GEO arc (\(\geq\)36,086 km) at end of mission, where they will not interfere with active GEO operations. The required \(\Delta v\) for this disposal maneuver is approximately 11 m/s for typical GEO satellites.

  3. Passivation: Within 5 years of end of life, all stored energy on the spacecraft must be depleted: propellant vented or burned, pressure vessels vented, batteries discharged through shorting resistors, and pyrotechnic devices safed. Passivation eliminates the risk of on-orbit explosions that have been responsible for the majority of fragmentation events.

  4. Collision probability during disposal: The probability of collision with a cataloged object during the disposal maneuver must be less than 0.001.

  5. Casualty risk at reentry: The probability of human casualty from surviving reentry fragments on Earth’s surface must be less than \(10^{-4}\) per reentry event.

docs.title: 28.6.2 FCC 5-Year Deorbit Rule
docs.text: In September 2022, the US Federal Communications Commission adopted a rule reducing the post-mission deorbit time for US-licensed satellites in LEO from 25 years to 5 years, applying to satellites launched after September 2024. This revision, informed by technical analyses showing that 5-year compliance substantially reduces the probability of a Kessler cascade at the densely populated 800–900 km altitudes, applies to Starlink (operating at 340–550 km where natural deorbit within 5 years is achievable), OneWeb, and future Amazon Kuiper deployments. Operators who fail to comply may forfeit bonds of $1 million per satellite and risk revocation of their FCC operating licenses.

docs.title: 28.6.3 Design for Demise
docs.text:
The casualty area (\(A_c\)) of a reentering spacecraft is the effective area around a ground impact point within which a standing person would be killed by fragment impact, computed as the sum of geometric areas of all surviving fragments augmented by the kinetic lethal radius:

\[A_\text{casualty} = \sum_i \pi \left(\frac{d_{\text{frag},i}}{2} + 0.6\right)^2 \text{ (m}^2\text{)}\tag{28.8}\]

where \(d_{\text{frag},i}\) is the diameter of the \(i\)th surviving fragment in meters, and 0.6 m is the assumed average human body radius. The IADC limit is \(A_\text{casualty} < 8\) m\(^2\) per reentry event; exceeding this requires a controlled reentry to an uninhabited ocean zone.

The Design for Demise (D4D) philosophy maximizes the fraction of spacecraft mass that ablates and vaporizes in the reentry heating environment (above 80 km altitude) rather than surviving to the surface. Aluminum alloy components (melting point 933 K) readily demise; titanium alloy components (melting point 1941 K) and carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) tubes with titanium inserts frequently survive to the surface. Tantalum capacitors (melting point 3290 K) are among the most likely components to survive complete reentry. Modern satellite design for demise replaces titanium fasteners with aluminum equivalents, eliminates CFRP tubes in structural locations, and substitutes aluminum electrolytic capacitors for tantalum types where circuit requirements permit. ESA’s DRAMA (Debris Risk Assessment and Mitigation Analysis) software tool propagates heat transfer through the satellite structure during reentry to estimate surviving mass and casualty area.

docs.title: 28.6.4 Passivation Design
docs.text:
Passivation failures—aging propulsion and battery systems exploding rather than passivating—represent the dominant source of debris fragmentation events. Engineering solutions implemented in modern satellite designs include:

  • Propellant venting: Self-pressurizing orifice valves or pyrotechnic line cutters open propellant tank vents after a programmable delay (typically 1–3 years post-EOL), allowing residual bipropellant or monopropellant to vent to vacuum in a controlled manner.

  • Pressure vessel venting: High-pressure helium pressurant tanks vent through burst disks or redundant solenoid valves actuated by EOL command; the delayed activation (1 year post-EOL) provides a safety margin before the command is executed.

  • Battery passivation: End-of-life controller logic applies a shorting resistor across battery cells, dissipating stored charge within minutes; some designs incorporate pyrotechnic cell breakers as a backup.

  • Pyrotechnic safing: Initiator circuits are permanently disabled by firing safety pins or removing bridge wire circuits, preventing accidental actuation of separation systems from accumulated electrostatic charge.

docs.title: 28.7.1 RemoveDEBRIS Mission
docs.text:
The RemoveDEBRIS mission (Surrey Space Centre / Airbus DS, 100-kg satellite, taken to the ISS in April 2018 and deployed in June 2018) conducted the first in-orbit demonstrations of active debris removal technologies:

  • Net capture (September 2018): A 5\(\times\)5 m Vectran braided net was ejected at 7-m range toward a deployed DebriSat target, successfully enveloping and capturing it. Net ejection was performed with four corner masses providing spin stability, and closure of the net mouth was achieved by a drawstring mechanism.

  • Harpoon capture (February 2019): A 1.5-kg CFRP target panel was deployed on a 1.5-m tether, and a spring-launched harpoon projectile at 20 m/s successfully penetrated the panel and retained attachment through barbed tip engagement.

  • Vision-Based Navigation (VBN) demonstration: AI-enhanced proximity operations navigation using monocular cameras tracked the DebriSat target over a range of 3–10 m.

  • Drag sail deorbit: A 10-m\(^2\) drag augmentation sail was deployed in February 2019, accelerating deorbit from the 400-km altitude by increasing ballistic coefficient drag.

docs.title: 28.7.2 ESA ClearSpace-1
docs.text: ESA’s ClearSpace-1 mission, contracted to ClearSpace SA (Switzerland) for approximately EUR 86 million, was originally to target the Vespa (Vega Secondary Payload Adapter) ring—a 112-kg CFRP structural ring left in a 664-km orbit by the second Vega flight in 2013. The concept was to capture the Vespa with four articulated claw arms with compliant contact fingers, and then to perform a deorbit burn to destructive reentry. The mission was later redefined (in 2023 ESA changed the target to its own PROBA-1 satellite) and its launch date has slipped more than once, so it has not yet flown. The mission serves simultaneously as a demonstration of ESA’s commercial ADR service procurement model and as a technology pathfinder for future higher-rate ADR operations.

docs.title: 28.7.3 Astroscale ELSA-d and CRD2
docs.text:
Astroscale’s ELSA-d mission (2021) demonstrated the magnetic docking plate concept: the 17-kg client satellite carried a permanent magnet docking plate, and the 175-kg chaser demonstrated approach, capture, release, and re-capture in multiple geometries, including with the client in a slowly tumbling non-cooperative attitude. The magnetic capture approach avoids the complex mechanical latching required for physical grapple mechanisms and tolerates some residual misalignment at contact.

JAXA’s Commercial Removal of Debris Demonstration (CRD2) Phase 1—the ADRAS-J (Active Debris Removal by Astroscale-Japan) mission, launched February 2024—conducted proximity operations around the intact H-IIA rocket body (3000 kg) at approximately 600-km orbit, characterizing the tumbling rate, surface condition, and approach envelope of a real-world large debris target without physical capture. Phase 2 will include physical capture and deorbit.

docs.title: 28.7.4 Ion Beam Shepherd
docs.text:
The Ion Beam Shepherd (IBS) concept proposes contactless debris removal by directing the exhaust plume of an electric propulsion thruster toward the debris object’s surface, imparting a net photon-plus-ion-pressure force that gradually alters its orbit. The effective force on the debris is approximately:

\[F_\text{IBS} \approx 0.7\,\frac{P_\text{thrust}}{v_\text{exhaust}}\left(\frac{d_\text{target}}{d_\text{beam}}\right)^2\tag{28.9}\]

where \(P_\text{thrust}\) is the thruster power, \(v_\text{exhaust}\) is the ion exhaust velocity, and the geometric factor accounts for beam interception by the target cross-section. For a 100-W Hall thruster at 60-cm standoff distance from a 1-m cross-section debris object, the effective IBS force is approximately 1 mN—enough to change orbital velocity by 1 m/s per week, or deorbit from 800 km in approximately 3 years. A secondary thruster on the opposite face of the shepherd spacecraft maintains formation flying at the required standoff distance. The primary advantage of IBS is that no physical contact is required, eliminating the risk of uncontrolled collision during capture of a tumbling target.

docs.title: 28.7.5 Laser Ablation
docs.text: Ground-based or space-based high-power pulsed lasers can generate a debris-deorbit force by ablating material from the debris surface. A 100-kW peak-power pulsed laser (pulse energy \(\sim\)1 J, repetition rate 100 kHz) focused on a debris surface at 500-km altitude generates a localized plasma plume via ablation, imparting a specific impulse of \(\sim\)1 cm/s per pulse and \(\sim\)1 m/s total \(\Delta v\) per 100-pass engagement over several months. The LODR (Laser Orbital Debris Removal) program explored this concept; key challenges are adaptive optics (AO) correction for atmospheric turbulence to maintain focused spot at 500 km, pointing stability (\(<\)0.1 \(\mu\)rad jitter), and the requirement to track tumbling objects with high fidelity. Laser ablation is particularly attractive for the 1–10 cm debris size range—too small to capture with mechanical systems but individually too numerous for one-by-one physical removal missions.

docs.title: 28.7.6 Harpoon and Net Systems
docs.text: Harpoon and net capture mechanisms have both been demonstrated by RemoveDEBRIS (as described above) and continue to be developed for operational ADR missions. The Airbus harpoon system fires a 150-g titanium barbed projectile at 20–30 m/s; on penetration of the target surface, a spring-loaded barb deploys to provide retention. A tether connects the harpoon to the servicer spacecraft; after secure harpoon attachment, the servicer fires its thruster to initiate deorbit. Net capture is preferred for large, tumbling targets where harpoon penetration angle is uncertain; net ejection speed, closing velocity, and net-mouth-to-target-ratio are the key design parameters for reliable capture at approach ranges of 5–20 m.

docs.title: 28.7.7 Electrostatic Tug
docs.text:
The electrostatic tug concept applies primarily to debris removal in GEO, where the long-range Coulomb force between charged spacecraft is significant due to the natural charging environment (no ionosphere, direct solar UV, energetic plasma). A servicer spacecraft and its target debris are charged to differential potentials of \(\pm\)kV using electron guns and ion beams, generating an attractive Coulomb force:

\[F = k_e \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{r^2}\tag{28.10}\]

where \(k_e = 9 \times 10^9\) N\(\cdot\)m\(^2\)/C\(^2\), \(Q_1\), \(Q_2\) are the charges on the two spacecraft, and \(r\) is the separation distance. At \(r = 20\) m, \(Q_1 = -Q_2 = 1~\mu\)C, the attractive force is approximately 22.5 \(\mu\)N—comparable to a small Hall thruster thrust—sufficient to slowly detumble and deorbit a GEO debris object over months of operation. The electrostatic tug avoids physical contact entirely, a key advantage for tumbling objects at GEO where synchronization maneuvers would require large propellant expenditure.

docs.title: 28.8.1 Space Sustainability Rating
docs.text: The World Economic Forum’s Space Sustainability Rating (SSR), launched in 2021 in partnership with ESA, EPFL and other institutions, provides a voluntary certification scheme for satellite missions that quantifies and publicly discloses their sustainability practices. The SSR evaluates missions across nine indicators including: collision probability and conjunction data sharing; adherence to deorbit timelines; passivation compliance; post-mission disposal reliability; propulsion capability for avoidance maneuvers; and transparency of operations. Scores are publicly published on a 1–10 scale, creating reputational incentives for operators to improve sustainability practices and providing investors, insurers, and regulators with standardized, comparable sustainability metrics.

docs.title: 28.8.2 Long-Term Evolution Projections
docs.text:
ESA’s DELTA (Debris Evolution Long Term Analysis) model projects the LEO debris environment 100–200 years forward under different launch traffic and mitigation scenarios:

  • Without ADR, current launch traffic: Debris population at 800 km increases by approximately 50% by 2100, with cascade probability \(>\)10% per decade beginning in the 2050s.

  • With 5 ADR removals per year at 800–900 km: Population at 800 km stabilizes near current levels; cascade probability remains below 5% per decade through 2100.

  • With 10 ADR removals per year: Slow population decline at 800 km; 200-year projections show environment recovering toward pre-FY-1C levels.

These projections underscore the conclusion that passive mitigation alone (even with perfect compliance) is insufficient to stabilize the environment at current levels; active removal at a rate of at least 5 large objects per year is required as a minimum.

docs.title: 28.8.3 International Governance
docs.text:
The COPUOS (Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space) Working Group on the Long-Term Sustainability (LTS) of Outer Space Activities published 21 consensus guidelines in 2019, covering space debris mitigation, space operations, space weather, and regulatory transparency. The guidelines are non-binding but represent the broadest international consensus on space sustainability practices ever achieved.

Key governance developments include:

  • US SPD-3 (2018): Space Policy Directive 3 established a US national policy for space traffic management, directing the Department of Commerce to provide basic SSA services to civil operators and directing development of a national STM architecture.

  • ASAT test moratoria: The United States unilaterally declared a moratorium on destructive direct-ascent ASAT testing in April 2022, joined by Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom, and other allied nations; the moratorium does not yet have international treaty force but represents a meaningful political commitment.

  • ITU milestone filings: The ITU has implemented stricter requirements for non-geostationary satellite system filings, requiring demonstrable deployment progress to prevent “paper satellite” filings that reserve spectrum without actual deployment.

  • National STM frameworks: The UK Space Sustainability Registry, ESA Space Safety Program, and France’s GRAVES radar form nascent national contributions to a future multilateral space traffic management system.

docs.title: 28.8.4 Economics of Debris Prevention
docs.text:
The economic case for debris mitigation is compelling when external costs are properly internalized. Cost to incorporate design-for-demise features (aluminum substitution for titanium fasteners, component redesign): approximately $100,000 per satellite at the design stage. Cost of deorbit propulsion capability for LEO satellites (5-year compliant deorbit): approximately $200,000–500,000 in propellant and propulsion hardware per satellite. Cost of a single collision event for the affected satellite operator: $200–500 million (satellite replacement, revenue loss, insurance claim). Cost to third parties from the resulting debris cloud: uninsured externality imposed on all LEO operators, potentially exceeding $1 billion in increased risk exposure.

The insurance market is beginning to reflect this reality: space insurers including AXA XL and Munich Re are reported to take mitigation practices into account when pricing cover. Post-Cosmos 2251, several insurers introduced conjunction-related policy exclusions for damage caused by cataloged debris—creating a liability gap that motivates operators to seek better SSA services.

docs.title: 28.9 Key Equations
docs.text:
Kessler Collision Rate.

\[R_c = \frac{N^2 \sigma V_\text{rel}}{2 V_\text{total}}\]

Cascade condition: \(R_c > N/\tau_d\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(N > N_\text{cr} = 2 V_\text{total}/(\sigma V_\text{rel} \tau_d f)\).

Alfano Collision Probability.

\[P_c = \frac{r_c^2}{2\sigma_x\sigma_y} \exp\!\left(-\frac{x_\text{TCA}^2}{2\sigma_x^2} - \frac{y_\text{TCA}^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\right) \quad \text{(dilute-miss approximation)}\]

where \(r_c = r_1 + r_2\), \((\sigma_x, \sigma_y)\) are the combined miss-plane standard deviations, and \((x_\text{TCA}, y_\text{TCA})\) is the nominal miss vector at Time of Closest Approach.

Whipple Shield Penetration Limit.

\[t_{\text{rear}} = 0.25\,m_p^{1/3}\,\frac{(v_r\cos\theta)^{2/3}}{\rho_B^{1/3}\,S_{cr}^{1/3}}\]

Deorbit \(\Delta v\) from Atmospheric Drag.

The \(\Delta v\) required to reduce perigee from \(h_p\) to reentry altitude \(h_r\) (assuming circular starting orbit at altitude \(h\)):

\[\Delta v_\text{deorbit} = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{R_E + h}}\left(1 - \sqrt{\frac{2(R_E + h_r)}{2R_E + h_r + h}}\right)\tag{28.14}\]

For deorbit from 800 km to 120 km reentry interface: \(\Delta v \approx 155\) m/s; from 550 km (Starlink): \(\Delta v \approx 45\) m/s for 5-year atmospheric-only deorbit at \(h_p = 300\) km.

docs.title: 28.11 Debris Altitude Distribution Diagram
docs.text:
Figure 28.1 illustrates the approximate spatial density of the tracked debris population as a function of altitude.

Figure 28.1. Schematic altitude distribution of orbital debris spatial density (relative units, based on MASTER-8 model data). The pronounced peak at 800–1000 km reflects the concentrated debris from the Fengyun-1C ASAT test (863 km) and the Iridium 33/Cosmos 2251 collision (789 km). The MEO region (2000–35,000 km) has lower density but contains radiation-belt trapped charged debris. The GEO operational band shows a modest density from intact but defunct spacecraft; the graveyard orbit at \(>\)36,086 km receives passivated end-of-life GEO satellites.

docs.title: 28.12 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter 28 Key Takeaways

  • The orbital debris environment comprises 34,000 tracked objects, \(\sim\)900,000 objects in the 1–10 cm range, and \(>\)128 million sub-centimeter fragments totaling 9,400 metric tons—a population dominated by fragmentation events (the majority of objects by count).

  • The Iridium 33/Cosmos 2251 collision (2009) and Fengyun-1C ASAT test (2007) collectively added \(\sim\)5800 new tracked objects concentrated at 750–900 km, the altitude range most susceptible to Kessler cascade.

  • Whipple multi-shock shields protect spacecraft against \(\sim\)1-cm objects; Probability of No Penetration (PNP) \(\geq 0.995\)/year is the NASA standard for ISS crewed modules.

  • The Kessler cascade condition—where collision rate exceeds atmospheric removal rate—is estimated to have already been exceeded at some altitude sub-bands at 750–900 km when untracked objects are included; NASA LEGEND modeling requires 5 ADR removals per year to stabilize the population.

  • Conjunction assessment with the Alfano \(P_c\) formulation uses combined position covariance; the maneuver threshold \(P_c > 10^{-4}\) drives \(\sim\)30 ISS avoidance maneuvers per year.

  • IADC mitigation guidelines (25-year deorbit, GEO graveyard, passivation) form the international baseline; the 2022 FCC revision to a 5-year US requirement is more stringent for LEO.

  • Active debris removal technologies—net, harpoon, claw (ClearSpace-1), magnetic capture (ELSA-d), ion beam shepherd, electrostatic tug—span TRL 3–7; the JAXA CRD2/ADRAS-J mission (2024) marked the first proximity operations around an actual large debris target.

  • Removing 5 large objects per year (preferably intact rocket bodies) from the 800–900 km band is the minimum required to stabilize the LEO debris population at current levels per LEGEND modeling.

docs.title: Chapter 29: Quantum Communications and Satellite QKD
docs.text:
“Anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it.” — Niels Bohr

The security of modern digital civilization rests on mathematical hardness assumptions—that factoring large integers or computing discrete logarithms is computationally infeasible. Quantum computers, leveraging Shor’s algorithm, threaten to invalidate these assumptions within the coming decades, rendering the public-key infrastructure protecting everything from financial transactions to military communications vulnerable. Quantum communications offers an alternative security paradigm grounded not in mathematical difficulty but in the fundamental laws of physics. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), the most mature quantum communication technology, enables two parties to establish a shared secret key whose security is guaranteed by the no-cloning theorem and the postulates of quantum mechanics—any eavesdropper necessarily disturbs the quantum channel in a detectable manner.

Satellite-based QKD is the enabling technology for global quantum-secure communications. Ground-based fiber QKD networks are limited by absorption losses: even at the optimal 1550 nm telecom wavelength, fiber attenuation of 0.2 dB/km means that photon survival probability falls to \(10^{-20}\) over 1000 km, making direct fiber QKD at intercontinental distances impossible without quantum repeaters. Free-space satellite links exploit a fundamentally different loss mechanism: diffraction spreading over vacuum, with the bulk of atmospheric absorption confined to the lowest 10 km. The Micius satellite, launched by China in 2016, demonstrated satellite-to-ground (downlink) QKD over slant ranges up to 1200 km, satellite-to-ground entanglement distribution over 1203 km, and an intercontinental quantum-secured link relayed through the satellite—milestones that validated the satellite QKD approach and triggered a global race to deploy quantum communication satellites (Liao et al. 2017).

This chapter develops the quantum mechanical foundations necessary to understand QKD, describes the major QKD protocols in mathematical detail, examines the physical implementation challenges in free-space and satellite environments, surveys current and planned satellite QKD missions, and addresses the longer-term vision of quantum repeater networks and the relationship between QKD and post-quantum cryptography.

docs.title: 29.1 Introduction to Quantum Communications
docs.text:
Quantum communications encompasses a family of technologies that exploit quantum mechanical phenomena—superposition, entanglement, and measurement—to perform communication tasks that are impossible or insecure classically. The field divides broadly into three areas: quantum key distribution (QKD), quantum teleportation, and quantum networks (including quantum repeaters and a future quantum internet).

QKD is the most technologically mature application. In QKD, the quantum channel transmits not data directly but random key material whose security is guaranteed by physics. Classical cryptographic algorithms (AES, ChaCha20) then encrypt the actual data using this key in a one-time-pad or cipher mode. The quantum channel need not carry high bandwidth; the security benefit is entirely in the key generation process. QKD is complementary to, not a replacement for, classical encryption algorithms; it addresses the key distribution problem specifically.

Quantum teleportation transfers an unknown quantum state from one party to another using a pre-shared entangled pair and a classical communication channel. It does not teleport matter or information faster than light; it consumes one shared entangled pair and two classical bits per qubit teleported. Teleportation is the fundamental primitive of quantum repeaters.

Quantum networks aim to interconnect quantum processors, sensors, and communication nodes via entanglement distribution, enabling distributed quantum computing and fundamentally new sensing and clock-synchronization capabilities. The term “quantum internet” describes a global network providing these services as infrastructure.

Core Principle of QKD Security: Any attempt by an eavesdropper to intercept or copy quantum states being transmitted necessarily perturbs those states, by the no-cloning theorem and measurement collapse. The resulting errors are detectable during classical post-processing, allowing Alice and Bob to bound the information acquired by any eavesdropper and amplify the remaining key privacy to an arbitrarily small information leakage. Security is guaranteed by physics, not by computational hardness.

The satellite link budget for QKD differs from classical satellite communications in one critical respect: the signal consists of individual photons. While classical links require \(E_b/N_0\) ratios of 5–15 dB for reliable demodulation, QKD links operate at the single-photon level. The relevant figures of merit are photon detection rate (key sifted bits per second) and quantum bit error rate (QBER). A QBER below approximately 11% (for BB84) is required for positive secret key extraction; satellite QKD experiments have reported QBER of a few percent during night-time passes.

docs.title: 29.2.1 Qubits and Superposition
docs.text:
The quantum bit, or qubit, is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a classical bit that takes value 0 or 1, a qubit can exist in any superposition of its two basis states. The general state of a qubit is:

\[|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle, \quad \alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{C}, \quad |\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1\tag{29.1}\]

where \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) are the computational basis (Z-basis) states, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are complex probability amplitudes, and the normalization condition \(|\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1\) ensures probabilities sum to unity. Upon measurement in the Z-basis, the qubit collapses irreversibly to \(|0\rangle\) with probability \(|\alpha|^2\) or to \(|1\rangle\) with probability \(|\beta|^2\).

Bloch Sphere Representation: Any pure qubit state can be parameterized on the surface of a unit sphere (the Bloch sphere) as:

\[|\psi\rangle = \cos\!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)|0\rangle + e^{i\phi}\sin\!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)|1\rangle\tag{29.2}\]

with polar angle \(\theta \in [0,\pi]\) and azimuthal angle \(\phi \in [0,2\pi)\). The north pole represents \(|0\rangle\); the south pole represents \(|1\rangle\). The equatorial plane contains equal-superposition states including \(|{+}\rangle = (|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\) (along \(+x\)) and \(|{-}\rangle = (|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\) (along \(-x\)).

Photon Polarization Encoding: For satellite QKD, qubits are encoded in the polarization of individual photons. The four polarization states used in BB84 are:

\[\begin{align*} |H\rangle &= |0\rangle \quad \text{(horizontal, Z-basis)} \\ |V\rangle &= |1\rangle \quad \text{(vertical, Z-basis)} \\ |D\rangle &= \frac{|0\rangle + |1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} \quad (\text{diagonal } +45^\circ,\ \text{X-basis}) \\ |A\rangle &= \frac{|0\rangle - |1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} \quad (\text{anti-diagonal } -45^\circ,\ \text{X-basis}) \end{align*}\]

The Z-basis \(\{|H\rangle, |V\rangle\}\) and X-basis \(\{|D\rangle, |A\rangle\}\) are mutually unbiased: measuring a Z-basis state in the X-basis gives a uniformly random result with no information about the original state. This mutual unbiasedness is the foundation of BB84’s security against intercept-resend attacks.

docs.title: 29.2.2 Quantum Entanglement and Bell States
docs.text:
A two-qubit system is entangled if its state cannot be written as a product of single-qubit states: \(|\Psi\rangle \neq |\psi_A\rangle \otimes |\psi_B\rangle\). The four maximally entangled two-qubit Bell states form a complete orthonormal basis for the two-qubit Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}_2 \otimes \mathcal{H}_2\):

\[\begin{align*} |\Phi^+\rangle &= \frac{|00\rangle + |11\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} \\ |\Phi^-\rangle &= \frac{|00\rangle - |11\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} \\ |\Psi^+\rangle &= \frac{|01\rangle + |10\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} \\ |\Psi^-\rangle &= \frac{|01\rangle - |10\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} \end{align*}\]

In the \(|\Phi^-\rangle\) state, measurement of particle A in any basis is perfectly anti-correlated with measurement of particle B in the same basis, regardless of their separation (Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen correlations). This non-local correlation cannot be explained by any local hidden variable theory, as demonstrated by violation of Bell inequalities. The E91 QKD protocol (Ekert 1991) exploits entanglement as the physical resource for key generation, providing security from Bell inequality violation rather than basis randomness.

EPR Correlations and Relativistic Causality: The correlations in entangled pairs are instantaneous and independent of distance, seemingly violating relativity. However, measurement outcomes are fundamentally random and cannot be controlled by either party, so no information is transmitted faster than light. Entanglement enables coordination but not signaling, preserving relativistic causality. The non-local correlations are detectable only through classical post-processing of both parties’ results.

docs.title: 29.2.3 No-Cloning Theorem
docs.text:
The no-cloning theorem is the fundamental quantum mechanical result that prohibits any device from creating a perfect copy of an arbitrary unknown quantum state. This theorem is the ultimate security guarantee of QKD, preventing eavesdroppers from copying transmitted qubits.

Proof by contradiction: Assume that a unitary operation \(U\) exists such that for any state \(|\psi\rangle\):

\[U|\psi\rangle|0\rangle = |\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle\tag{29.11}\]

Apply this to two orthogonal states:

\[\begin{align*} U|0\rangle|0\rangle &= |0\rangle|0\rangle \\ U|1\rangle|0\rangle &= |1\rangle|1\rangle \end{align*}\]

Now consider the superposition \(|\psi\rangle = (|0\rangle + |1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\). By linearity of quantum mechanics:

\[U|\psi\rangle|0\rangle = \frac{U|0\rangle|0\rangle + U|1\rangle|0\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{|00\rangle + |11\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} = |\Phi^+\rangle\]

But the assumed cloning operation requires \(U|\psi\rangle|0\rangle = |\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle\), which evaluates to:

\[|\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle = \frac{(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)}{2} = \frac{|00\rangle + |01\rangle + |10\rangle + |11\rangle}{2}\]

Since \(|\Phi^+\rangle \neq |\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle\), we have a contradiction. Therefore no such unitary \(U\) exists, and perfect cloning of arbitrary unknown quantum states is impossible. \(\square\)

The no-cloning theorem means that an eavesdropper Eve cannot intercept a qubit, copy it, and forward the original. Any measurement she performs collapses the quantum state, introducing detectable errors in the QKD protocol.

docs.title: 29.2.4 Quantum Teleportation
docs.text:
Quantum teleportation transfers an unknown qubit state \(|\chi\rangle = a|0\rangle + b|1\rangle\) from Alice to Bob using a pre-shared entangled pair \(|\Phi^+\rangle_{AB}\) and two classical bits. The four-step protocol:

  1. Alice holds qubit \(|\chi\rangle\) plus her entangled qubit. The joint state is \(|\chi\rangle_C \otimes |\Phi^+\rangle_{AB}\).

  2. Alice performs a Bell state measurement on \(C\) and \(A\), obtaining one of four outcomes with equal probability \(1/4\), and projecting Bob’s qubit \(B\) into a state related to \(|\chi\rangle\) by a Pauli rotation.

  3. Alice sends the 2-bit measurement result to Bob via a classical channel (two classical bits).

  4. Bob applies the appropriate Pauli correction (\(I\), \(X\), \(Z\), or \(XZ\)) based on Alice’s classical message, recovering \(|\chi\rangle\) exactly.

The original qubit at Alice is destroyed in the Bell measurement, consistent with no-cloning. Teleportation requires classical communication and does not violate relativistic causality. It is the operational primitive enabling quantum repeater networks: entanglement swapping is teleportation of one entangled particle to a distant location.

docs.title: 29.3.1 BB84 Protocol
docs.text:
The BB84 protocol (Bennett and Brassard 1984), proposed by Bennett and Brassard in 1984, is the first and most widely deployed QKD protocol. Its security against arbitrary quantum attacks (including coherent attacks by an eavesdropper holding a quantum computer) has been rigorously proven in the finite-key regime.

Protocol Steps:

  1. Qubit transmission: Alice randomly selects a bit value \(b \in \{0,1\}\) and a basis \(\beta \in \{Z,X\}\), prepares the corresponding state (\(|H\rangle\), \(|V\rangle\), \(|D\rangle\), or \(|A\rangle\)), and transmits it to Bob.

  2. Measurement: Bob randomly selects a measurement basis \(\beta' \in \{Z,X\}\) and records the outcome.

  3. Sifting: Alice and Bob communicate their basis choices (not outcomes) over a public authenticated classical channel. They retain only the approximately 50% of rounds where \(\beta = \beta'\). This forms the sifted key.

  4. Error estimation: Alice and Bob publicly compare a random subset (5–10%) of sifted key bits to estimate the QBER \(e\). Estimated bits are discarded.

  5. Error correction: An information-reconciliation protocol corrects discrepancies. Cascade is interactive and achieves \(f \approx 1.16\) efficiency; LDPC codes approach \(f \rightarrow 1\) with one-way communication.

  6. Privacy amplification: A universal hash function (Toeplitz matrix) compresses the error-corrected key by the estimated information leakage, producing a final key with arbitrarily small information available to any eavesdropper.

Secret Key Rate: The asymptotic secret key rate (bits per transmitted pulse) against general (coherent) attacks for weak coherent pulse (WCP) sources with decoy states is:

\[R \geq Q_\mu \left[1 - h_2(e_1)\right] - Q_\mu \cdot f \cdot h_2(E_\mu)\tag{29.16}\]

where the binary entropy function \(h_2\) is:

\[h_2(e) = -e \log_2 e - (1-e)\log_2(1-e)\tag{29.17}\]

Here \(Q_\mu\) is the detection rate (counts per pulse sent), \(E_\mu\) is the observed QBER, \(e_1\) is the estimated phase error rate for single-photon pulses, and \(f \approx 1.16\) is the error correction efficiency factor. For a channel transmission efficiency \(\eta_{ch}\), detector efficiency \(\eta_d\), and mean photon number \(\mu\):

\[Q_\mu \approx \eta_{ch} \eta_d \mu \quad \text{(for small }\eta_{ch}\eta_d\mu\text{)}\tag{29.18}\]

QBER Security Threshold: For BB84 with one-way error correction, the maximum tolerable QBER for positive key rate is \(e_{\max} = 11.0\%\) (solution of \(1 - 2h_2(e) = 0\)). Typical satellite QKD achieves QBER of 3–6%, well below threshold. Higher QBER, e.g., from strong atmospheric turbulence or eavesdropping, signals abort.

docs.title: 29.3.2 Decoy-State BB84
docs.text:
Practical QKD sources are weak coherent pulse (WCP) lasers with Poisson photon-number statistics: \(P(n|\mu) = e^{-\mu}\mu^n/n!\) for mean photon number \(\mu \approx 0.1\). Multi-photon pulses (\(n \geq 2\)) are vulnerable to the photon-number-splitting (PNS) attack: Eve intercepts the pulse, retains one photon in a quantum memory, and forwards one photon to Bob. She later measures when Alice reveals the basis, gaining full information on multi-photon pulses without introducing QBER.

The decoy-state method (Lo–Ma–Chen 2005) counters PNS attacks. Alice randomly interleaves:

  • Signal pulses: \(\mu \approx 0.1\) photons/pulse (key generation)

  • Weak decoy: \(\mu' \approx 0.5\) photons/pulse

  • Vacuum decoy: \(\mu_0 = 0\) (measures dark counts and stray light)

Differences in detection statistics between intensity levels allow tight estimation of the gain \(Q_1\) and error rate \(e_1\) of the single-photon component, enabling the key rate formula:

\[R \geq Q_1[1-h_2(e_1)] - Q_\mu \cdot f \cdot h_2(E_\mu)\tag{29.19}\]

In its 2017 QKD experiment the Micius satellite transmitted decoy-state BB84 signals from orbit to a ground station (a satellite-to-ground downlink), obtaining key rates of the order of 1 kbps at a slant range of 1200 km and roughly an order of magnitude more at the shortest ranges of a pass (Liao et al. 2017).

docs.title: 29.3.3 E91 Protocol
docs.text:
The Ekert (E91) protocol (Ekert 1991) replaces Alice’s photon preparation with a source of entangled photon pairs, distributing one photon to Alice and one to Bob. The source may reside on the satellite (satellite-to-two-ground-stations entanglement distribution) or at a ground station. Security is verified by measuring correlations that violate the CHSH inequality.

The CHSH (Clauser–Horne–Shimony–Holt) inequality for measurement settings \(A_i\) (Alice) and \(B_j\) (Bob) is:

\[S = \left|E(A_1,B_1) - E(A_1,B_2) + E(A_2,B_1) + E(A_2,B_2)\right| \leq 2 \quad \text{(local hidden variable theories)}\tag{29.20}\]

where \(E(A_i,B_j) = \langle A_i B_j \rangle\) is the correlation coefficient with outcomes \(\pm 1\). For the \(|\Phi^-\rangle\) Bell state with optimal measurement angles (Alice: \(0^\circ, 45^\circ\); Bob: \(22.5^\circ, 67.5^\circ\)):

\[S_{\text{QM}} = 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.828 \quad \text{(Tsirelson bound, maximum quantum value)}\tag{29.21}\]

The Micius satellite demonstrated \(S = 2.37 \pm 0.09\) across 1200 km separation, clearly exceeding \(S = 2\) and confirming that entanglement survives the free-space satellite channel. If an eavesdropper intercepts or measures the entangled pairs, entanglement degrades (the state becomes mixed), reducing \(S\) toward the classical bound and revealing the attack.

docs.title: 29.3.4 Continuous-Variable QKD
docs.text:
Continuous-variable (CV) QKD encodes key information in the quadrature amplitudes \((\hat{X}, \hat{P})\) of coherent laser states, rather than single-photon polarization. The GG02 protocol (Grosshans–Grangier 2002) operates as follows:

  1. Alice draws random displacements \((x_A, p_A) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, V_A N_0)\) from a Gaussian distribution with variance \(V_A\) in shot-noise units \(N_0\).

  2. Alice prepares coherent states \(|\alpha\rangle\) where \(\alpha = (x_A + ip_A)/2\) and transmits them to Bob through the quantum channel.

  3. Bob measures either \(\hat{X}\) or \(\hat{P}\) quadrature using homodyne detection, or both using heterodyne detection.

  4. Post-processing: parameter estimation of channel transmissivity and excess noise, reverse reconciliation (Bob’s data is the reference), privacy amplification.

The asymptotic secret key rate against Gaussian collective attacks is:

\[R \geq \beta I(A:B) - \chi(E:B)\tag{29.22}\]

where \(I(A:B) = \log_2(1 + \text{SNR})\) is the classical mutual information, \(\chi(E:B)\) is the Holevo bound on Eve’s information about Bob’s key (computed from the channel covariance matrix), and \(\beta \leq 1\) is the reconciliation efficiency. CV-QKD offers the practical advantage of using standard telecom components (no cryogenic single-photon detectors), with demonstrations reaching 100 km fiber at 100 kbps (NTT, 2021). For satellite applications, atmospheric fading channels require modified security analysis.

docs.title: 29.3.5 Measurement-Device-Independent QKD
docs.text:
Practical QKD implementations face detector side-channel attacks: detector blinding (bright illumination forces InGaAs APDs into linear mode, making them responsive only to bright trigger pulses), time-shift attacks, and after-gate attacks exploit imperfections in real detectors. All such attacks are eliminated by measurement-device-independent QKD (MDI-QKD).

In MDI-QKD, both Alice and Bob send independently prepared BB84 states to an untrusted relay node Charles, which may be controlled by the eavesdropper. Charles performs a Bell state measurement (BSM) and announces the result. The security proof shows that regardless of Charles’s actions, Alice-Bob correlations from successful BSM events satisfy the security requirements. The key rate with decoy states:

\[R \geq Q_{11}^{ZZ}\!\left[1 - h_2(e_{11}^X)\right] - Q_{\mu\nu}^{ZZ} \cdot f \cdot h_2(E_{\mu\nu}^{ZZ})\tag{29.23}\]

where \(Q_{11}^{ZZ}\) is the two-photon BSM gain for Z-basis transmissions, and \(e_{11}^X\) is the X-basis phase error rate estimated from decoy statistics. MDI-QKD requires Hong–Ou–Mandel (HOM) interference at Charles between photons from Alice and Bob, demanding sub-picosecond timing synchronization and sub-picometer wavelength matching—challenging but achievable with clock distribution over fiber.

docs.title: 29.3.6 Twin-Field QKD
docs.text:
The secret key capacity of any point-to-point quantum channel with transmissivity \(\eta\) is bounded by the Pirandola–Laurenza–Ottaviani–Banchi (PLOB) bound:

\[C \leq -\log_2(1-\eta) \approx \frac{\eta}{\ln 2} \quad (\eta \ll 1)\tag{29.24}\]

This linear scaling with \(\eta\) limits fiber QKD to impractical rates beyond \(\sim\)500 km (where \(\eta \approx 10^{-10}\)). Twin-field (TF) QKD surpasses the PLOB bound by using single-photon interference (not coincidence) at a central relay. Schematically, Alice and Bob each prepare phase-randomized WCP states and send them to a central station. The relay detects single photons by interference, and parity-check communication allows Alice and Bob to identify correlated outcomes. The key rate scales as \(\sqrt{\eta}\):

\[R_{\text{TF}} \propto \sqrt{\eta} \quad \text{vs.} \quad R_{\text{MDI}} \propto \eta\tag{29.25}\]

This square-root advantage enables TF-QKD over 500 km of fiber with positive key rate. In 2021, TF-QKD was demonstrated at 508 km fiber with \(R > 0\), using field-deployed fiber between two buildings in Shanghai with active phase stabilization. TF-QKD is the leading architecture for future ultra-long-distance fiber quantum backbone links.

docs.title: 29.4.1 Single-Photon Detectors
docs.text:
Single-photon detector (SPD) performance determines the achievable key rate and maximum distance. Key metrics are detection efficiency \(\eta_d\), dark count rate (DCR) in counts per second, timing jitter \(\Delta t\) (affecting pulse resolution), and maximum count rate. Table 29.1 compares the three major SPD technologies.

Table 29.1. Single-Photon Detector Technology Comparison for QKD Applications Parameter Si SPAD (800 nm) InGaAs SPAD (1550 nm) SNSPD (1550 nm) Detection efficiency 70% 25% \(>\)93% Dark count rate 100 cps 10,000 cps \(<\)1 cps Timing jitter 350 ps 200 ps \(<\)50 ps Max count rate 20 Mcps 10 Mcps 100 Mcps Operating temperature 300 K (TEC) 240 K (TEC) 0.8 K (cryocooler) Dead time 50 ns 10 \(\mu\)s (gated) 10 ns Wavelength range 400–1000 nm 1000–1700 nm 400–2000 nm Volume/complexity Small, low Moderate Large, cryocooler

Superconducting Nanowire SPD (SNSPD): The SNSPD operates by maintaining a superconducting nanowire (NbN or WSi, width 50–100 nm, thickness \(\sim\)5 nm) at \(\sim\)0.8 K, biased just below the superconducting critical current. An absorbed photon locally destroys superconductivity via a hotspot mechanism, producing a voltage pulse detectable with a room-temperature RF amplifier. SNSPDs achieve detection efficiencies exceeding 93% at 1550 nm with \(<\)50 ps timing jitter and \(<\)1 cps dark count rate. The requirement for millikelvin operation (Gifford–McMahon or pulse-tube cryocoolers) is the primary integration challenge for satellite payloads. Future missions targeting 1550 nm operation will require miniaturized space-qualified cryocooler systems; progress in Joule–Thomson and Stirling-cycle miniaturization is relevant.

InGaAs/InP SPAD: InGaAs APDs in Geiger mode are the workhorse of terrestrial telecom-wavelength QKD. Gated operation (100 ps–1 ns gates at repetition rates up to 1 GHz) suppresses afterpulsing, limiting effective detection rates. Detection efficiency of 25% and DCR of \(10^4\) cps are adequate for metropolitan fiber QKD but are inferior to SNSPDs for high-performance ground station receivers.

Si SPAD: Silicon APDs at 850 nm were used in the Micius satellite ground stations. High efficiency (70%) and moderate DCR make them suitable for 850 nm satellite QKD despite limited telecom-band response.

docs.title: 29.4.2 Entangled Photon Sources
docs.text:
Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is the dominant method for generating entangled photon pairs. A pump photon (\(\omega_p\)) is converted in a second-order nonlinear crystal (\(\chi^{(2)}\) medium) into two lower-energy signal and idler photons satisfying:

\[\begin{align*} \omega_s + \omega_i &= \omega_p \quad \text{(energy conservation)} \\ \mathbf{k}_s + \mathbf{k}_i &= \mathbf{k}_p \quad \text{(phase matching / momentum conservation)} \end{align*}\]

Type-II phase matching in beta barium borate (BBO) or periodically poled potassium titanyl phosphate (PPKTP) crystals produces polarization-entangled pairs in the \(|\Phi^+\rangle\) or \(|\Psi^-\rangle\) Bell state with fidelity exceeding 99% in optimized laboratory sources.

Source performance metrics:

  • Spectral brightness \(\mathcal{B}\) (pairs/s/mW pump/nm bandwidth): characterizes SPDC efficiency. Bulk BBO achieves \(\sim 10^4\) pairs/s/mW; fiber-coupled waveguide PPKTP sources achieve \(>10^6\) pairs/s/mW.

  • Pair generation rate \(R_{\text{pair}}\): total emitted pairs per second. The Micius SPDC source was reported to generate about \(5.9 \times 10^6\) pairs/s.

  • Entanglement fidelity: fraction of generated pairs in the target Bell state. for Micius the fidelity after the satellite-to-ground channel was high enough to violate the CHSH inequality (Section 29.3.3).

  • Multi-pair probability: heralded two-photon state purity limited by multi-pair events \(\propto \mu^2/2\); must keep pump power low enough that \(\mu \ll 1\).

Space qualification: The SpooQySats program (National University of Singapore) demonstrated a miniaturized polarization-entangled photon-pair source on a 2U CubeSat (SpooQy-1) deployed from the ISS in 2019, showing that an SPDC source can operate in the space environment, including thermal cycling and radiation.

docs.title: 29.4.3 Free-Space Optical Channel and Link Efficiency
docs.text:
Total link efficiency for a satellite quantum channel is the product of all loss mechanisms:

\[\eta_{\text{link}} = \eta_{\text{atm}} \cdot \eta_{\text{pointing}} \cdot \eta_{\text{optical}} \cdot \eta_{\text{detector}}\tag{29.28}\]

Diffraction loss: For a Gaussian beam with transmitter aperture diameter \(D_t\) and receiver aperture diameter \(D_r\) at link range \(d\) and wavelength \(\lambda\), in the far-field regime (\(d \gg D_t^2/\lambda\)):

\[\eta_{\text{diff}} = \left(\frac{\pi D_t D_r}{4\lambda d}\right)^2\tag{29.29}\]

At 850 nm with \(D_t = 0.3\) m, \(D_r = 1.0\) m, \(d = 1200\) km this ideal expression gives \(\eta_{\text{diff}} \approx 5 \times 10^{-2}\) (about 13 dB). Real Gaussian beams, finite pointing and the practical divergence of the transmitter make the diffraction loss larger; a value of about 22 dB at 1200 km has been reported for Micius. Together with atmospheric, pointing and optical losses the total link loss is several tens of dB, which necessitates single-photon detection and explains why satellite QKD key rates are of the order of kbps rather than Gbps.

Pointing loss: For a Gaussian beam with far-field divergence half-angle \(\theta_{\text{div}} = 2\lambda/(\pi D_t)\) and pointing error standard deviation \(\sigma_\theta\):

\[\eta_{\text{pointing}} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{8\sigma_\theta^2}{\theta_{\text{div}}^2}\right)\tag{29.30}\]

Micius achieved sub-microradian to microradian pointing accuracy, small compared with its beam divergence, with pointing loss reported to be below 3 dB. Such accuracy requires a two-stage pointing system: a coarse gimbal followed by a fast fine-steering mirror.

Atmospheric transmission: Transmission through the turbulent atmosphere, dominated by the lowest \(\sim\)30 km, follows Beer–Lambert attenuation:

\[\eta_{\text{atm}} = \exp\!\left(-\int_0^{\infty} \left[\alpha_{\text{abs}}(h) + \alpha_{\text{scat}}(h)\right] dh / \cos\theta_{\text{zen}}\right)\tag{29.31}\]

Zenith transmission at 850 nm is 0.7–0.8 in clear conditions; at 45\(^\circ\) elevation, \(\cos\theta_{\text{zen}} = 0.707\) increases the effective path by \(\sqrt{2}\). Nighttime operation mitigates sky background, which at daytime would saturate SPDs with \(\sim 10^6\) photons/s in a 1 nm filter bandwidth.

docs.title: 29.4.4 Polarization Control and Reference Frame Alignment
docs.text:
Polarization-encoded QKD requires aligned reference frames between transmitter and receiver. During a satellite pass, orbital motion, attitude variations, and satellite rotation cause the polarization reference frame to rotate continuously. Two approaches address this:

Active polarization compensation: A beacon laser at a different wavelength co-propagates with the QKD photons. The receiver monitors beacon polarization and feeds back corrections to a Pockels cell electro-optic modulator (EOM) or motorized waveplate actuator. Space systems also use a beacon for pointing and for tracking the polarization reference during the pass.

Reference-frame-independent (RFI) QKD: The protocol is redesigned so that security does not require shared reference frames. Alice and Bob measure in three bases; two share a common alignment (Z), while a third (X-Y plane) is frame-independent. An additional parameter \(C = \langle A_x B_x \rangle^2 + \langle A_x B_y \rangle^2 + \langle A_y B_x \rangle^2 + \langle A_y B_y \rangle^2\) replaces CHSH violation for security verification. RFI-QKD relaxes the need for active polarization control at the cost of a somewhat reduced key rate.

docs.title: 29.5.1 Micius/QUESS Satellite
docs.text:
The Micius satellite (Quantum Experiments at Space Scale, QUESS), launched 16 August 2016 into a roughly 500 km sun-synchronous orbit, is generally regarded as the first dedicated quantum communication satellite (Liao et al. 2017). Its mass was roughly 630 kg and its orbital period about 95 min. Key payload elements:

  • Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) source of polarization-entangled photon pairs at 810–850 nm

  • Decoy-state QKD transmitter at 850 nm

  • Optical transmitter telescope with a two-stage acquisition, tracking and pointing system

  • Beacon laser and timing synchronization with the ground station

Ground stations used in the experiments include Xinglong (near Beijing), Delingha (Qinghai), Lijiang (Yunnan), Nanshan (Urumqi), Ngari (Tibet, at high altitude, which reduces the atmospheric path) and, for the intercontinental link, the observatory at Graz in Austria.

Landmark Achievements:

  • Satellite-to-ground QKD (Nature 549, 2017) (Liao et al. 2017): Decoy-state BB84 from Micius to the Xinglong ground station over 645–1200 km slant range, with key rates of the order of 1 kbps at the longest range. Demonstrates the feasibility of satellite QKD (a downlink: the quantum signal travels from satellite to ground).

  • Entanglement distribution (Science 356, 2017): Entangled photon pairs were sent simultaneously from the satellite to two ground stations, Delingha and Lijiang, separated by 1203 km (Yin et al., Science 356, 2017). Bell inequality \(S = 2.37 \pm 0.09 > 2\): the first distribution of entanglement over more than 1000 km.

  • Quantum teleportation from ground to satellite (Nature 549, 2017): Independent photon prepared at Ngari ground station teleported to Micius satellite via entanglement shared between Ngari and the satellite, over \(\leq 1400\) km slant range.

  • Intercontinental QKD (Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 2018): Keys shared between Xinglong (China) and Graz (Austria) via Micius used to protect a video conference between the two countries over a ground distance of about 7600 km, with Micius acting as a trusted relay.

Trusted Node Limitation: The Micius intercontinental relay operates as a “trusted node”: the satellite holds intermediate keys from both national networks and XORs them to relay the combined key. End-to-end information-theoretic security without trusting the satellite requires entanglement swapping with quantum repeaters, a longer-term technology goal.

docs.title: 29.5.2 International Satellite QKD Programs
docs.text:
Table 29.2 summarizes current and planned satellite QKD missions.

Table 29.2. Satellite QKD Mission Overview Mission / Country Launch Platform Payload & Approach Achievement Micius / China 2016 \(\sim\)500 km SSO, \(\sim\)630 kg SPDC entangled source; decoy-state BB84 transmitter QKD to 1200 km; entanglement 1203 km; intercontinental key relay SpooQy-1 / Singapore 2019 2U CubeSat deployed from the ISS Miniaturized entangled photon-pair source Entangled photon source operated in orbit QEYSSat / Canada planned (launch later than 2025) LEO QKD receiver on the satellite; uplink architecture Planned ground-to-satellite (uplink) QKD demonstration Eagle-1 / ESA and SES planned (second half of the 2020s) LEO QKD payload; European QKD pathfinder Planned European QKD satellite demonstration

QEYSSAT (Canada): The Quantum Encryption and Science Satellite carries a QKD receiver on the satellite—a key architectural inversion from Micius. Ground stations transmit quantum states upward to the receiver, which simplifies the satellite payload and lets several ground transmitters share one orbital receiver. The mission is led by the Canadian Space Agency with Canadian university and industry partners, and its launch date has moved several times; as of 2025 it has not flown.

Chinese Ground–Space Network (2021): China integrated a 2000 km fiber QKD backbone between Beijing and Shanghai (32 trusted relay nodes) and metropolitan QKD networks with satellite-to-ground links, forming an integrated space-to-ground quantum communication network of about 4600 km extent with more than 150 users (Chen et al., Nature 589, 2021).

Eagle-1 (ESA/SES): A planned European QKD satellite developed by an SES-led consortium with ESA and the European Commission, intended as a pathfinder for a European space segment for quantum key distribution. Its launch date has been announced for the second half of the 2020s and may change.

docs.title: 29.6.1 Fundamental Limits of Direct QKD
docs.text:
The PLOB bound \(C \leq -\log_2(1-\eta)\) limits direct QKD to impractical rates at intercontinental distances. For fiber at 0.2 dB/km:

\[\begin{align*} d = 100~\text{km}: &\quad \eta = 10^{-2}, \quad C \leq 0.014 \text{ bits/use} \\ d = 500~\text{km}: &\quad \eta = 10^{-10}, \quad C \leq 1.4\times10^{-10} \text{ bits/use} \\ d = 1000~\text{km}: &\quad \eta = 10^{-20}, \quad C \leq 1.4\times10^{-20} \text{ bits/use} \end{align*}\]
