Even free-space satellite links are limited: at 10,000 km with 300 mm and 1 m apertures at 850 nm, ideal diffraction loss alone gives \(\eta \approx 8\times10^{-4}\) (about 31 dB), and atmospheric turbulence, pointing and optical losses add further loss. Multi-hop trusted node relaying (as in Micius) circumvents this at the cost of trusting each relay.

docs.title: 29.6.2 Quantum Repeater Architecture
docs.text:
The BDCZ (Briegel–Dür–Cirac–Zoller) quantum repeater divides a long link into \(N\) elementary segments, creating entanglement across each segment and then extending via entanglement swapping:

  1. Entanglement generation: Create Bell pairs across each elementary link of length \(L_0 = L/N\), storing photons in quantum memories at repeater nodes. Success probability per attempt: \(p_0 \approx \eta_{\text{elem}} = e^{-L_0/L_{\text{att}}}\).

  2. Entanglement swapping: Bell state measurement on two stored qubits at a repeater node creates entanglement across \(2L_0\) without requiring those photons to travel the full distance.

  3. Entanglement purification: Multiple lower-fidelity pairs are distilled to fewer higher-fidelity pairs via BBPSSW protocol: two pairs with fidelity \(F\) yield one pair with \(F' = F^2/(F^2 + (1-F)^2) > F\) for \(F > 1/2\).

The achievable key rate with ideal quantum memories scales as \(\eta_0^{1/N}\) rather than \(\eta_0\), enabling exponential improvement. First-generation repeaters (in development as of 2025) require quantum memories and linear optical BSMs; second-generation repeaters additionally need quantum error correction; third-generation (“all-photonic”) repeaters use photonic cluster states.

docs.title: 29.6.3 Quantum Memory Technologies
docs.text:
Quantum memories store and retrieve photonic qubits. Table 29.3 gives indicative values for several platforms; the best published results differ from experiment to experiment and no single memory yet combines all the properties a repeater needs.

Table 29.3. Quantum Memory Technology Platforms for Repeater Applications Platform Efficiency \(\eta_m\) Storage Time \(\tau_s\) Multimode \(M\) Notes Rb vapor EIT 50% 1 ms 10 780 nm; room temperature Pr:Y\(_2\)SiO\(_5\) AFC 90% 7.7 ms 1000 605 nm; 3 K; spin-wave Eu:Y\(_2\)SiO\(_5\) 25% 6 hours 100 580 nm; 2 K; record \(\tau_s\) NV centers (diamond) 10% 1 s (nuclear) 1 637 nm; room temp. possible Tm:LiNbO\(_3\) waveguide 50% 100 \(\mu\)s 100 Telecom compatible

A spin coherence time of 6 hours has been demonstrated in Eu:Y\(_2\)SiO\(_5\) (Zhong et al., Nature 2015), and optical storage for about one hour has been reported in the same material system. These results show that very long storage is physically possible, although not yet together with the high efficiency, bandwidth and multimode capacity that quantum repeaters need.

docs.title: 29.6.4 Experimental Quantum Networks
docs.text:
QuTech (Delft University of Technology) demonstrated a three-node quantum network of NV-center qubits in the laboratory in 2021 (Pompili et al., Science 372, 259). The nodes, called Alice, Bob and Charlie, were linked by short optical fiber, with entanglement heralded by photons emitted at 637 nm. The experiment demonstrated:

  • Heralded entanglement generation between non-adjacent nodes (Alice–Bob) via entanglement swapping at Charlie

  • Quantum state storage in \(^{13}\)C nuclear spin memories (\(\tau_s \approx 1\) s)

  • Classical post-processing for distillation and key extraction

This was a proof-of-principle of a multi-node quantum network with entanglement swapping between non-adjacent nodes. Later work has extended heralded entanglement between solid-state nodes to deployed fiber between cities.

docs.title: 29.7.1 The Quantum Threat to Classical Cryptography
docs.text:
Shor’s algorithm solves integer factorization (RSA) and discrete logarithm (DH, ECC) in polynomial time \(O(n^3)\) on a quantum computer, where \(n\) is the bit length of the modulus. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) capable of breaking 2048-bit RSA would need thousands of error-corrected logical qubits. Resource estimates by Gidney and Ekerå (2021) were about 20 million noisy physical qubits and 8 hours of running time with surface-code error correction at a physical error rate of \(10^{-3}\); later estimates are lower but still far beyond today’s machines. As of 2025, IBM Condor (1121 physical qubits, 2023) and Google Willow (105 qubits, 2024, error-correction demonstration) are examples of the state of the art.

The “harvest-now-decrypt-later” (HNDL) threat is widely discussed: an adversary able to collect encrypted traffic today could store it until a future CRQC enables decryption. Data that must stay secret for 10–20 years (state secrets, financial records, medical data) is therefore a concern. Standards bodies therefore recommend starting the migration to quantum-resistant algorithms for such data now.

docs.title: 29.7.2 NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards 2024
docs.text:
NIST finalized three post-quantum cryptographic standards in 2024:

  • FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, formerly CRYSTALS-Kyber): Module lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism. Security based on Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) hardness. Key sizes: ML-KEM-768 has 1184-byte public key, 1088-byte ciphertext. Replaces RSA/ECDH for key exchange.

  • FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, formerly CRYSTALS-Dilithium): Module lattice-based digital signature algorithm. Security based on Module Short Integer Solution (MSIS) and MLWE. Signature size: 2420 bytes (ML-DSA-44) to 3309 bytes (ML-DSA-65). Replaces RSA-PSS and ECDSA.

  • FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, formerly SPHINCS+): Stateless hash-based signature scheme. Security based solely on hash function security (SHA-256/SHA3), with no algebraic structure to exploit. Conservative but larger signatures (roughly 8000 to 50,000 bytes).

FALCON (NTRU lattice-based signature) was also selected by NIST for standardization (as FN-DSA, in draft as of 2025), offering smaller signatures (about 666 bytes for Falcon-512, with an 897-byte public key) for bandwidth-constrained applications.

QKD vs. PQC: QKD: Information-theoretically secure; guaranteed by physics; requires physical quantum channel and specialized hardware; limited key rate (\(\sim\)kbps) and distance; vulnerable to implementation side-channel attacks. PQC: Computationally secure against known quantum algorithms; may be broken by future algorithms; software-only deployment on existing infrastructure; arbitrary throughput; standard implementation maturity. Recommended hybrid: session key \(= K_{\text{QKD}} \oplus K_{\text{PQC}}\) (secure if either is secure).

For satellite systems, QKD provides quantum-secure key distribution over the satellite link (typically refreshing daily key material for ground network segments), while PQC algorithms protect routine command/telemetry channels and can be implemented in firmware updates without hardware changes. ETSI GS QKD 014 specifies the QKD application layer interface for integration with classical network security functions.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Quantum communications exploits the postulates of quantum mechanics—superposition, entanglement, and the no-cloning theorem—to establish unconditionally secure key distribution. BB84 and decoy-state variants provide practical QKD with proven security; E91 uses Bell inequality violation for device-independent-like security; CV-QKD uses telecom components; MDI-QKD removes detector vulnerabilities; TF-QKD surpasses the PLOB bound. The Micius satellite achieved satellite-to-ground QKD over up to 1200 km (key rates of order 1 kbps), entanglement distribution over 1203 km (\(S = 2.37\)), and an intercontinental key relay over about 7600 km, validating the satellite approach. Quantum repeaters based on entanglement swapping and quantum memories (demonstrated in 3-node QuTech network) are the path to intercontinental QKD without trusted nodes. NIST FIPS 203/204/205 provide immediately deployable post-quantum cryptography, with hybrid QKD+PQC the recommended architecture for critical satellite infrastructure.

docs.title: Chapter 30: 6G and Non-Terrestrial Networks
docs.text:
“The next generation of wireless will not merely improve speed—it will dissolve the boundary between the sky and the network.” — 3GPP Technical Report 38.811

The integration of satellite and aerial platforms into the mobile network is no longer a research concept but a rapidly advancing engineering reality. Third-generation Partnership Project (3GPP) standardization of Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) has moved from study phase in Release 15 to normative specifications in Release 17 (frozen June 2022), with enhancements ongoing through Release 19. Simultaneously, commercial and pre-commercial deployments are turning theoretical link budgets into products (as of 2025): SpaceX’s Starlink direct-to-cell satellites sent their first text messages to ordinary phones in January 2024 and entered service with partner operators later, AST SpaceMobile’s 64 m2 BlueWalker 3 test satellite demonstrated data connections to unmodified smartphones, and Apple’s Emergency SOS via satellite has been available on iPhones since late 2022 through Globalstar’s LEO constellation.

Looking beyond 5G NTN, the 6G vision encoded in ITU-R IMT-2030 requirements explicitly designates non-terrestrial networks as a native component of the 6G architecture—a fundamental departure from 5G’s terrestrial-centric design with satellite connectivity retrofitted as an afterthought. This chapter traces the standardization pathway from 3GPP Release 15 study items to Release 19 enhancements, analyzes the NTN architecture (transparent vs. regenerative payload, timing advance management, Doppler compensation), examines direct-to-device commercial deployments, describes HAPS (High-Altitude Platform Station) technology, and outlines the 6G Space-Air-Ground-Sea integrated network vision including terahertz ISLs, Open RAN for NTN, and energy efficiency targets.

docs.title: 30.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Non-terrestrial networks comprise satellite (LEO, MEO, GEO), HAPS, and UAV platforms that extend cellular connectivity beyond the reach of terrestrial base stations. The commercial motivation is compelling: the International Telecommunication Union estimated in 2024 that roughly 2.6 billion people were still offline, many of them in remote or rural areas where terrestrial infrastructure is economically difficult to justify. Maritime and aeronautical connectivity markets demand global coverage that only satellites can provide. Emergency communications after natural disasters require infrastructure independent of ground-based assets.

The technical challenges that historically separated satellite and cellular systems are profound. Satellite links impose propagation delays of about 2 ms (LEO at 600 km, directly overhead) to roughly 240 ms (GEO, user to gateway via the satellite) one-way, versus \(<0.5\) ms for terrestrial 5G. Doppler shifts at LEO range from \(\pm\)50 kHz at S-band (\(f = 2\) GHz) to \(\pm\)0.76 MHz at Ka-band (\(f = 30\) GHz). Cell sizes are enormous—a LEO satellite at 600 km illuminates a footprint 600–2000 km in diameter, compared to 200 m for a 5G small cell. These differences require fundamental protocol modifications: the standard 3GPP Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest (HARQ) process (8 processes with 8 ms round-trip timing) cannot function with a 600 ms GEO round-trip time.

NTN Altitude Regimes and Delay Budget:

  • LEO (160–2000 km): 1–13 ms one-way; orbital period 1.5–2.5 hours; coverage per satellite 300–3000 km

  • MEO (2000–35,786 km): 13–120 ms; period 2–24 hours; navigation satellites

  • GEO (35,786 km): 240 ms one-way; stationary; 3 satellites for near-global coverage

  • HAPS (17–22 km): \(<0.1\) ms; quasi-stationary; 140–200 km coverage per platform

3GPP NTN standardization addresses these challenges with protocol adaptations (extended HARQ timers, UE-based timing advance pre-compensation, Doppler pre-compensation) while reusing the maximum possible NR air interface functionality to reduce implementation complexity.

docs.title: 30.2.1 Release 15 and 16: Study Phase
docs.text:
3GPP NTN standardization began with study items in Release 15 (2018) and Release 16 (2019–2020):

  • TR 38.811 (Study on NTN, v15.4.0, May 2019): Channel model, propagation delay, Doppler analysis for LEO/MEO/GEO/HAPS. Identified key challenges: round-trip propagation delay impacts on HARQ and scheduling, frequency offset from Doppler, large cell size requiring large TA values, feeder link bandwidth, mobility management.

  • TR 38.821 (Solutions for NTN, v16.0.0, January 2020): Evaluated solutions including UE-side TA pre-compensation using GNSS and satellite ephemeris, Doppler pre-compensation, HARQ process adaptation, and timing advance extensions.

  • TR 22.822 (SA1 NTN use cases, v16.0.0): Service requirements including continuous broadband access in underserved areas, 3GPP service continuity between terrestrial and NTN, IoT connectivity in remote areas, public safety communications, and in-flight connectivity.

Four NTN scenarios were studied: LEO (200–2000 km), MEO (2000–35786 km), GEO (35786 km), and HAPS (17–22 km altitude), with both transparent (bent-pipe) and regenerative (onboard processing) payload architectures.

docs.title: 30.2.2 Release 17: First Normative NTN Standard
docs.text:
Release 17, frozen in June 2022, produced the first normative NTN specifications. Two work items ran in parallel: NB-IoT/eMTC NTN and NR NTN.

NR NTN Key Specifications:

  • TS 38.101-5: User Equipment (UE) radio transmission/reception for NTN (new part 5)

  • TS 38.300 Annex: Architecture enhancements for NTN

  • TS 38.213/38.214/38.321: Physical layer procedures and MAC for NTN

Key Features Introduced in Release 17:

Timing Advance (TA) pre-compensation: The standard NR TA mechanism (base station commands UE to advance its uplink timing) cannot account for the large and dynamically varying propagation delay in NTN. Release 17 introduces UE-side TA pre-compensation:

\[\text{TA} = \frac{2 d_{\text{feeder}} + 2 d_{\text{service}}}{c} = \text{TA}_{\text{common}} + \text{TA}_{\text{UE}}\tag{30.1}\]

where \(d_{\text{feeder}}\) is the gNB-to-satellite (feeder link) range, \(d_{\text{service}}\) is the satellite-to-UE (service link) range, \(c\) is the speed of light, and TA is expressed in units of \(T_s = 1/(30720 \times \Delta f_{\text{ref}})\). For GEO, the maximum NR TA value was extended to 67,800 \(T_s\) = 245 ms to accommodate the 240 ms one-way GEO delay. The UE computes \(d_{\text{service}}\) from its GNSS position and the satellite ephemeris broadcast in SIB (System Information Block).

Doppler pre-compensation: The UE pre-compensates its uplink carrier frequency for the satellite Doppler shift using GNSS-derived velocity and satellite ephemeris. Residual Doppler after compensation is \(<\)100 Hz, within the NR frequency error tolerance.

HARQ adaptation: Standard NR uses up to 8 HARQ processes with 8 ms round-trip timing. A GEO link with 600 ms RTT would require 75 processes—impractical. Release 17 allows HARQ process disabling (broadcast via SIB, or configured per bearer), allowing the gNB to operate with a simple ARQ mechanism or rely on upper-layer retransmission. For LEO with \(\sim\)25 ms RTT, HARQ is feasible with 4–8 processes and extended timing.

Scheduling offset extension: The parameter \(k_0\) (PDCCH-to-PDSCH offset) and \(k_2\) (PDCCH-to-PUSCH offset) are extended from the terrestrial range of 0–7 slots to accommodate NTN delays.

NTN Frequency Bands (Release 17):

  • Band n255: 1626.5–1660.5 MHz UL / 1525–1559 MHz DL (L-band, mobile satellite service)

  • Band n256: 1980–2010 MHz UL / 2170–2200 MHz DL (S-band, mobile satellite service)

  • Band n254: 1610–1626.5 MHz UL / 2483.5–2500 MHz DL (L/S-band, mobile satellite service)

  • Ka-band bands for NR-NTN (n510, n511, n512): about 27.5–30 GHz uplink and 17.3–20.2 GHz downlink, a Release 17 addition for fixed and very small aperture terminals

docs.title: 30.2.3 Release 18: Enhanced NTN
docs.text:
Release 18 (frozen March 2024), the first release of the 5G-Advanced era, introduced significant NTN enhancements under the eNTN work item:

Earth-Fixed Beam (EFB) Mode: In conventional LEO NTN, satellite beams sweep across the Earth at orbital velocity. EFB mode uses active beam steering to fix a beam over a geographic area (like a GEO footprint) for a configurable dwell time, greatly simplifying UE mobility management and cell reselection. The gNB adapts cell parameters on a beam-granular basis.

Enhanced Inter-Satellite Handover: Release 17 inter-satellite handover required full UE re-connection. Release 18 introduces conditional handover and early measurement reporting to reduce handover interruption time from \(>1\) s to \(<100\) ms, critical for voice and real-time applications.

UE Power Saving for NTN: Extended discontinuous reception (eDRX) periods are adapted for NTN satellite periodicity (\(\sim\)90 min for LEO). Wake-up signal (WUS) transmission allows UE to remain in deep sleep and wake only when data is incoming. Connected-mode DRX parameters are extended for GEO latency.

Multi-TRP Diversity: Multiple transmission/reception points (satellite beams) serve a UE simultaneously (MTRP), providing macro-diversity gain for link reliability in edge-of-beam conditions and improving SINR by 3–6 dB.

docs.title: 30.2.4 Release 19 and Beyond
docs.text:
Release 19 (expected 2025–2026) includes:

  • NTN Multicast/Broadcast Service (MBS): Satellite delivery of broadcast content (TV, software updates, emergency alerts) using NR MBS framework—highly efficient for one-to-many distribution.

  • MIMO for NTN: Multiple antenna techniques adapted for large-scale satellite antenna arrays, potentially 2\(\times\)2 or 4\(\times\)4 spatial multiplexing for GEO satellites with multiple beams.

  • eMBB throughput enhancements: Higher spectral efficiency per beam to approach 1 Gbps per satellite beam for LEO.

  • IoT-NTN enhancements: Power consumption optimization for NB-IoT over satellite, duty-cycle relaxation for battery-powered sensors.

Table 30.1 compares key features across NTN releases.

Table 30.1. 3GPP NTN Standards Evolution Summary Release Freeze Date Status Key Features Key Specs Rel-15/16 2018–2020 Study TR 38.811 channel model; TR 38.821 solutions; use cases defined; challenges identified TR 38.811, TR 38.821, TR 22.822 Rel-17 June 2022 Normative TA pre-compensation; Doppler pre-compensation; HARQ disabling; TA extension to 245 ms; NTN frequency bands TS 38.101-5, TS 38.300, TS 38.213, TS 38.321 Rel-18 March 2024 Normative Earth-fixed beam; enhanced handover; eDRX NTN; WUS; MTRP diversity; GEO NTN specific TS 38.213 v18, TS 38.321 v18 Rel-19 2025–2026 In progress NTN MBS; NTN MIMO; eMBB enhancement; IoT-NTN evolution TBD

docs.title: 30.3.1 Transparent Payload Architecture
docs.text:
In the transparent (bent-pipe) payload architecture, the satellite performs only RF frequency translation and amplification: the satellite receives the uplink signal from the gNB (via the feeder link) and retransmits it toward UEs (service link), or vice versa for the uplink path. The 5G NR gNB (gNodeB) base station logic resides entirely on the ground. Advantages: satellite complexity is minimized (no digital processing in space, reducing power, mass, cost, and software development risk); ground-based gNBs can be upgraded without satellite hardware changes; spectrum reuse between feeder and service links is straightforward.

The feeder link carries the Uu air interface (the NR radio interface) transparently. The gNB inserts timing corrections accounting for the double-hop delay before scheduling uplink resources. Starlink Generation 1 satellites operated as bent-pipe for cellular backhaul, and most current commercial NTN systems use transparent architecture.

The delay budget for transparent GEO architecture:

\[d_{\text{GEO}} = \frac{2 \times 35{,}786~\text{km}}{3 \times 10^5~\text{km/s}} \approx 240~\text{ms one-way}, \quad \text{RTT} \approx 600~\text{ms}\tag{30.2}\]

docs.title: 30.3.2 Regenerative Payload Architecture
docs.text:
In the regenerative architecture, some or all gNB functions are implemented on the satellite. The 3GPP functional split options allow:

  • Option 2 (DU on satellite): The gNB-DU (Distributed Unit, handling physical and MAC layers) runs on the satellite; the gNB-CU (Centralized Unit, handling RRC, PDCP, SDAP) remains on the ground. The F1 interface connects DU-to-CU via the feeder link.

  • Full gNB on satellite: Complete 5G base station on the satellite; UEs connect directly with standard NR. The feeder link carries only user data (N3 interface) and management.

Regenerative payloads reduce the effective RTT seen by the UE from the full GEO round-trip (600 ms) to twice the service link delay (2\(\times\)120 ms for GEO, 2\(\times\)2 ms for LEO), enabling HARQ to function and reducing scheduling latency. Inter-satellite links (ISLs) in regenerative systems allow routing without returning data to ground stations, further reducing latency (Telesat Lightspeed at 1325 km LEO: 4.4 ms per hop). The trade-off is substantially higher satellite complexity, power consumption, and software development cost.

docs.title: 30.3.3 Timing Advance Management
docs.text:
In terrestrial NR, the gNB measures UE uplink timing and commands TA adjustments via MAC CE (Control Element). This loop is untenable with hundreds of milliseconds NTN delay. Release 17 introduces UE-side open-loop pre-compensation:

\[\text{TA} = \underbrace{\frac{2d_{\text{feeder}}}{c}}_{\text{TA}_{\text{common}}} + \underbrace{\frac{2d_{\text{service}}}{c}}_{\text{TA}_{\text{UE}}}\tag{30.3}\]

  • \(\text{TA}_{\text{common}}\): feeder link delay, known to the gNB, broadcast in SIB as a common offset.

  • \(\text{TA}_{\text{UE}}\): service link delay from UE to satellite, computed by the UE from its GNSS-derived position and the satellite ephemeris broadcast in SIB1 (NTN-specific ephemeris IE added in Release 17).

The satellite’s position at any future time is predicted from the broadcast Keplerian elements or state vectors with \(<\)100 m accuracy, giving UE timing pre-compensation accuracy of \(<\)1 \(\mu\)s (\(<\)30 m position error equivalent). The NR TA range was extended from 3846 \(T_s\) (terrestrial) to 67,800 \(T_s\) = 245 ms to accommodate full GEO one-way delay.

For NGSO (LEO/MEO), \(d_{\text{service}}\) changes significantly during a pass: a LEO satellite at 600 km overhead moves from \(d_{\min} = 600\) km to \(d_{\max} = 2000\) km (at 20\(^\circ\) elevation) over a 10-minute pass, varying TA by \(\Delta\text{TA} = 2(2000-600)/(3\times10^5) = 9.3\) ms. The UE continuously updates TA prediction using ephemeris extrapolation.

docs.title: 30.3.4 Doppler Pre-Compensation
docs.text:
A LEO satellite at \(h = 550\) km altitude has orbital velocity \(v_{\text{orb}} = \sqrt{\mu_E/(R_E+h)} = 7.59\) km/s. The maximum radial velocity component (at horizon) is approximately \(v_r = v_{\text{orb}}\cos\phi\) where \(\phi\) is the elevation angle. The Doppler frequency shift on the service link is:

\[\Delta f_{\text{Doppler}} = \frac{f_c}{c} \cdot v_r = \frac{f_c \cdot v_{\text{orb}} \cos\phi}{c}\tag{30.4}\]

At \(f_c = 2\) GHz (S-band), \(v_r = 7.59\) km/s (overhead pass): \(\Delta f_{\text{Doppler}} \approx \pm 50.6\) kHz. At \(f_c = 30\) GHz (Ka-band): \(\Delta f_{\text{Doppler}} \approx \pm 760\) kHz. The NR subcarrier spacing of 15–120 kHz would be completely obliterated without compensation.

Release 17 UE Doppler pre-compensation: the UE computes its radial velocity relative to the satellite from GNSS position+velocity and satellite ephemeris, then pre-shifts its uplink carrier frequency by \(-\Delta f_{\text{Doppler}}\) before transmission. After UE compensation, the gNB sees residual Doppler \(<\)100 Hz from residual ephemeris error and UE position uncertainty, within the NR frequency error budget. The satellite-side Doppler on the feeder link is compensated by the gateway (gNB side).

docs.title: 30.4.1 Link Budget Challenge for Direct-to-Device
docs.text:
A standard smartphone has a nearly isotropic antenna (about 0 dBi gain) and transmits at 23 dBm (200 mW) maximum output power, giving an EIRP of about 23 dBm. The link to a LEO satellite at 1000 km faces free-space path loss (FSPL):

\[L_{\text{FSPL}} = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi d f}{c}\right) = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi \times 10^6 \times 2\times10^9}{3\times10^8}\right) \approx 158~\text{dB}\tag{30.5}\]

at \(f = 2\) GHz, \(d = 1000\) km. A terrestrial gNB at 100 m would see FSPL \(= 20\log_{10}(4\pi \times 100 \times 2\times10^9/3\times10^8) = 78\) dB—an 80 dB advantage for the terrestrial link. The satellite must recover much of this deficit with a very large, high-gain antenna array: a 30 dBi antenna at 2 GHz needs a diameter of about 2 m (for 60% efficiency), and higher gain and many narrow beams need still larger apertures. This drives the AST SpaceMobile BlueWalker 3 design to a 64 m2 phased array.

The satellite EIRP requirement is:

\[\text{EIRP}_{\text{sat}} = \text{EIRP}_{\text{gNB,equiv}} + L_{\text{FSPL,NTN}} - L_{\text{FSPL,terr}} + \text{Margin}\tag{30.6}\]

docs.title: 30.4.2 AST SpaceMobile
docs.text:
AST SpaceMobile’s BlueWalker 3 (BW3) prototype satellite, launched in September 2022, was used to demonstrate direct connectivity to unmodified smartphones:

  • Phased array: a 64 m2 deployable planar array, among the largest communications arrays flown in low Earth orbit

  • Frequency: low-band terrestrial mobile spectrum made available by partner mobile network operators

  • Demonstrations (2023): voice and video calls and data sessions with ordinary handsets; peak data rates above 10 Mbps were reported by the company

The first operational BlueBird satellites were launched from September 2024; the company plans a constellation of such satellites at roughly 500 km altitude, with separate feeder links to gateways, and has announced agreements with a number of mobile network operators. Performance, schedule and regulatory status of the commercial service were still evolving as of 2025.

docs.title: 30.4.3 Starlink Direct-to-Cell
docs.text:
SpaceX’s Starlink direct-to-cell satellites carry an eNodeB-type cellular payload with a large antenna, so that ordinary LTE phones can connect when the operator lends part of its terrestrial spectrum:

  • Air interface: LTE in a partner operator’s mid-band spectrum (the US service with T-Mobile uses the 1900 MHz PCS band)

  • Capacity: a few Mbps in total, shared across each beam footprint; the service was designed first for text messaging

  • First messages: the first six satellites were launched on 2 January 2024 and the first text messages were sent in January 2024; a beta service followed with T-Mobile in the United States

  • Partner operators: agreements announced with T-Mobile (US), Rogers (Canada), Optus (Australia), KDDI (Japan), One NZ (New Zealand) and others

The regulatory step is the permission, granted in the United States in 2024 under the FCC’s “supplemental coverage from space” framework, for a satellite operator and a terrestrial mobile operator to use the terrestrial operator’s licensed spectrum from space, which the conventional rules for mobile bands did not allow. Rules and services differ between countries and were still changing as of 2025.

docs.title: 30.4.4 Apple Emergency SOS via Satellite
docs.text:
Apple’s Emergency SOS via Satellite, announced with the iPhone 14 in September 2022 and available from November 2022, uses Globalstar’s LEO constellation (second-generation satellites at about 1414 km altitude) in the mobile satellite service band n53 (2483.5–2495 MHz):

  • Data rate: very low; the service sends short, compressed messages and the phone guides the user to point it at the satellite

  • Services: Emergency SOS to responders, location sharing through Find My, roadside assistance and, in later software versions, short text messages

  • Business model: Apple announced an investment of about $450 million in Globalstar’s infrastructure in 2022

The service shows that some consumers value emergency satellite connectivity built into a phone. How large the demand will be for broader satellite messaging and data services is not yet established.

docs.title: 30.4.5 Chipset Ecosystem for NTN
docs.text:
Commercial NTN requires chipsets integrating 3GPP NTN capabilities:

  • Smartphone chipset vendors (for example Qualcomm and MediaTek) have announced modems and platforms with satellite messaging support, some based on proprietary satellite links and some on 3GPP Release 17 NB-IoT NTN.

  • NB-IoT NTN modules for low-power sensors and trackers, which use the Release 17 narrowband NTN specifications over geostationary and low-orbit satellite networks, have been announced by several module makers.

  • Phone makers have added satellite emergency messaging to flagship models since 2022.

Table 30.2 compares direct-to-device satellite service providers.

Table 30.2. Direct-to-Device Satellite Service Provider Comparison Provider Satellite Band Peak Speed MNO Partners Status (as of 2025) AST SpaceMobile BlueWalker 3 / BlueBird low-band terrestrial above 10 Mbps (demo) AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone and others Test satellite flown; first BlueBirds launched 2024 Starlink D2C Direct-to-cell satellites operator mid-band (LTE) a few Mbps shared per beam T-Mobile, Rogers, Optus, KDDI and others Text service in beta/early service Apple/Globalstar Globalstar LEO n53 (2.4 GHz) very low (short messages) Apple (direct) Available since late 2022

docs.title: 30.5.1 HAPS Platform Technology
docs.text:
HAPS operate in the stratosphere at 17–22 km altitude, above commercial aviation and most weather but far below the Kármán line. The stratosphere at this altitude has low wind speeds (\(<5\) m/s in the equatorial region), enabling quasi-geostationary station-keeping. Solar-powered HAPS platforms can achieve effectively unlimited endurance by harvesting solar energy during daylight.

Airbus Zephyr: A solar-electric HAPS under development and test (as of 2025):

  • Zephyr S: wingspan of about 25 m and a mass of roughly 75 kg (ultra-lightweight composite structure)

  • Power: thin photovoltaic cells on the wings with rechargeable batteries for the night

  • Endurance: a flight of 64 days in 2022 was reported by Airbus as a record for an aircraft of its kind

  • Coverage: 140 km diameter footprint per station at 21 km altitude

  • Payload: Multiple spot-beam antennas; cellular frequency bands; ISR sensors

  • Station-keeping: Autonomous algorithm exploiting stratospheric wind layers; \(<\)1 km position drift

HAPSMobile Sunglider (SoftBank group): a solar-electric HAPS with a wingspan of about 78 m, designed for telecommunications payloads; stratospheric test flights were made in 2020.

docs.title: 30.5.2 HAPS Frequency Allocations
docs.text:
HAPS frequency allocations are governed by ITU Radio Regulations and WRC decisions:

  • User links: L/S/Ka-band shared with other services; HAPS used as International Mobile Telecommunications base stations are covered by ITU identifications in several bands below 3 GHz

  • Feeder links (HAPS-to-gateway): WRC-19 allocated 38–39.5 GHz for HAPS station links in some regions; V-band (47.2–50.2 GHz) used for HAPS-to-satellite feeder

  • HAPS-to-HAPS ISL: Ka-band 26.5–27.5 GHz

  • HAPS and mobile broadband: ITU-R Report F.2439 describes HAPS systems for fixed-service use

docs.title: 30.5.3 Path Loss Advantage of HAPS vs. GEO
docs.text:
The free-space path loss comparison between HAPS, LEO, and GEO at the same carrier frequency (\(f = 28\) GHz, Ka-band):

\[L_{\text{FSPL}} = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi d f}{c}\right)~\text{[dB]}\tag{30.7}\] \[\begin{align*} L_{\text{HAPS}} (d = 21~\text{km}) &= 147.8~\text{dB} \\ L_{\text{LEO}} (d = 600~\text{km}) &= 176.9~\text{dB} \quad (+29.1~\text{dB vs.\ HAPS}) \\ L_{\text{GEO}} (d = 35{,}786~\text{km}) &= 212.5~\text{dB} \quad (+64.7~\text{dB vs.\ HAPS}) \end{align*}\]

HAPS enjoys \(\sim\)29 dB lower path loss than LEO and \(\sim\)65 dB lower than GEO (the distance is shorter by factors of about 29 and 1700). This allows a HAPS to use smaller user-terminal antennas and lower transmit power for the same link margin than a satellite, which makes direct connections to handheld devices more practical than from LEO or GEO, at the cost of a much smaller coverage area per platform.

docs.title: 30.5.4 HAPS Use Cases and Economics
docs.text:
Rural broadband: A single HAPS station at 21 km altitude provides 140 km diameter footprint coverage, replacing approximately 20 terrestrial towers in flat terrain. Deployment is days (airfield launch) versus months–years for tower construction. HAPS backhaul links to satellite or ground fiber gateway.

Emergency communications: HAPS can be deployed to a disaster zone within 24–48 hours (ferry flight from nearest airbase), providing cellular coverage where terrestrial infrastructure has been destroyed. Endurance of 64+ days exceeds typical disaster response requirements.

Earth observation: At 21 km altitude with optical resolution \(\approx h \tan(\text{IFOV})\), an IFOV of about 14 \(\mu\)rad (for example 4 \(\mu\)m pixels behind a 0.28 m focal length) gives \(\sim\)0.3 m ground resolution. Persistent stare capability over a single region is impossible for LEO satellites (90 min orbital period) but natural for HAPS.

5G backhaul: HAPS can backhaul rural small cells at Ka-band, enabling 5G service extension without fiber deployment.

docs.title: 30.6.1 IMT-2030 Requirements and NTN Role
docs.text:
ITU-R Recommendation M.2160 (the IMT-2030 framework, adopted in 2023) sets out the capabilities of 6G systems; its indicative values are of the following order (the values are targets for the radio interface in general, not requirements specific to satellites):

  • Peak data rate: 50–200 Gbit/s

  • User-experienced data rate: 300–500 Mbit/s

  • Air interface latency: 0.1–1 ms

  • Connection density: \(10^6\)–\(10^8\) devices per km2

  • Mobility: up to 500–1000 km/h

  • Improved energy efficiency relative to IMT-2020 (5G)

  • Coverage: wider coverage, including remote areas, with satellite and other non-terrestrial systems expected to play a role

NTN is designated a native 6G component from initial standardization—unlike 5G, which treated satellites as an extension to be added after the terrestrial standard was mature. This means NTN-specific requirements drive air interface design choices including waveform, duplex mode, OFDM numerology, and control-plane architecture from the outset.

docs.title: 30.6.2 Space-Air-Ground-Sea Integrated Network (SAGSIN)
docs.text:
The 6G SAGSIN architecture integrates:

  • Space layer: LEO and MEO constellations (as of 2025: Starlink with several thousand satellites in orbit, Amazon Kuiper with 3,236 satellites authorized, OneWeb with about 650 first-generation satellites, Telesat Lightspeed with about 200 planned satellites, and SES O3b mPOWER in medium Earth orbit)

  • Air layer: HAPS at 17–22 km; high-altitude UAVs at 8–15 km; low-altitude UAVs at \(<\)1 km

  • Ground layer: 6G terrestrial base stations (sub-THz mmWave small cells; sub-6 GHz macro cells; 700 MHz coverage cells)

  • Maritime layer: Ship-borne user terminals; submarine fiber connected hub stations

A unified 6G control plane manages seamless mobility across all segments, with network slicing providing differentiated QoS: eMBB slice (terabit ISLs), URLLC slice (LEO with \(<\)20 ms E2E latency), mMTC slice (IoT-NTN narrowband). AI/ML-based network management (RAN Intelligent Controller at cloud scale) optimizes beam scheduling, handover, interference coordination, and resource allocation in real-time across the integrated architecture.

docs.title: 30.6.3 Terahertz Communication for Satellite ISLs
docs.text:
Terahertz (THz) bands (100 GHz–3 THz) offer bandwidths of 10–100 GHz per channel, enabling terabit-per-second links for inter-satellite links (ISLs) between adjacent satellites in a mega-constellation:

  • Atmospheric transmission windows exist at 120 GHz, 140 GHz, and 220 GHz (between water vapor and O\(_2\) absorption peaks)

  • At LEO ISL distances of 100–1000 km in vacuum, molecular absorption is zero; only free-space diffraction applies

  • Antenna aperture at 300 GHz: \(\lambda = 1\) mm; a 10 cm diameter aperture gives about 44 dBi gain at 25% efficiency (vs. about 24 dBi at 30 GHz)

  • THz ISL at 1000 km, 10 cm aperture, 100 mW transmit: FSPL \(= 20\log(4\pi\times10^6\times3\times10^{11}/3\times10^8) = 202\) dB; Rx power = \(20 + 44 + 44 - 202 = -94\) dBm; thermal noise \(kTB\) (\(B = 10\) GHz) = \(-74\) dBm, SNR \(\approx -20\) dB—requires higher power or larger apertures for terabit ISLs

Research toward 6G THz ISLs focuses on 100 W solid-state power amplifiers at D-band (110–170 GHz), photonic integration of THz sources, and beamforming antenna arrays with 1000+ elements at sub-THz frequencies.

docs.title: 30.6.4 Open RAN for NTN
docs.text:
The O-RAN Alliance’s NTN Working Group (established 2022) is adapting the Open RAN architecture for satellite networks:

  • Functional split: O-CU (O-RAN Centralized Unit) on ground; O-DU (Distributed Unit) on satellite (regenerative case); O-RU (Radio Unit) as satellite antenna

  • Open interfaces: E2 interface (gNB-to-RIC); F1 interface (CU-to-DU); eCPRI (DU-to-RU) adapted for NTN delays

  • RIC (RAN Intelligent Controller): Non-real-time RIC (Non-RT RIC) for beam resource planning and interference management; Near-RT RIC for handover optimization and interference mitigation with \(\leq\)10 ms loop latency (feasible for LEO, not GEO)

  • AI/ML xApps: Reinforcement learning for beam scheduling; federated learning across satellites for interference coordination; LSTM-based handover prediction from orbital mechanics

Open RAN for NTN promises multi-vendor satellite network deployments where ground CU, satellite DU, and antenna elements from different manufacturers interoperate through standardized interfaces, reducing vendor lock-in and equipment cost.

docs.title: 30.6.5 Energy Efficiency for 6G NTN
docs.text:
IMT-2030 aims at a substantial energy efficiency improvement relative to 5G IMT-2020. For NTN, the key efficiency levers are:

  • Digital beamforming with DPD: Massive MIMO phased arrays with digital pre-distortion (DPD) of power amplifier nonlinearity allow higher PA output power (better efficiency) while maintaining EVM. GaN PA efficiency of 45–55% PAE (power-added efficiency) at saturation vs. 20–30% backed-off is critical for solar-power-limited satellites.

  • RF-over-fiber feeder links: Highly linear analog fiber links from gateway to satellite (for GEO transparent payload) operate with \(<\)1 dB NF without active electronics in the up-path, improving satellite power budget.

  • Regenerative + solar: LEO constellations with regenerative payload and large solar arrays (Starlink Gen3: 3600 W BOL) can sustain \(>\)10 Gbps per satellite throughput. Specific throughput: \(\sim\)2.8 Mbps/W.

  • Sleep modes: O-RAN Non-RT RIC orchestration activates/deactivates satellite beams on demand (cell on/off analogous to terrestrial BS sleep), reducing per-bit energy consumption by 10–30\(\times\) in low-traffic periods.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Non-terrestrial networks have transitioned from vision to commercial reality through 3GPP standardization (Release 17 normative NTN specifications, June 2022) and commercial deployments (Starlink direct-to-cell text messaging from 2024, AST SpaceMobile BlueWalker 3 and BlueBird satellites). The key protocol innovations enabling NTN—UE-based timing advance pre-compensation via GNSS and ephemeris, Doppler pre-compensation, and HARQ process adaptation—are now standardized and chipset-integrated. Direct-to-device connectivity from unmodified smartphones to LEO satellites, enabled by large phased arrays (\(>64\) m2) and terrestrial spectrum sharing frameworks, is transitioning from demonstration to commercial service. HAPS platforms (Zephyr-S: 64-day endurance, 140 km coverage diameter) provide a complementary mid-altitude segment with 33 dB path-loss advantage over LEO. The 6G IMT-2030 vision integrates all of these into a native Space-Air-Ground-Sea architecture, supported by THz ISLs, Open RAN intelligence, and 100\(\times\) energy efficiency targets.

Key NTN Equations Summary:

\[\begin{align*} &\text{Doppler shift: } \Delta f = \frac{f_c \cdot v_r}{c} \approx \pm 50~\text{kHz @ 2 GHz, LEO 550 km} \\ &\text{NTN timing advance: } \text{TA} = \frac{2d_{\text{feeder}} + 2d_{\text{service}}}{c} \\ &\text{D2D FSPL @ 2 GHz, 1000 km: } L = 20\log_{10}(4\pi d f/c) = 168~\text{dB} \\ &\text{HAPS path loss advantage vs.\ GEO: } \Delta L = 20\log_{10}(35786/21) = 64.6~\text{dB} \end{align*}\] Figure 30.1. Integrated NTN architecture for 6G: LEO mega-constellation with Ka-band ISLs provides global coverage; HAPS at 21 km provides regional capacity augmentation; GEO provides broadcast/overlay; ground gNBs serve as feeder link gateways; diverse UEs (terrestrial, maritime, aeronautical, IoT) connect via service links. The 5G/6G core network runs in cloud infrastructure.

docs.title: Chapter 31: Future Concepts and Emerging Space Technologies
docs.text:
“The dinosaurs became extinct because they didn’t have a space programme. And if we become extinct because we don’t have a space programme, it’ll serve us right.” —Larry Niven

The space industry stands at a moment of profound technological convergence. Advances that would have seemed implausible in isolation—cheap reusable launch vehicles, on-orbit additive manufacturing, quantum-secured communications, and orbital solar power—are arriving simultaneously, catalysed by cross-pollination from artificial intelligence, advanced materials science, photonics, and nuclear engineering. Satellite technology is no longer merely an enabler of terrestrial services; it is becoming the substrate for a space-based industrial civilisation. This chapter surveys the most consequential emerging concepts across energy, manufacturing, communications, propulsion, quantum science, and observational astronomy, situating each within a technology maturity framework and projecting economic trajectories to mid-century.

docs.title: 31.1 Introduction: Technology Readiness and Convergence
docs.text:
NASA’s Technology Readiness Level (TRL) scale, originally developed by Stan Sadin in the 1970s and formalised across ESA and DoD acquisition frameworks, provides a standardised vocabulary for assessing the maturity of emerging technologies:

  • TRL 1–3: Basic research, proof of concept, analytical validation in laboratory

  • TRL 4–5: Component validation in laboratory and relevant environment

  • TRL 6–7: System prototype demonstrated in relevant and operational environment

  • TRL 8–9: System complete and flight qualified; proven through mission operations

Many of the technologies described in this chapter occupy TRL 3–6, meaning they have demonstrated physical plausibility but have not yet been proven at operational scale in space. The convergence thesis holds that several enabling factors must mature concurrently for transformative concepts to reach commercialisation: ultra-low launch costs, on-orbit autonomous assembly, high-capacity power systems, and AI-driven operations. When these enablers align—as they appear to be doing in the late 2020s—previously stalled concepts can transition from TRL 4 to TRL 9 within a single decade.

Cross-Cutting Enablers. Four enabling technologies underpin virtually every advanced space concept described in this chapter: (1) reusable launch vehicles reducing cost-to-orbit by 10–100\(\times\); (2) AI-driven autonomy enabling spacecraft to operate without continuous human oversight; (3) additive manufacturing permitting large structures to be fabricated in orbit rather than launched as monolithic assemblies; and (4) advanced photovoltaics and power electronics approaching the efficiency and specific mass targets needed for economical space-based power generation.

docs.title: 31.2.1 Concept and History
docs.text:
The idea of harvesting solar energy in space and transmitting it wirelessly to Earth is one of the oldest serious proposals in astronautical engineering. Peter Glaser of Arthur D. Little Inc. first articulated the concept in a 1968 paper published in Science: “Power from the Sun: Its Future,” which proposed placing photovoltaic arrays in geostationary orbit (GEO) and beaming the collected energy to Earth using microwave radiation (Glaser 1968). Glaser noted three fundamental space advantages: the solar constant at GEO is 1366 W/m\(^2\) continuously (unattenuated by atmosphere or night), collections are uninterrupted by weather, and the geostationary position permits continuous illumination of a fixed ground receiver.

The concept was taken seriously enough that the United States Department of Energy (DoE) and NASA jointly funded a $20 million Reference System Study between 1976 and 1980. The 1979 Reference System envisaged a single solar power satellite with a 5 km \(\times\) 5 km silicon photovoltaic array in GEO, transmitting 2.45 GHz microwave energy via a 1 km diameter phased array antenna to a 10 km \(\times\) 13 km elliptical rectenna (rectifying antenna) on the ground, ultimately delivering 5 GW of electrical power to the grid—comparable to five large nuclear power stations. The report concluded that the concept was technically feasible but economically prohibitive given the launch costs of the era, which would have required lifting approximately 50,000 tonnes to GEO using the Space Shuttle. The programme was cancelled in 1981 under budgetary pressure.

Interest re-emerged in the 1990s driven by concerns about climate change and energy security. NASA’s Fresh Look Study (1995–1997), led by John Mankins, revisited SBSP using modular architectures and lighter materials. The confluence of dramatically falling launch costs, improvements in thin-film photovoltaics, and solid-state microwave power amplifiers in the 2010s and 2020s has brought SBSP back into serious engineering consideration by space agencies and private entities worldwide.

docs.title: 31.2.2 Modern SBSP Architectures
docs.text:
The end-to-end energy conversion chain for SBSP involves multiple sequential efficiency steps, each introducing losses:

\[\begin{align*} P_{\text{ground}} &= P_{\text{solar}} \cdot \eta_{\text{PV}} \cdot \eta_{\text{DC/DC}} \cdot \eta_{\text{DC/RF}} \cdot \eta_{\text{prop}} \cdot \eta_{\text{rectenna}} \end{align*}\]

where a representative budget for a modern system yields:

SBSP End-to-End Efficiency Chain

Stage Efficiency Notes PV conversion (\(\eta_{\text{PV}}\)) 33% Multi-junction GaAs/Ge, AM0 spectrum DC-to-DC power conditioning (\(\eta_{\text{DC/DC}}\)) 96% High-voltage distribution DC-to-RF solid-state (\(\eta_{\text{DC/RF}}\)) 80% GaN MMIC at 2.45 GHz Free-space propagation (\(\eta_{\text{prop}}\)) 54% Gaussian beam, 1 km aperture Rectenna conversion (\(\eta_{\text{rectenna}}\)) 86% Schottky diode rectenna Net system efficiency \(\mathbf{\approx 12\%}\) \(0.33 \times 0.96 \times 0.80 \times 0.54 \times 0.86\)

Even at 12% net efficiency, GEO solar input is 1366 W/m\(^2\) continuously versus an average terrestrial yield of \(\sim\)200 W/m\(^2\) (accounting for night, weather, and latitude), providing a \(\sim\)6.8\(\times\) effective advantage before efficiency losses.

The microwave transmission parameters are chosen to balance beam efficiency and safety. The 2.45 GHz Industrial, Scientific, and Medical (ISM) band is preferred for regulatory reasons and low atmospheric attenuation. At GEO (35,786 km), the diffraction-limited beam from a 1 km aperture antenna has a central spot diameter of approximately 1 km at the ground. Peak power density is kept below 230 W/m\(^2\) at beam centre—substantially less than the 1000 W/m\(^2\) of direct sunlight—making the beam safe for humans and aircraft. Beam pointing is maintained by a retrodirective phased array system: the ground rectenna transmits a low-power pilot tone at 5.8 GHz; the satellite’s phased array detects this signal and phase-conjugates each element’s transmission to steer the beam precisely to the source, providing inherent safety since the beam cannot be redirected without the pilot tone.

docs.title: CASSIOPeiA (UK)
docs.text: The Constant Aperture, Solid-State, Integrated, Orbital Phased Array (CASSIOPeiA) concept, developed by Ian Cash of International Electric Company, is notable for its elegant solution to the attitude control problem. Traditional SBSP designs require either a complex dual-axis gimbal mechanism to keep PV arrays facing the sun while the antenna faces Earth, or a large rotary joint to transfer multi-gigawatt power across a rotating interface—both represent massive engineering challenges. CASSIOPeiA avoids these by using a conical structure that integrates both PV cells and transmitting antenna elements across its surface. The cone slowly rotates about its axis to maintain thermal equilibrium. Electronic beam steering via phase shifts allows the transmitted beam to be pointed at any ground receiver without mechanical reorientation. This “no moving parts” architecture dramatically simplifies manufacturing, assembly, and long-term reliability.

docs.title: SPIDERS (ESA)
docs.text: Modular concepts, studied in several programmes including the European SOLARIS preparatory work, use many identical tiles, each integrating solar cells, power conditioning and microwave transmitter elements into a planar panel of modest size. A gigawatt-class system would consist of very large numbers of such tiles assembled autonomously in orbit into a kilometre-scale structure. The key advantage is scalability: demonstration systems at small scale are structurally similar to the full system, differing mainly in tile count. In-orbit robotic assembly is the critical enabling technology, and studies of these concepts rest on very demanding assumptions about mass per kilowatt and launch cost that have not yet been demonstrated.

docs.title: 31.2.3 Recent Demonstrations
docs.text:
Between 2020 and 2023 small experiments flew in orbit that tested components of the SBSP concept: a solar-to-radio-frequency conversion module (the NRL PRAM, 2020) and, in 2023, the Caltech SSPD-1 demonstrator, whose MAPLE experiment was the first demonstration of wireless power transfer by a phased array in space. These are component-level demonstrations at tiny scale; no space solar power satellite has delivered power to the grid.

Caltech SSPD-1 (2023). The Space Solar Power Demonstrator-1 (SSPD-1) was launched in January 2023 as a rideshare payload. It carried three experiments: MAPLE (Microwave Array for Power-transfer Low-orbit Experiment), which used a lightweight phased array to beam power wirelessly in space to receivers on the same spacecraft, and was also reported to have sent a detectable signal to a receiver on the ground at Caltech (the first demonstration of wireless power transfer in space by a flexible phased array); DOLCE (Deployable on-Orbit ultraLight Composite Experiment), a deployable ultralight structure experiment; and ALBA, which exposed 32 different types of solar cell to the space environment. MAPLE showed that a phased array can steer a power beam electronically in orbit; the power involved was tiny compared with that of a utility-scale system.

NRL PRAM (2020). The Naval Research Laboratory’s Photovoltaic Radio-frequency Antenna Module flew aboard the US Air Force X-37B spaceplane from 2020 to 2022. PRAM was a small module that converted sunlight to radio-frequency power, demonstrating the solar-to-RF conversion element of SBSP in the space environment; it was not a beam-to-ground power demonstration.

JAXA SSPS Roadmap. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency has maintained one of the longest-running SBSP research programmes. Japanese plans include a small demonstration in low Earth orbit, with the longer-term aim of a geostationary system; dates are targets and have moved before.

ESA SOLARIS. ESA began the SOLARIS preparatory initiative in 2022 to assess whether space-based solar power could contribute to European energy needs; its studies concluded that the concept might be technically feasible but depends on large cost reductions in launch and in-orbit assembly. Any later demonstration depends on decisions not yet taken.

China OMEGA. China’s Orb-shape Membrane Energy Gathering Array concept is a Chinese space solar power concept with proposed staged demonstrations between about 2030 and 2050; the schedule is a stated ambition rather than an established programme.

docs.title: 31.2.4 Economic Analysis
docs.text:
The primary barrier to SBSP has always been launch cost. The 1979 Reference System required lifting approximately 50,000 tonnes to GEO at a cost that, even with shuttle economics, exceeded $1 trillion—completely non-competitive with any terrestrial energy source. The economics transform dramatically with low-cost heavy lift. SpaceX Starship is targeting a fully reusable launch cost below $100/kg to LEO; GEO delivery adds a further factor via electric orbit raising over months, but at $300/kg to GEO a 1 GW SBSP system weighing 2,000 tonnes (at 2 kg/kW) has a launch cost of $600 million—comparable to a large terrestrial solar farm.

\[\begin{align*} C_{\text{capital}} &= \frac{m_{\text{specific}} \cdot c_{\text{launch}}}{P_{\text{net}}/P_{\text{solar}}} \end{align*}\]

At 2 kg/kW specific mass and $100/kg launch cost, the launch-cost contribution to capital cost is $200/kW—competitive with offshore wind ($1,500–3,500/kW) and nuclear ($6,000–12,000/kW). Unlike terrestrial solar or wind, SBSP requires no land area (critical in land-constrained nations), produces firm (dispatchable) power without storage, and produces zero atmospheric emissions during operation. Transmission losses remain a key challenge: the 12% end-to-end efficiency is lower than ground-based systems, but the combination of 24/7 availability at full capacity and the high raw solar flux partially compensates.

docs.title: 31.3.1 Commercial Space Stations
docs.text:
The retirement of the International Space Station, planned (as of 2025) for around 2030, is motivating NASA’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations (CLD) programme to fund private successors. Multiple teams are pursuing distinct architectural approaches:

Axiom Space Station. Axiom Space has flown four private astronaut missions (Ax-1 through Ax-4) to the ISS, gaining operational experience before deploying its own modules. The first Axiom commercial module is targeted for ISS docking in 2026, with the full Axiom Station detaching as a free-flying platform when the ISS retires. Axiom has attracted investments exceeding $2 billion and signed agreements with NASA, ESA, and national space agencies.

Starlab. The Starlab station, developed by Voyager Space in partnership with Airbus, received a $400 million NASA CLD contract in 2021. It employs a large inflatable habitat module and targets a 2028 launch. The station is designed to accommodate four resident crew members and provide laboratory volume comparable to ISS US On-Orbit Segment.

Sierra Space LIFE Module. Sierra Space’s Large Integrated Flexible Environment (LIFE) inflatable habitat offers 82 m\(^2\) of usable floor area in a module that launches compactly and inflates on orbit. Three LIFE modules were planned for Orbital Reef.

Orbital Reef. The Orbital Reef partnership (Amazon, Blue Origin, Sierra Space) received a NASA CLD award and targets a 2030 operational date. Blue Origin contributes the core module and launch via New Glenn; Sierra Space provides LIFE habitats and Dream Chaser crew/cargo transport.

docs.title: 31.3.2 Microgravity Manufacturing
docs.text: The microgravity environment of orbit suppresses sedimentation, buoyancy-driven convection, and container-wall contamination, enabling the production of materials impossible or impractical to fabricate on Earth’s surface.

docs.title: ZBLAN Optical Fibre
docs.text:
ZBLAN—the fluoride glass system ZrF\(_4\)-BaF\(_2\)-LaF\(_3\)-AlF\(_3\)-NaF—has a theoretical minimum attenuation of 0.01 dB/km at 2.55 \(\mu\)m wavelength, more than twenty times lower than the best silica fibre (0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm). This extraordinary transparency arises from the absence of OH absorption bands in mid-infrared wavelengths. However, when ZBLAN is drawn into fibre in a terrestrial gravity environment, buoyancy-driven convection during solidification creates microcrystallites within the glass matrix, raising actual attenuation to 0.1–1.0 dB/km—still excellent but far short of theoretical.

Microgravity suppresses convective crystallisation, and orbital experiments by Made in Space (now Redwire) from 2017 to 2019 aboard the ISS consistently produced ZBLAN fibre with lower microcrystallite density than terrestrial control samples. If commercial-scale ZBLAN production in orbit can be demonstrated, the implications for transoceanic submarine cable infrastructure are transformative: 2.5 \(\mu\)m mid-IR transmission with 0.05 dB/km attenuation could support transpacific spans of several thousand kilometres without repeaters.

docs.title: Pharmaceutical Manufacturing in Orbit
docs.text:
Protein crystals grown in microgravity are characteristically an order of magnitude larger and more structurally perfect than equivalent terrestrial crystals, because the absence of sedimentation allows slow, diffusion-limited growth rather than the rapid, turbulent accretion typical on Earth. High-quality protein crystals enable X-ray crystallography with superior resolution, accelerating drug discovery and structural biology.

Varda Space Industries launched its W-1 mission in June 2023 aboard a Rocket Lab Photon satellite bus: a self-contained pharmaceutical manufacturing module processed crystallisation experiments in orbit for several months, then returned the capsule to a landing in Utah in early 2024. The mission demonstrated end-to-end commercial in-space pharmaceutical manufacturing and reentry logistics. Subsequent Varda W-series missions are planned with increased manufacturing volume and client pharmaceutical compounds.

docs.title: Advanced Materials and Biological Fabrication
docs.text: Metal foams—materials with engineered porosity that combine low density with high stiffness—form more homogeneously in microgravity because buoyancy-driven bubble migration is absent during solidification. Semiconductor crystal growth (particularly GaAs and InP for III-V photovoltaics) benefits similarly. Organic tissue engineering—growing three-dimensional organoids and vascularised tissue constructs—is significantly more effective in microgravity because cells self-organise into three-dimensional architectures without mechanical support scaffolding, enabling disease models and eventually transplantable tissues.

docs.title: 31.3.3 In-Space 3D Printing and Assembly
docs.text:
ARCHINAUT. Redwire’s ARCHINAUT concept (a successor of the Made In Space Archinaut work) illustrates in-space additive manufacturing of structures. The system employs a FDM (Fused Deposition Modelling) extruder for PEEK (polyether ether ketone) thermoplastic, operating in the space vacuum environment. A 3-axis robotic arm integrates with the extruder to deposit material into structural beams up to 10 m in length over approximately 8 hours of continuous operation. UV curing provides surface finishing. NASA awarded Redwire a $73.7 million Tipping Point contract for on-orbit demonstration via OSAM-2 (On-orbit Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing 2), which targets the fabrication and attachment of a solar array support beam in LEO.

Lunar Regolith Printing. ICON and NASA’s Project Olympus programme is developing the Olympus Construction System: a mobile construction platform that uses lunar regolith as raw feedstock for additive manufacturing of habitat structures via laser sintering of regolith to produce load-bearing walls and vaulted structures. ICON’s CHAPEA (Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog) 3D-printed habitat at Johnson Space Center was tested with human crews from 2023 to 2024, validating habitability concepts for lunar surface operations.

Metal Additive Manufacturing. In vacuum, electron beam additive manufacturing (EBAM) offers advantages over laser-based processes: the electron beam has higher energy density, can be rapidly deflected electromagnetically, and operates efficiently in hard vacuum. Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is also being adapted for space manufacturing environments. These metal AM capabilities are essential for on-orbit fabrication of structural brackets, propellant tanks, and thermal management components.

Self-Assembling Architectures. DARPA’s Phoenix programme explored the concept of repurposing components from retired GEO satellites using a servicer spacecraft. The broader vision of modular, self-assembling satellite architectures—where standardised mechanical and electrical interfaces allow heterogeneous modules to autonomously mate and configure—is pursued by multiple research teams. Key technology challenges include alignment (sub-millimetre docking accuracy), latching (secure mechanical connection), and electrical/data coupling (through-contact power and communications).

Economic Case for In-Space Manufacturing. The economic justification for manufacturing in orbit must clear a high bar: the cost of delivering raw materials and energy to orbit must be lower than the value premium of the resulting product. Currently, only products whose mass-specific value exceeds approximately $10,000/kg are plausible candidates: ZBLAN fibre (potentially $1M/kg), pharmaceutical compounds ($100k–$10M/kg), and semiconductor wafers ($10k–$1M/kg) all meet this criterion. Structural materials and bulk commodities do not, unless manufactured from in-situ resources (lunar regolith, asteroid material).

docs.title: 31.4.1 Next-Generation Deep Space Network
docs.text:
NASA’s Deep Space Network (DSN), operated by JPL, is the sole telecommunications infrastructure supporting all NASA planetary and deep space missions. The network comprises three ground station complexes at Goldstone (California), Madrid (Spain), and Canberra (Australia), providing near-continuous coverage of any sky position through their 120\(^\circ\) longitude separation. The current antenna fleet includes 34 m beam-waveguide (BWG) dish antennas as the primary workhorse for Ka- and X-band, and legacy 70 m antennas at each complex.

Ongoing upgrades include Ka-band capability at all three complexes, antenna arraying (combining multiple 34 m dishes coherently for effective aperture equivalent to a 70 m antenna), and Deep Space Station-23 (DSS-23): a new 34 m antenna at Goldstone commissioned in 2024 to increase network capacity for the growing fleet of planetary spacecraft.

DSOC (Deep Space Optical Communication). The most transformative near-term capability improvement is laser optical communications. The Deep Space Optical Communication technology demonstrator, carried aboard NASA’s Psyche asteroid mission, employs a 22 cm transmit telescope on the spacecraft emitting at 1550 nm (near-infrared), with the ground terminal using the Hale 5 m telescope at Palomar Observatory fitted with a photon-counting superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD).

DSOC achieved first light in November 2023 at a distance of about 16 million km. In December 2023 it demonstrated a downlink at a maximum rate of 267 Mbps from about 31 million km, and in April 2024 it maintained a link of about 25 Mbps from about 226 million km, rates well above those of a deep-space X-band link at similar distance. The ultimate goal is a photon-counting receiver sensitivity enabling 1 Gbps from Mars (56–401 million km depending on orbital phase), transforming planetary exploration data volumes from X-band’s 2–6 Mbps on best passes to streaming-quality video from the Martian surface.

docs.title: 31.4.2 Lunar Communications Architecture
docs.text:
NASA’s Artemis programme requires a dedicated lunar telecommunications and navigation infrastructure qualitatively more capable than the ad hoc relay arrangements of the Apollo era.

LunaNet. NASA’s LunaNet is an open, interoperable lunar communication and navigation architecture analogous to the terrestrial internet. Rather than a single NASA-owned and operated network, LunaNet defines interface standards—including Delay-Tolerant Networking Bundle Protocol (RFC 5050) and Contact Graph Routing (CGR)—that any conforming service provider can implement, creating a competitive marketplace for lunar communications services. Multiple NASA Tipping Point contracts fund commercial providers to develop LunaNet-compatible services.

Nokia Bell Labs Lunar 4G LTE. NASA awarded Nokia Bell Labs a $14.1 million Tipping Point contract in 2020 to deploy the first cellular network on the Moon. The system operates at 1.8 GHz LTE (4G standard), providing data rates sufficient for HD video transmission and EVA crew communications during Artemis surface operations. The network comprises a base station deployed by a NASA lander and user equipment integrated into astronaut suits and surface rovers.

ESA Moonlight. ESA’s Moonlight initiative, developed by Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd (SSTL) and Telespazio, proposes a constellation of four dedicated lunar relay satellites in highly elliptical orbits optimised for south polar coverage. The orbit design provides continuous line-of-sight to the lunar south pole—the primary Artemis landing target—from at least one satellite at all times. Moonlight provides both communications relay and a navigation service (Lunar Communication and Navigation Service, LCNS) analogous to GNSS, enabling surface position determination to metre accuracy without Earth-based DSN contact.

Intuitive Machines IDSN. Intuitive Machines’ IM-1 Nova-C lander, which achieved the first US lunar surface landing since Apollo 17 in February 2024, landed near the lunar south pole region. Commercial lunar relay and navigation services, offered by private companies with NASA and international agencies as anchor customers, are being developed, following the model of commercial satellite communications.

docs.title: 31.4.3 Mars and Deep Space Internet
docs.text:
The current Mars telecommunications relay network comprises NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO, 2 Mbps UHF relay), MAVEN, and international assets including ESA’s Trace Gas Orbiter and China’s Tianwen-1. The fundamental challenge of interplanetary communications is the one-way light travel time: 3–24 minutes to Mars (depending on orbital geometry), precluding real-time interactive protocols. The Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) architecture addresses this through a store-and-forward paradigm formalised in CCSDS 734.2-B-1. DTN’s Bundle Protocol implements custody transfer, enabling reliable end-to-end delivery across links that are interrupted for hours or days at a time. The Licklider Transfer Protocol (LTP, CCSDS 734.2-B-1) provides a link-layer retransmission mechanism tuned for the long round-trip delays of deep space links.

A future dedicated Mars telecommunications orbiter in Mars areostationary orbit (17,031 km altitude, 24.62-hour period) could provide 200 Mbps optical downlink to Earth and broadband relay coverage for surface assets. The Gateway lunar station, planned as part of the Artemis infrastructure in a Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbit (NRHO), will serve as a communications hub for cislunar operations and a relay node for the lunar far side.

docs.title: 31.5.1 Solar Electric Propulsion
docs.text:
Solar Electric Propulsion (SEP) combines solar power generation with electric thruster technology to achieve specific impulses of 3,000–10,000 s—an order of magnitude higher than chemical propulsion—at the cost of very low thrust levels (millinewtons to newtons). The thrust-power relationship for an electric thruster operating at total efficiency \(\eta\) is:

\[\begin{align*} F &= \frac{2\,\eta\,P}{v_e} = \frac{2\,\eta\,P}{I_{sp}\,g_0} \end{align*}\]

For a 1 kW system at \(\eta = 0.65\) and \(I_{sp} = 3000\) s, this yields approximately 44 mN—far too low for rapid orbit changes but extremely propellant-efficient for long-duration missions.

Notable SEP applications include NASA’s Dawn mission (NSTAR gridded-ion engines, three individually throttleable thrusters, \(I_{sp}\) up to 3200 s), AEROJET’s NEXT-C engine on the DART mission (6.9 kW power, 236 mN maximum thrust, \(I_{sp}\) 4190 s, xenon propellant), and SpaceX Starlink’s krypton Hall thrusters (approximately 1.6 mN thrust, 1500 s \(I_{sp}\), enabling orbit raising and deorbit for the entire constellation). For cargo missions to Mars, a 200 kW SEP system could deliver payloads too large for chemical propulsion in a 5-year spiral transit, providing mass-efficient transport at the cost of mission duration.

docs.title: 31.5.2 Nuclear Propulsion
docs.text:
Nuclear propulsion offers performance fundamentally inaccessible to solar or chemical systems, particularly for missions far from the Sun (where solar flux diminishes as \(1/r^2\)) or where high power density is required for rapid orbit changes.

Kilopower (KRUSTY). NASA’s Kilopower project, developed in partnership with the Department of Energy, demonstrated a compact fission reactor system in ground testing (Kilowatt Reactor Using Stirling TechnologY, KRUSTY) in 2018 at the Nevada National Security Site. The reactor used a highly enriched uranium core in a fast-neutron spectrum, with heat passed to free-piston Stirling convertors (heat pipes carried the heat from the core). The Kilopower concept covered electrical power from about 1 to 10 kW, and was proposed for lunar surface power in places such as permanently shadowed craters and for Mars surface operations where solar power is insufficient; as of 2025 no Kilopower unit has flown.

Nuclear Thermal Propulsion (NTP). NTP heats a propellant—typically hydrogen—by passing it through a fission reactor core, achieving exhaust temperatures of 2,500–3,000 K. The specific impulse is governed by:

Nuclear Thermal Propulsion: Specific Impulse

\[\begin{align*} I_{sp} = \frac{1}{g_0}\sqrt{\frac{2\,\eta\,R_u\,T_c}{M_{\text{mol}}}} \end{align*}\]

For hydrogen propellant (\(M_{\text{mol}} = 0.002\) kg/mol), reactor temperature \(T_c = 2700\) K, nozzle efficiency \(\eta = 0.9\), and \(g_0 = 9.81\) m/s\(^2\):

\[I_{sp} = \frac{1}{9.81}\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 0.9 \times 8.314 \times 2700}{0.002}} \approx \frac{4494}{9.81} \approx \mathbf{458~s}\]

With higher-temperature carbide fuel elements (\(T_c \approx 3000\) K), \(I_{sp}\) approaches 900 s—twice the performance of the best chemical engines. The NERVA/Rover programme demonstrated specific impulse of the order of 800 s in ground testing (the programme ended in 1972).

DARPA’s DRACO (Demonstration Rocket for Agile Cislunar Operations) programme, conducted jointly with NASA, was set up to flight-test a nuclear thermal rocket using high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) fuel; the flight date slipped and the programme was reported to have been ended in 2025. DRACO’s primary mission is to demonstrate rapid cislunar manoeuvring: a spacecraft that can change its orbit significantly in hours rather than the weeks required by SEP.

Nuclear Electric Propulsion (NEP). NEP couples a fission reactor to an electric thruster system, combining the high power density of nuclear with the high \(I_{sp}\) of ion propulsion. Russia’s “Zeus” nuclear tug project (the Transport and Energy Module, TEM) envisages a megawatt-class gas-cooled reactor driving a turbogenerator to power electric thrusters, with a demonstration planned for around the 2030s. The conceptual JIMO (Jupiter Icy Moons Orbiter) mission studied by NASA in 2002–2005 proposed 200 kW NEP to achieve orbit insertion around multiple Jovian moons successively—a mission impossible with any other propulsion technology.

docs.title: 31.5.3 Beamed Energy and Momentum Exchange
docs.text:
Laser Propulsion. Two distinct mechanisms enable laser propulsion: ablative propulsion vaporises a small mass of ablator material to produce thrust at specific impulses of 1,000–10,000 s; laser-thermal propulsion heats a conventional propellant in a heat exchanger irradiated by a high-power laser beam. The specific thrust is:

\[\begin{align*} F &= C_m \cdot P_{\text{laser}} \end{align*}\]

where the momentum coupling coefficient \(C_m\) (N/W) depends on the ablation mechanism, typically \(C_m \approx 10^{-4}\)–\(10^{-3}\) N/W for ablative systems. At 1 MW laser power and \(C_m = 5 \times 10^{-4}\) N/W, thrust is 500 N. The Myrabo Lightcraft concept demonstrated laser-propelled vehicles reaching 71 m altitude in 2000 using a 10 kW pulsed CO\(_2\) laser.

Electrodynamic Tethers. A conducting tether deployed from a LEO spacecraft, flowing current \(I\) through the ambient magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\), experiences a Lorentz force \(\mathbf{F} = I\,\mathbf{L} \times \mathbf{B}\). The force direction can provide orbit raising (electrostatic electron collection at one end, ion emission at the other) or deorbit (reversed current direction). The Terminator Tape (Tethers Unlimited) is a passive deorbit device: a 75 m conducting tape deployed from an end-of-life cubesat, which dissipates orbital energy via eddy currents induced by the geomagnetic field, deorbiting a 10 kg satellite in 25 days from 800 km without propellant.

Momentum Exchange Tethers (MXER) offer a propellantless approach to orbit raising: a long (100 km) rotating tether in LEO can capture a payload at the low end of its rotation arc and release it at the high end, transferring momentum from the tether to the payload and boosting the payload to a higher orbit or interplanetary trajectory while the tether descends—to be re-boosted by electrodynamic force.

Solar Sails. JAXA’s IKAROS (Interplanetary Kite-craft Accelerated by Radiation Of the Sun), launched in May 2010 (with its sail deployed in June 2010), was the first spacecraft to demonstrate solar sailing in interplanetary space. The 14 m \(\times\) 14 m polyimide sail, 7.5 \(\mu\)m thick with embedded thin-film solar cells, accelerated IKAROS during its Venus flyby trajectory, demonstrating measurable photon pressure acceleration. The Planetary Society’s LightSail 2 (launched 2019) demonstrated orbit raising in LEO using only its 32 m\(^2\) sail, by changing the sail’s orientation (face-on and edge-on to the Sun) around each orbit. NASA’s NEA Scout, a 6U CubeSat with an 86 m\(^2\) sail, was launched aboard Artemis I in 2022 as a technology demonstration for low-cost near-Earth asteroid reconnaissance, but contact with it was not established after launch.

docs.title: 31.6.1 Quantum Sensing and Metrology
docs.text:
Quantum sensing exploits the wave nature of matter to achieve measurement sensitivities that classical instruments cannot approach. Atom interferometry uses laser-cooled atoms as test masses whose quantum mechanical wave functions are split, routed along divergent paths, and then recombined. Phase shifts accumulated along different paths encode information about accelerations, rotations, and gravitational gradients experienced by the atom cloud.

The phase shift in a pulse atom interferometer (Mach–Zehnder configuration with \(\pi/2\)–\(\pi\)–\(\pi/2\) laser pulses) is:

\[\begin{align*} \Delta\phi &= k_{\text{eff}} \cdot a \cdot T^2 \end{align*}\]

Atom Interferometry: Phase Sensitivity

In equation ((31.6)):

  • \(k_{\text{eff}} = 2k_{\text{laser}} \approx 1.6 \times 10^7\) m\(^{-1}\): effective wavevector of the two-photon Raman transition (Rb at 780 nm)

  • \(a\): acceleration to be measured (m/s\(^2\))

  • \(T\): free-evolution time between pulses (s)

In microgravity, \(T\) can extend to 10–30 s (versus 0.1–0.5 s in ground experiments), enhancing sensitivity as \(T^2\). Microgravity sensitivity approaches \(10^{-12}\) m/s\(^2/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}\)—enabling detection of gravitational anomalies from underground water reservoirs, ore bodies, and subduction zones.

Space Gravimetry. ESA’s GRACE Follow-On mission uses laser interferometry between two satellites to map time-varying gravity anomalies at nanometre ranging precision, tracking ice sheet mass changes, groundwater depletion, and post-glacial rebound. A quantum gravimetry mission using atom interferometers aboard the two satellites would provide a 100\(\times\) sensitivity improvement, enabling weekly gravity maps at km-scale spatial resolution. ESA’s STE-QUEST (Space-Time Explorer and Quantum Equivalence Principle Space Test) mission proposal combines cold-atom gravimetry with a test of the Einstein Equivalence Principle to part-per-\(10^{15}\) precision.

Optical Atomic Clocks. The best optical lattice clocks (strontium or ytterbium) achieve fractional frequency instability below \(10^{-18}\)—equivalent to losing less than one second in the age of the universe. Space optical clocks serve two distinct applications: (1) relativistic geodesy, in which the gravitational redshift \(\Delta f/f = gh/c^2 \approx 10^{-16}\) per metre of height difference allows geoid mapping to 1 cm accuracy by comparing ground and space clock frequencies; and (2) next-generation navigation, providing timing signals that eliminate the dominant error source in current GNSS.

ESA’s ACES (Atomic Clock Ensemble in Space) experiment on the ISS, comprising a PHARAO caesium fountain clock and an active hydrogen maser, achieved \(10^{-16}\) fractional frequency stability during initial operations. The FOCOS (Fundamental Physics with an Optical Clock in Space) NASA concept extends this to \(10^{-18}\) with a space optical clock.

Quantum Magnetometers. Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) magnetometers achieve field sensitivities below 1 fT/Hz\(^{1/2}\)—six orders of magnitude more sensitive than fluxgate magnetometers. Space deployment of SQUID arrays would enable detection of magnetic anomalies from ocean-floor mineral deposits, submarine geological structures, and the magnetospheric structure of other planets at much finer resolution than achievable with classical instruments.

docs.title: 31.6.2 Quantum Communications Network
docs.text:
As detailed in Chapter 29, satellite quantum key distribution (QKD) uses single photons to distribute cryptographic keys with information-theoretic security guaranteed by the laws of quantum mechanics. The Micius satellite demonstrated intercontinental QKD over 7,600 km in 2020, proving the viability of space-based quantum communications.

ESA Eagle-1. ESA’s Eagle-1 mission (2025–2027) is Europe’s first dedicated QKD satellite, developed by SES and a European industrial consortium with QIA (Quantum Internet Alliance) involvement. Eagle-1 combines classical Ka-band communications with a quantum optical channel, providing hybrid QKD plus classical encryption to European government and commercial users.

China’s Quantum Internet. China has built the world’s most extensive quantum network infrastructure: a 2,000 km Beijing–Shanghai quantum-secured fibre backbone is connected to the Micius satellite for intercontinental links, and metropolitan quantum networks exist in 10 cities. Scale-up to a 13,000 km national quantum internet is underway, integrated with classical fibre and satellite relay links.

Quantum Repeaters. The ultimate quantum internet requires quantum repeaters—devices that extend entanglement over longer distances without classical signal retransmission that would violate the no-cloning theorem.
